First off, yes, I did receive this product for free; and that's very fortunate because the price of this game matches its content: worthless.
Unless you have all the time in the world while living in your mother's basement playing MOBAs, MMOs, and jerking off to anime, you won't want to dedicate the time needed to learn the characters, their abilities, the relics, potions, and items that work best for each character and best against each enemy, and everything else necessary to not be one or two shot every single death.
As you may have read from even positive reviews, there is a learning curve; it does take time to get good at this game, but why devote any of your precious time to this game? If you commit enough time to learn each character, the best result is that you learn to deplete your enemies' health in one second.  Until you've devoted a significant amount of time to this game, you will die very, very much.  You will be one shot and two shot by the type of people mentioned in my intro; and you WILL be battling them since matchmaking is a joke and doesn't match you with people your level.
The only time this game is remotely fun is when inexperienced players can have a prolonged skirmish with other inexperienced players.  There is absolutely nothing enjoyable about dying in one second, or killing enemies in one second. There are some relics that can help prevent this, but have fun waiting 2-3 minutes for their cooldown.  "But you usually deplete players' health within one second in first person shooters too" Ah yes, thank you for bringing that up.  Yes, it's true there are a great deal of games in which you can kill people this quickly, the difference is that they are not Smite and actually require a little skill and strategy, not just memorization of items, attack rotations, and pressing the numbers 1 through 4.  Smite requires minimal aiming, and the only skill it requires is the ability to read descriptions and the time it takes to read and learn those descriptions.  These types of games are usually designed to require multiple attacks, optimally used in a certain rotation, to kill enemies.  Therefore, this game feels very broken when one ranged area of effect attack can deplete 95% of my health instantly, rendering me dead by any additional damage.
Moving on, the community sucks.  They are mean and intolerant of new players, and one of my first experiences in Smite was during a 3v3 Co-op battle against bots, my two teammates through majority rule surrendered the game right as we were about to win, just to be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and prevent me from gaining experience; but hey, what can you expect from a bunch of weebs who are living in their mothers' basements playing MOBAs and jerking off to anime.  I can't blame them entirely for their hatred of new players, since having one bad teammate can throw the game entirely.  Unfortunately, this isn't the only imbalance in the game.  The gods themselves are horribly imbalanced.  This is easily observed after any brief gameplay, but is especially obvious when doing custom battles and studying how bots who are the same level and class perform very differently.
I'm not even going to mention the numerous glitches which, from reading other reviews, seems common with the Steam version.
Finally, I will admit that I am not a big MOBA player, MMO player, or a fan of any other style of game that utilizes attacks along the number bar.  They can be addicting, but not fun. So, if you're not like me (i.e. the type of person aforementioned), then maybe you will love this game; but I recommend against wasting any time on Smite unless you're a masochist who enjoys experiencing more anger than joy from the games you play.
I was never much of a MOBA player, never liked League or Dota. I think SMITE is a refresher and a much more fun approach to this genre

This is a very short game. According to Steam, it only took me 68 minutes to complete. I also didn't even look up any solutions for the puzzles. BUT that is a good thing because it's a testament to the game's INCREDIBLE hint system. Seriously, this is the best hint system I've ever seen in a puzzle game. The hints for certain, more difficult parts, always start out fairly vague so that you're not just simply given the answer. If you're taking even more time to figure out what to do, the hints will get progressively more and more specific. This is fantastic because it encourages you to keep trying for yourself and not google the answer.
For example, a certain part required me to use a key on a fairly small keyhole. I didn't see the keyhole at first, so I was unsure of what to do. The hint told me to simply find a keyhole, so I was made aware that a keyhole was indeed what I should have been looking for, but the game didn't just tell me exactly where it was. They give you *just* enough information. It's very nifty and other games should take notes!
The puzzles themselves are never too difficult but not too easy either. I enjoyed solving all of them. The biggest thing I didn't like about the game was the ending. It's seriously lame. Spoiler alert (not really): it's just a blank screen basically telling you that "you feel like your journey is over, but it has only just begun." Such a stupid cop-out. Anyway, get this game for a cheap price if you can and enjoy it while it lasts.

While I've seen action games that had funny moments, usually those are in the form of dialogue or at least cutscenes. Not often is the game itself humorous.
This is probably technically a platform hell game ... Eryi's Action has simple enough controls and goals but you will die over, and over, and over, and OVER to hidden traps, pop-up enemies, deadly items that look just like harmless ones you've already encountered, and "Kaizo traps" (places where, unless you plan ahead, you'll die while you don't even have control of your character).
Thing is, though, I'd more accurately call it a comedy platform game. It's slapstick, but it's hilarious. It's massively cruel, yet it's so blatant and cheerful about it. And, once you've learned all the traps in a level, completing it then becomes a normal platformer (not even actually that difficult of one).
If you've got enough experience with this kind of game that you'll be able to get the jokes, Eryi's Action is definitely worth it just for the laughs. If you're new to platformers, though, put it off for later. Much later.

Well, this was certainly a surprise! I'd only recently heard of Minimum and after looking up some videos about it, I decided to gamble $10 on it. I was not dissapointed in the slightest. Minimum is a third-person shooter set in a low detail, poligonal world where your team must defeat the other team in two of the competitive modes. The first mode available is the classic Team Deathmatch where you try to get more kills than the opposing team. The real meat on the bone for this game though has to be Titan mode. In this game type, you and your teammates must gather resources by killing creeps. Doing this will add strength to your titan. The objective is to overpower the other teams titan, have your titan bring down their defenses, and then have your titan destroy the opposing team's power core. Titan mode gets really hectic and is a total blast, especially when your team actually coordinates. The last game mode is a coop survival mode which was fun, but didn't keep my attention for long. The lack of other game modes is slightly dissapointing and I hope to see more in the future. The gameplay itself is very fast paced and chaotic as well. Gun selections are your standard fare of shotguns, assault rifles, katanas, snipers, and plasma launchers. What makes Minimum stand apart from other shooters, however, is the way weapons are utilized throughout the game. Everytime you kill an enemy, they will drop energy which will level up your weapon for that life. Every weapon has 5 levels and they become more and more powerful the more enemies you kill. Once you die, you'll start from scratch and have to level them up once again. You can also craft armor in the middle of a match which can give you certain stat boosts and unlike weapons, armor doesn't go away or level down throughout the entire match. This does lead to a slight complaint, that being game balance. The game does suffer from some bad balance issues and often you'll find yourself fighting several people with god like weapons at once. It's the classic scenario of "The rich get richer". There are instances in game where you will spawn at level 3, but this is usually near the end of matches.
One of the main "gimmicks" with Minimum is its simplistic art style. Not only does it give the game a unique feel so unlike any other online game I've played, but it also makes things very clear and distinct. The enemy team is always red and they can be easy to spot out of the enviornment. The maps also look really nice as well as the Titans. Speaking of maps, they're actually really well made in this game. All of the maps are well contructed with numerous routes for players to take and also have spawn protection. In fact, if an someone kills an enemy who just spawned, they will actually recieve a point deduction which is a good attempt at trying to prevent spawn camping.
The matchmaking in Minimum has worked out rather nicely for me. I've noticed some complaints about their game constantly crashing, but I have not experienced this very often (only one time). Due to its simplistic style, the game also has really fast loading times and everything renders rather well. I've also experienced very little lag during the time I've played as well. One thing I really like as well is the support Human Head Studios has put into the game. Since I've owned this game, there have been numerous updates and announcements for future content. There are actaully a lot of menus that are completely inaccessible which I can only assume is for planned future content. I really hope they continue to support this game throughout the years.
Overall, Minimum is unique, fast-paced, intriguing, and just downright fun to play. If you enjoy third person shooters like Loadout or Warframe, you'll most likely get a lot of enjoyment out of it. It was well worth the 10 bucks and I truly hope this game will live and grow in many years to come.

So how is it that this game is supposed to be fun?
In the few matches I played, there seemed to be little use in creating a strategy that would work against more seasoned players. This was compounded by the fact that swords seem to be overpowered (faster movement + more damage). Add it all up and what I was left with feeling was frustration that there seems to be little to no hope at 'getting better' since you only live a few seconds, die, and all that non-learning-curve losing just enables an already-knowledgable team to get even farther ahead in the match.
It's basically a snowball effect of initial loss creates greater loss, while people who have seemingly been playing longer exploit that to it's fullest. Which I suppose is fine for them...but I'd be worried by how far the community can grow, if the only incentive for playing is being crushed regularly, and thoroughly.
Which is a shame too - I bought a pack of this thinking it would be something fun for my friends and I to play. Now I will urge them against an installation altogether. I'm actually the one out of us who has some patience for punishing gameplay, and even I think the amount of overkill you can experience strangles any chance of learning and becoming better out of a losing match.
It's unfortunate, because mechanically Minimum is interesting. It reminds me of Monday Night Combat, except skills and classes are replaced by gear, and there's an emphasis on escorting Titans (at least in that mode) and improving them that, in theory, means different people could play different roles.
As it is though, the game is woefully imbalanced towards swords, and further punishing a losing team to the point of discouragement, than learning through loss. I'd rather take a more balanced experience like TF2 over this as it is.

I played Supergiant Games first game, Bastion a while after playing this one. Their games are quite similar and they both do what they aim to do incredibly well, although I must say I do like Transistor a lot more than its predecessor.
This game immidiatelly grabs your attention with its artwork and graphics. The sci-fi setting and the sleek graphics with the occational hand-drawn cutscene makes the game look absolutely breathtaking. The gameplay is also top notch. It takes Bastions simple concept and combat system and puts a grand twist to it. Bastion allowed you to upgrade your weapons while Transistor allows you to combine them, the feel of coming up with a combination of skills that both looks, feels and works great is quite the spectacle and this combined with the way combat is designed makes fighting both fun and creatively challanging.
The game is not only attributed to fantastic art, amazing gameplay and a wonderful story but also the greatest soundtrack of any game I have ever played, ever. The game is partly built around its music, and everything about how Transistor sounds is flawless. The game knows how good its soundtrack is and even occationally gives you the option to just let the main character Red put down her sword and hum to the music that played. Not once did I skip an opportunity to do so.
Also the voice acting is just like in Bastion, superb.
10/10, one of my alltime favorite games. Amazing soundtrack, top tier graphics, fantastic and innovative graphics, Supergiant Games deserves your money more than any other game studio out there.

Ever since its original release in 2011, Rock of Ages has managed to persist in my memory. This may not sound remarkable, but consider that this was six years ago now - and also the odd fact that I never actually owned the game until recently. You see, I remember seeing its many quirky trailers, and being intrigued by its gameplay; half rolling boulders down hills and smashing your opponent’s defences (in a way that recalls the classic arcade game Marble Madness), and half tower defence simulator where you struggle to stop your opponent doing the same to you. Wrap the whole thing up in an art style and sense of humour that’s very Monty Pythonesque in its nature, and perhaps you can begin to see how it avoided being a fleeting memory, even without me ever taking to the controls to play it myself
Being memorable in that regard is one thing, however, but until I actually played it recently the question remained – is it fun to play? Well, get past the brief but initial phase where you painfully have to work out what the heck you’re meant to be doing, and it’s certainly fun for a while. Each battle sees you face off against a different figure from history, introduced in genuinely funny cutscenes which pack in half a ton of film and pop culture references to boot; a particular highlight is Leonardo Da Vinci taking part in a total rip off of The Matrix, for instance.  What follows is the gameplay process of using a big rock to smash through their defences and eventually squish them to death, which is something that carries with it the innate sense of joy that you’d probably expect from what that sentence is describing. Indeed, for the first few levels you’ll perhaps think it’s the most genius thing that you’ve played in years – but then the cracks begin to show.
For one, many of the maps you’ll be staging your attack on are just plain irritating - you’ve got some with high speed ramps and jumps that’s you’d perhaps be hoping for when it comes to seeking out high speed thrills, for sure. Yet they are accompanied by many others which are just twisty and confusing, or have architecture that saps the joy out of things. Think slowly jumping a large and clumsy boulder up a flight of stairs sound fun? If you do, you’re in for a treat - and should probably seek the help of a psychiatrist. There’s numerous occasions where you’ll most likely require more than one run through of a level just to get the sense of where you should be going, which just isn’t an optimal design choice in the slightest.
Worse, however, is the AI you face off against, which only ever maxes out at the level of borderline idiotic. For example, one battle I played saw the opponent’s boulder roll around the map aimlessly after encountering a tiny set of defences it simply couldn’t work out how to pass; another saw their boulder harmlessly rub against my defensive wall for the entire length of the match, no attempt to fix the problem ever attempted. Too often the simplest of strategies that is “build a wall of towers” actually pays off, and even when you have to get a tiny bit more strategic than that I never really encountered a level that felt difficult to any great degree. The only advantage the AI seems to have over you is the ability to build seemingly endless defences that go way beyond your spending limits – yet all this does is end up creating a strange situation where is feels like the the game's being cheap and resorting to cheating, despite the fact it barely adds any real degree of difficulty.
This, in turn, means the story mode of the game (which composes the vast bulk of what’s on offer) can be completed remarkably easy – I was done and dusted in about three hours maximum. The reality is the fun and novelty that comes from boulder bashing has lost its lustre by this point regardless, especially when all the irritations and issues above have been thrown into the mix. Think online battles will breathe a new lease of life into things and keep you playing forever? Ha! Good luck – all my attempts at searching for a battle ended fruitlessly. There’s simply no-one playing any more.
The question as to whether I’d recommend Rock of Ages to others, then, becomes a difficult one. None of the issues listed above destroy all your enjoyment by a long shot, but there’s no denying that they do detract from the whole experience a considerable amount. In the end, however, there’s a degree of uniqueness and a sense of joy surrounding what’s on offer here. They’re things which helped the game persist in my memory for so long, and the things which make it so it squeaks through in gaining my approval, even if it does so only by a small margin. Know what you’re getting into, or (perhaps even better) wait for a sale and pick this up on the cheap, and you’ll certainly get some fun out of it. It might not rock your world, but at points it certainly gets on a roll.

After I got past the typically slow tutorial portion of the early game, I found myself really getting sucked into the great open world environment. I would love if more open world games were set in major cities outside of the US. This one, set in Hong Kong, is great at bringing the atmosphere of a crowded bright and noisy playground for you to test your martial arts or drifting skills. I thought the combat in this game was pretty solid, although you do end up spamming your favorite power moves in hand to hand combat. The gunplay was not anything ground breaking, which I don't even fault them for, ultimately Wei Shen's best weapon are his fighting moves. Some minor flaws in this game, like being too short at about 50 hours including all DLC and 90% achievements completed, and some clunky running and turning at times can lead to frustrating movements or random jumps off of any and all walls, trash cans, food vendors, or old women's faces. Like I mentioned earlier, the game also starts off too slow. I had to restart playing this at least 3 times and I almost didn't make it through again. But, I am very glad I did! I thought Wei Shen was a cool undercover cop and the right guy to be in Hong Kong to clean up the streets, and I was glad I got sucked in to his world to experiance it.

Lara “Don't you think you've seen enough” Croft
Another great entry in the series and for many the benchmark for all other TR games, Tomb Raider II is a bigger and tougher sequel with more adventures and puzzles that are going to push the player’s skills and logic to the limit.
Set after the hijinks of the first game, Lara is now on a hunt for the secret treasure that might grant the power of the Dragon to its user. She wants to hide it from getting into the wrong hands; while a mysterious cult at the same time is trying to retrieve what they think belongs to them and rule the world of course.  Set across 18 levels and many locations around the globe, you will visit the treacherous Great Wall, the breathtaking streets of Venice, secret installations, ancient Tibet monasteries and a sunken ship at the bottom of the ocean. Lara has a couple of new moves, such as rollback in mid air while jumping, rollback while underwater, and a gracious swan dive, along with new weapons to make the combat a bit more interesting, such as automatic pistols, grenade launcher and M16. Levels this time are bigger, more complex and more demanding, as you’ll have to use every single move set and the right weapon on the right enemy to reach the end. Graphics wise, everything has more polygons than TR1, including Lara, but new players will hardly notice a difference from the previous game.  Music and sound effects are perfect, as they show up at the right time to bolster the player when meeting a tough challenge ahead or to warn them to be careful due to many dangers nearby.
There are still some archaic drawbacks to the game: combat is still very primitive with its bullet-spungy enemies even though the new weapons make it less tedious; some levels and situations are a bit illogical and demand a suspension of belief, such as underwater levels that have mooks in them. Yes, there are a couple of levels inside the Titanic-like ship that is hundreds of meters below water, and enemies are there just waiting for you there with no stockpiles or a transport back to the surface. I can already image this situation:
Generic Enemy 1: Are you sure Lara is going to show here? I mean it’s cold and rusty here and the damn ship could fall apart every second?
Generic Enemy 2: Don’t sweat it! She’ll be here soon with a prescribed led poisoning!
Generic Enemy 1: But what after we stop here? We didn’t brought food or anything to pull us out of here?
Generic Enemy 2: Hey, looks at bright side! If we die here, I’m sure our boss is going to pay to our families a handsome MIA insurance that was guaranteed in the contract.
Generic Enemy 1: You mean the contract we never signed?
Generic Enemy 2: Yep! Our boss has thought of everything.
Generic Enemy 1: But I don’t have any family! That’s why I’m here with you guys at the bottom of the ocean floor with no equipment or supplies whatsoever.
Generic Enemy 2: Then you don’t have nothing to worry about, friend! Your destiny is in good hands.
Even with its shortcomings, the new adventures of Lara Croft more than successfully deliver that Indiana Jones vibe. Tomb Raider II gets two thumbs recommendation from me and it’s a classic piece of gaming history everyone should try. It is easily among the best ones in this franchise.

The primary objective in the campaign is to build a rocket to escape the planet on which you are stranded. But to complete the research and construction necessary to do so, you must build factories to automate the gathering and processing of natural resources, and the systems you design become gradually more and more complex as you attempt to automate new processes. Describing this game in full would take much more time than I have to spare, and you really need to experience yourself the amazing feeling of omnipotence that permeates each successful bit of progress to understand why this game is so amazingly good, so I recommend at least playing the demo before passing it up, even if it doesn't seem like your kind of game.

Overall, one of the best games i have ever played. When i played back in 2010-2011 on my PS3, i didnt realize how good it actually was. And im talking about both experiences: singleplayer and multiplayer.Now, 2016, i re-bough this game on the steam winter sale. And god, what a good choice this was.
About the multiplayer: its the strong point of MW2. The community may be smaller now, since there have been so many new CoD games, but there are still people playing. You can find a party even 4 am on a wednesday. The multiplayer quality is fantastic. The amount of content keeps you coming back for more. A lot of customization options, which includes call signs, emblens, perks, attachments... Killstreaks are a good reward for the players skills. I personally like the matchmaking system instead of dedicated servers, becouse it keeps the game alive, becouse everyone can become a host, we all know there are a lot of limitations to host a dedicated server.
There is also a mode that can be played both singleplayer and multiplayer, called Special Ops. Here you do some very cool missions, usually not very long. They use some locations from the campaing. But its very good becouse its VERY challenging. Its very skill based, and it will take you some time and patience to do all Spec Ops missions. Its much more fun to do with a friend rather than doing alone. Spec Ops gives MW2 a very unique perspective over the other CoD games, becouse in my opinion its a better mode than Survival and Zombies.
And theres the singleplayer campaing, which continues the story from MW in a very good way. The story is short, you can probably beat in in 5-6 hours in the regular difficulty, but its a very entertaing story about war. Although you probably wont spend a lot of time in this mode, you will enjoy the cinematics and the whole story a lot.
Is MW2 the best CoD game so far? Yes. Best FPS game so far? No, but one of the bests.
But wait, isnt the game too old? Yes and no. "Yes" becouse it was launched 7 years ago, but "no" becouse the game aged really well in all aspects. Im talking mostly about graphics and gameplay...

It takes Bastions simple concept and combat system and puts a grand twist to it. Bastion allowed you to upgrade your weapons while Transistor allows you to combine them, the feel of coming up with a combination of skills that both looks, feels and works great is quite the spectacle and this combined with the way combat is designed makes fighting both fun and creatively challanging.
The game is not only attributed to fantastic art, amazing gameplay and a wonderful story but also the greatest soundtrack of any game I have ever played, ever. The game is very linear. There's not really any option for sidequest, or anything resembling quests at all for that matter. It's just one long story. If you're the type of player that wants to run around exploring or go off on your own adventure then this game isn't for you.
That being said the story is great. Even during my second playthrough I didn't get bored with it. And the ending... it's something you have to experience for yourself. The gameplay feels fresh and yet familiar enough that you'll know the basics within a few min. There's still a few advanced things to figure out and once you've gotten the hang of those you can increase the difficulty (done through in-game mechanics, not a setting in some menu).
Two playthroughs took about 29 hours, including unlocking all the achievements. I could probobly have done it quicker, but there's some minor things in the game that doesn't matter from a gameplay perspective, but they help in telling the story and experiencing the world, and I didn't want to miss any of those. Also I took a few breaks from the gameplay to just listen to the soundtrack. The soundtrack is amazing!

First off, yes, I did receive this product for free; and that's very fortunate because the price of this game matches its content: worthless.
Unless you have all the time in the world while living in your mother's basement playing MOBAs, MMOs, and jerking off to anime, you won't want to dedicate the time needed to learn the characters, their abilities, the relics, potions, and items that work best for each character and best against each enemy, and everything else necessary to not be one or two shot every single death.
As you may have read from even positive reviews, there is a learning curve; it does take time to get good at this game, but why devote any of your precious time to this game? If you commit enough time to learn each character, the best result is that you learn to deplete your enemies' health in one second.  Until you've devoted a significant amount of time to this game, you will die very, very much.  You will be one shot and two shot by the type of people mentioned in my intro; and you WILL be battling them since matchmaking is a joke and doesn't match you with people your level.
The only time this game is remotely fun is when inexperienced players can have a prolonged skirmish with other inexperienced players.  There is absolutely nothing enjoyable about dying in one second, or killing enemies in one second. There are some relics that can help prevent this, but have fun waiting 2-3 minutes for their cooldown.  "But you usually deplete players' health within one second in first person shooters too" Ah yes, thank you for bringing that up.  Yes, it's true there are a great deal of games in which you can kill people this quickly, the difference is that they are not Smite and actually require a little skill and strategy, not just memorization of items, attack rotations, and pressing the numbers 1 through 4.  Smite requires minimal aiming, and the only skill it requires is the ability to read descriptions and the time it takes to read and learn those descriptions.  These types of games are usually designed to require multiple attacks, optimally used in a certain rotation, to kill enemies.  Therefore, this game feels very broken when one ranged area of effect attack can deplete 95% of my health instantly, rendering me dead by any additional damage.
Moving on, the community sucks. My first review, and I am happy that it is this game. I purchased The Room during the Steam Summer '16 Sale, and I can say this without regret, I am VERY picky when it comes to games. There has to be something about it that draws me in, and watching the trailers for the game, I was intrigued.
This wasn't just a "hidden object" point and click game like I was initially expecting. No, you were moving things, rearranging stuff, dragging levers and flipping switches. Turning keys in locks, pushing buttons, watching as everything you did had a purpose to it. There were no prizes, and even the achievements were simply only for completing a chapter, but I found myself more rewarded by seeing what my actions had an effect on regarding the next phase of the puzzle. Over half a dozen times, I found my eyes widening in surprise as I watched something amazing happen, and that has NEVER happened before in other "puzzle" type games.
Perhaps, for me, it was the fact that this was a "puzzle box" that made me want to see the treasure inside, rather than simply just a "push the box over here to reach the ledge" sort of thing. The puzzles were challenging, but I didn't feel like they were abstract. You didn't have to think too much outside the "box" (pun intended) to figure out how to find the solution, and even if you could figure it out rather easily, it was still a procedure to get to the solution.
As with anything, though, I fear the only complaint I can make was time. In less than four hours, I was finished. I was satisfied, it left me wanting more (but in an episodic way, not a lack of content way,) but six chapters in less than four hours...I have mixed emotions about it. It was perfectly atmospheric without it being "horror." It was progressively challenging without being abstractly difficult. It was just....short.
I will be buying the second game, and am looking forward to being just as satisfied, if not moreso, with that one.

A sequel to the classic Tomb Raider and also my all time favourite in the series. It should be noted that the release date shown on the store page is a reference to only the digital release of the game; episode number 2 was actually released back in 1997. The pictures do explain this is a 20 year old game, though.
There are still various animals in the game as enemies (our favourite T-Rex returns) but there are a lot of mafioso thugs Lara has to take on as she seeks the dagger of Xian. New locales in the game include Venice, an opera house, an oil rig, Tibet and even underwater areas full of sharks and deadly eels. Accordingly, there are new weapons - harpoon for the underwater sequences and some stronger guns against Bartoli's men such as a grenade launcher or a rifle.
The core concept did not change. We need to reach the exit on each level and in the process getting rid of the enemies as well as solving puzzles. The main menu still includes Lara's home mansion which acts as a tutorial level so it is always advisable to begin here before commencing the main quest. In bundle the classic five games are a great purchase if you have fond memories of them.

Never thought guys who created Aliens: Colonial Marines would come up with this.
So, Minimum is a 'Just-came-out-of-early-access minimalistic 3rd person shooter with MOBA elements'. But that description is wrong about what it says: The game is not complete nor really minimalistic. Apparently, it's version 0.5something, and even though the armor system, base gameplay, weapon crafting and devices are generally done, it features only a couple maps, and the planned weapon upgrade system, structures and all the options that brings into the game aren't available yet. It also has a load of bugs, mainly in the UI and drop system, alongside with some sttutering during loading screens and occasional fails to end the program. It doesn't affect the main gameplay too much, though.
The second lie is 'minimalistic'. That's not what minimalistic really means. Sure, it doesn't have stupid drawings on the walls, nothing is lying on the ground, but the models are just blocky rather than being simple. Funnily enough, that gives the graphics an interesting charm - the blocky Titans, one color ground and upgrades that look like small futuristic car batteries go very well with all the lens flare everywhere.
The game itself then has three gamemodes: Team Deathmatch, Survival and Titan Mode. But right now I feel the game has actually only one gamemode truly worth playing - Titan Mode. In this particular one, five players on each side are pinned down in a conflict on a simple map featuring one main 'lane' and one or two 'Jungle areas', much like a MOBA would. The 'lane' is where giant robots named "Titans" march trough - meeting in the middle to fight to the death, where the winner may continue on to destroy the enemy's base. Bases are then made out of several parts - Power core, which is what the enemy needs to destroy to win, Turrets, which are your best hope to damage the enemy Titan after it destroyed yours, Spawn Rooms, whch are exactly what they sound like, and defensive walls, an equivalent of MOBA towers, which can be damaged only by Titans, and that usually combo with Turrets to keep the Titans under as much fire as possible. Titans, however, don't fight alone - players can help damage the enemy titan and destroy turrets, while the enemy team must be stopped from doing the same.
But then, the time comes - both Titans down. Then, the Creep Phase begins. The teams are informed that harmless creeps start spawning in pre-designated areas in the 'Jungle' map parts, where each killed creep drops a powerup that increases your Titan's strengh, making it more probable that it'll win the fight with the enemy titan. Of course, the enemy will do the same - so part of your team should start farming, when the other one should go interrupt the enemy's farming process to cripple them. Alongside with that there is the Golden Creep - faster version of the standart creep with more HP and no restrictions on it's position on the map - wandering around before it gets killed and drops a powerup worth ten times as much as a normal creep's. When time for this phase is up, titans respawn with their newfound strenght and the Titan phase begins once again. Rinse and repeat until the match time is up or one of the sides wins.
The PvP combat is based around weapons and armor. You can carry two weapons, one of which may be a meelee, one rechargable device, currently limited to several variants of grenades and turrets, and up to three different pieces of armor: Helmet, Chest armor and Leg armor. Each of these armor parts is crafted on the battlefield from armor shards and polygons (see the pun?), and can be upgraded up to level three. These resources drop every time a Titan is destroyed, a Creep is killed, a wall is broken or a player is killed. Each armor upgrade adds a small HP bonus, and also some kind of a special bonus, which in some cases comes with a disadvantage to keep things balanced. These armors come in sets - each with three individual parts, to provide a bonus to a specific playstyle, but you can mix different armor parts to match your personal one. These stay on you even after you die.
Weapon upgrades, however, don't. Every time a turret is destroyed or a titan is destroyed, one blue weapon upgrade is dropped, which you or one of your allies may pick up to upgrade their current weapon by one level. Players, however, drop one upgrade if they don't have a weapon with level three or higher, and drop two of these if they do. Each upgrade increases damage and, beyond a certain differing point, adds the weapon a passive ability. Kills become necessary to have an advantage over your enemy, but with each level over them, the probability of you being focused down because you'll drop twice as much upgrades plus lose all your upgrades increases. This makes the action more dynamic, as you become more and more dangerous the longer you stay alive. Every weapon also features an rechargable active ability - dash, jump, burst fire or super powered projectile.
Over all, I think this game is an idea that got ahead of it's age, but the game is still too uncomplete to be fully judged. Just look at the structure plans - there is one that would spawn weak combat creeps all around to slow down the enemy. I can still recommend it though - as long as you can take the bugs and the darn stupid camera most 3rd person shooters share.

This game is quite peculiar, and one that make me wish there is a 'maybe' bottom.
The gameplay is practically non existent, but this is not necessary a bad thing, since the purpose of Fingerbones is to tell a story.
Ambients are... well, there are practically just three rooms in this game, so there isn't much to say.
On the other side, these few rooms make you feel really uneasy.
But let's focus on the plot, which is the true center of this game:
First of all, the themes of Fingerbones are not easy. I don't want to spoiler anything, but if you are a very sensible person, maybe this is not the game for you.
And I don't mean there are gory or terrifying jumpscares, but the story itself can be very disturbing.
The horror element is build only on the psychological level, and the only 'true' scares in Fingerbones are some sounds.
This kind of horror build-up is what I truly like in Fingerbones, since there are very few games that have managed to do that so well.
The anxiety is created as you read the notes and discover the terrible story of the protagonist and the place where you are, and the horror (or disgust) as you realize what has appened.
But, in my opinion, this is also the main flaw of this game: the focus on the story make it a bit sterile.
There is the story, and nothing else, and the plot itself is not completely explored as it deserves.
In the end, Fingerbones is not a bad game, and in many ways it succeeded where others have failed, but, it leaves the feeling that there is something missing, and the story could have been explained and expanded better

Fingerbones is a short yet very interesting experience. You can complete it in about 30 minutes without using a walkthrough, as the few puzzles aren't too difficult to overcome, and in my opinion this is a plus; you see it, you download it, and you play through it in barely an hour. This is the kind of games that benefit from its short length, in many different ways.
I will do my absolute best not to spoil anything in this review as it is much better to see the story unravel before you. The game takes place in what seems like a basement. You are given no apparent goal, but the game is quite clear on what you should do next, as the area you are in is quite small. The story is narrated through notes laying around, written by someone you may assume as the player character. Storytelling through notes is something that I don't particularly enjoy in video games, but it is quite well handled here.
The atmosphere is on point. The game takes advantage of its limited map to reinforce the claustrophobic impression it's creating. The visuals are great, it is dark, foggy, with a bit of light shining through the windows and that's it. The sound design is just as great. The horror is also different from what we are used to see (there are no jumpscares at all, if that kind of thing bugs you); I have not played the game Gone Home, but from what I have read of it it is rather similar; obviously, something has happened, but you don't know exactly what or who did it, and the tension builds up continually as you go further down the rabbit hole despite thinking you may not want to actually find out.
Just because it's free doesn't mean it's good.  Nothing happens.  You walk around, there's some noises, you read some stuff, and that's it.  There, I saved you half an hour.

Half-simulation, half-real time strategy, you create a disease with the objective to completely wipe out humanity. Choose from a variety of diseases, including Virus, Bacteria or Parasite. Grow your disease from Patient Zero to the last human on Earth. Participate in unique and randomly generated scenarios.
The game feels like a realistic interpretation of how a global contagion would work, whilst keeping in fun game-play elements and memorable storytelling. The game also features several fictional diseases, such as a zombie virus, and the Simian flu from the Rise of the Planet of the Apes movies. These add to the uniqueness of each scenario as you try to take over the planet with an army of zombies or an army of apes. The game now has a scenario creator which players can tailor the games mechanics to suit their own diseases they create.
All-in-all, a fun game that you can use to kill time for 30 or so minutes on a Sunday evening.

Smite always has a place in my heart. I've been playing now for nearly 3 years and hav yet to get tired of it. Yes, there will be times that the meta gets royally screwed up and it gets difficult to enjoy, but it almost always fixes itself. From events, to comp, to quests, to so many different Gods to chose from, I love this game so very much. You will always have something to do and have fun doing it. Even if you get completely demolished in a game you get this urge to just get better and better. The depht of customization is amazing. Dynamic skins, voice packs, announcer packs, emotes, global emotes, recall skins, laoding card borders, it's all a lot. Hi-Rez has been supporting this game since beta and it doesn't look like they'll be stopping anytime soon with a new patch coming out every 2 weeks. However...Smite isn't without it's flaws.
Matchmaking can get rather annoying. I personally rarely did comp, but when I did my team was always unbalanced to a degree. I wouldn't recommend comp unless you're playing with at least 2 other people. Even in casual you'll sometimes get a team of randoms against a six stack. There are some items and Gods that are very clearly broken that might take a while to get fixed (I'm looking at you thorns >.>). Before, exclusive and limited skins were much more rare than they are now and were meant for very special skins. But now with the inclusion of Adventures more than half the skins coming out now are exclusive. The number of limited skins, the almighty rarest of the rares, have gone up a lot lately as well. They'll encourage you to spend all this money for new these exclusive skins that very easily could have been able for open purchase. It gets annoying when your favorite God gets a skin that is stuck behind a pay wall or in a chest. But, these are cosmetics so I can't get that mad at this.
I've taken plenty of breaks from Smite but always find myself coming back. It's just all around fun, with or without friends (though it's twice as fine with friends with mics). Including the time I've played the game before it came to Steam, my time played is more around 1,000 hours. And honestly? Heres to 1,000 more. Smite has some obvious flaws that get bigger from time to time, but it doesn't fail in providing a good amount of fun that you'll be wanting to come back for. Aside from some balancing issues and hiding some skins behind events and chests I have no major complaints. Not a MOBA for everyone, but for sure a MOBA for me.

Pro's:
-Great artwork
-Great soundtrack

Cons:
-Poor Combat

For starters, the combat is a great idea but just didn't work out. They tried mixing real time with turn based which made the game into a run around until I can freeze again. While running they give you a dash if you equip it. The dash puts you so far, then freezes you in spot for .5 seconds and by that time enemies are upon you and your taking damage. A roll like Bastion would have been awesome, or at least take away that stun during the dash. Not to mention every attack has a brief stun. Some for as long as 2 seconds it seems. Making them only viable during the freeze. While equiping different effects to other you just end up using the same ones most of the game, finding a good combo and just keeping it. I think I had the same three the whole game only swapping out one of them.
TLDR: Combat gets repetitive fast.
The characters themselves, the two main. I enjoyed. Everyone else is a mystery. You never get to really meet anyone and nothing was built up onto them. You have to read a bio to really get to know anyone in the game under their attack they gave you. Everyone has a few paragraphs to read but why should I have to read when this game could show me? In 4 hours you could have extended the game to allow me to see more into these characters instead of read because we didn't put it in.
Long story short. I do not recommend this game. The story tries to be edgy, different, and Bastion-esque and only manages to leave the player wanting. While the combat become repetitive and wanting to be avoided.

I can safely say that Transistor is one of the most beautiful games I have ever played. Every inch of the game is dripping with style, and my goodness, the soundtrack is pure sex - Coasting (Hummed) is an instant favorite!
Combat has so much depth like you wouldn't believe: you can mix-and-match so many permutations of skills and watch them blow apart and break enemies in style; the Turn system is easy to pick up but hard to master; and the difficulty respects your abilities to think your way out of trouble. The story picks up really fast halfway through the game, and I'd say the voice acting was done well. Don't worry about the game being a little short (you can finish your first run comfortably under 5 hours), there's still Recursion mode afterwards (NG+) so there's space for some replayability.
I guess my only complaint is with the camera and the map direction. A lot of times the fixed camera can screw you over both in and out of combat - in combat, some foreground elements do not go translucent if you go behind them, which can get you in trouble (if you Jaunt yourself into the edge of the map and you can't see Red, for example); out of combat, it's not always clear where you have to go, which is still somewhat related to the camera.
But please, do pick it up, it's a super fun game!

A fun ride severely hampered by performance issues and clunky moments.
Rock of Ages has all the right ingredients for being an all timer in the "cult classic" category. Goofy premise, unique style, fun gameplay, and great delivery. It all comes together in a great package and niche-feeling theme. Its a really unique take on the tower defense genre. You build defenses to protect your gate against your enemy's weapon; A rolling rock. But the game also features offensive play. You roll your own rock as well. A ball rolling game is a simple concept but still has to control in a satisfying way and this does on both keyboard and mouse and controller. While there is strategy involved, there's also a touch of racing as you try to get your roll and hit in before the AI to get ahead. It makes for some great fun. But the game's faults make it hard to outlandishly praise and even make the simple recommendation difficult. It is plain fun when everything is working right though! And you get a good amount of fun if you go for all the extras and collectables or whatever they are.
The game felt really un-optimized for me as performance was lacking. Later levels with more commotion led to severe framerate drops. Severe. Even on the lowest of settings. There's people running it flawlessly on laptops so it was partial (bad) luck of the draw that it wasn't optimized for my toaster. But a quick search showed I was hardly alone and there were people even editing .ini files and such just looking for an extra frame. A little too messy and too much effort for a game that should run fine to begin with as far as I was concerned. So I just lowered the resolution and windowed it to tough out the last third of it. The story mode took me around 5hrs while going for all the extras. Solid length for such a "small" game. There's a few other modes left if I were inclined. The bosses while inventive departures from standard play and funny were usually quite clunky. They ended up a test of wills and a relief to finish rather than anything resembling a challenge and satisfaction. And the unique and inventive tower defense side of the gameplay did get fairly shallow once you developed strategies that worked against the AI well. Perhaps the depth truly lies in multiplayer, but that was never on my radar to play.
Was a great game to get in a bundle like I did somewhere along the line and I wholeheartedly recommend it if its a deal, bundle or other bargain. But if the theme and gameplay idea isn't jumping out at you, its an easy skip. Its definitely a niche audience that will get the most out of it. With its problems it probably won't win anybody over by actually getting your hands on it and playing. A book that can be judged by it's cover perhaps? I could be off base here. But hey, if the cover looks interesting, take a roll for sure! Sequel in the works as well!

About the multiplayer: its the strong point of MW2. The community may be smaller now, since there have been so many new CoD games, but there are still people playing. You can find a party even 4 am on a wednesday. The multiplayer quality is fantastic. The amount of content keeps you coming back for more. A lot of customization options, which includes call signs, emblens, perks, attachments... Killstreaks are a good reward for the players skills. I personally like the matchmaking system instead of dedicated servers, becouse it keeps the game alive, becouse everyone can become a host, we all know there are a lot of limitations to host a dedicated server.
There is also a mode that can be played both singleplayer and multiplayer, called Special Ops. Here you do some very cool missions, usually not very long. They use some locations from the campaing. But its very good becouse its VERY challenging. Its very skill based, and it will take you some time and patience to do all Spec Ops missions. Its much more fun to do with a friend rather than doing alone. Spec Ops gives MW2 a very unique perspective over the other CoD games, becouse in my opinion its a better mode than Survival and Zombies.
And theres the singleplayer campaing, which continues the story from MW in a very good way. The story is short, you can probably beat in in 5-6 hours in the regular difficulty, but its a very entertaing story about war. Although you probably wont spend a lot of time in this mode, you will enjoy the cinematics and the whole story a lot.
Is MW2 the best CoD game so far? Yes. Best FPS game so far? No, but one of the bests.
But wait, isnt the game too old? Yes and no. "Yes" becouse it was launched 7 years ago, but "no" becouse the game aged really well in all aspects. Im talking mostly about graphics and gameplay...
This is the best call of duty game ever. I highly recommend you.

Sleeping Dogs is not a terrible game, it got nice graphics (especially when it's raining), a great unarmed fight system, and a properly done interseting setting.
So why the negative review? Because the game has 2 big flaws that prevent me to consider this (i completed it without rushing) a truly enjoyable experience:
1-The driving mechanincs are bad, the awful and totally unrealistic vehicle handling (and dont get me started on the silly "ramming" mechanic) and the ridicolous damage model (cars and motorcicle are almost indistructible, taking huge amount of enemy fire or crashing at 250 km/h on concrete wall without consequences, but then you got one bullet on the tire and your car immediately explode in huge fireball for some reason). That's particulary annoying considering this game has A LOT of driving related mission, and games with much less focus on those like Mafia 2 or even L.A. Noire did an incredible better job when it comes to driving.
2-The story (the last part in particular). The story actually starts off very interesting, and it remain so for the first half of so, they truly manage to get the player the impression of Wei's conflicting loyalities, you also get a nice unexpected shock moment that makes things even more interesting but from that moment to end, the story become one of the most predictable and boring i've seen in a while.
You know when a crime or thriller movie, seems so much predicatable and obvious you are sure that there is going to be some huge plot twist near the end? Well this game second half of the story gives exactly that same impression, but in the end you get no plot twist and everything turns out to be exactly as lame as it seemed to be.
, in the end, extremely disappointing. Also your enemies are some of the most uniteresting and flat characters i've seen in while,"huh watch me i'm so violent and evil just for the sake of it!!!! i'm also stupid and short sighted (but somehow i became the most powerfull and respected Triad boss of Hong Kong) I'm such a bad guy!!!! do you hate me already???"
In the end this game got quite some nice aspects to it, but, if you are not fan of the setting (that's actually very nicely done) i'd say there far superior alternatives when it comes to this genre (especially if you are looking for a good story-driven title, coughMafia2cough) that are much more worthy of your time.

This week Factorio my mostly played game on Steam, seems appropriate to write a review about it now. I won't write about the graphics, sound or gameplay but I will describe how I played the game, because that's the reason why I keep playing Factorio.
First of all, don't think it is too complicated when you see those complex designs on reddit. There are a lot of different solutions to improve your factory. Sometimes I look on the internet for a solution, such as a way to evenly balance items on the belts (the belt balancer), but the biggest part of my factorio is created by just building something and see what works well enough and improve when it is needed. There is no need to do things perfect from the start.
I have a similar advice on mods, it may seem smart to look into these and install everything that seems nice to have but it's best to just start playing and think of which things you want to change. I found it annoying to have a small inventory so I choose the BigBags mod to increase the stack size and add warehouse buildings to have more storage space. If you start with too many mods there are too much possibilities to explore and when you have a problem you don't know if it's in the basic game or one of the mods.
So you don't need to do everything perfect from the start. That's exactly what I did:
When I created my first factory I thought I designed my stuff pretty good, I noticed there were some inefficiencies but it was good enough. Then I found out that producing 1 blue science/min wasn't sufficient for all the research and it wasn't that easy to scale up because of my factory layout. Some time ago I thought it would be fun to load this savegame again and it basically was a big mess of belt spaghetti and some assemblers in between. Somehow I spent 19 ingame hours on this and the farthest I got was some small scale oil refining for the blue science.
With the second factory the train track design became much more userfriendly. Finally it was easier to scale up production. So my factory was much bigger than the first one, and better designed because I built everything around 'the main bus', a central line of belts which carry the mostly needed resources. So it's easier to scale up production on the side and you always have the required items close to where it's needed. I started using construction robots to place my blueprints so once I had a good design I could just place it somewere and it would be built almost instantly. And I got logistic robots to keep my personal inventory stocked with the items I needed often so I didn't need to craft these anymore. This way expanding my factory went much faster than before. This time I actually managed to launch the rocket in about 80 hours, because I was mostly just having fun experimenting and exploring instead of focussing on the rocket. I made huge improvements compared to my first game, but still far from perfect. I got 30k of belts in stock, and I thought it would be more efficient if I could somehow pause the production of certain items once I got a certain amount of them so the copper and steel could be used elsewere instead.
This became the main improvement of my third factory, I knew that the solution was in using a circuit network to pause production for a certain item but it seemed very complicated to setup, even after watching some youtube videos on it. I finally found out and gradually implemented these circuits in my factory to prevent overproduction. I also started creating production lines for items which I always crafted personally so far because I didn't need them that much before, such as roboports and laser turrets. But it became annoying to craft these over and over again when I started to create more outposts, so then I automated production of these, and prevented overproduction with circuit networks.
Once I got more outposts my rail network became more complex and I had to look up how to place the rail signals to avoid collisions and deadlocks. Then I made more blueprints to make it easier to make a complete outpost with turrets, roboports and walls. To make sufficient products to expand I needed more green and red cercuits, because 500 green/min was way too less. I made cleared some space at the end of the main bus, and placed some assemblers in a much more compact layout than my old circuit production. Made a blueprint of this and placed this again and again. Before I thought it would cost much more time but in about 15 minutes I completed this and added 2500 green circuits/minute.
My latest project was to find more oil, and I decided to move as far to the right as I could for a certain time and found some oil wells and a lot of very rich ore fields (ore fields get richer the further away from your spawn point). Then created some distant outposts there so now there would be enough resources to build this rocket. But my next project will be to automatically supply my outposts with repair packs to repair the buildings after an attack and also some laser turrets and walls, in case these are destroyed. I want to use a dedicated train for this, but want to prevent that all the items keep being loaded in the train wagon because it's hard to pause production that way if my storage chest is empty but there are 1000 laser turrets in the train itself, turns out it can be done with the Inventory Sensor mod.
Thankfully this game has a great community so a solution to your problems if often found, and if it wasn't possible in the game someone will create a mod for it. If you want a game where you have lots of freedom to experiment and solve problems in your own way, and like to have a steady feel of improvement while playing, which I tried to describe in this review, this is the game for you.

I'm a huge fan of Bastion and I wouldn't be entirely truthful saying that I wasn't expecting a similar experience.  That said I do understand that this was an entirely different project and respect the things the team did well, considering the size and budget of the team.
The musical score is hands down one of the selling points of this game and a huge part of why the art style suits the game so well.  It elicits a very surreal feel to the game that sells the convulted story just a bit by being "beautiful and artistic".
Unfortunately the story is a bit forced and 5-7 hours in length, the gameplay repetitive even with the variety of combos you can create, the VATS like system when you press spacebar, with no side objectives to speak of or even interesting things to explore.  The lack of items or any other depth puts the weight of the enjoyment you feel while progressing on the combat... which are all scripted and repeated a few times.  Too few boss fights, limiters being fairly forced upon you to make the game challenging, and the entire linear experience felt more like a visual novel game rather than the action-rpg I was expecting.
A friend of mine has nothing but praise for this game's many attributes and I really wanted to like it as much as he did.  Unfortunately I found myself losing interest in the repetition and non-rpg elements of the game that I frequently took breaks for days at a time before finishing this short game.
I wouldn't personally recommend it for the full price tag but the game gets enough love from the Indie community that it goes on sale frequently so check it out if you're interested (at the very least to help the developers fund another game that might be different direction from this one).

Gameplay:
The idea of the Rock of Ages is unique, you control a rock rolling over various surfaces to destroy enemy's castle door, the enemy has the exact same goal, destroy your castle door first. It usually takes 3-4 rocks to destroy enemy's castle door. Once your rocks finish rolling or right at start of the game, there will be a period of time where you'll be waiting for a new rock to become available, giving you time to build defense units (towers, TNTs etc.) on the enemy's road to slow down the enemy boulder, or even destroy the rock completely. At start of the game you are given a specific amout of credits, allowing you to buy defense units from those. You gain credits when you hit enemy castle door and when you destroy the enemy defense units with your rock. There are 3 keys laid over every map, after every few levels, you'll require a specific amout of keys to be able to proceed further on in the singleplayer. The keys are easy to get and you can always replay any level, and even if you lose the game, you still get the keys you collected with the rock from the map, so there's no need to worry about the key part.
In boss battles you simply are 1 rock inside some sort of arena where you fight the bosses, the goal is to kill the boss by hitting its weak point with the rock 3 times without getting destroyed by bosses' attacks.
The rock HP system is quite complicated. The base rock has 3 layers each having some amount of hitpoints it can take before breaking. When a layer gets destroyed, your rock gets smaller, and inflicts less damage on enemy's castle doors, it doesn't affect boss battles anyhow though, except for the rock simply being smaller, making it a little harder to take damage, but also to hit the enemy. There are another types of rocks that you can buy for credits, such as a rock with 4th layer or a burning rock which basically has its first layer set on fire, making it easier to break through enemies, but it can get extinuished in levels containing water, changing it into normal 3 layer rock. Your rock can also fall out of every map, but it'll just respawn on the nearest checkpoint and it won't lose hp at all, so there's no need to be extra careful.
That should be everything important I found worthy of mentioning from the gameplay, with that out of the way, I'd like to describe the other parts of the game.
Game's art:
You start at south coast of nowadays Italy's borders in times of Greek mythology, every new level, you move a bit forward in time and across the map of Europe (Borders of today's Italy, France, Spain and Portugal) , starting on tutorial fight with Hades in ancient greek times, moving throughout the levels all the way to late middle ages, fighting characters such as Charlemagne, Leonardo da Vinci and many more. There are short cutscenes before start of every battle, showing the enemies you are going to fight in sort of comic way, it's up to your personality whether you find them funny or insultive to Europe's history. Personally I liked most of them, but few of them took it too far (fighting the Plague, displayed as some sort of skeletal figure of human body for example). The design of the levels themselves was pretty simple, yet still nice. I could see a lot of effort going into design of the game's bosses. Except for some of the cutscenes, I liked everything from the game art-wise.
Controls:
I've got nothing to criticize in this part, the controls are fairly simple and work as they should.
Performance:
I was able to run the game smoothly on a low tier laptop without a single problem in framerate.
Other:
-The game also has multiplayer, but I haven't had the luck in finding someone to play with.
-The singleplayer is pretty short, a good player will be able to finish the game within 2 hours. For average player, like I am, it shouldn't take more than 3 hours either.
-Majority of the levels are easy, you can just place several elephants at the same place, and on most of the maps it will screw over the enemy rock's AI in single player, as the rock will get completely blocked and destroyed by the elephant defense units. Some of the defense units may feel much stronger compared to the other. I only found 1/2 of the defense units effective for most of the maps
-The game could get repetitive after some time.
Summary:
Pros:
-Unique idea of the game
-Almost flawless design of the levels and cutscenes
-Perfect controls
-Perfect performance
Cons:
-The singleplayer won't take too long to finish, I'd be really suprised if it took someone more than 4 hours
-Jokes in some cutscenes were taken too far
Final words:
This is a first serious game review I've ever done. Took over an hour to do. I initially wanted to keep it short, but it seems like I failed doing so. Still only tried to include my view of the most important parts of the game, so hope I did not forget anything. At the time of writing the review, the game is 9.99€ in Steam store, I got the game with 75% discount due to a discount coupon for it I had, my friend reccomended it to me. I definitely don't regret spending those two and a half Euros on the game, it was worth it. If you're considering buying the game, I would say it's worth even its full price, but if it seems like too much to you, just wait for a discount, definitely worth taking at 5€ and less. I'm reccomending this game because the idea and its execution astonished me and I enjoyed the singleplayer all the way through.
Thank you for reading this review, if you have any feedback, leaving it in the comments would be appreciated, it could help me if I'd be reviewing another game in the future.

Best P2P MMO I've played in recent years. Been a few months since I have played so this might not be completely accurate. Here are my positives (+) negatives (-) and neutrals (o).
(+) All classes on one character, each levels individually, Mix and match (some) skills from one class to another. For example, if you plan to play a healer, "Swift Cast" from the offensive caster is absolutely required so you can revive people instantly.
(+) This is the ultimate callback game for fans of the more classic Final Fantasy games, though you'll find a little bit from every game here. You probably don't need to be an FF fan to enjoy this, it stands up on its own mechanically. I would basically describe this game as "WoW done better."
(+) Level scaling for Dungeons and FATES (Fates are over-world events that people can take part in as a community.) So no matter what level you are, you and your friends can play together. However, you cannot level scale on the overworld unless you're inside a FATE.
(+) Party Finder. It works wonders, just queue up and do most anything else while you wait for a party to be automatically formed for a dungeon. You can also join overworld parties. Tanks and Healers will be matched quicker because they are not as commonly played, expect to wait if you are a DPS.
(+) Glamour system, make any piece of equipment look like another. You can only unlock the ability to glamour at level 50, but people can do it for you before then. It IS possible to look like a classically colored Black Mage, if you have the currency for it.
(+) Mechanically difficult and exhilarating bosses. Knowing how each dungeon and boss fight works before going in is essential to success. This is a double-edged sword, however, you could be stuck on a difficult fight, wiping multiple times with a pub party that doesn't know what they are doing. Sometimes it can get a bit too stressful, you'll always be on the razor's edge, late game. Different classes and roles are easier or harder to play, I wouldn't recommend rolling a tank for your first class.
(+) Guilds, Guild Houses and Homes. I highly recommend finding a good guild, there are benefits to reap. Decorate your own Guild House, Personal House or Apartment Room inside your Guild House. You could make your own guild, but I recommend joining an existing one that has some legs and good community.
(+) Chocobo Companions. Train a Chocobo to fight alongside you on the overworld, good for soloing. They can be mix-ups of Tank, Healer and DPS. Though the tank isn't all that good, last I heard.
(+) Gold Saucer and Minigames! Gamble, collect cards and play tetra master across the world (love it or hate it), race Chocobos FF7 style, earn currency for rewards.
(+) Retainers, get one of these as soon as you can, you get up to two for free. They act as your bank and you can send them out on missions to get items for you.
(o) Crafting is still kind of a pain like most MMO's, you do not draw from resources directly from your bank like in GW2, so it's an inventory management headache, but there is money to be made and it's far from useless. Each crafting class works mostly the same, but each has some unique skills that can cross-class like combat classes do. Many of which are necessary. It's worth a try.
(o) Arena and Mass-Scale PvP is available, though I can't comment on it since it's not my playstyle. EDIT: Recent update added 1v1 dueling.
(-) Ability Icon Clutter, a carry-over from WoW. This can be mitigated with good macro building and UI customization management, though.
(-) Main storyline isn't interesting until around level 50, which is max level before the expansion. Before that, there are some highlights, but it's mostly a slog through lots of political dialogue. Post vanilla is a vast improvement, though. Also, side story arcs are a lot better, for example, each class has its own story arc.
(-) No cross-server play. If you have a max level character on one server, and your friend is on another, one of you will have to make a new character or pay money for a server transfer.

Smite always has a place in my heart. I've been playing now for nearly 3 years and hav yet to get tired of it. Yes, there will be times that the meta gets royally screwed up and it gets difficult to enjoy, but it almost always fixes itself. From events, to comp, to quests, to so many different Gods to chose from, I love this game so very much. You will always have something to do and have fun doing it. Even if you get completely demolished in a game you get this urge to just get better and better. The depht of customization is amazing. Dynamic skins, voice packs, announcer packs, emotes, global emotes, recall skins, laoding card borders, it's all a lot. Hi-Rez has been supporting this game since beta and it doesn't look like they'll be stopping anytime soon with a new patch coming out every 2 weeks. However...Smite isn't without it's flaws.
Matchmaking can get rather annoying. I personally rarely did comp, but when I did my team was always unbalanced to a degree. I wouldn't recommend comp unless you're playing with at least 2 other people. Even in casual you'll sometimes get a team of randoms against a six stack. There are some items and Gods that are very clearly broken that might take a while to get fixed (I'm looking at you thorns >.>). Before, exclusive and limited skins were much more rare than they are now and were meant for very special skins. But now with the inclusion of Adventures more than half the skins coming out now are exclusive. The number of limited skins, the almighty rarest of the rares, have gone up a lot lately as well. They'll encourage you to spend all this money for new these exclusive skins that very easily could have been able for open purchase. It gets annoying when your favorite God gets a skin that is stuck behind a pay wall or in a chest. But, these are cosmetics so I can't get that mad at this.
I've taken plenty of breaks from Smite but always find myself coming back. It's just all around fun, with or without friends (though it's twice as fine with friends with mics). Including the time I've played the game before it came to Steam, my time played is more around 1,000 hours. And honestly? Heres to 1,000 more. Smite has some obvious flaws that get bigger from time to time, but it doesn't fail in providing a good amount of fun that you'll be wanting to come back for. Aside from some balancing issues and hiding some skins behind events and chests I have no major complaints. Not a MOBA for everyone, but for sure a MOBA for me.

My love of games scewed towrds Space Quest and Robocod and the like.  The family got a crappy low end Mac when I went to Uni in the mid '90's.  By then I had become very removed from anything gaming.
When I started playing the demo of TRII I thought it was THE MOST amazing game I had ever seen.  I had never played a game like it, (DOOM was the closest).   That this 'unco' girl could figure out the keyboard controls amazed me and I played that one level over and over again.
Mac games in the late 90's in this part of the world were super expensive.  So needless to say when I did get this game I played it again and again and again.
My review can ONLY be biased on my experiece of 20 years ago.  I LOVE IT.  10/5 stars.  I love the game, the music, sound, story, secrets, cut scenes and challenges.  I particularly enjoy the Venice Scenes.  Gorgeous.

Part platformer, part puzzle game, part parody. Eryi's Action actively punishes players adhering to the standard genre conventions via a relentless stream of cheap shots. Eventually, you'll start to think you have the traps figured out, only to have the rug pulled out from under you once more.
Fortunately, the game is fully 'on rails'; once you figure out the trick to each segment all that's left to do is actually getting past it. Especially in the latter levels, this will require quite a bit of manual dexterity, however.
If you get frustrated easily, do not buy this game.
If you're looking for a cheap, shortish platformer that forces you to think outside the box on occasion, I would certainly recommend Eryi's Action. Being able to appreciate and laugh at the boundless creativity with which the game screws you over is just an extra bonus.

The best MMO available today bar none, and the only MMO I have liked since Ragnarok Online.
The visuals and performance are unbelievably good, and the gameplay system has a few quirks that make it more engaging that your average MMO (such as being able to dodge some attacks by moving out of their way), but two things truly set it apart: The story and the Duty Finder.
The story is a rather straightforward plus: It has an amazing narrative worthy of the Final Fantasy name, complete with unbelievably well crafted in-game cutscenes of the likes I would have never expected to see in an MMO. The story will also carry you through the leveling process, cleverly masking "the grind", much like offline JRPGs.
The Duty Finder, on the other hand, is a very well made matchmaking system that will pair you up with people that meet the necessary criteria so that you can tackle dungeons as a party. The standard setup is one tank, two damage dealers and one healer: Dungeons are balanced around a "fully featured" party like this, and the Duty Finder will make it a breeze to build such a party even with random strangers. Pretty much every single person I've been paired with through the Duty Finder has fulfilled his role well. The player base seems very mature in general.
In short, if you want to play an MMO right now, it has to be this one.
