The Room is a point and click examina-thon game that generally is targeting a very specific audience (people who enjoy stuff like MYST will probably like this) and although its demographic is niche, the game for me personally hits all the right spots to make it a very enjoyable and "comfy" game, despite not being a huge fan of these types of games.
The Room is exactly what it says on the tin I guess in terms of premise; you are in a room, and in this dark room you have in front of you on a table a puzzle of some kind, with the setting of the game being in the 1800s, I think anyway. These puzzles are generally very bizarre and extremely intricate, with little details and inklings on each set piece to allow you to examine or play with. The objective is relatively simple; open up each puzzle, and as each puzzle opens, another awaits inside. Picture those russian dolls that have little versions of each other inside them. There is some kind of hidden story involved in the game, but for me personally it was best to not know much for the sheer feeling of mystery involved.
The graphics are very photorealistic, volumetric, and pristine, which obviously allows for more obscure puzzles to be made that couldnt have been achieved on engines for games like MYST back in the 90s. The game's soundtrack consists of eery ambient music, sometimes with the rhythm of a heartbeat, probably indicating that your character is either panicking or focusing on solving each dimensional puzzle in the game. Clicking on things, usually ones with twisty handles or rotational movements, can be a little awkward and fidgety to work with, but besides that, the game controls pretty seamlessly.
The game unfortunately has the issue of being incredibly short, being around 2-3 hours probably depending on how gud you are at solving these kind of puzzles, but for me the money price was worth a pound or two, just for the sheer level of detail in each of the 5 puzzles.
If there is one issue with the Room that I will point out, it is the sheer unawareness of how comfy the game could actually be without its creepy atmosphere, but I suppose it would be considered some kind of clone to other point and click examination games, so the horror setting I suppose helps it be unique.
Overall, an enjoyable experience that was comfy to play while it was raining outside, filled with atmosphere and that Victorian-era feel to it.

Review: Alpha State and Focus on Low Skill Kills
First the good things. The game's graphics are, at least for my taste, very nice. And the low poly design, along with some more optimizations, could allow this game to have very low system requirements. It's potentially the only recent shooter i could run at a constant and stable 120fps/hz.
A little downside here, the game seems to be locked at 90 fps, which is a bit sad in times of 120Hz monitors. Probably an engine limitation, but most likely one that could be changed. Maybe even in the config files if one looks for it.
Also, the combination of a shooter with a moba, is extremely nice. Huge addictive potential here. The Titan game mode is spot on and could even survive as a single gametype in a shooter.
Unfortunately, that's already all good there is to say for the moment. So now to the weak sides.
First of all, they claim to have left early access. But this game is not even in Beta stage. In a Beta, most of the features are already there. In this game most feats are still placeholders. So what we got here is an alpha build.
The game's weakest point is, unfortunately, the combat part. Everything you found in the past 10 years in serious shooters, that was counted by top players as skill free, honorless or plain trolling, is what Minimum promotes at the moment.
That the weapon sounds, like the AR, sound like pea shooters, could be forgiven. But that the strongest "tactic" ingame is, to bunny hop (10 meters high, and nonstop) while spamming grenades (non stop), is ... well, i lack the words to put it in a nice way. It seems to be a bad joke, and one wonders how old the devs of this game are. Serious combat looks different.
Next worst thing is the amount of melee in this game. An honorful melee kill is one where you sacrifice the chance for an easy kill, to get a cool kill with a melee weapon. In Minimum however, you get super speed, insane dashes, selfheal and whatnot, to get free kills.
This doesn't mean that you rack up insane numbers of kills this way. But it means that you get a lot of undeserved kills. Which is never a good thing in a game, because that is what makes a lot of gamers move on to other sources of entertainment. Very bad idea when you are trying to build a playerbase. One of the worst ideas in fact. So your main choices now are, to also go the crappy way of melee in a shooter. Or increase your armor, and thus becoming slower and slower...
The developers cleary point into a for me very strange direction. Instead of promoting proven to be addictive shooter combat, they degrade this game to a sort of hack'n slash'n spray'n spam fest. It's fun for a short while, but gets boring rather fast.
But this most likely strongly depends on what type of game player you are. If you are not happy by dominating through the use (or abuse) of certain game mechanics to gain an advantage, then this game is defenitely not for you.
On the other hand, if all you need to be happy is rack up kills, no matter how skillfree or honorless, then this game has a whole lot to offer. It basically combines all those mechanics that are frowned upon in serious matches in one game.
Also, one thing that i find very worrying, is an option in the menus. The game seems to support gamepads and has options for aiming assist. This is an absolute no-go in a shooter on pc, and i hope they will make sure that controllers do not even come close to the accuracy that can be achieved with a mouse. This would be almost as bad as officially allowing aimbots.
Keep in mind though that this game appears to be in early alpha still though. So a lot can still change. And spending 5 bucks for it on a Steam sale is certainly not a mistake. Not only because some good laughs can be had, but also to give the devs more time to fine tune this game. This game could be very long term addicting and lure out of lot of cash out of peoples pockets for skins and the like if it were more serious.
One thing that would be very nice to see, if the general direction this game seems to go is maintained, would be if in the stats the different types of kills (shot/explosives/melee) would be visible seperately.

The best MMO available today bar none, and the only MMO I have liked since Ragnarok Online.
The visuals and performance are unbelievably good, and the gameplay system has a few quirks that make it more engaging that your average MMO (such as being able to dodge some attacks by moving out of their way), but two things truly set it apart: The story and the Duty Finder.
The story is a rather straightforward plus: It has an amazing narrative worthy of the Final Fantasy name, complete with unbelievably well crafted in-game cutscenes of the likes I would have never expected to see in an MMO. The story will also carry you through the leveling process, cleverly masking "the grind", much like offline JRPGs.
The Duty Finder, on the other hand, is a very well made matchmaking system that will pair you up with people that meet the necessary criteria so that you can tackle dungeons as a party. The standard setup is one tank, two damage dealers and one healer: Dungeons are balanced around a "fully featured" party like this, and the Duty Finder will make it a breeze to build such a party even with random strangers. Pretty much every single person I've been paired with through the Duty Finder has fulfilled his role well. The player base seems very mature in general.
In short, if you want to play an MMO right now, it has to be this one.

Pros: Loads of content, loads of stuff to do.  Easy to get into multiplayer content, incentives for veterans to help rookies out, storyline quests progress your levels quite efficiently.  Interesting crafting mechanic, no-fuss travel, lush scenery and classic Final Fantasy aesthetics.  Loads of punny quest titles and memes hidden throughout.  A marriage mechanic that does not restrict (or even ask questions about) gender combinations.  Multi-rider mounts so you can haul your friends around.  Tons of quests and collections, a completionist's dream.
Cons: Extremely technical, precise, minmax-y and a lot of poor communication, both between the game and the player and between player and player.  Terribad voice acting, overly flowery and verbose script, a plot that is hamfistedly dramatic and full of predictable and frustrating tropes, ugly "basic" gear practically until max level with few to no alternate options.  Gear-gated content and rng-based gear acquisition (this is a con, to me, take that as you will.).  Story quests force you to solo content, even in a game where no class is built to safely run solo.  Passive-aggressive elitism in the community.
I ran out of game time, and I won't be renewing it.  This game is not for gamers who play games to have fun.   This is an MMORPG that is designed for people who feel good about themselves by getting very good at, or completing, extremely difficult or complicated content.   I'm not what one calls a "hardcore gamer" and thus the restrictive, overly specific Holy Trinity of RPGs gameplay left me feeling drained more than refreshed.  After failing a solo story quest duty five times in a row, and finding that I was doing everything right, I just simply should've gotten hit less, I decided I wasn't the kind of player Square-Enix had in mind when developing this game.
I'm told Heavensward is much better story and much nicer mechanics, but if you can't even make it to the Heavensward  expansion's content, which begins only after you've completed your entire A Realm Reborn story quest, it's not worth even the cost of the base game.  I'm not going to muddle through a difficult, unsatisfying and frustrating game just in the hopes that I can pay more money to see if the expansion is more to my liking.

Replay Value: Transistor features a multiple challenge rooms and a new game plus.

Here's my short summary/review of the game.
The game starts slowly, but that's actually a good thing (I'll elaborate shortly). Once you get through a few days , the game becomes challenging. It tests your attention to detail when inspecting passports, permits, ID cards, etc., and when you get a written warning for sending someone through to the country when you weren't supposed to, it is completely your fault. All the information is present for you, and it's up to you to keep it in mind and use what you've got to get through as many people in the day as you can. Why go through a ton of people quickly than take your time inspecting? Well, for every correct inspection you make, you earn money -- money that you use to pay the bills at home. So you aren't just doing your job well, you are doing it well to support your wife, son, uncle, and (for whatever reason) your mother-in-law, and I think that's a neat thing to motivate you to be efficient. That being said, do not take your first two days for granted. The rules are simple enough that you can run through 15-20 people per day. I like that this game keeps me engaged by demanding my focus on details, and the aspect of earning my paycheck to support my family is a very nice use of motivation. Make bank, keep your family fed and warm, enjoy the game :)
It's definitely not the longest game nor does it have a lot of replay value, but it is and will be a uniquely pleasing experience.

I was a little hesitant to get this game when I saw that it was on sale for the summer sale, but seeing the low price I figured it was worth the risk and the worst that would happen is that I would get some trading cards that would recoup a little bit of the cost. It was surprisingly than I expected and I've compiled a list of pros and cons about the game.
Pros:
-Low cost for a game with a surprising amount of content
-A fair amount of strategy required for a game that's only about drawing a line on your screen
-Incredibly low stress game and its perfect for just sitting around
-Surprisingly a lot of ideas for such a simplistic concept
-Quick achievements, but also the "other achievements" which make you attempt the levels in a different fashion.
Cons:
-Gets a little repetitive for the more difficult levels. While the first few that you see in the advanced pack and maybe a couple of the others can be truly difficult, eventually you start seeing the same patterns and they fall in place easily for you.
Conclusion:
The game is well worth the price no matter how much you get it at. The game is a fantastic concept, which can be executed in a surprising amount of different ways. The achievements make you think about the levels in a little bit of a different way as well (if you care about those) and overall add another layer of difficiulty to the game. I loved the game other than the few "easier" levels due to repitition in the final advanced pack. Overall though, a solid 9/10 game well worth the price!

The high quality animation and sound effects definitely help with that. The aesthetic is gorgeous; I caught myself rotating the view just to gaze at the scenery a few times.
On a sour note, I can't say I liked the hints popping up constantly and tempting you to click them, only to tell you something obvious. It's a bit insulting to be told "hey, maybe if I turned the thing up there, it might reveal things down there" after about 30 seconds of exploration. In the end it's a satisfying work of art to interact with, and well worth the price. 15/20

Tomb Raider 2 - Review
Tomb Raider 2 continues the adventures of Lara Croft. One year after Tomb Raider took over the world, the team at Core design return with what is considered by many, myself included as the very best Tomb Raider game in the original series.
The story of Tomb Raider II surrounds the mythical 'Dagger of Xian', a weapon which was used by an Emperor of China to command his army. By plunging the weapon into its owner's heart, the weapon has the power to turn its bearer into a dragon. The last battle fought with the Dagger ended when the warrior monks of Tibet removed the knife from the Emperor's heart, whereupon the Emperor died. The Dagger was then returned to its resting place within the Great Wall of China. This will take Lara all over the world and she will battle a dangerous cult intent on getting their hands on the dagger.  As before this is told through FMV cut scenes and in game clips, these are an improvement on before and there is more voice acting than in the previous game which helps improve the story telling experience. As before however it’s not always easy to tell what’s going on but you always have a rough idea and it keeps the game moving well.
I personally preferred the story in Tomb Raider 2 to the first game and it takes Lara from the Great Wall of China to Venice then onto an underwater shipwreck, then to the mountains of Nepal and back to China. The level design is fantastic here and all the levels feel unique. One of my complaints about the first game is that many levels felt similar in design, but in Tomb Raider 2 this is not the case, they all stand out with tough, puzzles, great exploration and improved combat. Special mention must go to the Barkhang Monastery level that sees Lara explore an ancient monastery that’s full of great puzzles, many enemies and monks that if left un harmed, aid Lara against the cult members. In 1997 this was very impressive and it made the level stand out in gaming let alone Tomb Raider 2 with the impressive number of people on screen and AI.
Graphically Tomb Raider 2 is much improved over the original. Lara’s model has been improved with a higher polygon count, her famous ponytail also makes its first appearance here and reacts impressively to the way Lara moves, running over her shoulder and reacting to wind ect. Environments also look improved with more varied textures, Lara will find herself in more modern surroundings such as Venice and an oil rig rather than just ancient tombs. Dynamic lighting has also been added, Lara’s weapons will cause light to bounce off the environment as she fires them and she now has flares to help brighten up darker areas.
Game play has been greatly improved this time around, from the moment I picked up Tomb Raider 2 Lara felt more responsive and allot less “tank” like. It makes it much easier to play Tomb Raider 2 in 2017 than say Tomb Raider 1. Combat has been improved with more guns added to Lara’s arsenal, a grenade launcher, M16 assault rifle and harpoon for underwater combat have been added alongside the classic duel pistols, uzi’s and shotgun. The amount of gun fights in the game has been increased with Lara fighting many more human enemies this time around, the AI is rather standard for 1997 and at times can be relentless in their pursuit of Lara. The combat to exploration balance in Tomb Raider 2 feels perfect and adds a new dimension to the game play. The save system has also been changed, dropping the save crystal’s from the first game for a save anywhere system that makes the game far more forgiving than before, no longer will you have to play through the same sections of the game over and over again when you die.
Tomb Raider 2 is an impressive achievement, in one year Core Design has managed to improve on the original in almost every way and create an all time classic. Not only is it one of the best games in the original Tomb Raider series, it’s one of the best games on the original PlayStation.
If you’re a fan of Tomb Raider, Lara Croft or action adventure games, it’s a must play!

First off, keep in mind that this game is 19 years old and will require some minor tweaking if you want it to look at least semi-decent. I absolutely don't recommend playing it as is, it looks really bad. Download and install the widescreen patch
first, then download this patch if the game displays a Windows border in fullscreen mode
. The cutscenes are interlaced and look awful, but I remember them looking just as bad back in 1997.
Now you're all set to play what many consider to be the best Tomb Raider game ever made. Compared to its predecessor, Tomb Raider 2 is much more action oriented. Personally I always liked this game more than the original, even if the combat is still the same lackluster "run around like a headless chicken while holding the Fire button" kind of thing. Other than being combat heavy, it's your standard classic Tomb Raider. Puzzles, platforming, deadly traps, mysterious artifacts, it's all there.
Even after all these years, TR2 still has a charm that cannot be matched. There's something about its low poly enemies and silence only occasionally interrupted by bursts of music that makes this game scarier than the latest photorealistic reboot.
I'm probably biased since this is a game I've completed many, many times since the 90's and I consider it to be the best game in the entire Tomb Raider franchise, but to me everything about it is perfect. Its controls are outdated but solid and you get used to them quickly. The sound design is amazing, the atmosphere creepy. The levels are huge with lots of nooks and cranies to explore and secrets to discover.
Even if you're not an old Tomb Raider fan and you've only just discovered the franchise, do yourself a favor and play this game to see how the legend started.
Oh, and whatever you do, do NOT press F12 while playing. It'll force the game into windowed mode and cutscenes will stop working. You'll then have to quit the game, go back to Steam and change the game settings back to fullscreen.

Graphics wise the game is great, unlike minecraft that is still stuck in dev graphics because notch is incompetent, Minimum is deliberately minimalistically styled. This game is Asian GTA. If you like GTA or Saints Row you should definitely buy this game. Among the game's many positives are: Hong Kong culture, Triad culture, a great variety of soundtrack, a focus on martial arts instead of just shooting up everything, and an amazing story. The tension in the story comes from Wei Shen's equivocal position between being an undercover cop, and being a rogue who has a personal vendetta to dominate Hong Kong's underworld.
There are a few frustrating things about the game. If you're playing the PC version, the menus feel a bit laggy, and there are a couple of missions where counterattacks just do not register consistently (Death by a Thousand Cuts). Read the YouTube comments on this mission for hilarity. Another bug is when you throw a knife at someone, and it bounces off of them at high speed and instantly kills you (even from full health).
If there is one piece of advice I can give you, it is to look up what the fastest vehicles are for each type of race and to buy them, because some races are absolutely impossible to win without the right vehicle (try winning a B-class race with the HKPD SUV -- use the Terre GT instead) . In the races, the computer-controlled drivers will often ram you at the start (asian drivers), and if you find yourself being overtaken on a straightaway it's because you have an underpowered vehicle.
Another tip is to use the uniform that gives double cop XP for all of the missions that are colored blue. Even without the uniform, it is easiest to max out cop xp for the bonuses, almost as easy to max out face xp, and very difficult to max out Triad XP.
Other than trying to win races without buying the fastest vehicles, and the sometimes inconsistent fighting mechanics (laggy registers on counterattack timings), this game truly has an amazing story that should not be missed by anyone who is a fan of the open world GTA style games. Buy Asian GTA.

Note that this is for the base game, not the game plus expansion.
Pros: Loads of content, loads of stuff to do.  Easy to get into multiplayer content, incentives for veterans to help rookies out, storyline quests progress your levels quite efficiently.  Interesting crafting mechanic, no-fuss travel, lush scenery and classic Final Fantasy aesthetics.  Loads of punny quest titles and memes hidden throughout.  A marriage mechanic that does not restrict (or even ask questions about) gender combinations.  Multi-rider mounts so you can haul your friends around.  Tons of quests and collections, a completionist's dream.
Cons: Extremely technical, precise, minmax-y and a lot of poor communication, both between the game and the player and between player and player.  Terribad voice acting, overly flowery and verbose script, a plot that is hamfistedly dramatic and full of predictable and frustrating tropes, ugly "basic" gear practically until max level with few to no alternate options.  Gear-gated content and rng-based gear acquisition (this is a con, to me, take that as you will.).  Story quests force you to solo content, even in a game where no class is built to safely run solo.  Passive-aggressive elitism in the community.
I ran out of game time, and I won't be renewing it.  This game is not for gamers who play games to have fun.   This is an MMORPG that is designed for people who feel good about themselves by getting very good at, or completing, extremely difficult or complicated content.   I'm not what one calls a "hardcore gamer" and thus the restrictive, overly specific Holy Trinity of RPGs gameplay left me feeling drained more than refreshed.  After failing a solo story quest duty five times in a row, and finding that I was doing everything right, I just simply should've gotten hit less, I decided I wasn't the kind of player Square-Enix had in mind when developing this game.
I'm told Heavensward is much better story and much nicer mechanics, but if you can't even make it to the Heavensward  expansion's content, which begins only after you've completed your entire A Realm Reborn story quest, it's not worth even the cost of the base game.  I'm not going to muddle through a difficult, unsatisfying and frustrating game just in the hopes that I can pay more money to see if the expansion is more to my liking.
I game to have fun, not to hate myself.

Concept: Play as Red, a woman who wields a powerful weapon called the Transistor in order to purge the Process.
Graphics: The visuals are breath taking; all the levels are hand-drawn masterpieces, and the character designs are simple but memorable.
Sound: I found the soundtrack to be forgettable, but the opening theme was catchy. What little voice acting that is provided is superb.
Game Play: Transistor can be played in real time or paused at anytime to plan out your every move. Every function in the game can be augmented with any other function to create interesting and hilarious combinations, and experimentation is highly suggested. The game scales nicely, and no battle I encountered seemed overly difficult or too easy.
Entertainment: This game is incredibly short; most players complete their first play through in 6-10 hours, but every moment feels masterfully crafted. Nothing about this game feels tacked on, padded, or repetitive.
Replay Value: Transistor features a multiple challenge rooms and a new game plus.

Hello, reader. Different folks read different reviews based on which ones have the most thumbs up, thumbs down, or even only the positives, or only the negatives...and some folks try to read as many as they can, regardless of rating or positive/negative opinion of the game, hoping to figure out if it's right for them before purchasing. For Hero Defense, I would specifically encourage you to look at what almost everyone agrees on, whether positive or negative:
.
This is a competent tower defense with a nice visual aesthetic, some alright gameplay, and a corny plot (those can be fun in games). However, upgrading your weapons and your heroes requires a very large amount of runes, gold, and experience, which requires playing the same levels many, many times. The positive reviews and negative reviews will both quite frequently point out that there is a grind, and I will say that it is a very prominent part of the game.
The grind in the game both looks and feels to me like a mobile free-to-play game at times, which I found very disconcerting, personally. There are no purchases in this game using real money as of right now, but it has a grind reminiscent of a "freemium" game, with little stars filling in next to each level as you complete different difficulties, and a second currency (runestones) which you can buy with the less-useful and more plentiful currency (gold). Character progress stagnates without these resources to increase XP gains, weapon damage bonuses, unlock more equippable bonuses, etc.
If even the slightest sensation of a game feeling like a freemium game turns you off on a game, then Hero Defense is not for you, as was the case for me. If you love the feeling of a freemium game without spending real money and dealing with the grind that entails, then Hero Defense might be something you would enjoy if you like the other aspects of the game.

OF COURSE I locked the butler inside the walk-in freezer. Who hasn't?! Now that we've dealt with that, let's see what we have here.
Let me get this over with quickly and painlessly:
- yes, the graphics and animations and whatnot are VERY dated and don't play along well with modern resolutions. The game, however, runs well enough for me, and that's all I care about (but I'm very forgiving in terms of gfx and resolution).
- the platforming and puzzles are awesome and in my opinion, that's what the game is about. This game is pretty slow and methodic and if you want to find all the secrets, items, and explore every nook and cranny in general, then this is your cup of tea. The environments are varied, the gameplay never gets stale although some levels (like the motherfreakin' sunken ship) drag on for a bit too long.
- the combat, however, is A-T-R-O-C-I-O-U-S. Whoever thought this game needed shooting should jump into a spike pit, seriously, I canNOT stress enough how clunky, unfair, cheap and absolutely unnecessary this aspect is. Let me give you an example. You can take around 10 shots before you drop dead. The bad guys in the later levels need 2 to 3 GRENADE SHOTS. Let that sink in. I don't care if it's "just a game", no videogame iteration of a human grunt-type enemy should be able to withstand three grenades to the noggin.
That said, for me, the platforming outweighs the terrible combat just enough to get a "Recommend" from me. Oh, and definitely get during a sale, not worth full price at any rate.
TL;DR version: graphics/presentation meh, platforming/puzzles BIG thumbs up, combat: NO, NO, NO, NO, NO!

Classic Tomb Raider games have pretty much disappeared from the collective consciousness and it's a damn shame, because more games started here than just Uncharted. Contrary to popular belief, Tomb Raider 2 aged like fine wine.
From the perspective of level design philosophy, this is straight up Dark Souls. Locales vary greatly, rooms and corridors intertwine, and dread is trying to overcome you every step of the way. Even though every environment is blocky, the blocks are layered and textured in such a way that every level feels like an environment first, and a video game level second.
People will say that controls in classic TR games are clunky, but they are actually the antithesis of clunky. They are precise and deliberate, is what they are. Somewhat obtuse and with a learning curve, but not clunky. If you endure, you will be flipping, jump-rolling and running jump grabbing without a second thought.
Enjoy the fact that the controls are easy to map to a controller, and that the PC version of the game allows you to savestate, because most things in this game are lethal. But it really makes you soak it all in, much like Dark Souls does. Sometimes, you just have to slowly walk to the edge of a platform to make a jump. And the jump is missable. You literally earn every jump you make. Nothing ever railroads you or rushes you forward.
I have played TR2 immediately after finishing Uncharted 2 for the first time, and there is just no comparison. TR may have inspired Uncharted's design, but there is really next to nothing left of it anymore.
I don't understand how they managed to make a 3D game this good back in 1997.

[BRIEF]- Minimum is a great, fast-paced, well-rounded 3rd person shooter. I have recommended this game to several of my friends. This is a cheap shooter game that stands out from other games such as CoD and BF simply because it's a geometric-like game. A game can have blocks without being compared to Minecraft, so let it go. The developers chose to do this sort of art style most likely for two common reasons: They wanted to stand out and they wanted to spend more time on the engine. The game runs very well on my computer, the servers are 90% reliable, and there are many more features that are currently being implemeted in the game.
[MICROTRANSACTIONS]- I'm sick of them, you're sick of them, he's sick of them.. who isn't? The developers have cut the price of the game from $20 to $10. They need the extra cash. At the time of me writing this review, they are purely cosmetic aswell. Each "cosmetic" item in this shop has an equivalent that can be obtained by playing the game.
[GAMEPLAY]- I love this game. It runs so smoothly! I was amazed that the game was actually exactly how the trailer showed. I have enjoyed a couple of hours playing this game and I play on spending many more. It's like a mixture of Call of Duty, Titan Fall, and League of Legends.
[GRAPHICS]- The game is pretty. It's not meant to have top-notch graphics, the developers wanted to make a fun game that's really cheap and can run on computers that are in mint-condition.
[IMPROVEMENTS AND SUGGESTIONS]- Some weapons are clearly better than others. Anyone that has played Minimum for at least 15 minutes can honestly say that the swords are too op. I believe that swords should be at least half of the power that they currently have. I have purchased the grenade launcher and the fork launcher, I believe that the launchers should get at least a 25% speed buff because anyone with the starter weapons can kill you more efficiently. To get a kill with these weapons, you need to basically steal someone else's kill! I feel awful doing it so I stick to starter weapons most of the time.
[MOST IMPORTANT SUGGESTION]- If I had to choose one thing, I would ask if the drops from players can have a 3-5 second shield on them for the killer because figuratively speaking, 75% of the time some dude with a sword rushes my kill and takes the drops.
[ENDING THOUGHT]- In conclusion, I would highly recommend this game to anyone who likes games such as Dota, League of Legends, Call of Duty, Battlefield, and Gears of War.

I had high hopes for this game, as I loved the concept and MOST of the execution of the flash game, though not the flash game itself for reasons I will discuss shortly. I was hoping that this fixed the biggest issue I had with the flash game, but it appears not to have. My issue is simple: The game wants you to win the way the developers want you to win. That doesn't sound so bad, but experimentation is almost DISCOURAGED unless it's to find the way the developer wants you to win. That would be passable if the iteration time wasn't so LONG. Even on maximum speed, this is a SLOW game. It's ridiculous. Such a good concept, so bad in practice. If you get spotted, you're pretty much screwed too, unless you kill EVERYONE, because developing a cure is easy and screws you so hard that an industrial power drill made to drill through hardened steel couldn't do it faster.
On top of that, to get ANYTHING done you need to beat the game several times. You unlock genes randomly, you unlock new pathogens in a linear fashion, proceeding from one to the next to the next... Winning is more about beating the system, rather than working with the system for a solution you like. The guides I've seen and my own experience is that the only way to win is to infect EVERYBODY undetected, then stockpile points until you've got a completely harmless pathogen turning into a disease more deadly than nuclear bombs fast enough to make Sonic blush.
On top of that, they frontload you with NO information and don't even HAVE a tutorial beyond popups explaining SOME of the UI, just a "How to Play" hidden under the Escape menu with extremely unhelpful information.
TL;DR: Iteration time too long, solutions MIGHT number more than 1 for any given pathogen (discounting minor differences), pathogen solutions nearly identical in approach, tutorial effectively non-existant, being cured is INSANELY easy and, to top it off, the majority of symptoms are only useful as paving stones to others. 2/5, at least it's not broken, but that's about all I like about the game itself.

*This is my first proper review*
Final Fantasy XIV is something that will change your point of view on MMORPGs -- it will broaden your vision. This is something I only came to realize recently, from being away from the game for a while. You'll just want back, because you're addicted.
FFXIV is simply put LOVE. The amazing soundtracks, the stunning visuals, the challenging combat... it's all there, and it's all in harmony. Nothing fights with each other.
Pros:
-- the stunning visuals (even on low-end PCs the game looks beautiful. thank you cross-platform)
-- the amazing music. you'll find yourself listening to it and being sucked into it (it might get boring though, if you spam a specific dungeon many times *I just listen to music while raiding*)
-- the world. it's beautiful.
-- challenging combat system (I say challenging because of complex skill rotations - especially on DPS classes. and all those damned AOEs) that will not make you bored. the fights require your unshaken, full attention (unless you're a healer in a 4-man dungeon...))
-- great variety of mounts and cosmetics
-- no p2w in sight.
-- friendly community, no matter where you are.
-- newbie friendly. it doesn't matter if this is your first MMORPG or 10th, you'll learn your way within the game.
-- really well thought out gathering and crafting system that works and gets you the gil (in-game currency).
-- the game's rich main story will break your heart. the amazing, funny side story quests won't leave you bored either.
-- the game is friendly towards different players. casual? you got it. medcore? you got it. hardcore? you got it. PVP? you got it!
Cons:
-- the dungeons' replayability can get dull over time. leveling up your sixth class and lashing out at the possible newbies in your party? that's a no-no, no matter how annoyed you are. you were once at similar situations too. you were, and still are, learning.
-- silly run from point A to point B, then back to point A and through point C to point D just to turn in the quest at point B-quests are somewhat annoying if you are looking forward to progress in the game.
-- character creation lacks in not letting you to edit more than the face and boobs (and tail). you can still create very unique characters, though personally I am not a fan of skinny legs. damn japanese.
-- maps are locked. as in, you cannot jump off the ledge of a cliff. there's an invisible wall (though there are some secrets...)
-- gilspammers (goldsellers) and the very laid-back measurements taken to counter them.
Overall, the game is perfect even with its imperfections. The devs are very hard working and as the game has not been around for very long -it just recently got its first expansion pack- I think they deserve a round of applause.
Get the game and get sucked in it. It's well worth its monthly fee and I will continue playing this masterpiece.
It's unique and it will go a long way.

This is a passport stamping simulator, and much more. The game starts off simple: You play as a passport inspector in a 1984-esque totalitarian country, deciding who to allow into the country, with a single stamp. As the game progresses, more and more odious regulations are added, making your job harder over time. At one point I had to inspect FIVE different documents just to decide whether that 80-year old bearded grandpa was a smuggler or not (he was). Right, and there's rents to pay and family members to feed at the end of each day. Tough choices are to be made every day - detain a poor sod for that extra 5 dollars in bribes, or let your son starve for a day. Fail to earn enough money over time, and your family starves to death and its game over.
The graphics, though rudimentary at first glance, as well as the simple 8-bit music perfectly complement the dystopic atmosphere of the game.
But the beauty of this game lies in its masterful storytelling. Through the stamping of passports and little dialogues between characters, you begin to learn more about the world of the inspector; the stories of the characters that pass through your passport booth (including the likeable/destestable smuggler Mr Jorji), as well as the truth of the country he lives in. Between the geopolitical tensions between Arsotka and its neighbours, the terrifying inspector from the "Ministry of Information" and a border guard's long-lost love, the game draws you in with its simple, yet riveting storytelling.
Glory to Arsotska.
This game is a great detective game, well worth the money.

A solidly made game that's incredibly unique. Everything about this game is so different than other games I've played. I played Bastion and thought this might be similar because it had a very similar POV, but the game is completely different.
Good:
- Refreshing setting and gameplay.
- Everything in this game feels like it's of high quality. Art direction, voice acting, music.
- Gameplay is very well done. The mechanics feel like they're finely tuned and well thought out. To summarize, the game revolves around these powers you can equip your character with. You can equip them 3 ways:
1) As a direct attack that you use by pressing a button.
2) As a modification to a direct attack (see 1.)
3) As a passive ability.
Every power you get has a distinct behavior/properties. Your powers do not get upgraded, you simply gain various different ones. The way you equip these changes the way you fight. For instance, you can equip a power that pierces enemies in a straight line. You can equip another power to make the line split into 3 instead, each doing less damage individually, but more damage combined. This now forces you to get closer to enemies with your attacks to do maximum damage, and changes the way you position yourself in combat. Instead of trying to line up the enemies, you try to get them all in front of you. To aid this you can equip a power that will pull enemies into a specific area. There are TONS of combinations like these, producing various strategies.
What's more the game actively encourages you to implement new strategies in quite a few ways without flat out telling you. One of the ways is that by losing in combat, the powers you're using become unavailable for some time. This means that you'll need to re-equip some other powers and rework your strategy. Another way is the game has these "challenge" maps where you can test yourself. You are put in a room with enemies and forced to use preselected abilities. And of course, there are a good variation of enemies that force you to fight certain ways.
I really enjoy how succinct the game can be. There are no stats. There are no powers you have that eclipse each other. They are all completely separate and have their own use cases. It's really quite brilliant.
- Customizable difficulty. This is something I would really like to see more games adopt. The only game I know that does this is Bastion, which is made by the same developers. Difficulty is managed by equipping things called limiters, which have various effects on gameplay such as limiting how many powers you can equip, or producing a shield on the weaker enemies. These do much more than just giving enemies more health or having them deal more damage.
Not so good:
- The story can get a little muddled in lingo. There's a lot of talking that sounds natural to this world, but doesn't always explain what they're talking about. It can make the story a little difficult to follow at times, but you can still get the general idea of what's happening.
This game is great. If you're looking for to play a unique game that's solid all around, play this.

Tomb Raider 2 is undoubtedly the best old game of the Tomb Raider franchise done. The first game was revolutionary but overly "square", and Tomb Raider 3 had better graphics, but it was very difficult and "more of the same". Tomb Raider 2 got the middle ground: maintained the essence of the first game with improvements in graphics and gameplay, but without being confused, "more of the same" and unnecessarily difficult as the third game. In short, Tomb Raider 2 bordered on perfection. While Tomb 1 is visually dark and claustrophobic, the phases of Tomb 2 are more colorful, biggest and very memorable. The four phases of the wreck of Maria Doria are by far my favorite phases of all Tomb Raider serie, for its immersive atmosphere, symbolically and literally. Novice players of this new generation will certainly face major difficulties with the game controls, which are well archaic. No movement is automatic or fluid: from one platform to another, all the leaps and Lara moves must be calculated accurately by the player himself; otherwise it's instant death. The good news is what the PC version is possible to save the game any time you want.

This game is a classic. It was one of the games that helped spawn the mighty fandom of the Tomb Raider franchise. It's graphics were likely pretty good for the time, but I only played it a few years later, and I still loved it. The water is particularly impressive considering it was released in 1997. However, I can't recommend buying this. The reason why is that it appears they did nothing, or next to nothing, to make it more capable of running on modern machines. When I first launched it, the setup appeared behind the main window, so I couldn't edit it. I didn't even know it was supposed to appear, so I just clicked return, and the game loaded up, with most of the right side black, and part of the left side cut off. I checked for settings, to no avail. Like a few extremely old games, the video setup is separate from the game (and not exactly intuitive to access from within Steam). Opening it, I wasn't able to change the full screen resolution from 640x480 for some reason. After disabling my second monitor, and setting my main monitor to 800x600 (the smallest resolution where I could still see the apply button), I managed to get the game to appear correctly. A bit of a hassle to say the least. I also installed the widescreen patch. After restarting to re-enable my second monitor, I then tried it in windowed mode. Steam absolutely will not launch it in windowed mode. I had to open it from the exe. It was a travesty. It kept switching the resolution to 640x480 despite being in windowed mode, and was impossible to play. But, somehow, after that, I restarted, and tried it again from steam, and it magically just worked, in full screen mode, without disabling my second monitor. It was still in 640x480 unfortunately, but there was no black bar on one side, and it appeared correctly. I played it for a few minutes before my computer switched to another application on it's own, because the standard keys are set for alt to be the jump key.
So, I will play through this game once more, and keep it on my Steam to occasionally play, but I really don't suggest anyone else buys it. They didn't do a thing to try to remove any bugs or anything from what I can tell. They simply took the old retail version and packaged it for steam. Frankly, I would be embarrassed if I worked for them. They should either hand the code to some of their team to squash some bugs occasionally, and clean up the code, or open source it, so maybe someone out there somewhere will choose to clean up the code for them. This game is barely playable on a modern machine. I'm likely gonna have to set up a virtual machine just to play this and a few other old games giving me trouble.

Your goal is to protect your titan while trying to destroy your opponents and their titan, but the strategy pretty much always boils down to a free-for-all. I was getting waxed over and over again. I was just running around most of the time hoping for a kill and would suddenly find myself sliced in half by a high level player with a lightsaber katana. I really, really REALLY want to like this game, but I have doubts that there will be a player base willing to stick around long enough for the game to reach its potential.

An interesting little game that's one part skeeball, one part tower defense, and one part that age old joy of rolling down a hill as a kid. Rock of Ages is a nice pickup on sale to spend a few hours on.
The main gameplay is split into two sections: a 20-30 second phase where you place obstacles onto your opponents course (a mirror of your own) and then a phase where you control your rock as it rolls through a course, avoiding stage obstacles as well as any your opponent may have placed. At the end of the course is a castle gate, which you must smash into 3-5 times in order to break it open and defeat your opponent.
The gameplay depth comes from your rock's health, which crumbles as it takes damage, reducing it's size and power. As a  mostly undamaged rock can take down a gate in 3 rounds, but a damaged rock guarantees at least a 4th attempt. Thus you must place your obstacles in the best positions to slow and damage your opponent, while you attempt to avoid the same fate. The obstacles come in three tiers of different types, ranging from walls and ballistae to fans and income generating mines.  Choosing whether to take the damage to permanently remove an opponents obstacle or try to avoid it on each of your runs makes for interesting choices. There are also one use ball power-ups that can be purchased instead of obstacles, giving you some extra durability, power, or mobility for that round.
There are a few issues however: the momentum physics can lead to some obstacle areas entirely pointless, the morbid humor in the single player cutscenes is largely hit-or-miss, and the music ranges from pleasant to forgettable.
All in all, a game worth a fair few afternoons spent on the campaign or with a friend. Bonus points for having a story inspired by Sisyphus.
Note: this game was purchased by me for $2.00 during a sale.

Great idea, some poor design decisions really hinder this game though
Notably,
1.  Going up the stairs after going down is very frustrating, you move at a snails pace, I thought maybe this was a decision but I'm leaning more towards it's something in the character controller as it gives that "pushing through" feeling that box colliders in Unity will often give if the controller isn't accounting for something.  Maybe not casting enough rays or something, allowing the character's collider to move into the surfaces temporarily and move through like in "sludge"
2.  The sound of "errrrt" when you enter a correct password is initially... confusing.  This seems like the noise it should make when you incorrectly enter something, as incorrectly entering something yields no noise.

However I noticed that some of these samples gave a clicking/popping sound when repeating.  That's a sign of the sample not being perfectly seamless or not restarting at the proper point (if it is)

Moving slowly by it felt painful wearing headphones.  I am leaning both ways on this one.  For someone who is into this style of game I'd tell them to play through it as it gives insight into a few great things to do in this genre, but there's also a few things that very much bothered me.  For someone new to the genre I would definitely not recommend this, as I feel it could leave a sour taste in their mouth. Let me start by saying I have this game on my Android tablet, but I couldn't resist picking up the PC version at a discount during Summer Sale. I'm glad I did.
First of all, this isn't just a puzzle game. There's an entire narrative going on here that involves the ancient art of alchemy and the pursuit of the "aether," the fifth and final element that would unlock the secrets of the universe. This is real stuff, history-wise -- intellectual heavyweights like Plato and Isaac Newton used the concept to explain things they didn't understand about stars, planets, space and even the realm of the supernatural. To physicists and philosophers in antiquity, the aether couldn't be directly observed, but revealed itself in the forces of gravity and light.
The ornate boxes in the room are left there for you by an alchemist on the precipice of discovering the secrets of the aether. But he won't share his hard-won knowledge with just anyone, and as he explains, the devilishly clever mechanisms safeguard the alchemist's secrets "from lesser minds." Fortunately, you're one of the enlightened, and the secrets of the boxes will reveal themselves to you if you open your mind and look at things from a different perspective. (Often, that's literal -- the answers to some clues will not be apparent until you look at a particular mechanism or clue from all angles.)
It doesn't take long to realize the alchemist you're trailing is losing his grip on sanity. One of the impressive things about the game is that you not only recognize his descent into madness through the notes he leaves behind, but also by the increasingly bizarre and obtuse challenges he leaves for you.
So, is there anything different about The Room on PC?
Yes indeed. I was pleasantly surprised to find out that this is a port that gives a nice array of options, and the difference in visuals is dramatic compared to earlier versions of the game on Android and iOS. The lockboxes look magnificent, with ultra-high resolution textures and new detail worked into their surfaces, nooks and crannies. There was obviously work put into making this game look fantastic for PCs, and I appreciate any developer who respects the PC gaming community instead of taking the easy route and doing a straight port without improvements.
If you haven't played The Room, you're really missing out. I wholeheartedly recommend this game.

Average game.
Devs took TD idea and replaced towers with heroes. If there are usually a lot of towers in other TD games, there you can find only 5. Only 5, really? Yeah, it's the main game idea. You need to use heroes to defeat enemies. Every hero is strong against special type of monsters; the guy with arbalet kills vampires in a couple of shots, the old mage with holy water wipes out a pack of skeletons.
There is a city, where you can power up your heroes. You can learn skill for each of them. Tree skill is small, but anyway it's interesting to choose which skill you will learn right now.
Also, there is rune system. You can put different runes into hero's weapon and when you charge him (upgrade) in the battle, he will receive this bonus. For example, there are damage runes, range runes and more interesting tunes, like "75% change to attack with extra projectile".
So, you pass a mission, go to the town, unlock new heroes/buildings, upgrade your heroes and start new mission. Easy to understand.
What I like
- Awesome 2d art
- Fresh gameplay idea
- Easy to undestand
- Good voice acting
- Tree skill for every hero
What I didn't like
- There are only 5 towers/units. It's a really small amount. Also, you summon them all in every battle, so every mission you play with the same towers.. It's quite boring.
- The TD game is supposed to be strategy game. You need to think about tactic, find the best spots for towers and etc. The main part of gameplay of this game is relocating these 5 towers. When a wave starts you move them to a start point, some of them pass through, you move heroes to the end point. When new wave starts, enemies go on another road, you need to move heroes there. Repeat these actions X times (x - number of waves in the mission) to complete the level.
- The gameplay is the same in all missions. Yeah, there are different roads, some bosses come, and there are shrines for heroes. But, you play the same mission exactly is previous. I would like to see more diversity in enemies, more special skills, something new, which could let me give a desire to continue the game.
- Story is boring. Characters are usual. Dialogues bring nothing interesting to the game.
- Game requires playing previous stages to unlock new ones. I got stuck 3 times because of it. I couldn't finish the game, because i was forced to replay 6 stages to unlock the final mission. But I didn't want to do that.
- I would like to see active heroes’ skills. It's really boring when you can only move them around the map and upgrading them. For example, KR series has 2 active spells, meteor shower and reinforcements. It's really enjoyable to use them. There are no such spells.
- Rune system reminds me free-to-play mobile games. Grind gold, buy runes, combine runes to get stronger one. Repeat. I think, it wasn't a good idea to put this mechanic in PC game. Also, when you make an upgrade you don't feel what your hero become stronger. You start with "+10% damage rune". Really? The price of upgrading is equal to price of new hero. So, it's better to summon heroes instead of upgrading them.
- There are no numbers. You can't see amount of health of monsters, you can't find how much extra damage hero does. It's a bad for mw. I would like to see more information. It's an important part of a strategy game, which helps players to find the best tactic.
So, why have I given this game a positive review, if there are so many minuses? I have almost finished the game.  I suppose, if you play the game and could complete it, it can't be a bad game. The 15$ price tag is too high, I am sure. But i got this game with 70% discount, and this price is fair.
P.S. I hope, devs will notice bad design decisions and make the next game more interesting. Because, the main idea is good, but the final result is really average.

Here is an example, the runes you have to grind for are extremely limited in different types, there are only a handlful of them, and better ones are only a slight increase over the previous one. I don't mind the slight increase part, but they really need to give you more options of the type of runes you can choose from.
More choice means more strategic depth rather then pigeonholing you in to the same playstyle for just about every map. This is a game that would shine if it had 20-30 heroes and you had to pick and choose the type of combination you wanted to bring with you. Hero Defense is a Tower Defense with movable and upgradable heroes for Towers. You can modify the heroes by applying different quality and type of runes you earn through playing. My gripe is, and it may be silly to some, you don't have access to all your heroes right away... just like you don't have access to all the towers on level one of most TD games. The Co-Op is fun, but you can only play endless, co-op campaign would be awesome. It takes some time to unlock all the stuff you need to fully enjoy the game, but in my time with it, it's very fun.

Do I recommend this game? Well...
What can I say about Eryi's Action that hasn't been said already? No idea, but I can tell you that this game will likely make you hate everyone around you. Go on.
Play it.
Play it for an hour. Play it for one hour and try to stop playing. You can't. You'll keep playing because this innate arrogance inside you will not let you give it. It will not let you believe that you are a creature that exists in this world that is incapable of surpassing the agonizingly cruel traps and hazards within this sickeningly adorable game. You will continue to play. You will play past your limitations.
You will play, and you will die, and you will die and die and die. And you will keep playing.
Try to stop though, and look around yourself briefly. You might not notice it at first but your reality has changed. Nothing is how it once was. Birds no longer chirp, the sun has lost some of it's glow, your walls seem to sweat with a dreadful dew, and the faces of those around you seem to sag with a pulpy gloom, like bubble wrap. You want to pop every single bubble wrap face you see, except the bubbles are filled with habanero sauce, that spits into your eyes as you pop them so it only enrages you more.
You will hate everyone you ever met and will meet because of this game. And yet you will find it within you somehow to continue to play this hellborn game.
So do I recommend this game?
Yes.
Yes I do. Because I refuse to be the only one who is overcome by the grueling hatred for all life. I refuse to let you not share in this misery. Play it. Now.

As much as I want to like Transistor -- and I really, really wanted to like it -- it just fails on so many levels.
The story is an incoherent mess. The gameplay is way too short. The boss battles are so few and far between (and feel like some were just dropped entirely to get the game shipped). The turn based combat system can be overly clunky at times. There is no tutorial or explanation for many things. The save points are in very weird places, often requiring you to re-watch cinematics if you lose. Combat becomes overly repetitive with the same choices being the best in almost every situation (even with every Limiter on). And so much more.
I wanted to love this game like I love Bastion. The art, visuals, music, and voice acting are top notch. Heck, even the attacks and combat systems are neat (despite being a bit clunky). But there are just so many little issues that makes the game average at best and definitely not worth the overall cost.
If you can pick up the game for under $5 I'd recommend checking it out, but otherwise it is best to just look at the beauty of the game from afar.

This brings back memories!
When I was a child this game's difficulty scared the @#$% out of me. It's so dark and unforgiving.
I was all like: "Oh no! I'm so short on medpacks! I might get stuck with low health and never be able to complete this godforsaken level with all those bad guys shooting at me!" or "Oh no! I'm trapped in a scrapheap of rusty metal which sunk 40 fathoms below sea level! (I don't even understand how mutch that is but I guess that must be very very deep since I can't see any sunlight from here.) The water is leaking inside and there are sharks all around me! How the hell am I supposed to get out of here alive?" or "Oh no! Those baddies on machinegunned snowmobiles are shooting me to death and I can't do anything about it!". Obviously it's my favorite amongst the first six Tomb Raider games.
What a badass woman! A female equivalent of Chuck Norris!
However the game can be so mutch better if somebody sits down and makes a couple of changes to the engine (or releases the engine as open source like idSoftware does it with its games).
1. The stretching for aspect ratios other than 4:3 needs to be fixed. It makes the main character look like Gabe Newell on new widescreen monitors.
2. The processing power of GPUs increased by several orders of magnitude in comparison to 1997. Who needs distant objects to be turned black and/or thrown out completely in order to save computational complexity nowdays?
3. Z-Buffer is buggy. By turning it on and off you just select between different types of glitches. With it there is Z-fighting. Without it some objects further away appear in front of objects that are closer. Both was forgivable back in 1997, but not in 2016.
4. I reccomend playing this game with bilinear filtering disbled. Back then textures were VERY low-res and more like something we call pixel art nowdays. Bilinear filtering is a good idea for the new games with highres-textures, but in Tomb Raider 2 it messes up that nice pixel art by making it look smooth and ugly. Like smeared out oil paintings.

Minimum is a pretty fun third person shooter relying on twitch based shooting mechanics similar to those of old school classics such as Quake and Unreal Tournament.
It's main draw is the Titan Mode which is a very original and involved game mode that somehow manages to have a high scope, but keep the combat tight. Players have to escort giant titans to the enemy base while destroying the enemy titan. If both titans are destroyed, neutral creeps are spawned and must be killed to collect powerups for your titan. After a set time the titans (now powered up based on how each team did in the previous phase) will fight it out again. Titans are stopped by walls which only the titan can damage. Once gone however they are gone permanently, making them feel somewhat like the turrets in Mobas.
Mid match progression, much like that of mobas such as League of Legends means that battles will get more intense as the game goes on. However this may cause a balancing issue with one team levelling weapons and armor at a faster rate early on, dominating the rest of the match. This has both postitive and negative side effects. Unfortunately this can result in public matches being very frustrating if you get a bad team and get completely dominated, but in more competitive matches with friends to communicate with, it means that teamwork is far more valuable. A fully powered weapon is lost on death, so it only takes a single kill to bring your opponent back to your level. And creeps also give materials to upgrade armor so it is possible to strategically avoid combat and 'farm' creeps to upgrade armor.
Weapon balance is an odd beast, as most weapons take quite a few shots to kill, whereas swords are nearly instant kills. This may result in melee seeming over powered, and certainly it can be frustrating to have someone unexpectedly dash into you with a sword and kill you when you thought you where in control of the battle, or get stabbed from behind, but due to the high mobility of the characters there are plenty of ways to counter swords.
The game is missing many features but is already a very complete experience, and will only get better.

Minimum is a neat little game with a nice art style and fast paced fun multiplayer, that is not to say, however that it is without problems. Although there is a nice variety of choice for melee and ranged weapons, it's only once you begin to observe the interaction through playing the game that you start to notice the problems with balance.
Firstly, although the swords are a nice edition it makes the gameplay in multiplayer somewhat frustrating as there is little balance of ability to defer a sword attack if you have a ranged weapon, especially with people spamming the jump button every second (I will return to this point). The problem you get particularly with this is that you will damage a sword wielder to close to their death but with all the hopping around they do, ultimately they will run around an object that covers them before running back out with recovered health and quickly spamming to kill you.
The second major problem stems from some of the purchased armour which to an extent makes parts of this game "Pay to win" wherein I have seen people buying outfits to make them jump higher over and around players with large weapons making them very hard to hit and avoid their attacks due to their ability to jump far higher than any other average player, this is a serious problem in terms of combat balance in multiplayer as it means that not only can they jump above you and kill you faster, but it also means that they can escape to areas you would not be able to access as easily yourself without paying for the same privelege of armour.
Bar this the gameplay is very fun and engaging and there is a lot of potential for great things once player balance is focussed on a little more.

The game revolves around a concept that you don't see often within puzzle games. The idea that you have something that has other facets inside hidden within layers of a box that unlock secrets. What might appear as a plain box with a few panels and holes turns into a box full of trinkets, keys, notes, storage compartments, etc. The more you find, the more you unlock within the boxes. This is a fun game, nice presentation. It reminds me a lot of Defender's Quest, which is a pretty big complement. Basically, if you took Defender's Quest, bumped up the graphics (by a lot), and gave it a Halloween vibe, you'd just about have this game. The "towers" you get are heroes, and you only get the ones that come with the game. Instead of placing towers you move your heroes around, which gives you lots to do during each map. You also get upgrades in the form of skill unlocks, runes to add to your weapon, the weapons themselves, and various buildings in your town that, when upgraded, give you bonuses.
The game isn't easy. I'm not the best gamer in the world but not the worst, and if you just play straight through each map on easy, you'll eventually hit a wall. To get over it, you have to go back and play previous maps on higher difficulties, or in challenge mode, to earn gold, runes, and XP.
The game has personality, the different characters have dialog they speak during missions, and there's a bit of a story there.
There are a few things I think they could have done a bit better. Choosing maps requires you to scroll through a horizontal list, which is a little clunky compared to just clicking on a map. Also, the camera is zoomed in a bit on maps, requiring you to scroll around to move your heroes where you want them. This wouldn't be so bad except scrolling is either done with mousing to the edge of the screen or using the arrow keys. WASD is reserved for consumables you deploy during fights.
I haven't tried the multiplayer, but supposedly it offers both co-op and PVP. I can't speak on it since I don't know how it works, but it's there.
All in all though, this is a pretty cool twist on the tower defense genre. The Halloween vibe is awesome if you're into that sort of thing, and I am.

I had high expectations for Transistor, following the success of Bastion. Sadly, Transistor doesn't quite live up to them. That's not to say Transistor is a bad game. It just doesn't surpass Bastion. The story is fine: light, not too complicated--fitting for as short as the game is, similar to Bastion's even (Kudos for that ending though). The art style is beautiful, unique; again, similar to Bastion in that regard. Music is great; fitting for the cyberpunk world.
Where Transistor fails is combat. Hybrid turned-based combat is a mess. Other than the final boss, combat resolves to nothing more than buttom mashing one ability in real-time. Using turned-based attacks, though more focused, has too much of a cooldown, allowing enemies to easily overwhelm. 'Spray-and Praying' from a distance tends to be the way to go. This is such a dissapointment, as Bastion's real-time combat was so tight.
There is one component Transistor trumps Bastion, and that's ability customization. One ability can either be used as a straight attack, modify another attack, or give an overall passive boon. This adds a great amount of depth to picking an ability loadout, and is great improvement over Bastion's static main hand/off hand.
Overall, I recommend Transistor, although it is nothing more than a pseudo-remake of Bastion. That in and of itself isn't a bad thing, just dissapointing.

From True Crime streets of Hong Kong To Sleepign Dogs.. Thier Best Decision Ever

+ Excellent graphics
+ Professional voice acting keeps cut scenes entertaining
+ Solid driving physics (not as good as GTA)
+ Many activities and collectables, but some are repetitive fillers
+/- Tricky fight mechanics make early game segments frustrating, but it does get easier as you acquire new techniques
+/- Story starts strong but runs out of fuel toward the end, Wei is an unconvincing protagonist
+/- Beautiful city filled with lots of things to do, but doesn't feel alive and real (like GTA)
- Spamming attacks and combos to slowly wear down the same crowd of bad guys (always about 10 of them, come in 4 different flavors)
- Limited gun availability/action detracts from open-world fun

I would say that Sleeping Dogs is more akin to Saints Row than GTA. The world is a beautiful and lively representation of Hong Kong, although not a recreation. Still, you always get the feeling of restriction rather than freedom. Almost every part of the world is built with a purpose in mind, for a mission, a shop, or an activity. There isn't any part of the world that is just there to add to the world, like in GTA. There's not much reason to just explore, because if you do all the activities, you'll see every set piece, and the nooks and crannies in between, because they are all filled with collectables and things to do, much like Saints Row. Nothing really wrong with that, put it makes the game world feel more like a mouse maze filled with numerous pieces of cheese.
The story starts strong, with the very intriguing prospect of playing as an undercover cop trying to bust up a Mafia operation, and builds apprehensively toward protagonist Wei being forced to make to a difficult moral decision, but in the end, uses a corrupt police boss as an easy out for what could have been a very intriguing good guy/bad guy choice for the player to have to make. Instead the story flames out into a (mostly) happily-ever-after ending that was, well, a major letdown. This is easily the worst part of the game, and a great reason why there won't be a sequel.
The combat, which has been compared to the Batman: Arkham series, is the bread and butter of this game. It can be both very satisfying and very frustrating. You're given a multitude of ways to dispose of your enemies: punch combos, throws, weapons, environmental kills, tossing them over balconies, and of course, counter-attacks, which are crucial to master early on if you are to deal with the crowds of bad guys who will surround you for most of the game. Thankfully, they tend to only attack one or two at a time, much like the movies, and once you learn when to mash the counter button, you'll be alright. After a while, even the better moves feel lame and repetitive, and you're never able to mow through the garden variety baddies even in the late game, you'll have to spam the same power moves at least 3 times to make them stay down. Ugh.
The shooting bits, which become more numerous as the game progresses, are standard cover shooting fare, and for the most part, pretty easy. Except for these certain parts, you will not carry a gun around the open world. You can, but they are not easy to aquire, so you won't be able to run about and cause havoc, or have standoffs with the cops like in GTA. I suppose that makes sense given the context of the game, but it definitely subtracts an element of fun from the game.

There are many activities and collectables that fill the game world, some fun, others repetitive, but at least you can't say there's nothing to do. I know there are differing opinions of collect-a-thons, especially in games like this that mainly focus on the action, but I like it because it's a nice incentive to go see and experience the game world, steering you towards places you might otherwise ignore. Sleeping Dogs makes it super easy, too. Putting all the collectables on the map so you won't waste one bit of extraneous time searching for them. Other activities include standard fare like racing, strongholds, assassinations, and a dull yet very appropriate karaoke activity.
8.25/10
As a fan of sandbox, GTA style games, I definitely enjoyed Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition. The story kept me going most of the way, but in the end was a bummer, and I don't think I would have sank as much time into this game had I known the writers would have taken what I felt was the lazy way out of the good cop/bad cop dichotomy that hooked me to begin with. Recommended for all Saints Row and martial arts fans.

Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn is a pay to play MMO by Square Enix.
The game looks absolutely stunnig and has a varied gameplay with about 9 classes of War or Magic and even more crafting classes and gathering classes. The game takes a weird aproach to their class-system in which you, whatever you play as, can change the current class just by switching your weapon. Also you can get a "Job" at level 30 with one of the classes of war or magic . And no you don't get to work as a cashier. With a job you can better support a party in a dungeon or raid. Also you are able to use some skills from other classes which heaviely affect your gameplay.
For instance: I play a bard which is the job of the Archer. I also played pugulist to level 42 so i could get a skill I could use for my bard.
All together is the class system pretty deep and you can do a lot of stuff with it, but on the downside, it's also pretty hard to get the hang of it.
The Story of the game just screams Final Fantasy. Won't say anything more about it just because I wasn't listening to it that much.
The visuals are astonishing. It's the best MMO I've looked at in years. The shadows look awesome and the graphics insanly good for a MMO. I may be praising it a bit to much, but compared to the basic pay-to-win MMOs it is really a lot better looking.
You can also have a lot of fun with your friends (that you maybe don't even know yet). There are a lot of emotes (like 2 pages) so you can have a great time expressing yourself. There is also a marriage system so you can even marry your loved one. All characters have a first and last name just to push the immersion a bit further. You can even pick a birthday for your character.
There are 5 races. Miqo'te a race of cat-humans, Roegadyn the pumped doods, Elezen the elves, Hyur the humans and the Lalafell (pretty much the lolitas of this game). There's also a DLC race that comes with Heavensward called Au Ra. Pretty much like the Miqo'te but with dragons.
To sum it all up, its a pretty great game. 9/10

Now that that's out of the way, enjoy your opening scene filled with you stuck in the back of a cart/ship on your way to one of Eorzea's city states, which you pick based on your starting class. Along the way, you are introduced to a bunch of nobodies who become sombodies and then nobodies again when all is said and done. If you feel attached to a particular character, get ready to hate them as soon as the voice acting starts (even japanese dub is bad). Luckily this was rectified somewhat in the HW expansion as beginning with the first quest all NPCs save for a few have new VAs' that are actually british instead of the Sam Riegel and Liam O Brian being hammered into your ear for 3/4ths of the story.
When starting out at lvl 1 you will only have 1 skill to use in combat, as you level you'll get more and more skills and eventually your class will become very complex to manage, such as the case of Lancer to Dragoons. Once you get a feel for your class (around ilvl 200) and you've wiped to titans landslides or other easily avoidable AOEs and shouted "Lag" in the party chat at least 15 times, you will start to get the hang of prioritizing mechanics over moves. Being able to simultaneously DPS/Heal while a guy shouts THE EDGE IS CALLING TONIGHT and you're getting punched off the edge is truly an experience to behold.
If you are less combat focused and just want to fiddle the market with outdated gear so people have an excuse to use gil on something, then look no further then crafting. But unfortunately if you want to make any money off crafting you have to become an Omnicrafter which means getting every crafting class to 50 or 60 (if you like putting razer blades to your neck). The true end game for a crafter is crafting the newest glamour gear and selling them for millions of gil only to realize you have nothing worthwhile to buy and you go back to selling and making more of these things until a new patch comes out that does the same thing. With HW being an Omnicrafter is no longer necessary for the lvl 60 renditions however the new skills that were added in HW for crafters are just dumbed down versions of the other skills, which is bad. Gathering is also another avenue but theres no point in telling you about sitting for 2 hours trying to catch a fish with a green color instead of none.
Ibuki recommends this for the constant stream of content and the communication between the devs and the players despite being in different continents across the globe. This has problems atm but at least its not sitting there for almost 2 years with no new content added until the next expansion. As time has shown anything can be fixed in this game as long as Yoshi dedicates development towards it, which he is. My only complaints from 1.0 to ARR are the belts getting removed from the visual model of the character, Mi'qote asses being flattened out and lightning tiered for the sake of development costs, and the fact that when you turn around you instantly snap to ot the animation whereas 1.0 you actually turned around and moved realistically, also the cutscenes were far superior in 1.0.
