provides a different take on the Tower Defense genre. Instead of building and managing towers, you’ll actually be controlling a small roster of heroes, as you make your way through a series of levels on a haunted island chasing the Count, the father of one of your heroes. The game features an overall nice collection of music tracks and, in terms of visuals the game looks pretty good, and it reminds me of Dota 2 to some extent.
In a genre filled with tons of clones and some games that are barely worth playing, where Hero Defense distinguishes itself from others in the genre is in the fact that your “towers” are mobile, or more they are heroes. Given the fact that there is are only 5 heroes for you to choose, this also means there is not much to choose from. Since each wave usually features a specific type of enemy, each one of these types of enemies has a specific counter hero that will be better in dealing with said enemy type. However, enemies move rather quickly along their path, and there are multiple entry points to the level, as well as different paths that they can take, which ends up forcing you to keep your heroes constantly on the move so they can keep up with the enemy waves. This might seem like somewhat of a hassle at first, especially if you’re used to playing traditional Tower Defense games but after a while you quickly get the hang of it. Also, instead of having towers, what you have are what the game calls shrines, which are basically various spots on the maps that, if you put a hero there, those shrines will grant them a buff, like increased range or double damage.
In the same way, as you might be used to upgrading towers in other games, here you’ll be leveling up your heroes by spending orbs, which are dropped by the enemies you kill. Each of these level ups will grant a specific bonus to that character, which you can change if you see fit in the “Town”. The Town represents the structure for permanent progression and is something I quite enjoy. As you play the various levels you’ll gain gold, you can then spend this gold to restore the town which was destroyind by the vampire count. You can upgrade your Academy, granting you more skill options for each character, the Forge, which will allow you to upgrade your character weapons more and more as well as change their runes (the bonus effect you receive upon leveling them up mid-game) and last but by no means least, you also have the Vault/Bank, which you can use to exchange gold for gems (gems can be used to level up your heroes weapons, for example). This progression element made “farming” on previous levels a lot more enjoyable because I knew I was actually going to get something from it.
One of the things I can’t really decide how I feel about it is the story. While I don’t think that the one in this game is terrible, I found it to be rather cliche, and while the characters themselves are distinct from each other, I feel like they don’t have that much of a character. It just felt like they’re there for the unrolling and for gameplay purposes.
One huge annoyance I do have with Hero Defense is the fact that even though I found the controls to be intuitive, I think there should be an option to move multiple units at the same time, without having the need to order them one by one to go to the same spot, because sometimes, when there are a lot of enemies coming at you, you’ll have to keep moving your heroes from one place to the other while trying to get them in the best posssible spot. Also, it would be nice to have some actual control over the camera, having the ability to rotate it would be pretty nice and would help in some cases.

Pretty standard. If you've ever played Battlefield, CoD, Star Wars Battlefront, Counter Strike, Gears of War or Halo then you've played this.
Rather than bring anything new, this is just a competent, run of the mill and safe third person shooter with no new or interesting mechanics, no dedicated server hosting (as of yet), one somewhat interesting game mode (titan mode) and a few flavors of gun to play around with.
The controls are very responsive, but movement is limited to sprinting and jumping with a few weapon specific boosts/bonuses. The starting katana teleports you forward, the starting shotgun lets you super jump.
The Weapons are, like everything else about this game, standard. You have your starting shotgun, sniper and assault rifle. Every weapon has an alternate fire and the prices for unlocking them are something you can manage in 10-15 games, assuming you win/perform well. You can unlock the weapons in whatever order you want. There are a few different flavors of sniper, rifle, shotgun, grenade launcher and Sword.
As you play in a match, you gain points which unlock armors that improve your health and give you a stylish look. Different armors can be bought. Killing a player drops a boost which upgrades your held weapon. If you're using the starting Katana, you get two that attack faster/deal more damage. If you're using assault rifle, you get 4 extra barrels that shoot in a fan in front of you.
The audio is present, by which I mean you can tell where enemies are by their gunfire and movement.
You and your enemies can take a good deal of damage and only the snipers can deal one shot deaths, though performing a headshot is tricky as the animations are quite erratic. You're unlikely to die without warning unless you get ganged up on.
This game has Microtransactions, but they are cosmetic only. Kudos to the devs on that.
The game requires a log in and creation of an Mber account.
TL;DR Minimum is a standard and decently executed third person shooter that brings nothing new to the genre and lacks a few key features needed for a successful multiplayer shooter (dedicated servers/custom games), though these MAY be added at a later date. The games lifespan depends on this.
I recommend it only because its 5 dollars as of now. It's dirt cheap, so go for it. I likely won't be playing it again.

I really, really wanted to like this game, and there was a short period of time in which I felt quite attached to it, but it's far too repetitive for me. The battle system is quite dull and doesn't require too much skill (just enough grinding) and too much time is spent going back and forth. Consequently, the locations become quite old.
Throughout the game, you are asked to complete quests which may include:
- Fetch these items from X, Y and Z
- Speak to X, Y and Z
- Fill this bucket with water (yes, seriously - I have done this for at least two people)
- Inspect these areas
- Fight enemies and collect X from them
- Fight this boss.
There are dungeons in game, but you must first connect with other players who are in specific roles. It has taken me over ten minutes to access a dungeon before, even though some of these are essential to progressing through the main story. Whilst I would normally read articles online to pass the time, you have to watch the screen in order to see when the game is full. You have to accept the mission again, too, so if you miss that moment, you're back in the queue. I can understand why this is - playing with someone who is AFK is even more frustrating than waiting for ten minutes - but it is a shame when you can't progress through a game because there are no players around who want to join your next mission.
As far as player interaction goes, this game does not encourage very much of it. I have tried to contact other players after completing a dungeon with them, but I have been told I cannot connect with them at that point in time. I haven't yet been able to connect with a single player after leaving the dungeon.
Finally, the monthly fees are too high for those who want to play more casually. I appreciate the fact the servers are well-managed, but £7-£9 a month is quite a lot when you only play once a month. I absolutely love Final Fantasy - I even enjoyed XIII and XIII-2 - but I'd rather return once in a while and play the game slowly. However, this is not an option. You cannot pay for a month and have a day deducted each time you log in - the fee would last me a year at the rate I currently play.
There is a positive though - I must find one as a Final Fantasy fan. The music is lovely; I would recommend listening to the OST if you're a Nobuo Uematsu fan.

Ok, I finally beat the game with -316 lives.
The deaths are just not your fault at all (unless you have a bad memory) - they're all due to the level design.  Each death is comically absurd, because they happen beyond the expected mechanics of the 2d sidescrolling platform genre.
This game is basically "map memorization", however, maps are segemented by frequent checkpoints, to keep annoyance to a minimum.  The levels aren't "hard" like they are in games such as Super Meat Boy, but more of a puzzle setup.  You instantly die at a spot, and then you have to remember where that spot is, as well as figure out how to get around that trap.
There are crystals "hidden" in every level, which are placed in really hard super ultra mega challenging spots.  None of them are easy to get - I was only able to get one of them.  I assume the "??????" on the main menu opens up when all crystals are collected.

This is a PC Dōjin made by two people so I'm excusing its lack of polish in some areas like display size, etc. Respawning enemies and timed missions might be a dealbreaker for some, but I think that's part of its retro charm.
It's pretty fun and has a reasonable difficulty curve. Mech enthusiasts craving a good mech game will find lots to love with this action packed side scroller.

Hero Defense - Haunted Island is a tower defense game with a generous dollop of action and RPG-style progression stirred into the mix.  The main twist of the game is that instead of building static towers to stop the usual waves of enemies, you must instead coordinate your party of heroes to defend various routes, moving them around the map to defend the cowardly townsfolk from monstrous baddies.
The unique action-based defense system is very well done and surprisingly challenging.  Each of your five heroes effectively acts as an incredibly mobile tower (you can move them around the map at different speeds), and each has their own special means of attack as well as strengths and weaknesses against certain enemy types. Additionally, you are free to develop these five hero-towers as you like, choosing which skills and weapon upgrades your heroes will have access to during the map.  This means you must not only coordinate your party's movement and placement during battle, but also gear up with an appropriate combination of upgrades before each scenario to make sure your heroes stand a fighting chance.
The campaign mode is nicely polished, with a story that is a bit on the light and silly side, but is *much* meatier than tower defense games usually offer.  As you progress through the story and unlock various maps, you also unlock harder difficulties and map-specific challenges that will take much more skill (as well as grindable upgrades) to beat.  This adds a great deal of extra replayability to the game.
Hero Defense also offers another potentially exciting feature: multiplayer.  Right now, this is a competitive mode, where doing well on your own map gives you powers to try and trip up your opponent.  You compete with other players in weeklong multiplayer seasons, developing your party of heroes as you choose according to the specific rules and restrictions for that'season', then trying to reach the top of the ladder ranks before the season is up.
As Hero Defense is relatively new (released just a couple of weeks ago), currently there are not many players searching for multiplayer matches - however this may change as the playerbase grows.  The developers also seem to be making every effort to encourage and support multiplayer, and have been very active in the community in order to do so.  In addition to encouraging competition with ladder rankings for weekly multiplayer seasons, they have even hosted a tournament with gamekeys as a reward for the top finishers.  I would not expect this kind of event to be a usual thing, but it certainly shows their dedication to making the social portion of the game a success. The developers have also confirmed that they are working on a cooperative mode for release in the near future, so I have high hopes for the multiplayer side of the game - even if it's not quite there yet.
All in all, Hero Defense - Haunted Island is the kind of game that just makes me happy to play it.  The game offers a reasonable amount of challenge, a quirkily entertaining story, plenty of replayability, and a progression system that is simple enough to understand, but offers enough complexity to make choices extremely relevant, especially in the tough (but optional) challenge maps.  Plus, everything is layered with a nice coat of polish, from the pleasant graphics to the in-game voiceovers.  With all these checks in the positive column, Hero Defense is a refreshing style of tower defense game that even people who don't usually love the genre can enjoy.

Hero defense: Haunted island is a tower defense game where there are no towers. You might ask “how is that even a tower defense game?”, well what this game does is substitutes towers with heroes. This makes for a very interesting idea and much needed variety from the typical tower defense games. The story is Count Necrosis has betrayed his Vampire race by embracing the darkness they had been fighting all along. His son Jack has sworn to destroy his father and along the way he meets different heroes who join him on his quest.
The game looks very pretty with some nice effects. For a tower defense type game like this the blur and all the filters look pretty good and don’t interfere with your overall view. There’s V-sync option, resolution option, UI scale options which is nice in my opinion and more games should include this feature. The graphics quality presets ranges from low to ultra. I ran the game on ultra graphics with v-sync off and FPS was over 60 and never dipped below that.
The game features fully voice acted dialogs. Each hero has their own voice over dialogs. These voice acting acknowledgements of the user commands can be turned off from the options menu, so if you get tired of hearing the heroes say the same things, you can always turn this feature off.
The soundtracks of the game are in my opinion are very good, especially the theme music of the game is pretty awesome. It has that creepy Halloween feeling. The other soundtracks are also very atmospheric and make the game feel much more themed.
This is a hero defense game, meaning there are heroes you use instead of towers and you try to defeat waves and waves of enemies and bosses. The game features 5 heroes and all of them have their own unique abilities. Unlike tower defense games this is a much more interactive game, once the waves start you’ll have to keep repositioning your heroes for best efficiency against the enemies. The hero system is pretty neat as you require certain heroes for certain types of enemy waves. For example, the vampires can be best dealt with by Jack who is a crossbow attacking hero, the Igors can be best dealt with by Jane Doe who is a melee attacker.
There are 5 heroes in the game you can use. Plenty of enemies as well including Vampires, skeletons, Igors, wolves, zombies. Each hero has their own unique weapons. Jack who is the main character and trying to kill his father Count Necrosis, his main weapon is the bow and he is most effective against the Vampires. Burrows uses holy water to damage monsters. Burrows wants revenge from the skeletons for taking away his wife, naturally he’s most effective against skeletons. Sam Hain is an orphan girl whose parents were killed by zombies and he uses pumpkin bombs to deal with zombie hordes, she is most effective against the zombies. Jane Doe is a woman who was brought back to life by Dr. Amalgam who wanted her to be his bride, she has lost all her memories so she doesn’t even remember her name, hence, Jane Doe. She uses her club to melee attack enemies and she is most efficient against the Igors. Last but not the least is Wylde half-blood who is a human/werewolf hybrid. He does ranged attacks with his hatchets and can counter the wolves pretty well.
The heroes also have power-ups in-game, just like you can upgrade your towers, you can also upgrade (or ‘charge’ as the game calls it) heroes in the middle of the game. When the map starts you have 150 souls, you can purchase a hero with 100 souls. Once you start killing enemies in the first wave you’ll start earning more and more souls which you can use to purchase other heroes. Once you have all the heroes you can use these souls to upgrade the heroes. The upgrades for each hero are called runes. You can equip all sorts of runes in the order you want from the forge and in-game you can use the upgrade button and the runes will become available in the same pattern as you selected before. Each additional upgrade will cost 100 more souls then the last. E.g. first upgrade will be 100 souls, second will be 200, so on and so forth.  The upgrade runes include things like certain percentage of more damage, certain percentage faster attack speed, earn more orbs/coins etc.
The map layouts are pretty basic. You get waves coming from one part of the map to another part of the map. Some maps have 2 different places where the waves go from. The waves of enemies are displayed at the top of the screen and underneath each type of enemy wave is a color, either yellow or green. These 2 colors let you know where the waves will be coming from and which route on the map they will take, so you can adjust your heroes accordingly.
You have to rebuild and upgrade your town as you progress through the game. Building and upgrading town places will give you upgrades for your heroes. There’s a forge which will let you upgrade each heroes’ weapons and attach runes to them. The academy lets you spend your skill points for each hero to improve their attacks. You must upgrade the academy to newer levels to be able to level up your characters to as well. E.g. you need level 3 academy to be able to purchase the level 3 upgrades for each hero. There’s also a bank which lets you exchange coins for gems. Gems can be used to purchase weapon upgrades from the forge. All the levels can be replayed over if you want to improve your gameplay. Furthermore, you can play with different difficulties as well and higher difficulty will earn you more stars. Stages in the later part of the game require you to have certain number of stars to be able to play them so you must grind your way back to the earlier levels in higher difficulties.
The camera can be a bit problematic in my opinion. You can’t rotate and change the angles at all. Due to this I had difficulty in keeping track of enemies on a couple of levels. On most maps it’s fine but can be a pain in a few maps.
Multiplayer also seems to be dead as I could not find anyone playing online, so you might want to keep that in mind if you are planning to play this game in multiplayer mode. Though co-op mode is coming (as the developers have stated), that should make up for the multiplayer part and you can play with your friends which is always fun.

The game is extremely fun and can be addicting. If you’re a tower defense genre fan, this game is a very good game in that genre. The story is also nice with all characters brining something different in the game. The game is surprisingly well polished and I did not notice any unusual behavior, glitches or problems. At $15, I think it’s very reasonable but if you think it’s steep I’d suggest you wait till the upcoming big sale and most likely the game will go on sale.

I decided to review this game upon my return to it, this being as of patch 3.2, and I have tried to include as many details about the good and bad that I can scribble down:
Pros
- This is the foundation all MMO's should have, everything scales beautifully to keep old content relevant and accessible.
- Perhaps the only MMO I've seen that champions actually helping other players, doing so giving you rewards. This leads to a very friendly playerbase.
- 'Realistic' player housing, owning one or a mansion is costly but reflects your success with the game's trade skills, or that of your Free Company. Even housed in an instanced neighbourhood with other people.
- The choice of having all classes on one character, or multiple characters(*)
- The story, while cheesy in places, is a lovely little fantasy epic that really hits its stride moving into the Heavensward expansion, and believe me there is a lot to do here.
- The game is a challenge compared to others like WoW. With dungeons, raids, and trials as part of the levelling progression you can be assured that anyone that has made it to the endgame knows how to dodge attacks like a  Mushihimesama pro. The challenge is gradually muted if the same party fails repeatedly, so it is at least forgiving.
- It has cutscenes (most voiced for the main story) for nearly every quest, so you feel involved in the plot of even the more trivial run-about's.
- The music is amazing, personal favourites being the dungeon Pharos Sirius and Iahgard's (foundation) night theme.
- Subtle touches that make the experience feel more immersive, you can change the appearance of items much like wow's transmog system, targeting people has your character look at them, clothing reacts to weather, etc.
- Because you'd tend to favour one character, re-customisation is more of a breeze and is significantly cheaper than in WoW or the like.
- The Hildibrand quests are a hilarious change of pace.
- The meat of the game's jobs comes with the requirement to play other base classes, such as Black Mage requiring a 30 Thaumaturge and a 15 archer.
-The quests to get you on the path of your chosen class are a nice addition to your own personal development, and are very helpful to newcomers venturing into unknown territory, these are even provided for the game's trade skills.
- The encounters in the game are epic in scale, you feel very involved when bosses role out their special attacks to try and kill you.
Cons
- The races effectively feel the same. They have the same haircuts and little diversity in facial options. You are literally picking your character's physical build with them more or less, be it tall and slim, tall and bulky, etc. The Au Ra might be an exception with all the scales, tails and such but still has the same premise.
- (*) Having multiple characters will mean you have to play the immensely long story again, good if you enjoy it, but highly taxing otherwise.
- The story length as a whole, it will take you hundreds of hours to get to the most recent content, my play-time is purely from levelling one character in one class (job) from the vanilla content to 3.2 Heavenward content which is almost 400 hours alone.
- The game could do with a few more muted customiation options, all the excessive anime hair and weird choices for facial hair feel a bit limited.
- Some of the content and the community can be a bit strange. This is anime culture after all, mixed with a solid FF playerbase. While I enjoy both, it is easy to see why the feel of the game can repel people, some are so engrossed they anounce every attack they make with macros or you may feel unsettled by people in your party playing young girls in skimpy outfits and bunny ears.
- The depth of the game comes mainly from repetition with the main playable jobs (or classes). Some can feel very similar and many of the cross-class skills have little use beyond very low levels (aside from the valuable crafting ones). Crafting is the same process but reskinned each time more or less, but you at least feel more involved with the process.
- While I have no personal experience with it, the PvP content is said to be rather hollow. The lack of exclusive gear leads the most DPS-orientated jobs at the top in most cases.
- By the end you will absolutely loathe moogles.
Final Note:
While it took a few hours of investment to really get into the swing of the game it delivered an unexpectedly good story that builds towards a grand coclusion in A Realm Reborn and is much expanded on by the unique feel of Ishgard in the subsequent expansion. Always having access to all the content which provides up-to-date rewards for back-tracking is what all MMO's should have without fail. I was never left bored and without anything to do because there is simply so much to get involved in. Though, this fact also makes the game feel quite daunting, as even with many hours played I still don't feel I have progressed past being the noobiest of noobs. You are required to have a wide breadth of skills at high levels to really get the most out of the game, and while this is good, it can feel like a carrot on a stick held too far away for you to care. Though, the game can be forgiven for many of its flaws by delivering a unique experience that mirrors what a real MMO should be, co-op focused, challenging, and full of heart.

Transistor is one of my most favorite games ever.
I picked it up after I accidentally stumbled upon Bastion and fell in love with it, only to experience the same, if not better, feeling again. The art is unique, the soundtrack incredibly good, and the overall atmosphere is enthralling and beautiful.
The fighting system is a kind of a mix of real-time and turn-based combat. You are given a certain number of points represented as bar and you can spend those points on performing abilities uncluding movement, think mana or energy. This whole "picking a move" phase happens when the game is paused, but the excution itself is real time. You can use your moves any time on their own too, but this "tactical" way is more effective.
You level up through gaining experience points, but since the individual game levels are pretty much straigthforward corridors, there's no grinding involved and the experience points come sort of naturally, without any big effort. What matters though is what you spend them on. You can either buy a new skill, unlock an upgrade slot for a move you already have an older one, or increase your memory, which in turn increases the number of moves you can have at any single time. You can't always do all of the above, but that's pretty much how it works.
On death, you lose some of your moves untill you "recharge" at specific bind points or lose all of your moves and die. That can be kind of irritating since if the move randomly deactivated happens to be your main source of damage, you're pretty much screwed. Although it brings in a certain level of challengem it can be a lot painful.
The story is captivating, reflecting the overall mood of the game. Similarly to Bastion, there's only one narrator, which only adds to the unique feelings of the empty city.
Great game, totally recommend it.

A deeply inspired game. Transistor not only has a nice aesthetic, but a handful of well implemented and creative gameplay mechanics. It is a healthy marriage of arcade power-ups and tactics, where player experimentation is key. For games that promise both live and turn based action, the player is usually given the choice between either - in Transistor you will want to master both forms of gameplay if you wish to gain the edge.
The most intriguing part of the game is the power-up system. Throughout the game the player collects a series of "functions". These functions can be used as new attacks - choosing up to a total of four moves. Each function has a unique effect, letting the player choose from sneak attacks, long range strikes, clustering explosions, summoning minions, and more, or any combination of these. But the functions aren't limited to simple attacks. In addition to the four move slots, the player also has four passive slots to install their functions, and each move has two upgrade slots. The upgrades are really something special, allowing the player to improve and expand on or even change completely the nature of a move. As the player collects more of these functions, playstyles can become more and more diverse. The number of possibilities are staggering.
The gameplay itself is challenging enough that certain combinations may be found ineffective or require careful planning and skill to use. This is what makes the game whole as an interactive experience. The player has to strategize, adapt, evaluate, refine, rearrange. You can't just brute force your way through (though certain combinations do give a whole new meaning to "brute force"). You can't just grind to max stats and max gear.
If you like games that emphasize tactics and positioning, and enjoy making lots of experimental play styles. THIS is the game for YOU. If you don't, well, do me a favor, play it anyway.

NOTE:  I had to use a third party piece of software to be able to be able to map an XBox 360 pad in a sensible configuration.  I'd give this game a 7/10 score though because although it has many timeless elements of game design that still make it quite a bit of fun to play through, it does not have as clear and interesting a story as the first Tomb Raider, it falls short of that mark on most measures; and additionally it shows it's age graphically.  Is it still worth playing, yeah, but it could play much better with a bit of modernization.  The character model for Lara is of course excellently done for the time, as are her animations; but I think there may be more polygons in her model than in the rest of the game.  The modelling though isn't really where the game suffers;but rather in the low resolution textures.  The cut-scenes look extremely grainy on modern resolutions and the textures on the environments are sometimes poor enough to really pull you out of any immersion you may have.  I will say that there are a very wide variety of environments and some of them are quite in interesting, although if you're like me, you may not be able to clearly understand why you are actually going to all these peculiar places.  The story just isn't particularly clear or engaging.  The platforming controls are somewhat finicky.  You really end up using a set of manuevers in kind of the same way you might in a fighting game to clear these challenges.  Once you get those moves down, it's usually more a matter of finding where you need to platform to rather than the execution that is the challenge.  There are some block pushing/lever pulling puzzles as well and these are solid, usually not too much of a challenge but that's fine as they don't overstay their welcome.  As far as the combat, it's very similar to the first Tomb Raider as well, and the added weapon, and enemy variety is one of the real clear improvements over it's predecessor.  Overall, the game is dated, but fun.  If you are considering taking a look at the classic roots of the franchise though, I'd start with Tomb Raider 1 (better story, somewhat better level design, and native x-input support for the PC), and if you enjoy that .. heck yeah TR 2 is worth the time investment.

Tomb Raider II brings back the iconic charismatic archaeologist, Lara Croft, on another epic journey around the globe to investigate the legend around the Dagger of Xian. Her second adventure takes her along the Great Wall of China, the snowy terrains of Tibet, Italy’s city of Venice and a sunken shipwreck, accompanied by more complex series of jumping puzzles and death traps, lever activated time puzzles and the merciless killing of treasure hunting goons and exotic animals that stand in her path.
The game grants Lara the ability to climb ladders and craggy walls, to roll in the air and underwater for trickier puzzles, and to drive vehicles such as speedboats and snowmobiles around certain levels in the game, which can be incredibly fun and very tedious at the same time. Flares have been thrown into the game to allow Lara to explore particularly dark areas with ease, which come in handy for some of the later levels, along with new weapons packing serious firepower like the M16 assault rifle, a grenade launcher and automatic dual pistols (which replace the dual magnums that were available in TR1), along with all weapons within the previous game.
Enemies now have the intelligence to climb surfaces in order to reach Lara and carry pretty damaging weaponry, making combat somewhat more difficult, especially when they corner the player in tight spaces. Meaning there will be more ammo to find, a few more medicine packs to collect, and there are 3 secrets to find throughout each level; the gold, jade and silver dragons.
For those who have played Tomb Raider I, you will be pleased to hear that instead of having to save your progress at a save crystal and having to restart tedious levels every time Lara plummets to her death from that point, Tomb Raider II allows you to save your progress from your save manual whenever and wherever. It makes life much, much easier.
All environments and graphics appear to have been enhanced both in colour and in quality in this game, ultimately keeping movable blocks and secret areas better hidden, so it’s very easy to overlook a potential secret or an area full of loot if you aren’t actively exploring the entire level. The soundtrack in the game has been heavily built off its predecessor, only playing on certain cues like when the protagonist steps into the path of a rolling boulder, as it did in the previous game.
Another change to be noted is the change in voice actress for our fearless protagonist. Personally, I felt that her new voice fitted Lara better as she sounds much more experienced and capable of handling herself like a badass, whereas, her voice in TR1 portrayed her to be more of an arrogant adolescent.
The tutorial area in Lara Croft’s manor has developed greatly from its elder. The crates blocking most of the large manor have now been removed, inviting the player to explore the charming home more thoroughly. The gymnasium and the swimming pool reappear in this game, but with much obstacles to manoeuvre through and a prettier pool to swim around in.
Here is where you are introduced to Winston, Lara’s old butler who is intent on following her around the house while groaning and carrying a tray of rattling tea cups. On the odd occasion when I accidently ran into him, there is a chance that he will break wind. It can be pretty fun for a while, but eventually having him dog you around the manor will grow tedious. My solution was to have him follow me to the meat locker in the kitchen, wait for him to follow a certain distance behind, then perform a well-timed leap out of the area, and lock him in. I found watching him try to walk through the door grunting and groaning to be quite amusing. Cruel, but amusing.
Lara can now venture outside the manor and explore the maze behind it. The main section behind the maze is an assault course the player can now test out their skills on obstacles that are a bit more challenging than the gym.
All in all, if you’re looking for a game where you can relax and enjoy shooting lead into your enemies, but still challenging enough that it keeps you wondering about any potential death traps around the corner, Tomb Raider II is a classic game with plenty of everything and is generally fun to play, even when using the Playstation controls, although the PC controls are much more fluid.

This is what an era-homage game should be. They say they're paying tribute to Cybernator and Front Mission: Gun Hazard, and they deliver with all the new-gen hit detection, framerate, and lush backgrounds you couldn't get back in 16-bit. Be warned, though; that hit detection works both ways. There are bosses who will shoot at you from multiple directions, hitting you regardless of your blocking. From hard mode onward there are areas where you will rely on your shield so heavily that it will break, and you will mourn its passing. That being said, there are two pixel boss dodges and quick blocks where you will feel like you're owning the battlefield.
...until you play hard mode, where you will cling to health drops like your mother's teat. You will painstakingly ask yourself if it's worth it to spend an irreplaceable special shot on a mid level boss with the main boss around the corner and your health precariously low.
But really the difficulty is very well balanced. There are enemy design decisions that seem forehead slappingly easy which become deviously difficult on the higher difficulties. Even little things like level traps and boss patterns scale with difficulty. The pacing on normal was such that I squeaked by the last boss with a last ditch melee attack for the no-continues-used-win while I myself was a hair from death. Thankfully, there is a ONE BUTTON return to menu function, and the intro is about 3 seconds long when you spam the skip button. You will be glad you have this if you're going for the "beat one mission without getting hit" achievement from normal difficulty upwards.
Cons: lack of resolution options, game doesn't recognize gamepad unless it's active when you start the app, game wants to recognize analog stick (which you won't want to use) including switching over to analog only if you accidentally nudge  it in a firefight and frantically try to figure out why you are not aiming properly anymore. I also think the options for one button dash and one button melee would be welcome (being that I have so many buttons on this 360 controller), but all in all these are very minor complaints. The main con is that I wanted it to be longer, which is also really just indicative of the game's quality.
TLDR: I got it for three dollars. Pew pew 5 hours of fun with some rewarding moments. Go for it.

Gigantic Army is a simple arcade action mech game in which you customise and pilot a mech throughout 6+ level in one sitting until the end.
- The graphics look really cool. It's nothing new or outstanding but it looks awesome in it 16 bit aesthetic.
- The sound and music are extremely well done. Gun fire sounds on point, explosions sound powerful and your mech sounds weighty.
- Controls are stiff, your mech feels as if it's weighted done as jumps grant you very minimal upward velocity.
- Simple combat you have 6 weapons, 3 main and 3 sub. You pick 1 from each and begin your playthrough.
- It's short about 1 hour or less in length with minimal deaths
- No save feature, you gotta beat it in a single play through. You can play as long as you have enough credits.
- Movement is a bit too stiff, I know it was on purpose but it feels too stiff.
- Story is a walls of text that scroll to quickly.
- Gameplay is limited by a time limit and once it runs out you take damage until you die. How do you counter this, dash, melee and never stop firing.
- I wish the dash feature was given a specific button rather than double pressing left or right on the dpad.
Gigantic Army is a fun mech game with simple combat, customisation options and awesome audio\visual directions. It's annoyances don't hold it back from being a fun, yet short ride and for $5.00 (cheaper on a sale) you can't go wrong if you're a mech fan.

So apparently, "Games that hate you" is a genre now.  Possibly inspired by games like "I Wanna Be The Guy" and "Kaizo Mario World", Eryi's Action is designed to be intentionally frustrating.  Do not be fooled by the cutesy graphics.  Everything in this world wants to kill you, and you will waste many lives learning where all the deadly traps are hidden.  And yet, somehow it's a really good time.  You'll spend hours laughing at all the stupid ways you find to die.
If you're looking for a cute Mario clone with balanced gameplay... get Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams.  But if you're an expert gamer who is thinks Mario is for babies, get Eryi's Action.  It will appeal to the masochist in you.

This game is ♥♥♥♥ing hilarious and basically Cat Mario Redux: Just In Case You Thought It Needed To Be Even Harder, also known as Cat Mario 2: Electric Boogaloo. Everything, from you to the enemies you get constantly murdered by (which will happen on average every 1.5 seconds) is a kawaii-uguu, rainbow-puking, flower-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ taking part in the extremely sadistic Moeshit Apocalypse of You Dying A Lot Except Also Kawaii or Something.
On multiple occasions you will get completely brickwalled by seemingly impassable hazards and roadblocks that you have to work around, often inventively and in unexpectedly hilarious ways. Every time you start up the game you begin in Eryi's house and have to evade being bonked to death by falling pans that will virtually always outsmart your movements and send your negative lives remaining count that much closer to infinity. You can even get killed while on the world map, because even the background props have murderous intent: there is pretty much nothing in this game that can't or won't deliberately kill you in some bizarre way.
So on the one hand there's you screeching and raging at the absurd difficulty of this game as a more or less perfectly programmed torture simulator, but on the other hand the outright unpredictable ways in which the game communicates to you just how much it hates you are literally nothing short of hilarious. This is a game about dying literally thousands and thousands of times, and you're more likely to get into a plane crash and be abducted by aliens at the exact same time than you are to clear this game without dying even once. You can't pull off a perfect no-miss run in this game because you were never meant to: nobody was. Otherwise you wouldn't have infinite lives and a counter that's always more than willing to rub in your face the number of times you've died. The object of the game is not preventing your death count from continuously rising, but solving platform puzzles which can be bypassed only via methods comparable to the unintentional exploits that let you fling yourself outside of the world map in the N64 version of Zelda OoT, except this time they're both deliberate and lying in wait to be discovered to hilarious effect.
I don't think this is a kind of game you can just rate out of 10, so I won't. I just think it's positively hilarious and enjoyable unless you're literally some tryhard moron who thinks platformers are SRS BSNS or some♥♥♥♥♥♥

I really enjoyed the time I've spent playing this game so far. The characters feel like the embodiment of the classic tower defense tower archetypes, but the mobility of the characters and the special power up ground runes adds a strategy to the game that makes it more interesting than static towers placed along a path.
Characters both have different ways of dealing damage and also different strengths. For example, the vampire hunter guy with his crossbow is strong against vampires but weak against most other types of monsters. The priest guy is good against undead with his holy/frozen water damage-wise but can do little more than slow down other monster types. The third character you get is the typical aoe character to stop large, fast streams of week ghoul-like creatures in their tracks. The fourth character seems to me like a heavy-hitting melee type character who fights the larger ghouls and I haven't unlocked the fifth character yet.  Each character feels fleshed out and unique.
There are ways to upgrade the weapons of the characters with runes that you can either buy with in-game currency or find for completing missions. Then, as the characters kill waves of monsters, they collect points which allow them to use their weapon powerups in times of need. Each character also has a pretty robust and interesting skill tree that keeps your characters getting progressively stronger as the game progresses.
Villagers play an important role as an "oh crap" button. A wave of villagers can come streaming out of the town hall every so often to crash into a wave of particularly troublesome enemies. They're best used as a last ditch effort to protect your "base."
Overall, having played around 1.4 hours so far at the time of this review, I really enjoy this game so far and look forward to completing it and then going back to complete the levels on harder difficulties.

Hero-Defense – Haunted Island:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The noble town of Almanac is under extreme pressure from “the Count Necrosis” army of creeps. This terrifying Vampire overlord also known as Jonathan Sanders . . .  excuse me, who? Jonathan Sanders use to be a vampire hunter three decades ago before betraying his cause and his family! Now, it is all up to his son Jack to destroy the brutal “Count Necrosis” and restore his family name. Armed with a clove of garlic and a wooden cross. . .  What am I talking about, that is so old school. . . Armed with his crossbow and a tremendous amount of courage, Jack will have to defend and secure every building in Almanac before the ultimate battle against his dad, well Count Necrosis!
Hero-Defense – Haunted Island is a Tower Defense / Action game where you take control of a Vampire hunter, “Jack Sanders” and his companions (four unlockable characters).  At the start of the game, you will be introduced to the burning town of Almanac and you will attempt the save the remaining villagers by holding back a couple of waves of enemies. The first couple of missions are basically very good tutorials where you will learn the fundamentals of the game. What I really like straight off the bat (lol) about this game is the fact that you constantly move your heroes around the levels, which is different to your typical Tower-Defense game. Hero-Defense has fourteen levels to beat and each of them can be played or replayed on four different difficulties. The campaign mode is set on the lowest difficulty, which is good and gives you a chance to study the level a bit better before you decide to take to the next difficulty.
As in most defense-tower games, you have to defeat the incoming waves of foe. As I mentioned above, instead of placing your unit in specific positions, here you can move your characters across the level. Your heroes will not take on damage but you will find your enemies quite challenging to kill. To beat a level, you have to make sure to eliminate all waves without losing the barricade constructed by the villagers, which is located at the end of each level (or at the end of the path).  Every time you destroy an enemy, you will get a certain number of blue orbs. These orbs can activate a new booster attack for one of your heroes each time you reach a specific number of orbs. To give you an example, the first boost attack can be trigged when you accumulate 100 orbs. Some of your enemies will drop coins which you can use to either upgrade buildings in town or exchange them for gems.  Some levels will have shrines here and there; you will be able to position one of your heroes on it and will get an extra boost. Some of them are specific to each hero, so make sure you position the right one on it.  Also, make sure that no creeps reach any houses where villagers are hiding. Save them and you get additional points at the end of the level. Also, you need villagers to launch them as a mob if one of two waves are too close to the barricade. This game is just fun!
When you successfully beat a level, you will receive points and your characters will get experience and might even level up. Every time your character levels up it will receive two skill points which you will be able to use at the academy to improve their skills set. Don’t forget to upgrade the academy so your character can learn better skills.

Darkarta, A Broken Heart's Quest is perhaps one of the better Hidden Object Games on Steam that wasn't developed by Artifex Mundi, which to me should be a standard for quality Hidden Object Games.
Let me start off by saying that communication between development and the players are pretty good. They may not be fully prompt in their responses, but they are active enough to keep the ball rolling. That in itself should be a note towards a positive vote towards whether this is a good recommendation or not. In this case, yes.
The game itself did have bugs, up until their latest patch which came out August 13th, 2017. Prior to that, I wasn't able to progress beyond a scene where I had to put materials together to start a fire. The developer tried to get to the bottom of the issue, but ultimately, could not figure out where it went wrong. He suggested I start a new game to see if it happens again. Not attracted to the idea of starting anew, I put the game off until two days ago, when I noticed the update and continued my game. This time, I saw that they introduced a work around that allowed me to progress through the previous bug. This is fantastic, because I am eager to see where the story will take me.
Now about the story. Unlike many HO games, Darkarta ABHQ actually has a pretty engaging story line. I won't spoil it for you, but it's not run-of-the-mill, cookie cutter stuff you see in most HOG. There is a of time travelling, a story of love for your child, vengeance and rebirth. While slightly cheesy, definitely not badly written.
The visuals are pretty good as well. Lush and vibrant in all of the right places. The character drawings are a bit off, but hardly noticeable. For example, the character faces seem to be drawn by someone who doesn't have enough expertise in the specific field, but still a good illustrator overall.
Voice overs are okay, though I find the volume levels a bit imbalanced at times. Music is also good too and has variety throughout the scenes and cut scenes.
Game play itself is tight. There are a lot of different types of puzzles. My only major complaint is that the back-and-forth between scenes are plentiful and annoyed me after visiting the same scene over five times.
Overall, I give this game a rough 4/5 or in this case, a thumbs up. $6.49 Cdn is totally worth the content and support this game outputs.

So this is an incredible time-killer. Amazingly involving and moddable if there's anything you don't like. Primarily the game revolves around the gathering of just a few primary resources, processing them and turning them into baisic components, which can then be combined to make more complex components, which can then also be combined into even more complex components....you get the idea. There are also hostiles on the planet to deal with who REALLY aren't keen on you tearing down and poisoning their environment, so you need to construct defences and maintain them, power your factory and stay alive.
Ultimately your goal is to be able to construct the (incredibly complicated) rocket and a satelite to put in it, then launch the thing (you have to produce the fuel to feed it as well of course) For me though though the joy lies in the solving of logistical problems; moving what you need to where you need it. Overall, a decent game.
Technically, this game holds up quite well, despite being almost 20 years old.  There are some technical issues that the game can have, especially on 64-bit versions of Windows, but I've noticed that Compatibility Mode (run in Windows 95 mode on Windows 7 x64 Pro) tends to take care of most of the issues I've experienced with it.  You'll also want to create a custom resolution in your video card for your native resolution's 4:3 aspect ratio.  So with 1920x1080 as an example, you would create a 1440x1080 resolution to run in full screen, or run in windowed mode to see the game in its proper aspect ratio.
As for the game itself, it's not bad.  I think the biggest downfall to the game is that the developer went for the "more is more" approach, and it ended up backfiring on them.  Instead of fixing some of the core game mechanics, Eidos just pushed for a bigger tomb raider game.  We get more weapons, more bad guys, larger levels, more challenging puzzles, and more moves for Lara to execute.  But on the negative, Lara still controls awkwardly, combat is still horrible, and the locations are just straight-up boring.  How can I put this... Tomb Raider II doesn't really have tombs in it.  Oh sure, there's the first level, and the few near the end.  But for the most part, Lara is running around places like the canals of Venice (huh?), opera houses, naval bases, and shipwrecks.  And what's worse, is that the game actually starts out pretty good!  The first level has you romping through a section of the ancient Great Wall of China, and its fantastic.  It's full of booby traps, and generally keeps you on your toes.  The immediately after that, you're thrust into Venice, where you must run around the canals in search of the main bad-guy's hideout...  Weird.  In the end, Tomb Raider II just feels like a tedious and boring version of the original.  While Eidos did make a few touch-up improvements (more polys for Lara, the ability to walk in water, real-time lighting, etc.), they neglected to fix any of the core gameplay issues.  In all fairness, the original Tomb Raider was released in 1996, and this sequel was released just a year later.  So I'm pretty sure that it was a lack of time that prevented Eidos from fixing these issues.  Also, I believe that the third Tomb Raider also came out a year after this, and it also continues the trend of "more" - again, without any fixes to the same gameplay issues that the first game had.
If you're a nostalgic fan, go ahead and get this game on sale.  It's not as tedious as the third installment, and if you've already beaten this game, there's no reason you can't romp through it again.  If you've never played the Tomb Raider games, I would strongly advise to start with the first and probably end with the first.  It just goes downhill from there until Crystal Dynamics revived the series with Tomb Raider Legend.
TL:DR - Not a bad game at all.  But if you've never played the series, go ahead and start with the first one.  If you have played the first one, just know that the little improvements they made to the game don't outweigh its bigger flaws.  Still recommended though.

***A MOSTLY SPOILER-FREE REVIEW***
Eryi’s Action is a game as funny as it is fun, which is to say - very both.
A satirical take on plat-forming, reminiscent of games like “I Wanna Be the Guy”, Eryi’s Action is an indie title with surprisingly high production quality and a great deal of humour. Developers
have created something really solid here and if you like a particularly challenging pick-up-and-play platformer
then you could do much worse than this.
Firstly, all the assets in this game are great. The animation is really smooth, the sounds fit well without being distracting and the art is a top-notch stylistic nod to the games of yesteryear without being overly retro
. The characters and world design are very likeable, and hint at a much bigger universe behind the slice you see. It’s hard not to get a little sucked in by it all.
The
is particularly enjoyable, but annoyingly, it restarts every few seconds when you meet yet another grizzly end. The result is that you’ll never hear a full track unless you pause the game. I suppose if you were perfect at the game you might get the bonus of hearing each track uninterrupted and in full, but I very much doubt that this was an intentional feature so much as a happy accident. Having said that, I imagine the game would be less of a parody if the music were to continue oblivious to your untimely demise, so I can live with pausing every now and then if I want to take in the tunes.
What stands out the most
are the
. They’re pretty much perfect and never really get in the way. If you make a mistake, it feels like your mistake - not the controls, and that’s incredibly important for any game
. There’s only a couple of questionable things about them. The first was in the very beginning - I somehow missed that there was a run button, and checking online it appears others have missed it too. I think it’s likely due to the slow acceleration, but once you know about it, it stops being an issue. The second problem is that there's a slight inability to jump when landing on descending platforms, as if you get glued to them, so you have to wait a second before jumping. I suppose that could be just another part of the challenge, but it feels a bit clunky given how polished and reactive the rest of the platforming is.
The game is not without its other minor
either; most notably the difficulty curve which is a bit naught-to-ninety. Eryi’s Action has you thinking outside the box, and while that’s a fantastic thing for a plat-former to achieve, I can’t help but think it will drive a lot of players away by demanding too-much-too-soon.  I admit that I had to consult a walkthrough on a couple of occasions, one of which was at the end of the very first level. It wasn’t even a case of ‘obvious when you see it’; it was just a bizarre solution that wasn’t really hinted at. They really could have left that challenge to a later level and given the player the knowhow to clear one first. Another chink in the armour is the first boss you face. I definitely had a good chuckle when I figured it out, but it really appears to be impossible at first and I could definitely see people rage-quitting here. This is thinking outside the box stuff, and I love it, but I fear it was implemented a little too early.
Get through that much of the game however and you’ll be wise to its various trickeries, so it’s
clear sailing after that… at least as clear sailing as repeatedly dying can be! The game becomes a battle of wits to guess what the developer is thinking and counter it, and it results in hilarity almost every time you are killed in another unexpected way. This game really made me laugh a lot, and that in itself was worth the money paid and then some.
What gets me about Eryi’s Action is this: with all the fantastic music, sound, art, controls, character design, level design, etc… why did
choose to make the game like this? A game designed to be so hard it will stop many people being able to enjoy it. A niche game that misses out on a potentially huge audience. It’s immediately clear that a lot of effort when into getting it just right, so why not make it a full-on plat-former and keep the over-the-top traps as a B-Type game for hardcore players who want a greater challenge? I suppose time and effort are limited and in the end this was a good solution, but I for one would love to see a return of Eryi in a more forgiving world, if only so more people could enjoy it.

Gigantic Army is pretty cool, I guess.
Remember the 90's? I do, because back then I lived in a house. Apparently almost every indie developer remembers the 90's as well, but I digress. But unlike most of those games that look like a strange pixely butchery of what SNES and Genesis games actually looked like, Gigantic army looks like something you could actually get in cartridge form, which is neat.
Gigantic Army starts in the year 2009, the same year I found out who my real dad is, and then regretted finding out who my real dad is. Humanity, having discovered warp travel at the turn of the 21st century, goes about it's business doing what humanity does best. That is to say tenderly loving any other species that happens to get in our way.
You are a pilot of an MCR, that's a fancy name for giant robot that may or may not be a VOTOM. Your duty as the ground pounders of the Terran Defense Force is to drop on the home planet of the Romulans,  I mean the Ramulons, I mean the Klingons, no wait I got it the second time.
I think.
At the start of the game you choose a main weapon and a special weapon before going about your business of killing everyone that doesn't look like you. And what you get for this is a pretty sweet side scrolling mech game that should probably be on a MS-DOS PC or a Super Nintendo.
Seriously, they even got that whole Mode-7 thing going on, it's really cool.
I'm told the game plays like Cybernator or Assault Suits Valken, two games I've never actually played before because I live behind a convenience store and yell at passerby's. What do you want from me?
But like a SNES game, it's short but kind of challenging. It can be beaten in around an hour or so if you don't constantly get your teeth smashed in by one of the few cool bosses that out class you in every way but still get punched into mulch by your MCR's giant piston wang.
Your MCR, the Saladin
, moves like a giant battle robot should. It's clunky, heavy, and makes a satisfying BOOM whenever it lands on the ground. It's also slow and only has a short quick-dash to get from place to place a tad quicker.
Your weapons can include an assault rifle, a shotgun (called the riot gun), and a grenade launcher as well as your choice of missile spam to ruin someone's day.
But should you play Large Posse?
For 6 dollars? It's not that bad, I'd say get it on sale though. If you're hankering for some good ol fashion 90's mech shooting, then here you go. It's a SNES game in PC form, the story is simple, the gameplay is easy to pick up, and the bosses are pretty cool. It's a time waster if anything.

Quite a fun tower defense game, it looks good, and it is fun to play, overall I'd Recommend it.
However there were a few problems I had with the game,
1. The main guys voice acting is somewhat silly, or at least doesn't flow well
2. music is a bit reppetitive, its not bad just not a lot of veriety

✔
Hero defence was clearly designed by someone who knows their stuff! The choice of colour, and combination of fog with a cartoon environment simply looks awesome! But you can see that from the trailer!
✔
It’s aesthetically pleasing, scales correctly, and just looks and feels great. It doesn’t need any explanation, you just know what everything does, the skill menu especially!
✔
Every action has a different sound, and it’s very noticeable! No corners were cut with the sound design!
✔
Some games start slowly and build up the difficulty, but not in hero defence. Right away, you’re thrown in the deep end, with one moment of concentration loss losing you the game.
✔
It’s very interesting to play a tower defence where you can move your units!
✔
The multiplayer definitely has potential. In short, it’s an extended singleplayer. Instead of playing by yourself, your friend’s singleplayer map is put next to yours so you can see how they’re doing. It has to be said though, there isn’t much time to watch them! It throws you into the end levels regardless of how far through the singleplayer you are.
✔
I definitely saw an option to skip it! It’s such a burden when games don’t offer this functionality!
✖
You have to move your units back and forth a lot. Their range isn’t enough to kill everything from one spot, so you have to shift them along. Then, move them back to the spawn so there’s enough time to kill the next wave. Over and over again.
✖
To move a unit, you left click it, and then right click the location you want them to move to. It took me a while to get the hang of this. There are key binds, but no option to change mouse control, unfortunately!
✖
For the most part, you’ll want to move all your units together! But you can’t select multiple units, so you have to do it individually, which wastes a lot of precious time! Also, units push each other out the way to get past, but the unit that got pushed doesn’t move back after.
✖
Instead of an option list, you’re presented with a burning city. However it’s not obvious as to what each building does. You just have to click them all until you find some gameplay! Floating text would be really helpful!
✖
This isn’t a game you play for the storyline, but even so. All the characters lack empathy or personality, and it all just feels slapped together. The protagonist told a guy who literally just lost his wife to a fire to “mourn her later”.
✖
Enemies don’t move smoothly around corners, they snap quickly, which is very noticeable. The rune inventory is set. It looks like a standard inventory slot system, except you can’t put stuff where you want, everything has a default place. The heroes crossbow arrows come from the hero rather than the bow. Just little details like this that need fixing!
✖
As awesome as some of the voices are, it honestly sounds like it was all recorded by one actor, using different inflections and pitch distortion software.
★
I really would love to experience some more engagement between you and the other player! Maybe a mode where both you and player 2 can move all the units together. Or to prevent exploitation from strangers, maybe you take control of 3 heroes, and they take the other 2.
★
The joy of tower defence is that you can build more and more units! But here you’ll always be stuck with the main characters. If you could rescue citizens for certain levels that you could also control, to help tackle each wave, that would definitely add some replayability!
★
I enjoy doing things quickly. One major issue I had with the skill menu, is that you have to close each skill after upgrading it before selecting the next one. I’d love to be able to click the next skill immediately without needing to close the info!
★
The tutorial mainly consists of clicking on what the arrows tell you to click. However sometimes, it’s easy to miss where the arrows are on screen! Make the rest of the screen darker or something, just to highlight where I’m supposed to be looking!

Back when Call of Duty was actually good. I remember I put so many hours into MW2 with me and my friends on Xbox. The game was literally an addiction for me. So when I transitioned for Xbox to PC, My friends and I grabbed MW2 to relive some memories. And while we did relive our addiction for the game, we noticed a few flaws for the PC port. Now make no mistake. It's still MW2, but note that the PC port feels a bit downgraded than the console versions.
PROS:
-Great story, many twists and well written for what it's worth
-Great gameplay
-Special ops is a great feature, especially co-op
-Great voice acting
-Many weapons
-Many perks and equipment to choose from
CONS:
-Multiplayer is flooded with hackers. I won't hold it against the game's score, but be careful when looking for a match
-Death streaks, many are completely unbalanced
-No controller support. Really Infinity Ward?
-Shotguns are completely overpowered
-Multiplayer is easily exploitable, which can lead to an unbalanced match
Despite minor complaints, this game is truly the last of Old School Call of Duty. Every time my friends and I decide to play a match of SND or TDM, it becomes and competitively tense match with lots of fun every minute. Such a shame how the current games are so focused on catering to the younger audiences with the futuristic garbage instead of taking risks and going back to the modern era or World War 2. However, Call of Duty won't change. Because the money talks. And the series is still successful with millions of dollars rolling in each year. But during each release, I feel more and more bored with the games. Literally feeling like they're trying to make it more complicated than it should be. Hopefully one of the developers will try to make something different in the historical or modern timeline and make something fun, intruiging, and simple like MW2. And then stopping for a few years so the game can have the lifespan it deserves.

- Satisfying kills
- Snipers are pretty useless.  Huzzah.
Cons
- Servers are beyond terrible at the moment.  A lot of "rubber-banding" and flat out disconnecting.
- Not very beginner friendly.  There is a tutorial, but the game lacks a map screen and directive for new players.  Can leave you feeling bewildered.
- KATANA IS OVERPOWERED.  Oh.  My.  God.  The game would be about 5x better if this thing was nerfed.  The maps are rather small and the corners are plentiful, so someone rocking a maxed out Katana can turn a corner and annihilate you in a couple seconds while you scramble to jump and get away, which is damn near futile since the range of the swords seem immense.  My biggest gripe of the game so far... Even worse than the connection issues.
- Some guns just feel useless, and the amount of resources it takes to unlock a new one will leave you running a grindfest for quite the while.
- Microooooooo traaaaaansaaaaactiooooooooooons.  Booooooo.
Overall, I feel as if the game shouldn't have been released yet.  The connection issues and the occassional glitch are rather overwhelming at times, and the weapon balancing is poor.  For a "Shooter".... The melee weapon sure is the primary choice of almost everyone.  If you buy this, expect at least 60%+ of a lobby to be running swords.  That's if you can connect and stay in a game, anyways.
6/10.

While at the time of my review, I did not have a lot of playtime (about 2 hours or so), I'm already having a fair amount of fun.
Now, while I recommend the game, it does have some issues, but it does not stop the enjoyment I get out of the game so far.
The controls, especially while running or driving, are a bit odd. If you move the mouse, it reacts, oddly. The good news however, is that you do not really need to move the mouse during those. It is an odd control scheme, considering all other fighting/driving games use the camera differently during those actions, but it's not bad per say, simply different.
One small issue if you have an azerty keyboard, car hijacking while driving is mapped to Q by default. While movements will correctly assign themselves to ZQSD, the Q remains for hijacking while driving, which of course means every time you try to turn left, if a car is in range, you'll hijack it. It can however be remapped just fine in the options under the driving bit :), so not a major issue once you know about it. On the plus side, it was amusing to see my toon open the door every time I turned left...
The graphic art is a bit strange, while it's fairly nice, it has a slightly odd look to it that I can not define, but it does seem to work just fine.
The vehicles are on what I call easy mode. There seems to be very few (if any) loss of control, considering the rain and the speed, it is a bit unrealistic, but then again, I'm not playing this game to have a realistic feel.
I can not really judge the story, since at the moment I'm really at the beginning, and I spent most of my time running over pedestrians, beating pedestrians to a pulp to get a bit more familiar with the controls during fights (since most die quickly, and with little fight, they're a bit like statues you can kill kinda).
The fighting controls are slightly different from what I'm used to:
Left click to strike, E to parry, F to grab (and throw), shift + left click to jump kick. There might be other things, but I did not go deep in it yet.
There are many collectibles it seems, and since there are 40 briefcases, which seems to have 5K in it everytime,  and you just need to run over parking meters to steal the cash (I could not find a way to do it on foot, unfortunately), money probably won't be a big problem in the game.
I'm not yet familiar with the level ups, but there seem to be 4 areas, cops, gangsters, face recognition (popularity with the common people from the look of it), and health upgrade. I'm not sure if there's any customization to be done in those area, or if all will be available in a single game play. There are quite a few awards in game, on top of steam achievements. One of them being "safe driver". It's simple, it counts the time you drive, without hitting anything. I do mean anything, as hitting the pavement seems to reset the counter if you are going at max speed, as does going on the other side of the road on freeways (making a tiny jump).
There's a social leader board, where all your friends playing the game will show up. Which is a nice plus, without being a constraint or anything.
I also forgot to mention that your fights are rated. The rating seem to include style, in some fashion, and how well you're doing. If you counter, then do a combo (which so far are very easy), you get more points. You also have some interactions with the environment (fairly brutal kills in general), which gives you more points, but also frighten/intimidate enemies, making your HP regenerate slightly faster during fights, which I thought was a rather good way to implement fear (by making the fight a bit easier), without the mobs running like scarred chickens (although if you are really brutal, the last enemies do seem to stop fighting - not sure if this is normal or a bug, but I killed them anyway, just to be safe).
You can of course, steal cars, motorcycles, etc. You can also ram other cars (or people if you wish). The cops so far have the IQ of a sleeping statue, but I'm expecting as your level wanted climbs, their IQ increases a bit. I somehow managed to block a car, but simply pushing it in a wall. They never backed or got out of the car. There does seem to be a possibility of knocking off drivers by ramming cars, so it could be why, I will have to try again to see if that is what happened or not I guess. Ramming cars a lot, will eventually make them go BOOM.
You also get "streaks" of , well, virtually anything so far... Amount of pedestrians ran over, amount of cars disabled in a row, amount of flying kicks in a row, amount of kills in a row, and I'm sure more will come in time ^_^.
Basically, it's like GTA4, but in china, with a lot more jumping and kicking, kung fu, and what not.
I expect a lot of hours and fun on this one.

The main aesthetics for this game are challenge and submission. It's a puzzle game (challenge) and it's repetitive enough that it's a good time waster (submission). The mechanics are simple as you just trace a path with your mouse and the line follows. The music is pretty soothing and something about the sound effects are pretty satisfying to hear, especially if you run your mouse down a line quickly.
The game has 4 levels of difficulty and each level has a lot of puzzles. It's easy to get to the advance levels pretty quickly and there are about 60 advanced puzzles, so there isn't a lack of things to do.
Pros:
+ They advertise a puzzle game with a simple mechanic and that's exactly what you get.
+ Difficulty tiers all have numerous puzzles so there's plenty to solve at your desired difficulty
+ Sound effects are fun. Music is soothing, though a little sleep inducing because it's so calm
Cons:
- Eventually you'll run out of levels (though there are specific achievements for specific puzzles)
- I have a short attention span so this isn't going to be a game that I'll play for a long time.
In short, if you want a simple puzzle game that has varying levels of difficulty and you like what the screenshots have, then this is a pretty nice game to have.

An incredibly simple mind-bending puzzle game that will draw you in and take all of your free time. After picking it up, I had trouble putting down, even when frustrated with the later puzzles.
The game itself is fairly easy to understand, and the basic mechanics are easy to grasp. However, despite the simplicity of understanding the game, mastering it is a completely different story. The game starts you off on the Beginner difficulty, but as you progress you will eventually unlock Easy, Medium, and then Advanced. The puzzles in Beginner are easy to understand and can be solved in minutes, but as more mechanics of the game are revealed to you (namely neutral tiles and crossing lines), the puzzles start to suck away more and more time. Some of the Advanced puzzles eventually ended up taking hours of my time as I struggled to figure out what to do. Despite the difficulty, they remained enjoyable.
The achievements, for all of those that enjoy 100%ing games, are split between two different kinds: complete X number of puzzles of a certain difficulty, and completing a certain puzzle in a certain way. The second type of achievement listed is actually a ton of fun to go for, as it requires you to go back to a familiar puzzle and look at it in a new way. These special challenges presented through the achievements gives you even more time with the game, although obviously not required to do so.
Overall, Unium is a complete blast to play and your time will disappear before you know what's happening. For the low price tag, even if you complete the Beginner/Easy puzzles, you'll be incredibly satisfied with the purchase. Unium is a fantastic, beautiful puzzle game that everybody should give a try at least once.

Darkarta a broken hearts Quest Collectors Edition comes with the main Game, a bonus chapter, some extras & an integrated comic book. HOWEVER the Soundtrack is not included and is available on steam for purchase for more then the base game.
Before we begin here is a little information about who made this game:
TuttFrutti Studios which have been "working" their way up from Greenlight with promising game keys and other Methods finally made it into the Steam Store. Looking besides that I thought why is a game this beautiful in need of such shady methods? Well let me tell you.
Before we begin with the actual bad parts lets appreciate the beautiful Art this game is giving you. The colours are vibrant and beautiful, which in my eyes is always a huge plus. Another Plus was the Fast Travel Option. However this is all of the positive that I can give you.
The Game itself is badly translated and the Story is awfully explained. I can see what this developer was trying to go for, but the way it was put together, is not only making any sense but also seems like different kinds of people just threw in their own style of translating and then left it at that.
You would also think that before publishing the game someone must off read the translation before releasing it. Yet I keep finding not just awfully translated sentences but also horribly spelled wrong words or even double words such as "the The Guardian".
Some people might not be bothered by this and trust me if it would be just a one time thing I wouldnt mind, but it was not just a one time thing. Infact it was almost on every page including the additonal comic book.
The Hidden Objects Scenes are either way so unseeable that you need to search for hours or so easy that you are done within a couple of seconds. Whilst I played other HOP Games which were challenging in that part, this did not seem the case here.
The Characters in this Game were also rather confusing as most of them had similiar names and didnt look that much different from each other, which half of the time gave me trouble understanding what even was going on and thanks to the not well explained / translated diary it was even harder to see what was going on. Some of the Characters are just one hit wonders and you never ever see them again either.
The Voice acting was acceptable but nothing too special.
All in all this Game was overhyped and is very unpolished, I believe that TuttiFrutti Interactive should off worked harder on the game rather on doing shady advertising buisness.
Another thing that annoys me and irritates me at the same times is that this is called the Collectors Edition and the game itself is 6€. Yet the Soundtrack is not included and you will have to buy it for an additional 10€ off steam. Generally Soundtracks are included into Collectors Editions and if they are available for seperate purchase on Steam they are never more expensive then the base game. I am not sure what this is all about.
One more thing I'd like to mention is that the Developer has been paying people to give out good reviews for this Game which I beg you please do not look at.
Do I recommend this Game? No. I would recommend it once the Developer has taken the Problems into consideration and revamped their Game to what it could off been and not what it currently is.
