is a 2D hidden object puzzle adventure game fueled by the story of a mother searching for her kidnapped child and accented with Indian mythology and beauty. This is Tuttifrutti Interactive’s first game to appear on Steam -the platform I used to play this game on my computer- however this does not appear to be their first game. Either way, I was attracted to the title because of my love for hidden object games, henceforth referred to as HOGs. The game showed much promise and caused some buzz among fans of this genre though I jumped in with no bias, ready to have a fun time.
You step into the role of Mary who is both a wife and mother as well as a Harvard graduate, nice life if I do say so myself. Your family of three is on a boat sailing to a remote island after an invitation from your previously-assumed-to-be dead grandfather. Tragedy strikes as your boat is attacked by Darkarta and your daughter Sophia is taken away. With your husband now injured, Mary alone must save her beloved offspring as well as uncover the truth about herself, her family and why she was brought there in the first place. Your journey to save Sophia will take Mary to many different locations, from beautiful islands with Indian mystique to even the underworld itself.
Mary is determined to save her child, no matter what the risk, and the game makes sure to remind us of this constantly. Many cutscenes are just of Sophia crying and asking for her mama and Mary restating her resolve to find her child. The mother searching for her child is a common and very overused trope with HOGs so I wasn’t to impressed with the choice to go down that route here. The game does try to add variety by also mixing in the story of doomed lover Ameeha and Anantha as well as linking the two to Mary’s past life. The story does get a bit convoluted in terms of this, Mary is shown as a very nice woman and caring mother but the entire game is really a product of bad choices her past self made and lingering curses. I felt slightly insulted that because of actions in a past life now Mary is suffering and an innocent child is kidnapped and about to be killed, everything seemed like a melodramatic soap opera. However, I did not dislike the story and I did feel invested in seeing it until its conclusion despite it being predictable.
Whatever this game lacks in story it makes up for with gameplay. This title offers a striking amount of variety that isn’t often seen in HOGs. There are a lot of puzzles in this game that offer a decent level of challenge to players. Some are pretty easy and others will require you putting on your thinking cap, however I didn’t find myself frustrated with any of them. Another plus are the hidden object scenes, while I would have personally enjoyed having more of these in the game, you do get a good variety of them and none are revisited which is always a plus. While there are a few of your standard scenes where you’re given a list of items to find some border on actual puzzles themselves. Having to find certain items, put them in the right spot, move items around and a lot more. There aren’t many “simple” scenes in this game, players will either enjoy this or be disappointed. I for one was happy with the assortment of challenges.
Since this is a point and click game, players need only use a mouse to get through to the end. You click on characters to chat with them, you click on items to interact with them as well and of course for the puzzles and hidden object scenes. You have an inventory to hold items you find, some items you need to take a closer look and even combine with other items, a feature I personally enjoy. Another bonus point, you can lock the menu and keep it from minimizing. This is minor but I really love when HOGs have this feature. You have a map that allows quick teleporting, a journal that keeps track of what you’ve done so far and has interesting nuggets from Mary’s perspective about the story. There are morphing objects to collect as well as memories of Sophia which manifest as items lying around the scenery. Another nice feature, if you’re not a fan of hidden object scenes or find yourself stuck, you can opt out and do a match three mini game instead.
Even at a casual glance, it’s obvious that the graphics for this game are excellent. The backgrounds and scenery in this game are beautifully done with lively colors and great attention to details. HOGs in general have really improved in this category and this game proves that it can compete with titles by more experienced and well known developers. The hidden object scenes themselves are where this is most important, as they look like total chaos and clutter but also must be able to function and not leaves players on a frustrated search for items. The scenes in this game rise to challenge, I had no issues and didn’t even have to squint much to find any item. The characters are also well done as are the cutscenes, though animations while speaking are a bit hit or miss and I personally found Sophia to look very odd and unappealing. Audio wise things are fine, the music isn’t memorable but it helps set the atmosphere well as does the wealth of ambient noise around you. The game has voice acting as well which is full of emotion and for the most part enhances the game. While I do admit that there are some cases of overacting, I think this is also tied to the melodramatic nature of the plot as I mentioned earlier.
Fans of hidden object games need look no further,
is a solid addition to your library. It’s also a good title for newcomers to test out, especially given the amount of variety in puzzles and hidden object scenes. There is also a bonus chapter which wraps up the events of the main storyline, however, this was very short and while it did give resolution to the main story it didn’t add much overall. Being a collector’s edition, there a lot of bonuses besides the addition chapter, you also have a comic book that acts as a prequel, you have access to the soundtrack and can look at visuals from the game as well as replay puzzles or hidden object scenes if you like. Another nice feature, if you're ever stuck, the game comes with a strategy guide as well. On Steam, this title has many achievements to go after and it also as trading cards. This is a very solid game and I recommend it wholeheartedly.

Pretty sure this is the best HO game I've played. Cost more than I usually pay for them, but I don't regret it at all. I really didn't want it to end. In fact, the only thing which is stopping me starting over immediately is that I want to forget it a bit before starting again.
Some people watch TV while they eat. I often play HOPs instead. Because they are not time-dependant, are pretty relaxing, and you can usually just pick one up, play a bit, then leave it for another time. I'm almost reluctant to call them 'puzzles' actually, as most don't really require much brain-power or logic to solve. They're 'puzzles' in the jigsaw sense. It's mostly time-filler. But relaxing and entertaining still, if you like that kind of thing.
But with Darkarta I found myself enjoying it so much I pretty-much didn't stop playing until it was finished.
I felt the story starts off pretty generic and a bit naff, although it does get better towards the end. But the story isn't why I play HOPs.
The puzzles here are really very good. Not hard; not even mind-blowingly original. But clever and very well put-together. Even the cookie-cutter HOP staples have been added to, or have extra twists which make them feel fresh. I played through as much in anticipation of what they'd come up with next as enjoying the puzzles themselves.
Works nice in HD (which many don't) and graphics are beautifully done. (The cut-scenes are a bit rough around the edges, but I can live with that. I actually find it pretty amazing that in-game GFX can actually be
now than pre-rendered sequences.)
Oh; and one other thing I really liked. It's never made any sense at all to me why someone in the middle of such an adventure as this should discard an obviously useful item like a knife or a box of matches after only one use. Only to have to solve a similar problem later. (Or why they can't simply return to where they left them and pick them up again, for that matter.) In Darkarta, you occasionally get to use an item multiple times for different things. It's still not quite true-to-life, but it's a solid step in the right direction.
From a new developer this is a fantastic achievement. I suspect that when you start off in something like this you actually think a bit more carefully about what you are doing, rather than churning out endless slight variations on the same theme. If that is the case, then
continue with more of the thinking, less of the churning! :)
Edit: it seems since I got it, it's dropped considerably in price. So now definitely worth picking up.

To begin with I am not one to have made a lot of concise reviews and am looking forward to that changing, with that in mind please bear some mishaps in style here and there. I will try to make it rather short, but still give enough inforomation about the title !
To begin with I am not a great fan of the HOG(Hidden Object Games) genre and was absurdly sceptical about the title despite the postive reviews and recommendations from many HOG players.
is exactly what such a game needs to be from the initial minutes, its menus are intuitive and easy to use.
Again, as a skeptic towards the genre I do not expect too much of a story, but honestly speaking this one despite being among the somewhat an overused "something/somebody is lost, we have to find the thing/the person" the little notches to eastern mythology was both a freshening and nice experience and it did not feel too forced, especially the way it was presented.
Still, there are a lot of times when I was thinking isn't my character falling a little too often, from a little too high, a little too many times without any serious scratch. Despite some moments the character felt a little more resilient than a normal human being, that left a bad taste for a small while, the story progresses nice and is both entertaining and interesting.
Unusually beautiful and detailed HOG without the feeling of "the artist tried to fit too much things". Everything felt quite modest and the cutscenes were just amazingly rendered.
As far as cutscenes go though, going towards the end, when we start learning more about the other characters, those cutscenes felt a little too much, to the point where once it was - a puzzle or maybe two, rather fast - cutscene. This adds to storytelling, but gladly it seems like the devs realized that at some point and decided to make shorter cutscenes and on larger intervals.
Voice acting is one of the best found in the genre in the recent years if not in the top 10 of all times. The music felt right at many places, but sometimes I felt like it needed a little more in the more darker, scarier places.
After all, who doesn't like music which makes the eerie feeling of being alone in the creepy forest/cave/etc. just a little better.
In all honesty, most of the times I was focused on fidning a specific thing or solving yet another puzzle, but the times I heard the music, it just always felt like it needs a little more.
The diversity of the games and the option for some puzzles to be played in a Match 3 was something I found very interesting and noted to myself that this might be used if I find something too hard. Gladly I almost never got to Match 3 as the puzzles are always pulling the player towards solving them instead.
Despite that near the end some of the puzzles feel rather the same one after another, it is well done story-wise which is a definite plus, despite the feel of doing the same task 3 times in a row(Whoever reached the final chapter will know !).
Still the very colored and detailed world of Darkarta manages to mesmerize the player and pull him in again and again. If only I had more free time I would gladly do the playthrough in a single sitting.
You will notice that it seems like a package of two games but the second is more like the epilogue of the whole story but I strongly recommend to play through it too as it is rather short.
Some minor bad things(CONS), at least as far as my opinion goes is:
- Set at a video resolution that seems that can't be changed.(through menu)
- Some repetitive puzzles especially towards the end.
- Would feel too noob-friendly to old-time HOGers(which is a plus to people like me !)
There is something called Price-Entertainment Value, and in this case it the entertainment factor is too high to talk abuse of this factor :P
If we had to put a rating of this game in percentages it would be
and a must try-out(you can download the demo !) of every HOGer !

DISCLAIMER: I received this product for no cost for the purpose of reviewing. However, this does not affect my views and opinions of the game.
Darkarta: A Broken Heart's Quest is a 2D point-and-click, hidden object adventure. The game was developed by TuttiFrutti interactive and is their first title on Steam. The player assumes the role of Mary, a wife and mother of one. During a family trip to meet Mary's long lost grandfather, and only remaining family member, Mary's daughter; Sophie was abducted by a mythical immortal man. As Mary and her husband wash up on the shore of their destination, Mary's husband is in need of medical attention, leaving Mary to scour the land, looking for her missing daughter while solving puzzles and learning more about this strange situation along the way.
--------

The graphic assets of hidden object games are quite important. Striking a balance between having a presentable scene, with interact-able objects, and having the scene not seem so cluttered, is key. Fortunately, the game does a good job of striking this balance. The object fields are very pleasing to the eyes and have a good amount of detail. The game's scene's don't feel too cluttered, yet can still provide a challenge in locating hidden objects.
In terms of the actual visuals, the objects and scenery within the game are quite high quality. The character design is also quite decent though some of the character's interactions/animations, such as talking, are quite strange looking, and the game may have been better without these small animations. The game runs perfectly fine on any CPU and GPU as it is not a very demanding title.
--------

The sound assets are well done. The music within the game changes depending on the situation, and where the player is. The soundtrack is good and combined with the environmental noises of the game, add to the atmospheric experience.  The voice acting in the game is also well done. The voice actor's bring a good sense of emotion to their roles and actually enhance the game's experience.
--------
The mechanics of a hidden objects game are very simple, the player must find certain objects within a scene in order to progress. This title does this and does it well, though in addition to this, it also has a good amount of enjoyable puzzles, object-matching, and sequencing challenges. It stands out a bit above other hidden object titles and although many of the puzzles aren't that difficult, they are enjoyable and satisfying.
Many of the puzzles will have the player clicking, moving, sliding, and pushing around objects in certain orders. Though depending on the difficulty level of the game, the player can utilise hints or even skip puzzles altogether. This allows players of all different skill types to participate in these puzzles (or not).
--------
This is a very different hidden object game from what I've experienced in the past. That being said, I don't usually play that many of them, I think of titles in this genre as games like; "I Spy", or "Where's Waldo?", with nothing more than finding the hidden object. This title goes a little above and beyond, and in addition to locating objects, you also get puzzles and other nice little mini games thrown in. As someone who isn't very good at puzzles, and kind of dislikes them, I actually enjoyed these and had a good time with them, despite spamming the "hint" button and even skipping a few of them. Though the freedom to do those things is really nice.
My only real complaint with the game is that the opening scene with the little girl crying, and actually all of the mouths moving, looked really strange to me, and made me feel uncomfortable. It's a very minor gripe and doesn't hamper the game-play in anyway, but it's still stuck out as something very strange to me, though this also many have been intentional.
Thanks to the devs for giving me the opportunity to review the game, as well as anyone who took this review into consideration, I hope it helped.

An incredibly fun mecha game, Gigantic Army brings me back to the days of playing action-packed sidescrollers on the Genesis, PSX, or Saturn. The weapons feel good to use, and it's simple to just pick up and play. It's not an extremely deep experience, but it's the polished controls that keep me coming back. This game just feels good to play. I highly recommend it if you're looking for a nostalgic run & gun 2D platformer, and/or you have a mecha fetish.

Gigantic Army is an arcade style run and gun shooter characterized by its attempt to emulate the heavy, powerful feeling of a gigantic mech suit.
The first thing you will notice about GA is that your mech stomps along at a somewhat slow speed. Your jumps too,  also feel heavy and weighed down, even with your jetpack which allows you to continuously ascend further upward by holding down the jump button. All your weapons (including the proximity based melee attack) are balanced in some way too to be more methodical in use, some having brief reload times or requiring to be precisely fired with your 360 degree aim. You also have a ground dash, but it has quite some acceleration and must be used carefully. Lastly,  there's the shield which can block enemy fire, but using it requires careful timing and planning as it cannot be brought up mid air, or immediately after landing or firing.
Do these limitations make Gigantic Army feel slow paced? Not at all. GA shows that player move speed and pacing are two completely different things, and that seemingly cumbersome controls can feel profoundly smooth once fully mastered. While your mech may at first seem like a big clunky hunk of junk, mastering the subtle physics and techniques of jet packing, landing, and dashing will allow you to pull off rad dodges and close calls as you blast enemies.
The level and boss design is also quite solid, with the bosses being a major highlight and the most enjoyable part of the game. The levels offer great variety, making up for your slow move speed by being tailored around quick dashes, jumps, and fending off enemies from both sides. They also do a great job of mixing things up with frequent mini boss encounters. The bosses, especially the later ones, are the real show stealers though. Each of them has a number of attacks which are tricky to dodge whether on the ground or in the air, and will have you weighing the strategic benefits of attempting to out space them on the ground or out maneuver them in the air, two options that require very different technique but are both challenging and rewarding.
The game does a good job in terms of replayability, too. There are two extra difficulties, which feature much more challenging bullet dodging action, and the game has a scoring system in which you are rewarded a bonus for how fast you can speed run stages. Each of the three available weapons also causes you to use a slightly different playstyle, so attempting to master the game with all three should add a lot of replay value for anyone who enjoys the game enough to do so.
I generally prefer more nimble, ninja like controls for my action games, but Gigantic Army shows that a methodical, heavy metal shooter can provide an awesome change of pace.

So by this time you should know it's pay to play. You pay for ammo, you pay for gear. You can't even figure out which direction the wind is travelling in without paying for a spray. I'm not reviewing that aspect, although the model seems to be working for the company, it's probably holding back what would be a 90% positive game if it just went fully subscription based. As it stands, you subscribe you can hunt everything, but it won't give you any of the gear to hunt the specific animals, which means you'll be forking out you money or grinding missions to get any decent gear.
That being said, my 75 minutes with the game was fun. I've been watching Steve Rinella on Netflix, and had an itch for a hunting game. Unable to buy the newest game in the series, I was left with this one. The tutorial pretty much covers everything you need to know about tracking animals (Although it doesn't talk about camoflage, scent or wind direction). Tracks or clues come up in a red spot on the ground, which are easy to spot. My first tracks I found, (four different set to be exact) where Mule Deer, which I believe used to be in the free rotation. Lamenting my loss of hunting a Muley, I kept moving east, occasionally hitting my Deer Call. A call sounded out behind me, another Muley, and I kept moving to a red dot on the map through open fields. About 500M from my starting area, a call sounded to my North East, and I found some White Tail tracks. Annoyingly, when I found some other deer tracks, it began tracking another Mule Deer. This is pretty annoying that everytime you select a track, it loses the animal you were just tracking, and the Deer tracks to me, all look the same.
I hit another call, and suddenly something calls back. I check my GPS and the call is close. Really close. I crouch down as a large 8 pointer white tail moves over the hill towards me. Everything the game has told me so far tells me stay patient, wait for a good side lung shot. But I also have no idea which direction the wind is travelling, and I'm not camoflaged. Still standing, I take aim, hold breathe with space bar (what kind of game developer uses space bar as hold breathe?!) and aim for the chest, right of his sternum. I fire, and he turns and runs. At this point I'm certain I only wounded the animal and I'm upset that I rushed the shot. I curse myself, and move over the hill ready to track the wounded white tail. I find a blood trail, atleast I hit him. Then about ten metres down the hill my average sized 8 pointer is laying dead. I cheer, not expecting to even see a white tail I bagged a pretty good one. I take a couple of screen shots, and a trophy photo. My first kill scored a 162, not an insane score. After collecting the tag, the read out showed exactly where I hit it, lung and liver, he ran for about 2 seconds before dropping, the shot was 81M. If a hunter told you he bagged something like this in real life on his first trip fifteen minutes into a hunt, well, you wouldn't believe him that's for sure.
So happy enough I tagged one animal, I begin my calls and walking East again. Not long after there's another call to my North. I hit my call a couple more times and a smaller four pointer walks over the hill, giving me a good side on shot. I aim just above the shoulder, and back a little. I was pretty sure from my last successful kill that the wind was behind the buck, but again I didn't waste much time. I hit the young buck and he shot off, confused as to how he managed to drive off after what looked like a direct hit, I walked over the hill to find it. This one only scored 59. The kill was clean, he ran for about 2 seconds, and fell there.
So finally, is the game good? Yes. Is it worth a subscription, maybe. The game is scructured around a pay to play model, if you want to walk out like I did, make a few calls and hunt white tail with pretty much no idea what the hell you're doing, go nuts. I got really lucky. My hunt was exciting and I bagged a very respectable buck. I saw a heap of Pheasant too, which are also on the 'Free to play list' although I didn't have a shotgun. Subscribing won't pay for unlimited rounds either, bullets cost about 30 cents to a dollar for ten rounds.
It's a fun game, it's not fast paced, and it's certainly challenging in the free to play mode. I'll give it a thumbs up, but I wouldn't suggest paying for it unless you're really to spend a heap of money.

is among the best games ever made.  Its first xpac is an insulting, lazy, step backwards, and is on par with the rest of the early access garbage released on Steam nowadays, the 2nd xpac is even worse.

It also changed the quick & mobile ranged classes into non-mobile cast-time mage-equivalents.  The original classes offered great variety in playstyle, aside from Monk and Dragoon being similar. In all my years of RPG and MMO gaming, I have never seen a more pretentious story as the one here in FF.
Let me break down every single story mission in the game. You will watch some cutscenes, all awkward, all alien with the emotions being strange and foreign when translated to English, there will be a big powerful enemy to fight, but you will not fight him. Instead, your companion who was introduced in the cutscenes, will fight him, acting as a tank, DPS, and healer on in one, while you try your best to fight the minions, while not trying so hard as you actually take on to much DPS, where the god mod NPC cant heal you while fighting the boss.  If you think that sounds to idiotic to be true, It sadly isnt. You get to watch some NPC, save the day, while they will thank you for helping them out, even though your contribution was pitiful at best.
Its almost as if Square was trying to tell a far more interesting story, with far more interesting characters then you (I mean who the hell are you anyway?) and decided to instead tell lots of these little, more interesting stories about actual heroes, not your pathetic excuse of a plot cog. Your main characters special power, is LITTERALLY reliving cutscenes!!! You have the power to see things, that have happened because... reasons. So you spend alot of your time reliving the past through cutscenes, while this pretentious♥♥♥♥♥plot, force feeds you exposition! This is the laziest, sloppiest writing Ive seen in an MMORPG, AN MMORPG! They dont even need a good plot, they just need a decent premise to work, but this one fights you, this one is trying to make you feel as meaningless as possible, and not in a grand scale way, but in a "Im not even the main character of these stories!" kind of way.

Which is quite puzzling, because the game is so bright and friendly, and has some of the best emotes and head tracking, I mean the lips move when you type dialogue, its great! But... they decided to do this odd instanced thing, so the game ends up being very unfriendly to people wanting to talk to friends, its bizarre.
Game has housing, does it handle it well? Nope, you guessed it. Housing is tied to guild management, so only the old, long standing guilds have plots, so you have to join them to have a house. Want to make your own guild and own a house? Uh... to bad I guess. Why do I say this? Because there's only so many plots... they could have made infinite mirror plots... but decided only a few were enough. Guess what? There's a huge shortage of houses, not enough to go around, and like I said, this could be fixed... but they decided not too. Good job, you give us housing, but then take it away through miss management in the same breath.
Gameplay/Combat: You will be BEGGING to play WoW, after a few days of leveling. Every class that Ive played (Pugilist/monk, lancer, Rogue, Gladiator, Maurauder, and the healer, whatever it was called.) Was... BORING. Boring at the best of times, nonsensical at the worst. Take the Pugilist for example, how would FF screw up a ki using fist fighter who can self heal and fight fully armed and armored bad guys with only their fists? Well, make him a leather armor wearing back stabber, thats how. They spend alot of their time performing the same button combos (They try to pass this off as a unique game mechanic, but it means you literally HAVE to use your moves in a certain combination, making it even more rigid/boring) over and over again, switching from the rear, and side of their enemy to maximize damage/status effects. What if your fighting solo? Well then, all your moves will do less damage!
Because... your a martial artist! Why would you ever fight an opponent face to face? I mean, remember in Dragon Ball Z when Goku snuck up behind Freeza and smacked him a thousand times while Krillain distracted him? Me to, what a hero. No but, they seemed to have completely missed the point, what a monk in these types of games are... they are not ROGUES, Rogues back stab, they have daggers, right?  Wrong! Rogues do just as much damage from the front, as the back! They actually are better for solo fighting then a monk... what is wrong with this picture? What kind of logic is this, where the sneaky rogue with daggers fights face to face, but the martial artist monk, sneaks around and punches them in the back. Its called "Back stab" for a reason, the reason is if you slide a dagger into someones back when their not looking, its pretty much game over. Not back... punch barrage...
In short, this game is for Final Fantasy addicts. If you love all things Final Fantasy, you wont even see these glaring faults, and you'll love every second of it. For the rest of us who have played other, far better MMO's, this one will either fall short, or go out of its way to annoy you.

For starters, I want to say that I've beaten this game once so far (617 deaths), and I liked it. Thus comes the question: "Would I recommend it?" The short answer is "maybe, if you like stupid hard games." But, please, allow me to try to explain my reasoning.
Let's begin thinking about Eryi's Action in terms not as a piece of merchandise you (likely) have to hand over a specified amount of money to get your hands on, but as something that was made to entertain its users, or, in other words, let's think about it as "art", if you will, for a little bit. Around the internet (YouTube and Reddit, mostly) I've found people slamming this game because they think that the level design is flawed, not because it's hard as all ♥♥♥♥, but because it's difficulty usually stems from that which very easily feels like cheating: Spikes that come out of  the ground without previous warning that there might be such a thing in that area, those same spikes that jump at you if you initially evade them but stand there for a little too long, blocks that you can get stuck on and shot at or disintegrate when you try to stand on them, masses of solid ground that move so you fall into a pit... Compared to other games like Super Meat Boy or the Binding of Isaac, where you can see the level and are aware of mostly everything before venturing on (enemies and/or traps), and if you die it's entirely your fault and not because the game tricked you, it's clear that Eryi's Action doesn't follow the conventions games with similar difficulty level share. In this one, if you don't already know what's ahead, you will die. And you need to die in order to learn what you have to do to advance. It's a lot of trial and error.
It's true that sometimes it feels like it pulls cheap tricks to kill you, but does that make it "a bad game"?, or, changing the question a little, is it "flawed"? As I see it, no. At least not in terms of level design. The creators did exactly what they wanted in order to make the player fail numerous times in different ways. It feels like they created fairly standard levels that you'd find in the initial stages of old Mario games, then went back and proceeded to rig them with traps of all kinds. It's made to play with your expectations of what a level should do and to make you doubt of what you see or can't see. But once you have the knowledge to pass that part, it depends on your skills.
This isn't a game that's hard only for the sake of being hard. Every time you die you can tell what killed you and why, the puzzles you encounter are never random. Pure chance doesn't have a place in this game. To beat this you need skill, patience and simple abilities to memorize traps. If you don't finish this game it's not because it's an irredeemable cheating sack of♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's because you quit... or forgot you have it.
Some have called it a "deconstruction" or a "parody" of the genre, and to that I say: There are movements in the world of arts that go contrary to each other, and if videogames can truly be considered "art", then I fail to see a reason for that to not apply to videogames as well. In other words, I agree.
Now, back to the real world, videogames are made by an industry that feeds off of money, and in this case it's your money. At the end of the day, as much as you want to call a game "art," it's a product usually made to produce money for whoever developed it, and to do that it has to be entertaining. That brings us to the question: Is the amount of entertainment enough for your dough? I honestly don't know.
I did not buy this game, it was a gift. Someone I follow on Twitter posted "Who wants Eryi's Action?", I replied with "I don't know what that is, but I do" and now it's in my library. But no matter how I got it, this game is not free, it cost someone 5 USD, and down here in México that's enough to take the bus and get a cheap meal. I've already said that I enjoyed this game, even if I found it frustrating at times, but it's
. With 7 levels and 4 bosses you can finish it in one lazy afternoon when you have nothing to do. The cute graphics, although they helped make my frustration a lot bearable (in my case), are not of uniform quality. Having some sprites (like Eryi's) being well animated but all of the bosses having very few animations is weird and jarring. Some of the common enemies suffer from that too, like the flames that have no animation at all. Overall it looks pretty but at the same time rushed and unpolished.
People have mentioned that this is a game that should be free, but I don't think I can agree. For one thing the developers need to eat; they made a game that I consider short, but at the same time it's packed with a lot of stuff and is fun to play. And on the topic of length, I still don't know if it's a detriment or something that helps it succeed because it doesn't overstay it's welcome.
A big reason why I don't think it'd be good for this game to be free, is because when something has a price attached to it people tend to start paying attention and taking it seriously. As good and awesome as some free games are, if I was told "there's this super hard game that you can download for free over there", I likely would've replied with "eh, I'll check it out later, maybe", then probably proceed to completely forget all about it. But if I was told that there was a really hard platformer that's on the store, and seemed fun in videos, then I would've been interested. It's basic gut feeling, not purely logic, that makes you care about something when your money is potentially involved, even if it's not a lot.*
That's why I can't give it a strong recommendation. Even though I consider it a fun unconventional game, it lacks stuff that could make it
like a complete game. I'd love to see Eryi's Action 2 with better graphics and slightly longer story mode, but at the same time I don't know if that'd be a smart move for the company.
I hope this review helped some of you decide whether to buy it or not. Thank you for reading.
*This is a conclusion I reached after discussing it with a few friends. Hopefully I'm not making a gross and mistaken generalization.

After reading all the reviews I decided to add my own. It will be short.
Transistor is beautifuly hand paint game with a magicaly composed soundtrack. The Gameplay combines turn-based, live, RPG and Isometric facets to create a unique gaming experience. The story is not spoon fed and you are left to ponder the plot as you travel between 'encounters'. These encounters are at, from what i can tell, in set locations along the linear map. Once the encounter begins you cannot leave the area until all enemies are defeated. Despite this the game plows smoothly as you run to through the map.
Through out the game there is no chance for boredom. There are no grinds and clever thinking is required both in combat and when customizing your attack choices, to defeat your enemies. As you progress you unlock new ablities that can be combined in Hundreds of ways to create different attacks that all interact with each other.
This game is certainly not a point and click.
I recommend this game whole heartedly to any one who wants a genuine gaming experience.

I’ve long been a fan of the tower defense genre. I especially love games within the genre that attempt to be innovative, those that attempt to tell a story rather than just spit out increasingly more difficult levels at you and those that possess a high presentation level with a lot of charm. All three do a good job of summarizing Happy Tuesday’s fantastic Steam debut in Hero Defense: Haunted Island. It’s the type of game that I know that I will not be able to get enough of and will find time to play throughout my reviewing and playing of future games for Steamified. It’s just that damn good. I am thoroughly enjoying to the point of loving what I have played thus far.
One of the great things about Happy Tuesday’s game is that they haven’t stopped working on it since launching it into the Steam Early Access program. There have already been six updates and patches to the game since it launched on January 26 (the morning of January 27 in Australia which is what date Steam provides me so if my dates are slightly off for some of you you’ll understand why). They’ve planned for a two month early access period so we’re coming up to just under two weeks from an estimated launch date.
Without a shadow of a doubt the game’s greatest strength is its customization. You can practically play the game, as the descriptor says, the way you want to play it. Of course, there will be those who are such avid players of the game that they will argue that there is one best way to play the game – maximizing all of a certain skill set combined with what they consider to be the best runes, etc. but those of us who are more willing to play the game without spending a lot of time looking at all of the statistics to prove one theory right or wrong have a lot of different avenues to play. I’m not suggesting for a moment that those who do choose to maximize the game are going about it the wrong way as that can achieve a deeper level of enjoyment from the game and I’m certain that Happy Tuesday are hoping that their game has such avid fans.
Another feature that I like is that you can move your heroes around the map to put them into the position that you believe is the most productive. This certainly has a massive impact on the employed strategies. If your enemies move too fast then positioning your heroes at the start of the map can be disastrous because by the time that you react it can be a case of too little too late. However, if your enemies are slow and strong positioning far from the beginning can have the opposite effect – you don’t kill them before they get to the end of their path.
There are five heroes in the game. You begin with Jack Sanders who is a vampire slayer and then you unlock Barrows who is a grisly old gravedigger who has lost his poor wife. Barrows is best against skeletons. The next hero that you’re introduced to is the charming Samantha “Sam” Hain whose a precious little pumpkin thrower and zombie killer extraordinaire. The fourth hero is Jane Doe whose brain was used to create a Frankenstein’s monster. The final unlockable hero is Wylde Halfblood who is half-man and half-wolf so your werewolf character which is pretty cool.
Another thing that I very much enjoyed was the fact that the next level isn’t just given to you upon completion of the last. You have to meet certain criteria to unlock many of the zones in the game. What this means is that you need to unlock a certain amount of stars before advancing. You gain stars by completing levels – one star per successful level completion. For example, the first time that you complete a level you will be awarded a single star for that level. The second time you complete the level you will receive a second star and so on and so forth. This is a very good way of level and area progression.
Speaking of progression each character progresses similarly to how they would in many RPGs. As each character levels up you unlock skill points which you can utilize on a skill tree. Each hero progresses individually and has a number of different arcs that can be upgraded. Thankfully if you feel that at any time your character isn’t performing the best that you think it can you are able to reclaim skill points and redistribute them into the skills that you believe will perform better. As I said previously the customization within the game is incredible.
From a technical perspective I really cannot fault the presentation. The graphics are perfect to capture the feel and aesthetic of the game that the developers had in mind for the game. They allow you the freedom that you desire to navigate throughout each map and add just the right amount of character to the game. The soundtrack and the sound are spotless as well. They aide the game to establish the mood and the ambiance that you would imagine from a horror themed tower defense game. It’s simply a superb game no matter which way you look at it.
Finally, there is an online multiplayer component to be added to the game which I am very much looking forward to. If anyone would like to play together then I am very much welcome to your invitation. There will be unique runes available to be won through the multiplayer mode. The multiplayer was not available at time of review but from the descriptor, below, it appears that it will be a combination of MOBA and tower defense. My only hope is that the game comes without latency issues as coming from Australia some online multiplayer games are impossible to play because of it.
My hope for this game is that when it is feature complete and released out of Early Access that the critics do not ignore the game. It deserves to have its time in the spotlight and I believe that many critics will be pleasantly surprised by how well-developed and polished this game actually is.
An easy recommendation to practically everyone. There is so much for everyone who likes playing video games to enjoy here even if you’re not traditionally a fan of tower defense games.

A surprisingly pleasant take on tower defense games that I ended up enjoying  despute going in worrying about the potential for poor dev practices.
Hero Defense - Haunted Island is a tower defense style game where as opposed to building towers you control a hanful of heroes with thier own strengths that can be moved around the map in order to chase down the last few monsters. I enjoyed this feature since it made for less resetting every time  something got past me. All the usual suspects are here: Pure DPS, Slow effect, AEO, Mellee spawns in the middle of the enemy path, each of the heroes fill a basic purpose within the game that would otherwise be filled by a tower. Beyond that though if you ever played a tower defense game ever you can fill in the blanks on what happens during the defense portions of the game.
In the overworld there's a town on the outside of the level map where you can spend the gold and a secondary currency you earn and level up your heroes like you'd upgrade towers. I have to admit I initially thoughth that the secondary currency was going to be something you wither had to pay for or farm for endless periods of time to get, but I was proven wrong when a few levels in you can construct a bank that becomes your primary means of getting the blue currency by exchanging it for excess gold.
The game runs smoothly and I only had one crash shortly after my first boot of the game. Other than that initial crash it easily stays at 60 frames per second and hardly ever fluxuates for any reason.
If you're willing to turn the audio down and miss out on some corny voice acting and storytelling this makes for an excellent podcast game or something do do while you're waiting for a large download.

Fully customizable classes, smooth fast-paced gunplay and a sharp geometric artstyle, all brought together in a tight game mode with moba elements to keep things dynamic.
For those of you that are afraid of "moba elements", don't worry, there are no towers. The main focus of Titan Mode is fighting for creeps in side lanes, spawn zones, to buff up your giant robot so your giant robot ends up whooping the opposing giant robot. and while the two giant robots fight the players act as support units for their titans, fending off enemy players and attempting to damage the enemy titan and escort their titan to the enemy base core.
It's fast, it requires quick maneouvers, teamwork and keeping a balance between shooting the enemy in the face and buffing the titan. Moreover it's one of those games where a missed shot makes you cringe, because shootouts are tight.
Although there are slight unbalances here and there, nothing radical, nothing that can't be averted by thinking out a different armor and weapon combo. That's the fun in Minimum. A player's character is defined by his headpiece, chestpiece, legpiece and weapon combo. Armor bonuses are extremely varied and promise a host of possible combinations. Weapons fall into several main categories, each playing out differently. There's also a catch: the game has a killstreak system. Each kill upgrades your weapon. The longer you stay alive, the deadlier you become. Once you're dead, you start over or lose several weapon levels, which makes staying alive crucial.
Plus the game has still lots of content yet to be implemented, just got out of early access.
Long story short: it's fun, it's promising, and it nails down the basics of any good shooter. Looking forward to new content! As I've heard a few times over I'll go and say it again: there's nothing minimal about Minimum.

Options include four difficulty modes (including Custom!), Custom Cursor, Full-screen, and Wide-screen, plus a retractable inventory bar which you can lock in place, if you prefer.
I wanted to get all of the achievements - one of which is for playing on Expert Mode - so that's the mode I chose to play on.  That means NO sparkles, period.  Do you know how hard it is to find hotspots without sparkles??  Pretty hard, I'd say, since the game took me over 7 hours to complete.  In my defense, I was reading every scrap of story, examining every memory, and used NO hints, and NO skips.
Our diary has four tabs: Journal, which chronicles our journey thus far; Objective; Map (insta-travel, and is also accessible outside of your diary); and Characters, which gives us background information on the people we've met.
The first thing I noticed about the game is the artwork, which is stunningly gorgeous throughout.  The music was always appropriate, never jarring, and beautiful to listen to.  The voices are very well done, and the sound effects well-suited to the environment.
Gameplay is adventure-heavy, and starts out with most of the hidden object scenes ALSO being puzzles, which I really enjoyed.  I was disappointed that they weren't ALL HO-puzzles, but at least the ones that are there are replayable!
If you're not in the mood to find all (or any) of the hidden objects, you can switch to Match-3 mode (à la Phantasmat), and finish up the scene that way.  It takes two clicks to swap gems - you can't just drag it where you want it to go - and you have to wait for the pieces to stop moving before you can make another match.
The story of a woman trying to save her daughter is something we've seen many times over, but there were plenty of surprises along the way, and it was beautifully-told.  As a side note, it was refreshing to see that there's actually a loving husband involved - something I've rarely seen in this genre.
- Concept Art
- 51 CutScenes
- 32 Mini-games
- 30 Memories (I missed ONE! >_<)
- 17 Hidden object-puzzle games
- 33 Wallpapers (each in three different resolutions)
- 12 music tracks (though I don't see a way to download them to my hard drive
- 36 achievements
- Back-story Comic Book
It's not the best strategy guide I've seen... There are grammatical errors (which thankfully are NOT present in the game), and it's super-confusing.  The guide automatically opens to the page that references the place where you're standing, but this is not a chronological-order-type of thing.  It shows you everything you need to do on that scene, even if you're missing half of the inventory items.  'Pry open the car trunk with a crowbar'.  OK, but WHERE is the crowbar?  Good luck finding it in the guide, especially if you don't want any spoilers!  It IS very useful if you're looking for specific items in a hidden object scene, though - it has everything circled for you.
Short, puzzle-heavy, and the most beautiful graphics in the game.  It's a nice closing to the story, too.
If, like me, you're an achievement-hunter, be warned:  Some areas will become inaccessible even within the current chapter, so try to find all morphing objects and "memories" when you first enter the scene... You might not be able to come back later!  Also, once you finish the game, you can't restart on your current profile.  You'll have to delete that profile before you can re-use that spot.
This is a gorgeous game with a TON of content.  You can tell that
was a labor of love - it really shows!  A truly enjoyable game, and highly recommended.

Darkarta: A Broken Heart's Quest Collector's Edition can be far better categorized as a HOPA (hidden object puzzle adventure), since it features a wider variety of puzzles and also far more cutscenes and voice acted dialogue than as yet another run-of-the-mill HOG (hidden object game). This explains why it has been in development for over 4 years. Its developer is an enthusiastic newcomer onto Steam, but such dedicated folks have proven that hard work pays off eventually.
It’s a story driven experience, no doubt about it. A tale filled with intricate details pertaining to the mythological and cultural aspects of the Dharmic faiths (Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism and Jainism) of the Indian subcontinent. A subject rarely touched by video games in general, let alone adventure titles on Steam. Of course the history lesson had to be made more “digestible” by the inclusion of present day subplots such as one mother’s quest to find and save her daughter from sinister supernatural forces.
Players shall thus guide Mary in her search of Sophia. Along the way, many mysteries await discovery and only a sharp wit can get to the bottom of this. I strongly suggest you never skip a cutscene, dialogue or puzzle in this game. Even if you had next to no previous experience with this genre, the story by itself deserves your full attention and rushing or skipping parts of it would spoil the atmosphere beyond imagining.
Beautiful hand drawn and near-photorealistic locations and objects, aren’t a new or revolutionary feature in titles similar to Darkarta: A Broken Heart's Quest Collector's Edition. Indeed the animations of certain characters appear to be more detailed than in my previous forays into this genre, but overall the game looks just as you’d expect from its quality and time spent into development. It’s unfortunate though that even the longtime gaming standard of 1080p, doesn’t have any support.
As a dev team member explained to me, the game assets have been modelled and optimized for 1366x768 resolution in order to occupy less space once installed and if I were to throw an educated guess, in order to ensure a wider playerbase. Alas, the option to switch between resolutions would have been welcome. It’s a weak point in my perspective, since I enjoy taking as many in-game screenshots as I can and form my own archives and wallpapers from them. You can imagine how well that has worked out for me in this game, playing it on a 4K monitor at 768p.
Partial voice acting is still better than the silent treatment you get from many of Darkarta’s similar titles in the Steam Store. Why partial? Because not all written descriptions to everything you click, get followed by a recorded voice over. The soundtrack hits the right mood though and when you can hear the actors performing their lines, it’s obvious these weren’t hired amateurs. No complaints from me, as far as the sounds are concerned.
A HOPA  differentiates itself from a HOG in both scope and complexity. Instead of an almost randomized succession of object-filled locations, Darkarta: A Broken Heart's Quest Collector's Edition does an amazing job at stiching one scenery to another in the obvious pursuit of a coherent story. The dialogues with different characters have no branching options so you just click either Continue or Skip. And I already warned you about missing out on a lot if you’re not interested in reading/hearing what NPCs have to say.
I’m certain that you’re fully aware such games should be approached with patience at all times. The puzzles are in great number and they never seem to repeat themselves. That is to be expected but also a clear sign of attention to detail. Yes, there are still plenty of hidden object segments that have you rummage more efficiently than a homeless dude at a garage sale.
I’m just glad the HOG aspect of the game plays second fiddle to the more interactive puzzle sections which truly put your gray matter to the test. Picking up items and combining them is not as intellectually stimulating as pieceing together Chinese Boxes or finding the meaning behind a painting or bas-relief. You won’t be left wanting for more, once you get the hang of it and accept that the only way to play, is by not asking for any in-game Guide or Hint. There are even Achievements which reward exactly this natural manner of progression.
Think them through since more than half the fun within such games, is the sense of accomplishment you feel after spending 10 minutes in front of an abstract shape before finding out that the key you were desperately looking for, was in another room all along. I’m just kidding, of course. You have every reason to be proud when playing HOPA/HOG titles without the “training wheels”.
This is simply put, one of the best 2D Adventure games I played in recent years. And I’m talking of an original story and a brand new title, not a LucasArts or Double Fine remaster of an established classic. There aren’t any flaws to its storyline or excellent selection of brain teasers and if it wouldn’t have forced me to play in a resolution I thought I’d left behind years ago, I would have rated it a perfect score.
So it’s just near-perfect, but still an admirable feat rarely achieved by some of the Steam indie games i'm privileged to write about. Believe me when I tell you that this game’s production value is still not reflected in its current price tag. For all that it offers, Darkarta: A Broken Heart's Quest Collector's Edition deserves to be purchased on Steam, even outside of special discounts and bundles.

A while ago I voted for this game on greenlight. It looked shiny, colourful, just what I like in these games. A bit later there was a thread about highlighting it on one's profile (and vote), to then get a key for it. That was a very short window, so I don't think too many got in, but I did. :)
They finally got greenlit, released on Steam, and I got my key too. :)
Summary: I think they did a great job, with care and attention to detail.
I play these games mainly for the colourful graphics and minigames/puzzles. And man, there's tons of that here! :)
Highlighted features:
Nice customization options, including custom difficulty where I can turn off skip!
Fast travel map with indicators for morphing objects and collectibles too!
The subtitles/text stays until click/long enough to read comfortably, unlike some other games where it's too fast for me to read.
A feature I've not seen before in these games: Histories of the characters. I rather like that.
Interesting, new, and varied minigames.
Original and different HO scenes, with minigames inside even! :) (Plus an alternative match block game if you don't want to do them.)
Extras where you can replay scenes, minigames, cutscenes and more.
A guide to help when puzzles turn out mystifying. :) (There was one puzzle where I didn't understand what it wants, but with a brief look at the guide I got it, and could solve it myself.)
Enchanting, charming, colourful scenery of mystic places!
Plenty of cutscenes and heartbreaking story, if you're into that kind of thing. :)
And last but not least: When you change windows and back to it, you aren't thrown into a popup menu.
Also: Brief bonus adventure
Oddities:
With music turned off, some voices seem to be missing in cut scenes. (Like what the grandfather says during and after him 'telling you what he knows'.)
At least some exclamations at what's happening have no subtitles.
Sometimes near the end music just turned itself back on while focussed on something (like a letter, or a place to assemble stuff). Going back to main menu fixed some of that, in some places only exiting the close-up did (and music was back when zooming in again).
Somewhat negative:
I notice a slight pause when clicking on stuff/changing areas. I know at least one friend wouldn't even notice, and I think most people might not.
Need to wait for an animation to finish before I can do the next thing.

Anyway, there's lots of side missions, collectibles, places to explore, minigames, and citizens to beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of when they make rude remarks about your clothes, hit you with their car, or just simply exist. Honestly, I didn't need reasons to act like a total sociopath (even moreso than I do in the Saints Row games, which is really saying something), so I had a tendency to act like one...
...except during alot of missions when it actually has negative effects. Basically you have three leveling systems: Police (which you get xp for by obeying the law and punching criminals on police missions), Triad (for punching people or slamming their head into... woah that was uncalled for), and Face (for helping people, which I find funny since pride pretty much never involves being a benefactor). It's pretty obvious which of these three leveling systems I didn't get much XP for. The minigames were kinda silly, particularly that karaoke stuff and the whole collecting girl phone numbers thing (which I never called because I never got
bored). At least the combat is pretty good.
There is a story, and it's actually pretty good. At times predictable, and I often felt as if my main character was being way too antagonistic towards his police handler. But it's good. Also its crazy-violent, because gangsters who talk about codes and honor are the last people to actually respect such things. And while I was not torn at all about whose side I was on (because Triad people are scum), I did cheer a few times when they did stuff I wanted them to do, such as when the character I hated the most (because he pulled a Walder Frey, which made me think about the "RW" and all that comes with that) ended up being killed by a crazed lady feeding him one of his henchmen and chopping him with a meat cleaver. And while that was certainly satisfying, it wasn't one of the
ideas I had between the "Hong Kong RW" and that scene about what way I would have ended that guy (or Walder Frey). I had an alarming tendency to ponder what outrageous act of violence I wanted to see end the lives of certain characters, most of which were more brutal than what actually happened. I really must be a psycho. >_<
Anyway... sandbox crime, violence, betrayal... all that horse♥♥♥♥♥♥ There isn't really anything new here, and while I certainly prefer other games (like the Saints Row series) for this type of fun, this is alright. So I guess that's a "yes" from me.

I bought this, downloaded it, and played it. I spent 15 hours playing it on my first day of owning it.
Now, the Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition goes through various improvements from the previous version. I will now go step by step describing them.
Graphical Stuff: 9/10
The trailer boasts about graphical and texture improvements, and they weren't lying. There aren't much improvements to the graphics as there are to the textures. Lighting is very clearly improved and clothing and hair are no longer static. There is a few minor glitches to this kind of things but nothing too noticeable.
Audio: 5/10
I personally cant see much difference.
Gameplay: 8/10
Sleeping Dogs: DE has a few changes to the gameplay. For example, the city of Hong Kong feels much more immersive, there is more pedestrians and traffic making Hong Kong feel more like Hong Kong. The driving mechanics feel much smoother and better. But now for cons. some of the walking controls feel very wonky and sometimes it is more difficult to actually do the parkour in the game. The game is also no longer able to generate everything in your general area, so sometimes you'll take a few step and all of a sudden the game will span a group of civilians right next to Wei. and sometimes people spawn in the sky and fall to Earth. but overall, really good gameplay.
That's why my final rating for this game is 9/10.

If you want originality, this is probably the game for you. Just think about this :
This is just a few examples of the crazy things that can happen in this game. And it's not just about the humor : the gameplay is also interesting.
To summarize it, it is a duel between two players (using crazy historical figures avatars) who both are on one side of a symmetrical map. The game alternates between a phase where you buy traps to set on your opponent's side, and a phase where you try to roll your boulder down your side of the map.
Your opponent obviously has set up traps on your side (as you did on his), and you have to try taking as little damage as possible from them in order to damage the door at the bottom and eventually break it.
All of this in real time so you have to be quick as well.
It's a bit of a shame that the AI is fairly easy to exploit (a wall with catapults behind will usually wreck it). The AI also isn't the best at laying down the best trap combinations on your side of the map. Because of this the campaign will not resist you for long if you are a veteran gamer. Casuals should like this relaxed experience, though.
If you can find a friend to play with online then the true potential of the game mechanics shines through.
The game isn't very expensive anyway, so I still recommend it if you don't have a human opponent : the few hours it'll take you to see all the jokes and complete all the solo games modes are well worth it already.

I have ambivalent feelings about Transistor. As much as I love the overall aesthetic and atmosphere of the game, I could not get into the combat at all. Unlike Bastion (which was developed by the same company), Transistor suffers from somewhat repetitive combat while enemies lack variety.
Whereas Bastion was more action oriented, Transistor puts emphasis on planning and requires you to pause the battle – i.e. initiate a Turn() –  and queue up your attacks, execute those attacks, and then spend some time running away from enemies during Turn() recovery, until you are able to repeat the process. You wield only one weapon (the sword Transistor) augmented with various functions: you can have up to four functions installed at a time and each can be upgraded with up to two other functions. You can change your functions at every access point (which are save points in the game and are quite frequent) but mostly you find a combination that works and stick with it – since enemies are not very varied, you don't need to change your strategy much between different battles. As a result, the combat starts feeling repetitive.
Another thing that doesn't work as good in Transistor as it did in Bastion is the narrator. In Bastion he was an omniscient narrator who recounted the protagonist's adventures and described the post-apocalyptic world the game was set in. In Transistor, the narrator is the voice of the protagonist's lover trapped in the sword and his comments are directed at her – and frequently they are reduced to inconsequential passing comments, small talk, comments on whether you've entered some door or what the weather is like and similar. The developers clearly wanted a narrator to accompany you on your journey, but too often he is reduced to just making passing remarks that are in no way necessary, illuminating, witty, etc. As a result, many of his remarks feel superfluous and unneeded. On a second playthrough he becomes downright annoying at moments.
The narrator would have worked a lot better if only the developers allowed him to talk more about what was happening in the game, about the motives of the antagonists, about past events that took place, about the world of Cloudbank in general. But they made the story purposefully vague, so that you have to uncover it by reading the terminals and the descriptions of the functions, which begs the question – why have a narrator at all?
I wanted to like Transistor much more than I did because the art design and the atmosphere of the game instantly attracted me. The game is absolutely gorgeous looking and at every step I wanted to see more of that world. The story also drew me in right at the start – it started as a murder mystery and I needed to piece together what happened and why, and where my character was even going. A lot of the story is told through terminals you can interact with and through the descriptions of functions, which are not available until you have equipped a function in three slots (active, passive, and upgrade) and used it. However, much is also left unexplained or at least ambiguous, and I'm not sure if this was done on purpose or if it is the result of the fact that not everything can be delivered adequately through terminals and function descriptions.
Despite some of its flaws, Transistor is an interesting game. I just wish I found the combat more fun.

To be honest I wan't sure if to write this review.
Why? Well, at almost 9500 positive reviews that most likely covered what I might have to say it seems a bit pointless. Nonetheless - after the 2nd playthrough - I decided to write one as a 'thank-you' note to Supergiant Games.
If you have already played Bastion you probably know what to expect here. The game is in the same vain albeit with some different mechanics. I'll keep it short and by points.
Pros:
- Story: the story isn't mush new, but so was Bastion. What differentiates it from others is the narration and progress.
- Visuals: the style consists of a beautifully drawn sci-fi world and blends nicely with the story.
- Music: what's more to say? It's from the music director who worked on Bastion [+more songs this time].
- Combat: I found the attack customization engaging in developing different play-styles. Plus, the option to play either a hack-n-slash or take your time and plan the attacks can be refreshing when you get tired of one or the other.
Cons:
- Short: the game can be finished in less than 10 hours [my stats are inflated for idealing for cards and achievement hunting]. I don't regret for buying the game, but I did buy it on sale.
-Replayability: it really becomes an issue only because the game is rather short.
Overall:
Get it if you liked Bastion and if the shortness bothers you, get it on sale.

My very subjective verdict:
Hero Defense is a tower defense game with 5 heroes that you can move on the map. The controls are spot on but I recommend to use the keyboard and learn the few shortcuts... this can save lives, especially in later levels.
You collect gold and runes in the game. Gold is needed to upgrade the buildings in the town in which you can level up your characters and weapons. You can also convert gold into diamonds in order to build so called hero shrines on the maps. Additionally you need diamonds to add rune slots to your weapons. In those weapon slots, you can place runes which are a lot of fun top experiment with. Each rune comes in 5 diferent tiers and there are 9 different runes per tier. In general, the metagame is very satisfying. You always enjoy to go back to the town and play around with your precious loot.
Graphics are very polished with some nice effects like fog, lightning and bloom but I wouldnt regard the visuals as the game's strong point but they definitely are nice too look at. I totally like the music and the sound fx as they do a perfect job in creating a very nice atmosphere that is second to noe when compared to other tower defense games.

This is an early access review, and WOW what an impact this game has.
The game is beautiful to look at and plays really well, and I would not have thought this was an early access had I not already known.
The game itself at its core is a basic tower defence game, mobs follow one or more set routes through the map trying to survive to their goal and you have to stop them with a small number of "Towers", but this is where things start to diverge from the standard format.
Your "Towers" are one of several hero characters which have a full RPG style item system and skill tree that allow you to customize and level the characters up in the way that you want them to.  This allows for you to consider how each hero works with the others to give you a synergy in killing the attacking army because oh no! while you can hurt the enemy with all of the hero types, each hero has a specific type of enemy that they really excel at defeating and this can be seen by their colour coding for each wave meaning you need to plan ahead to make sure your hero is in the right place.  Thats right because this is where you again depart from the old tower defence format as your Hero characters are mobile around the map and can stand in many different places allowing you to take advantage of well placed shrines to boost your attack speed, range, or damage output.  But again watch out, only certain heroes can use some of these to your advantage.
Over all this is a very fun game, a little easy on the lowest difficulties needed to progress the story but you can go back and re-do a map to gain more rewards and give you an extra challenge as you level up your Hero.
All in all I recommend this game and I cannot wait to see what they have in store for the future

Many people complain that this game's controls suck and that it's so old it looks ugly. While the graphics aren't as good as the current games (obviously!) and some people might not be able to overcome this, I can't agree with the controls complaints. You need to understand that this game came out in 1997 when the current WSAD system wasn't the standard. Sure, it takes time to get used to the controls, but when you do, you will find out this is one of the most precise control systems.
Now, finally to the review. I have very fond memories of this game and consider it one of the top games in Tomb Raider franchise. Great choice of locations (China, Venice, wreck of Maria Doria, Tibet), thick atmosphere and simple, but sufficient story...yes, there aren't as many movement options as in its successor, Tomb Raider III, but I never thought that matters. The only downside to this great game is the Steam port - what the flip is the problem with FMVs? They're all windowed and in small resolution. But other than that, this game is brilliant. If you aren't an impatient kind of gamer who hates games that really take some effort to finish, get it. It's classic and fun even today.

In this sequel Laura gets....let me see...one new move. You know the roll that has you facing the opposite direction at the end of it? You can do that in mid-air now. That's it for the new side of things. Oh wait, you also drive a boat in one of the levels. It's so forgetable that it slipped my mind.
As for the old, game mechanics (I refuse to say 'gameplay') remain exactly the same. Early 3D platforming with nothing inherently wrong in its structure other than being so god damn outdated. Laura's repertoire of moves are so basic with no growth throughout the course of the title that everything you do in the first area will be replicated in every area afterwards, with the only change being the placement of the jumps and ledges. Modern titles keep an adventure fresh throughout by moving the plot in unexpected directions, keep you lured in through character interactions, or throw in a new mechanic to bring freshness to the ongoing story. Not Tomb Raider II (Or 1, for that matter); everything you will ever do or experience is introduced in the first level.
That wouldn't be such a bad thing if Laura didn't handle so rigidly. Imagine platforming with classic Resident Evil controls. Surprisingly it works, but it's still pretty damn stupid. The shooting on the other hand is so terrible it shouldn't even exist. Part of what drags down the old games in the series is the rigidity in movement that turns particular jumps into 8 second affairs when they can be instantaneous. Mario 64 was released a year before this title, and it puts this title to shame. Mario moves quickly; he grabs onto ledges and jumps across gaps seamelessly. Laura on the other hand requires you to slowly walk up to a ledge, jump back once, run forward and jump, grab onto the ledge and slooowwllyyyy rise up. It becomes tedious and analogous to platforming with a damn tank. Somewhat saving the woeful mechanics is the open-nature of the game: you are plotted somewhere in the map and, well...you look for switches and levers to pull. It's explorational; you are expected to make your way through it all with absolutely no guidance or narrative dictating the exact circumstances you find yourself in. Amazingly you don't get lost easily, which is a pretty big credit to the way the levels were designed. A bit of the positive that can be further elaborated in my Tomb Raider 1 review (since the titles are incredibly similar) is that the base level design remains competent.
Despite all the faults it's naturally received through aging, I still don't feel like this title is absolute trash. Just like in my review for Tomb Raider I, I can't bring myself to hate the game. And just like in that review I'm also not strongly recommending this. To me a thumbs down on a review means that it's best to stay away from the title due to it's overwhelming faults. But this game really has no faults other than age, and when it comes to age then every title is theoretically a bad title. I've played plenty of retro games that were obviously outdated, but the core of the game was still solid and I could enjoy it while understanding the place in time it was created in. I wish there were a ''give it a pass'' option on reviews, because even in its graphic the thumbs down implies that the game is bad.
This title isn't bad, it's just really ♥♥♥♥ing old. Maybe I'm getting far too hung up on the 'yes or no' aspect of the review; you should actually read the contents of the review anyway and not rely on an aggregate or a thumbs up or down. So you know what, I'm not gonna give this a number and ignore the recommendation; focus on the actual contents of this review and take it for what it's worth.
