OLD DOG, NO NEW TRICKS
→ OCTOBER 8, 2014 Many open-world, non-linear drive-and-gun games -- with some notable exclusions -- tend to tack on a story merely to loosely justify whatever it is you're doing. But the main thing I made clear in my original review of Sleeping Dogs on Xbox 360 and PS3 back in 2012 is that while it's a blast to play, its story is actually the star of the show. The Definitive Edition for new-gen consoles carries over both of those great traits and adds a decent facelift, and it's just as fun and just as memorable as it was the first time around. An engaging plot littered with memorable characters and a ton of slowly building tension is artfully coupled with solid melee action, gunplay, and driving to create a multi-faceted game that satisfies on all fronts.

As far as the aesthetic is concerned, Sleeping Dogs was never an exceptionally pretty game, but The Definitive Edition resolves some of its biggest visual faults and brings it more
Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition
Inspired by classic Hollywood and Asian cinema style action thrillers, Sleeping Dogs follows the story of detective Wei Shen as he infiltrates one of Hong Kong's notorious Triad crime syndicates.
→ MUCH MORE
in line with the PC version. On the Xbox One version I played, draw distances are vastly extended, textures are much sharper, and the overall gloss of the entire convincing recreation of Hong Kong is improved. It doesn't look like a native new-gen game by any stretch of the imagination, however - and it’s disappointing that the framerate stutters a bit when you're on foot running around and exploring, and the camera is still a bit messy in certain circumstances.
Again, though, I have to sing the praises of the story. Sleeping Dogs revolves around an undercover Hong Kong detective named Wei Shen. Shen – who's voiced wonderfully by Will Yun Lee in both English and Cantonese, is an interesting protagonist, one with true depth. Shen’s embedded himself with the Hong Kong underworld in order to unravel it from within, and watching him get sucked further and further into peril is fascinating. He's not a nameless hero or a loosely constructed anyman. He seems as real as a character in a movie.
Of course, Sleeping Dogs has plenty for you if story isn't your thing. Its driving mechanics are on-point, with lots of different vehicles toting unique feels, from run-down motorcycles and hulking industrial trucks to supped-up sedans and expensive sports cars, and everything in between. Developer United Front Games has crafted a believable and incredibly busy version of Hong Kong that's simply a blast to drive around, explore, and uncover. Likewise, fighting -- whether with your fists, a melee weapon, or a firearm -- is also a lot of fun. There's a ton of collectibles to discover in addition to its meaty campaign, with tons of offshoot side quests to complete. In short, Sleeping Dogs is bound to keep you very busy not only when keeping up with its story, but in simply doing everything within it there is to do.
Content-wise, the only notable difference between the old-gen version of Sleeping Dogs and the Definitive Edition is the inclusion of DLC. Both the supernatural-themed Nightmare in North Point and the cop-centric Year of the Snake are included, though I wasn't blown away by either. These separate packs -- which feel disjointed and aren't a part of the campaign -- don't stack up with the likes of GTA IV’s The Lost and the Damned or The Ballad of Gay Tony in terms of the amount of content, the quality of the new characters, or even new objectives. But, it's pretty cool that they're here in case you want to mess with them.
Testing out Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition reminded me of a facet I hadn't thought much about since I last played it in 2012: its multi-tiered leveling system. This experience rubric provides Shen with rewards in three different categories: as a cop, as a member of the criminal Triad, and as a citizen of Hong Kong. Earning experience points in these three categories often conflicts with one another, and each category has unique skills associated with it. Delving into this system is a ton of fun, and it's really cool watching Shen get stronger based on how I chose to behave. Displaying disregard for the citizens of Hong Kong won't net you much love in your Face meter, for instance, but upholding the law will surely bring you plenty of cop experience points.

THE VERDICT
Back in 2012, I called Sleeping Dogs one of the biggest -- and most pleasant -- surprises of the year. Two years later, the surprise has obviously dissipated, but that doesn't take away from what United Front Games achieved here. Playing the Definitive Edition reminded me how much I enjoyed its excellent story and characters, combat, and city, but also made me pine for a true new-gen sequel. The differences here might not be worth paying for a second time, but if you missed out on this great open-world action game the first time, you shouldn’t repeat that mistake.

Hey TuttiFrutti  Above and beyond 10 stars.
This game is off the chain.  All I can say is awesome awesome awesome.  The story, the graphics, the VO's, and the cutscenes brilliantly done.  The cutscenes are the best I have seen in a long time.  You do have collectibles which are memories and morphing objects.  There is also a walkthrough in the book which is very well done.  Don't know how they did it, but what ever scene you are in the game, the walkthrough is there.  I've never seen that done and I love it.  It also shows you the hidden object scenes and where the items are.  Kudos to who did the walkthrough.  Now Darkarta is eye candy for the ladies, but evil evil evil.
Story:  You, your hubby and your daughter were enjoying a lovely time in a boat when out of the blue an evil entity came out of nowhere and reeked havoc on you and your family kidnapping your daughter.  The evil dude of course was Darkarta.  The reason for it is he wants your daughter's soul and because he is thinking your another woman by the name of Nagin and he wants revenge.  Naturally you have no idea what the heck is happening.  All you want to do is to save your daughter's life and get the heck out of dodge.  So now you're on a journey to save your daughter and kill Darkarta.  Even though your grandfather said not to, what kind of mom would you be if you didn't put your life in jeopardy to save your baby.  And the story goes.
Graphics:  Absolutely gorgeous.  The kind where you like to just stop and look a moment before continuing.
Music:  Beautiful music.  A lot of voice.  Very nice to listen to whilst playing the game.
MIni games:  Except for the slider puzzle, all the mini games are different.  I never played them before.  And I have except for three games all CE's known to man lol.  Very nice variety.
HOGS:  They have a match 3 game if you don't want to do the HOG.  One word list had to where you could hover over the word and see a silhouette of it.  They had silhouettes, use one item to use on the scene, and find symbols.  Also they mini games in the HOGS, and what I noticed is that I couldn't complete the mini game, but instead of skipping it, I did the match 3 instead and didn't get a count for skipping.  It seemed to count it as part of the HOG.
Hint:  I didn't use it in the HOG, but on the outside it was awesome.  Told you what exactly you had to, what items to use and where to go.
Map:  It has the exclamation points telling you you have something to do there.  Also it tells you if you have a collectible yet to get.  And yes it's a jump map.
Kudos to the team on a very superb done game.  I highly recommend this game.  Free to try, and $8.99 to buy.  Can't beat that price.  :-)

Major game devs would do well to take notes from Fingerbones because this is the recipe for great horror games. "The Room" is really cool. It's like Myst in a way, except the exploration doesn't happen with caves and islands – it happens with tables and safes.
In this first-person puzzler you're searching for the two dozen secret nooks and crannies on each piece of furniture, along with a breeze of the supernatural and for lite narrative via letters.
What bugs me the most is how ridiculously overloaded each level is, which results in a very laggy experience *and* unresponsive controls. It seems like the FULL level is loaded completely at the beginning of each chapter, with all the secret drawers, compartments, switches and items. And all that stuff has to be handled by the CPU with each new camera angle. Why is the polygon count so high? This is just a puzzler? Why does the game need to load the small ball of the final puzzle part when I haven't even opened the box in the box yet? It's way too convoluted!
Oh, and it's way too short.
But other than that, this game was mindblowingly satisfying for me.  And there are sequels, too? Can't wait to play them on Steam.

Yes, believe the hype. The awards this game received... The 'overwhelmingly positive' Steam reviews... The Room is the best puzzle game I have ever played and I've been playing them since the 1990s. It's puzzling in its most basic form. There is no real story, you just tackle one big puzzle, although it's divided into five chapters. It's hard to describe in a few words why this game is so good, but simply put: it's fun! And playing The Room feels exciting and rewarding. They just got "it" right - "it" being everything a game like this should be, while being a completely unique experience unlike any other puzzle game I know of.
Maybe just a few short additional notes, though, that may help you decide whether to buy The Room if you're still not sure:
- it's a short game: it takes only about 3 hours if you take your time, so you may want to pick it up when it's on sale
- it's a rather easy game: for me the game was just challenging enough but if you're the sadistic kind of puzzler who only likes being challenged to the point of migraine, you will not find that here. On the contrary, there is a hint system in the game so if you feel stumped at any time, you can click a button to give you some pointers.
- the Steam Achievements are the most basic: one achievement for completing each chapter of the game.
I would recommend this game to everyone, not just to people who like playing puzzle games. It's really that good. But since it's a pretty short game, you may want to wait until it's on sale to buy it.

The good:  A nice visual style, unique enemy designs, decent parodies of a few genres here and there.
The bad:  There are some pixel-perfect jumps that you have to get JUST RIGHT. This wouldn't be so bad if the whole of Eryi was what you were considering when you were making the jump. But the hitbox does not incorporate part of her feet and (during the final boss) the very top of her head, which makes figuring out where she'll collide with enemies, projectiles, and the ground itself, iffy to say the least.
It's a fun little rage platformer if you're into that. But be prepared to break the connection in your head to her body and her hitbox. Keep this in mind during the last boss fight especially and don't be afraid to let her toes touch the fireballs that the boss shoots. It's really the only way to win.

Absolutely one of the most under-appreciated games ever made, hands down probably my favorite open-world game. I'd say it's a Chinese-American version of Yakuza, but less people know about that than this probably.
Pros:
-Combat: The hand-to-hand combat is fantastic, it's a slightly more complex "Arkham style", with counters, grabs, and actual button combos, which lead to visceral fist fights, ending in the always enjoyable slow-motion knockout/kill. This is probably what sells the game for me, it's just so much fun getting in huge fights that range from fists, to melee weapons, to all-out gun fights.
-Story: Playing an undercover cop in a Triad gang is a great start, as we watch the main character grapple with needing to enforce the law, but also being in a gang that he comes to respect/love. Spoilers aside, it's pretty great. The voice-acting is fantastic as well, with enough actual Mandarin that it doesn't feel like Disney Presents: Sleeping Dogs.
-Driving: Some people aren't a huge fan of the car physics in the game, which I can respect, but I love it. It feels rather Arcade-y, with hairpin handbrake turning, and the ability to jump from your car to others, it's just a blast to drive around causing havoc. It's true, sometimes I felt cheated by getting caught on something only to spin out and get stuck, but that's a rare occurrence.
-Customization: There are tons of outfits for your character, which actually changes how you play, with some getting bonus XP, and others giving you increased gun accuracy or melee strength. You can't change his hair or anything like that, but watching him enter a scene dressed like a '90s rocker is always fun.
-Length: There is plenty to do, my first playthrough on the PS3 got me about 20-25 hours of messing around and plot, and now this version has even more added content, with new missions and side-activities, it's definitely not a game to speedrun.
Cons:
-Guns: I did say I enjoy the gun fights, but it's hardly a terrible thing they're not too frequent. You never feel very accurate when shooting, and will most likely miss more than you hit, especially in the driving sections that ask you to protect the car. They're far from game-breaking, but you can really tell they focused on the fisticuffs and threw in guns afterwards.
-Level Up System: One of the cruxes of the game, is how you level up. There are 2 level up paths; Triad and Cop. Each mission will award XP to both in a "star-sytem", that is, maximum XP is 3 stars, and minimum is no stars. When you start a mission, cop XP starts at 3 full stars, but when you mess up you lose from that potential reward pool, by either hurting innocents, or driving like a maniac. Triad XP is earned  by fighting and general killing, and builds from 0 stars. What you have to do is try and be as bad aas possible, while still being good. Interesting on paper, but in reality it's rather annoying. It is so much easier to get cop XP that you may be fully leveled on Cop, and on level 5 of Triad. While also not game-breaking, it just feels unbalanced.
World Size: It says it's open-world, but in reality it's about 3 or 4 small cities attached by roads, circling a large empty area. It looks far larger than it really is, and seems rather deceiving.
Other than that I can't think of anything right now, it's a hell of a game, and I would certainly recommend it to anyone looking for a new twist on an old genre. It's fun to play, easy to get into, and will swallow your time if you give it the chance.

UPDATES FOR 3.21
*Perspective of a WoW loyalist since vanilla*
"Probably the best quality MMO since Wrath of the Lich King WoW."
BOTTOM LINE: If youre a PVPer, ignore the reviews prior to 3.2, PVP is slowly gaining popularity and the new modes have a ton to offer. You will be almost overwhelmed with things to do in this game. Theres a lot to offer for everyone.
Pros:
---Beautiful design for all of the zones, cities, and dungeons.
---Awesome sound track I actually enjoy hearing each unique dungeon theme (most of wow was played sound off)
---Balanced (for the most part) PVP. This game did what WoW should have done since vanilla. Theres a separate level up     system for pvp that gives you specific skills used solely for that mode. It fixes the whole PVE vs PVP balance conundrum most MMOs face
---THE FEAST: This is probably what saved it for me long term. Just release this past week was The Feast which is a competitive PVP mode with rankings. Matches here gave me more of a thrill here than playing in the 2.4k arena bracket in WoW
---The ability to play whatever class you want on a single character. This function also allows you to bring in skills from other classes to further customize your playstyle
---High quality and difficult end game content (unlike WoW, which has people farming the content within a week of release)
---Great community
Cons:
---People love the story but for me.... meh a lot of it was blah blah chosen one and tons of pointless fetch quests (like really homie i just saved the kingdom now i have to fetch water for 3 privates?)
---UPDATED: PVP was originally dead however theres been a resurgence with a competetive pvp arena mode added with seasons (as said above).
---Lack of Battleground diversity (However this is slowly and allegedly being addressed by producers)
---This game forces you to choke down 15-20 hours worth of dead level 50 content in order to even unlock the expansion pack

* There are two types of jump. One is "short-distance jump" which can be achieved with Jump key + forward (up arrow), second one is "long-distance jump", you have to gain some velocity to achieve this jump. My 10-year-old self and I can't recommend this game enough. It's classic puzzle-solving at its finest. In fact I'm pretty sure that playing it made me smarter. There's no AI holding your hand here, nor any obnoxious button graphics that flash on-screen and yell at you to mash the Y key to perform some entirely gimmicky and circumstantial roundhouse backflip to the face that you'll never need to do again. Just Lara and her lovably awkward polygons running straight ahead with the arms fully stretched out at a stiff, perpendicular angle to the body. On occasion, you can make her say "No," in a charming British voice, over and over again, and then kill her in a variety of exciting ways.
Serously though, the levels are rendered beautifully, leaving just the right amount to the imagination, and many of the puzzles actually require more than three brain cells to figure out. There are no journal entries offering fluff faux "immersion," no toggled map overlays to tell you where you are, and very little clues to help you out - just you and an often convoluted and action-packed pathway from the start of a level to the exit. The levels themselves, especially the memorable Venice series, have personality and often make you feel real suspense and a sense of danger. While some puzzles might frustrate the modern gamer (certain ones depend on very exact placement of Lara to perform a series of jumps with no room for error, for instance, which can get pretty tedious), the feeling of accomplishment you get after finally landing that horrendous jump, or opening that goddamn door, is so worth the effort.
In my opinion, this and the original Tomb Raider are the best installments in the series, mostly thanks to their simplicity. What it lacks in modern graphics, the game makes up for tenfold in gameplay and creativity of story and design. Plus, for the first time, Lara gets to use vehicles, which add a great deal of fun to the levels they appear in, by which I mean you can drive them off cliffs and explode.
All in all, you won't regret giving this a try. Yeah, you'll probably laugh at Lara and make fun of the dated graphics, and swear loudly at the controls, but these days, that's part of the fun. Definitely a must for 90s action/adventure gaming fans and especially people who don't mind video games not insulting their intelligence for a change.
Oh and you can lock the butler in the freezer.

I believe the developers jumped the gun with this early release. Don't get me wrong, I expect issues with early releases, but I'd like to think the developers would get some of the more basic, fundamental parts of their game to be more functional before letting the players get their hands on it. The game often crashes when trying to quit using the exit game button, and don't expect to craft and try out alot of different weapons in any reasonable amount of time, as the game eventually decides that you shouldn't get what you need to craft the different weapons in the game (Which there are quite a few of, all with their own unique perks.)
There are only 3 gamemodes to play in the game: Horde, Titan, and Team Death Match (TDM). TDM is what you expect, and quite entertaining, but alot of people complain about the spawns, and for good reason. Other than Titan mode, there is no set spawn point for your team, so you may just be spawning to your doom (Although the developers did put in penalties for killing fresh spawns, that's not really going to improve your experience).
Titan mode is the staple of the game, seeing as how its part of their title screen. This mode involves two massive bots going at it, and its up to you and your team to see it safely to the enemy team's home base. No problems with this mode, its quite entertaining.
Last up is Horde mode, where you and a bunch of your team members fight off against hordes of astronauts, ninjas, velociraptors, etc. Don't be fooled though, they might start off dumb and relatively easy to kill at the start, but they grow hard very quicklly. This mode needs more armor resources to drop off more creeps, as without the extra protection the later waves will destroy you quickly unless you have a fully organized team of pals to watch your back, but I will admit its very fun to try surviving the unrelenting hordes that turn almost any strategy you can come up with against you.
This game also has many features yet to be fully implemented (as expected, its a early release!) which I feel will make the game feel much more rewarding. Do I enjoy this game? Yes. Do I recommend it in its current form? No. I suggest you hold on for awhile and wait to see if this game's developers get on the ball with fixing its bugs.

Pretty darn good riff on the TD genre.
Great "tower" (character) customisation options. The Skill trees are functional and don't really offer a lot of variety (as you'll eventually unlock everything), but the Rune system for varying upgrade options is excellent and allows some interesting synergies and styles.
Only 5 "towers" (characters), but each of them is completely unique and has their own strengths and weaknesses. They're also mobile, and may even benefit from constant management, meaning this game is much more active than many TDs.
Some clever level design. Some of the levels are a little bland, but others have multiple paths, sub-objectives, objects that block line of sight, and shrines that buff your characters.
Good variety of difficulty. Map length ranges from a minute or two to half-hour grindfests. Challenges are available for each level and many are unique.
All in all, good little TD with some dedicated developers. Single player campaign is feature complete and is just being tweaked at this point. Buy and enjoy.

I own Eryi’s Action twice. Once on Desura and again on Steam, but if you think that makes it so good I’d buy it twice, no its so awful I’d buy it twice just to warn you all what a terrible 2D side scrolling torture platformer it is. Now for starters, I love 2D platformers and side scrollers. I love Mario, Super Meat Boy and I’ve even played hardcore platformers like “I wanna be the Guy.”
Eryi’s Action is a painful sort of difficult. Its a game based on memorization instead of skill. Each level forces you to remember where every obscure death trap is located. Its as if the developers read documents on how not to make a Mario level and used it to make this game. If an area looks like typical grass, you might think its safe to jump on, but that just means there could be spikes that jump out. Climb a ladder? Well that triggers spikes to fall on you. Try to hop on an enemy that 30 other enemies that look exactly the same…. it will hop into you, causing you to die. Think that platform is a platform? Nope you can’t walk on it and you go straight through.
Its all about remembering where the traps are and avoiding them. Its not fun. Deaths are constant, too constant to enjoy the game. The music is bad and repetitive, the death sound is like a cheese-grater on your nerves. You’ll die so much that the life counter will go into the negatives. That’s part of the joke. You don’t have lives, you have negative lives. It just keeps going. I think the real fun people are having is recommending it to unsuspecting shoppers.
Looking at Steam’s achievement page, its odd that so many people can love this game and review it so favorably when a mere 60% of people score the first achievement. You can tell how tough a game is by the drop off in achievement percentages. If you endure, you’ll memorize a level enough to get plenty of achievements in less than thirty minutes, but most people can’t even do that. Thirty percent of players have made it to the first goal flag. That should be staked as a warning for anyone that dares buy this game.
I didn’t find joy in Eryi’s Action on Desura and I couldn’t find any fun in it on Steam. This game tests your endurance. How much can you endure before you quit? I didn’t feel any sense of happiness or joy that I had finished a level. In fact completing a level means there are more traps even after you think you’re safe. When you complete a level you have no control over your character and no way to prevent falling into a death trap.
If you’re into memorization platformers, this game is for you, but I strongly recommend everyone avoid it. Even at a paltry $5, the risk is still to great that you won’t enjoy it. Unless you need material for Youtube.

What a delightful and refreshing change of pace in HOPAs! Great gameplay with innovative and challenging puzzles, unusual and fun HO scenes, and some clever adventure steps. All wrapped in absolutely stunning visuals, great voiceovers, and with a novel (and touching!) story to boot. This is definitely the best game of its genre that I have played in a long time.
The extras are extensive & include pretty much all typical fan favorites, plus a well-drawn comic book that provides a great backstory for the game. Be sure to check out the “Memories” section in Extras for some engaging depictions of little Sophia. Darkarta provided easily more than 7 hours of gameplay for me. Congratulations to Tuttifrutti for providing such a fascinating, beautiful, different, and fun addition for any HOPA-lover's library.

One of the best HOPA games I have played. An intriguing storyline, a different mythology and innovative puzzles make this game a cut above the rest. Have some snacks on hand, because you will want to play this one straight through. As a hardened game player, I didn't expect the few 'tugs at the heartstrings' I encountered.( Don't worry, everything turns out OK). Lots of 'extras' including an excellent comic book which explains the events leading up to where the game starts. Beautiful graphics which reflect the rich  Indian heritage,  wonderful music and interesting characters, make this a game you will want to replay. Tutti-frutti are a developer to watch out for, I'm already looking forward to their next production!

I purchase approximately 50 hidden object/puzzle games a year (on a different game site as I found Steam not long ago) and have done for the last 10 years. I'm also on Pond Friends in case any of you are curious. That's how I found out about this game. Out of all those games I can state that Darkarta is absolutely the best I have played.
Graphics are just amazing. The colors used, the location and setting, the detail...I could go on for days. Every single scene had so many things to look at and admire.
Hidden Object scenes - wonderful and multi-layered.
Puzzles - some puzzles are similar to what other developers are doing, but above and beyond. Many are unique and unlike other puzzles I've seen before. Absolutely great fun and they really made me think.
Setting - India with all its grandeur, beauty and lushness is explored in this game. I loved the setting and really didn't want to quit playing when I had to.
Storyline - different than other games I've played recently. Interesting take on the story of a child taken from her parents.
Collectibles - different as well. These pertain to the taken child and are fun to look for.
Game play - smooth and enjoyable.
Music - absolutely fits the setting and is peaceful and enjoyable.

This is truly a beautiful game, a tribute to the Indian culture by an up-and-coming new developer, tuttifrutti.  Based upon an ancient folktale, it blends that story with a modern-day tale about a mother in search of her daughter. The story behind the game is and emotional adventure - a heart-wrenching trek for a mother who all obstacles to locate her kidnapped daughter. It also helps her to come to grips with her own nightmares from the  past.  The graphics are amazingly beautiful and well-depict the lush Indian landscape.  The background contains a musical score reflecting the exotic melody of India.  The HOP scenes demonstrate the genius of this developer.  They are thematic and include some new concepts in portraying HOP scenes.  In one example, there is a scene in which you locate fragments on a crystalline ball. The puzzles are varied in difficulty and variety and are thematic as well.  In one example, you choose the correct hand positions to create a shadow animal.  The game explores a new concept not common in most HOP games, namely reincarnation.  This game is a must-have for serious casual game lovers.  It is truly a work of art and is truly a tribute to not only the country of India but the great love of this developer for their rich heritage.

I was recommended the game by a friend in college who got in on it during its limited release. He described as Halo meets Leage of Legends with a robust suite of weapons and complex and varied combat, complete with a per match upgrade system reminiscent of item building in League.
After about 4 hours of play I can't say I disagree with his characterization, and I'm very pleased with the overall direction the game is going. As long as it keeps the price tag where it is, I would certainly recommend it.
That said, there are still a large number of balance problems. I read in an update that the programers were trying to improve balance by increasing the time to kill across the board. I agree with this method of improving balance completely. Its unfair to players to constantly whack weapons with the nerf hammer and hope everything comes out ok, and increasing time to kill seems like a much better option than just dulling down the sword (which is clearly the most favored weapon at the moment)
This is the essential difference I see between Halo and Call of Duty: in CoD over half the weapons in the game have the capacity to kill you long before your character can do a 180. In Halo however you get some breathing room against most weapons; the assault rifle, DMR, battle rifle, pistol, even most of the plasma weapons won't take down even your sheild before you have time to react to them, and seek cover if you wish.
It is essential that combat occurs in this manner, if it is not possible for you to disengage after being fired on from behind and recover to the same HP as your assailant then overall gameplay suffers because players constantly run around the map hoping to catch other players from behind, and in fear of being caught themselves.
I'm not a particularly big fan of the weapon unlock requirements, especially considering that a number of them are strictly better than the stock items, but I am pleased that they were all made the same cost so that anyone who could identify the good items could quickly acquire them instead of having to slog through hours of gaming.
Finally (I promise!), USB game controller play is sketchy at best. I understand steam supports the PC gaming master race, and Xbox controllers are generally frowned upon, but just do this one for me, plz?
I apologize if this seems overly critical, I enjoyed the game, but there is significant room for improvement. I hope this gets to the right place.

Boy, oh boy, was I in for a rude awakening.
The very first match I played ended with the whole enemy team having fully upgraded weapons and armor, while we were struggling to even power up our Titans. I was salty, and I was sad to see that my playstyle from the early days of the game didn't work anymore.
I played five more games. The same thing happened: Enemy team got powered up completely, using high power weaponry (nothing but that, I might add), and fully upgraded armor. My team was getting slaughtered just walking out of spawn. This went on for all five matches.
In a salt-fueled rage, I hard-shut the game window, and uninstalled Minimum.
That was maybe three months back. Now, seeing Minimum's grayed-out name in my library, I'm reminded of how I used to like it. It also reminded me that I needed to edit my review. So, here's that.
If you are seriously considering getting this game, be warned: It will chew you up, digest you, $#!t you out, and repeat the whole cycle again and again until you do one of two things: You either give in and stoop down to your enemies' level and use heavy firepower to dominate your opponents, or you make the sanest decision you will ever make and uninstall the game.
The decision is yours, friend.

I have ambivalent feelings about Transistor. As much as I love the overall aesthetic and atmosphere of the game, I could not get into the combat at all. Unlike Bastion (which was developed by the same company), Transistor suffers from somewhat repetitive combat while enemies lack variety.
Whereas Bastion was more action oriented, Transistor puts emphasis on planning and requires you to pause the battle – i.e. initiate a Turn() –  and queue up your attacks, execute those attacks, and then spend some time running away from enemies during Turn() recovery, until you are able to repeat the process. You wield only one weapon (the sword Transistor) augmented with various functions: you can have up to four functions installed at a time and each can be upgraded with up to two other functions. You can change your functions at every access point (which are save points in the game and are quite frequent) but mostly you find a combination that works and stick with it – since enemies are not very varied, you don't need to change your strategy much between different battles. As a result, the combat starts feeling repetitive.
Another thing that doesn't work as good in Transistor as it did in Bastion is the narrator. In Bastion he was an omniscient narrator who recounted the protagonist's adventures and described the post-apocalyptic world the game was set in. In Transistor, the narrator is the voice of the protagonist's lover trapped in the sword and his comments are directed at her – and frequently they are reduced to inconsequential passing comments, small talk, comments on whether you've entered some door or what the weather is like and similar. The developers clearly wanted a narrator to accompany you on your journey, but too often he is reduced to just making passing remarks that are in no way necessary, illuminating, witty, etc. As a result, many of his remarks feel superfluous and unneeded. On a second playthrough he becomes downright annoying at moments.
The narrator would have worked a lot better if only the developers allowed him to talk more about what was happening in the game, about the motives of the antagonists, about past events that took place, about the world of Cloudbank in general. But they made the story purposefully vague, so that you have to uncover it by reading the terminals and the descriptions of the functions, which begs the question – why have a narrator at all?
I wanted to like Transistor much more than I did because the art design and the atmosphere of the game instantly attracted me. The game is absolutely gorgeous looking and at every step I wanted to see more of that world. The story also drew me in right at the start – it started as a murder mystery and I needed to piece together what happened and why, and where my character was even going. A lot of the story is told through terminals you can interact with and through the descriptions of functions, which are not available until you have equipped a function in three slots (active, passive, and upgrade) and used it. However, much is also left unexplained or at least ambiguous, and I'm not sure if this was done on purpose or if it is the result of the fact that not everything can be delivered adequately through terminals and function descriptions.
Despite some of its flaws, Transistor is an interesting game. I just wish I found the combat more fun.

If you have already played Bastion you probably know what to expect here. The game is in the same vain albeit with some different mechanics. I'll keep it short and by points.
Pros:
- Story: the story isn't mush new, but so was Bastion. What differentiates it from others is the narration and progress.
- Visuals: the style consists of a beautifully drawn sci-fi world and blends nicely with the story.
- Music: what's more to say? It's from the music director who worked on Bastion [+more songs this time].
- Combat: I found the attack customization engaging in developing different play-styles. Plus, the option to play either a hack-n-slash or take your time and plan the attacks can be refreshing when you get tired of one or the other.
Cons:
- Short: the game can be finished in less than 10 hours [my stats are inflated for idealing for cards and achievement hunting]. I don't regret for buying the game, but I did buy it on sale.
-Replayability: it really becomes an issue only because the game is rather short.
Overall:
Get it if you liked Bastion and if the shortness bothers you, get it on sale.

I bought it because I saw it on Steam Train, and i'm glad I did. This is certainly one of the more charming "unfair platformers" out there. It's got nice graphics and a good sense of humour, I found myself chuckling quite a few times at some of the traps I encountered.
Of course it goes without saying that if you hate unfair/trap platformers, you probably won't like this. That said, it shouldn't be compared to Unfair Mario. I actually found Unfair Mario really annoying, yet I still enjoyed Eryi's Action. If you really want a good idea about what this game is like, look up a free browser game called Syoban Action (also known as Cat Mario). Eryi's Action was produced by the same guy who made Syoban Action (hence the similar names), and as such Eryi's action could be considered a spiritual successor; if you like Syoban Action, there's a good chance you'll like Eryi's Action.

This game is indeed balls to the walls HARD! This game is the ulitmate test of patience and skill. If you're the type of person who often cries "Well how was I supposed to know that!?" do NOT play this game. It is feindishly hand crafted to discourage any and all players with little or no resolve, yet is not impossible.
I find that the eye-pleasing graphics takes some of the edge off the fustration one would feel from hundreds and hundreds of lives lost while trying to advance just mere inches away from the most previous checkpoint. This game is for expert gamers ONLY, casual gamers need not apply. If you do, then you only have yourself to blame.

It is not often that a platform game is really different from another platform game. Eryi's Action is very different, because it is a platform game in which you will die all over again. There are traps everywhere, which makes this videogame very frustrating. Although it is a nice twist in this old genre, I am not quite sure it is much fun. Still work the $1 I payed for the bundle though!

I love this game.  I think it's one of the best video games I've ever played.  It's weird, though, because it's not a game that comes without a load of the problems typical of MMOs.  (This is totally my opinion here, so if you're a reader who loves everything about MMORPGs and you disagree, that's totally fine.)  For long stretches of the leveling game, combat can be extremely dull depending on a variety of things: what job you've chosen, whether or not you have any companions (e.g. solo questing as a gladiator/paladin is going to be feel pretty slow when it takes you a moment or two to kill anything), and you're going to be sitting in queue after queue waiting for your turn in the dungeons.  Combat for some jobs is not very interesting until you're level 50 or 60 and you have access to dungeons and raids that will test your skills (often with boss mechanics that seem weird or even overwhelming at first, but are satisfying to pull off as a group overcoming a unique challenge), and that's an investment I'd want anyone to be aware of when getting into something like this.  You'll spend a lot of time pressing a few keys in sequence while you whittle down the HP of this or that monster.
Thankfully, most of the queues are pretty short and there are tools for getting people together for something even if the Duty Finder isn't pulling together a party for you.  And there's plenty to do while you wait: keep on questing, do some gathering or crafting, play Triple Triad.  Very importantly, for me, it's a world that feels good to hang out in.  The first and larger paragraph up there probably seems overly negative for a game I'd recommend to others, but here's so much that I enjoy about Final Fantasy present here — my bard's equipment is glamoured to look like early FF character designs by Yoshitaka Amano, and there's tons of armor (and other designs) in the game that support this style and atmosphere.  It is a legit as heck hangout/comfy game.  The challenging (hardcore raiding) stuff is there if you want it.
Just some thoughts here; not really a full review or an attempt to convince anyone to play.  It's my jam, tho.  I may come and go, and frankly I'm extremely relieved that it's a game I only want to play for a few months at a time between extended breaks, but when I'm into it... well, I'm pretty into it.

Staying true to the Final Fantasy name, Final Fantasy XIV delivers very great gameplay as Square Enix's 2nd Final Fantasy MMORPG.
It's pretty, now supporting a DirectX 11 client, with improved Tesselation and water effects, causes the game to look slightly better than DirectX 9, which the game originally supported.
It's very well optimized for PC. I run a i7 4790K and a GTX 970 with 16gb Ram. Not only can I run this game in 1080p maxed out at 60fps, I can also stream it with those same settings at a 3.5 bitrate, and my computer doesn't cripple in performance.
It has quite a variety. Final Fantasy XIV boasts multiple classes you can pick from. A wide diversity, that is simplified for dungeon play into 3 categories: Healer, DPS, and Tank. Players will be required to form parties with the minimal 1x Healer, 2x DPS, and 1x Tank. You can't just run in a dungeon and expect to solo the entire thing, you need your party members.
The only downside to this game is, you need friends. So you better know people who are already in the game to join, or go alone and make friends on your own. If you don't have anyone to play with, I can't really justify the monthly subscription fee of $13~15.

I thought it would be nice to write a straightforward review for those who appreciate it, because a lot of the reviews here so far just rely mostly on hyping up their experience to make the game sound good. Minimum is a fun and solid game, possibly on track to be the next big thing for PC shooters.
However, when looking at Minimum it’s hard to find anything terribly unique about the game after playing the games that make up its core. Honestly, it’s just a hodgepodge of mechanics different games: creep farming from MOBA/ARTS/ASS♥♥♥♥♥♥S, civilian escort from TFC (payload from TF2), armor tiers from Quake, in-game crafting from RPGs, etc. It’s a very minimalist style of game that still manages to not look like a piece of indie garbage (aka the game has an artstyle instead of just “I LOVE X TYPE OF GAME LET ME JUST COPY ALL OF THE AESTHETICS FROM IT”). It’s a very functional game and has lots of potential to be fun, but it’s just nothing terribly special and I can’t really give it a whole lot of praise for breaking any new ground.
“B-b-but it’s just fresh out of Early Access!”
Relax.
In a time where the shooter market is focused mostly on console shooters and CounterStrike, it’s good to see a multiplayer arcade FPS take the scene with the promise of a fun multiplayer experience. The game is very fair in terms of hardware specs and can run on a variety of semi-modern setups. Getting kills and watching your gun go from basic to a beast of warfare makes me grin. There are lots of weapons to choose from but your basic weapons are still VERY viable, and it’s very easy to get the weapons you think might be fun to play with by just playing the game. You can customize several class loadouts for plenty of situations, and there’s a little cash-shop for alternate skins if one so feels the need to grab one to be a special snowflake. The maps are for the most part well-designed: it’s easy to get from point A to point B and figure out the general and some specific nooks & crannies of a map within a single round. There aren’t any particularly terrible parts of the maps that I’ve played where one player has been able to lock down a certain area just by existing. A majority of the weapons are Unreal Tournament/Quake derived (more UT than Quake), and there are old standards and familiar faces returning like a grenade launcher, rail gun, lightning gun, shotgun, plasma, and so on.
It should be easy to deduce from the trailers and Steam page that you’ll be playing in third-person. It’s got controller support but I can’t imagine why anyone would want to put themselves at that much of a disadvantage for a team-based arena shooter with a twist. When playing in-game, the more kills you get, the more damage you weapon can do and in some cases, the wider of an area of effect it has. You counter this by building into two currently existing armor types (to start): Knight and Berserker. The former is focused on protection and anti-Titan ability at the cost of player speed, and the latter is focused on dealing damage and brawling other players at the cost of protection and health. Using these armor types, players have to work together to keep their Titan safe while doing whatever they can to destroy the other team’s Titan. When both teams have their Titans destroyed, the game goes into a “creep farming” phase where both teams hunt small creatures for personal resources to upgrade their weapons and armor, while each creep kill boosts your Titan’s power. There’s a Golden Creep that gives a very large bonus to a Titan’s power, and it can keep the field even if a team lacking in creep farm grabs it or be the key to victory for the dominant team.
However, there are some problems that plague Minimum. As with any game that has some element of MOBA/ARTS/ASS♥♥♥♥♥♥S in it, it’s easy for one guy to feed the other team and let them climb the armor tiers a lot easier (one game I played just recently had me and one other guy with 2+/1 KDR while the guy at the bottom of our team was 2/35 and it took us an age to move forward). It’s also easy to just have everyone completely forget about killing creeps and just have underpowered Titans keep brawling each other; conversely, it’s also easy to have one team completely remember and the other completely forget and have a super-fast game.
There are quite a few connection issues with the game because there are a lot of moments where I end up thinking that the game is peer2peer. Rubberbanding is prevalent everywhere, but most commonly with those who end up dashing around with melee only. This is generally frustrating because someone will just hold W into you and you’ll shoot him, and suddenly he’ll stretch behind you and you’ll miss that one shot needed to keep yourself alive. It’s probably the biggest issue I’ve got with the game so far because it’s really easy to abuse with the Taser Shotgun, which will segway into the next paragraph.
In terms of complaining about balance, I’m not a fan of movement-impairing effects. I haven’t had any problems with anyone using the Cryo Rifle, but the Taser Shotgun is simply frustrating to play against. It goes against the arena shooter maxim of having freedom of movement and is a carry-over from the MOBA/ARTS/ASS♥♥♥♥♥♥S themes of the game. I also am not a huge fan of the deployable player turrets because it’s particularly easy to deploy any time (beginning, middle, end) during a fight and at the very least make the job of a teammate getting an avenger kill for you that much easier.
“B-b-but they’ll patch it!”
“G-g-g-git g-g-gud!”
Relax.
Like any other multiplayer or co-op game, Minimum is best played with friends. I wouldn’t mind seeing a LAN option or true private server option in the future, and by the looks of it Minimum can have a bright future ahead of it. I just hope Human Head Studios doesn’t fall to the cries of the majority begging for melee-only hold +forward to win or some other vocal group. I also hope that those XP-based mod slots on weapons don’t become a thing. I really hope they don’t. I hope Human Head Studios learned from the mistakes of Loadout. I really hope they did.
All in all, even though I can’t really praise Minimum for setting any standards or breaking any new ground, I would recommend Minimum if you’re looking for a new yet familiar experience in the shooter market. I'm ready to see how Human Head Studios keeps Minimum going, and I hope it's in a good way.

In-depth Review about Gameplay & Game Mechanics -
Hero Defense Haunted Island is a Tower Defense game where Towers are replaced by 5 different Heroes. It contains a lot of RPG elements such as, levelling Heroes, Skill/Talent Management, Gear management and mid-game decisions. It plays a little like a Warcraft 3 mode with a bit of extra polish, story mode and more persistent elements.
The game does have its flaws though, one being A counters B which counters C style of balancing, it’s not just certain Heroes cleave or certain Heroes deal well with single targets, just some people will deal little to no damage to certain mob types. Think of Pokemon and trying to use Electricity on a Ground type.
Overall I enjoyed the game quite a bit, the issues I listed above can be addressed during Early Access. Leveling up your Heroes, getting stronger after each battle, having a decent variety of control and Hero types is a good start and shows promise for other game features.

I played the game in Alpha and Early Access and I can recommend it to everyone who likes Tower Defense and needs a new spin in the genre. I can see myself returning to this game, doing a quick level, building up my heroes and see where the story takes me. Especially the artwork and voice acting does it for me at the moment. I will be back with a bigger review once I got to the meat of the game and tested multiplayer.

While the terrain and landscapes are very well done, the draw distance is very limited (meaning the animals disappear from site within a very short distance from you) in this game, and that is something that a hunting game SHOULDN'T have. Name: Sleeping Dogs
Developer: United Front Games
Genre: Beat Em Up, Kung Fu, Action, Stealth, Racing
Personal Verdict: Ever wanted to put a leg up someones face? Do so in HD.
Originally Sleeping Dogs without the Definitive Edition tack to it this version sees square enix adding and adjusting the entire DLC released in Sleeping Dog previous version into something well errr, better. Anyways to the game itself.
Sleeping Dog is a visceral game of Kung-Fu, betrayal, triads and friendship as we follow one Wei Shen as he does his job in the brilliantly rendered world of Hong Kong, Wei must choose between his allegiance to the triads or to his police officers as he delivers justice. One Kung-Fu at a time.
Playing the story of Sleeping Dogs [SD] reminds me of the old action Kung-Fu movie where the story moves at breakneck speed and emotional rollercoaster happens all the time. Which is to say the story kick♥♥♥♥♥ It delivers them in spades and is not afraid to hold back from doing all sorts of nasties that the player will no doubt witness and feel.
Usually I do not like to talk much about graphics because what the heck am I suppose to write?! Exception of course are made. Sleeping Dogs treats the world of Hong Kong is pretty bland with repetitive civilian, normal texture etc etc but it really comes alive during the night and rain! Especially night and rain together in tandem!
Skins exude a sheen, cars has powerful reflection upon them and everything is generally 10x better than it is during daytime. Not to say the standard graphics are bad but upping it up and witnessing the full glory of the engine in rain and night is a breathtaking experience.
United Front Games pulled no punches in making sure we get the most authenthic experience for our stay in Hong Kong. Random quips in Cantonese can be heard as you walk the streets, Character that do not speak english instead does full Cantonese dialogue. The crisp clear audio makes subtitle a secondary thing as oppose to be a mandatory on for most games and every effect down to the last mission complete evoke a strangely nostalgic chinese feel.
Ah Sleeping Dogs, I turn you on, kick a few citizen stuff them into the boot of their car then kill them right in front of the hospital with my KUNG-FU. What better way to start a monday.
In an otherwise typical fare of open world game Sleeping Dog does the competition shame by focusing on one aspect many game have neglected: The melee system. While initially the melee system seems easy with 1 hko object scattered all over the enviroment and enemies come in weak and puny form they soon ramp it up especially towards midgame where you will be punching, kicking and hurling foes off rail while covered in blood. Essentially press counter when enemy glow red, punch them up till they die and then when the meter is full use face mode to recover health and make your enemy fear you.
Along the way explore the world! Beat up people in side activities to uncover drug raids, beat people up again to obtain chests of money and clothing. Turn Wei into the most fashion savvy freak with the game large customization option. Engage in daring fights as you beat up people to get money and more face value!
Or perhaps you're a picky one eh? Want a bit of dialogue and action in your beat em up? Look no further. Turn into a cop hunt down people as you become the scourge of the underworld, help your eccentric group of buddies as they get into random hijinks that often ends with beating people up. Or you know, just help around the citizen of Hong Kong, they could use a help from a friendly people-beating gangster.
But alas the gunplay fall shorts, since most resources went into fighting people up the gun lacks recoil, feels plasticky and holds no weight. Cleverly the game wave them away from most mission by stating "HONG KONG DON'T ALLOW GUNS!" it works for me it should works for you.
The car good to say however is awesome and a joy to ride, and since you can simply steal a car it doesnt matter if you're walking on foot, simply steal a car and be on your way. Or you can use the car valet. Eh. Fun feature includes the ability to steal cars within a car without going out. Amazing when you think about it since you don't have to dismount but can happily continue your ride in a shiny new car as the wreck of your old ones burns behind you.
Completing mission earns you triad points by being brutal and police point for being civilised lawful cop. Leveling up gives you a choice of perk within the skill tree.
An oddly choice of collectible, side missions and all that jazz ensures you won't be bored of the game anytime soon.
How I wish i could experience it all over again, the powerful gunfight, desperate Kung-Fu action and emotional story. Why does more game can be this way? Alas a few minor issues does bog it down though. But does this makes it a bad game? It is an excellent game released suddenly to our world. Buy it already I am tired of typing this all out. Basically this game is awesome.

As far as this game goes, if you loved the game on your mobile devices then your going to go nuts for this spawn of it. The game is highly playable right now as it stands, there are still some  bugs but the producers have been valiant in releasing a stream of updates that have significantly upgraded the Plague Inc experience! So, i say to those who are loyal fans, get on board now, the game is highly playable as it stands, updates are constanly coming fixing minor bugs to major ones, wouldnt you like to be a part of one of the greatest games of the year, so Come on, get in line for your immunizations because i predict Plague Inc: Evolved to spread and become infectious to alarming levels, be a part of a legend in the making!

One fine day, Eryi went to eat the melon that she had been SO looking forward to... but it was nowhere to be found! Then she noticed a note on the table. She picked it up and read: "Your melon looked delicious, so I took it. From Farta X"
Fuming with rage, Eryi set out from her house to get her melon back from Farta.
Eryi's Action is a 2D ‘trapformer’ by developer Xtal Sword that is visually inspired by Super Mario, but has gameplay akin to games like I Wanna Be the Guy. Don’t be fooled by its adorably charming looks – this game abounds in traps and wants you to die! However, where IWBTG was murderously difficult, Eryi's Action is additively challenging and FUN!
Trap placement is often laugh-out-loud funny and seriously engaging. Some traps simply need to be learned to avoided, but others are puzzles that will require your skill and wits to beat. Either way, Eryi’s action delivers laughs, frustrating and satisfaction & all...

Eryi's Action may look like your typical platformer at first glance. However, this assumption is horribly... HORRIBLY WRONG. While guiding Eryi through 10 stages filled with peril to reclaim her stolen melon (Yes... a melon), you will encounter enough booby traps to make your hair fall out from pulling it so hard. That's right, it's THAT type of game. You know the kind. It's one of those games where you're all like "I'm gonna jump on this block over here." and the game's like "NOPE! YOU JUST GOT EATEN! YOU LOSE!" that just stomp at any tiny bit of sanity you had left before you started.
While saying that, this game is still addicting and fun with tight controls and colorful visuals. Most of the traps have very specific trigger patterns and you'll eventually memorize these and be able to advance. While most of the ways you die in this game are indeed traps that you don't see coming, most of them are comical enough to where you'll get a chuckle out of each one. For example, a spinning windmill falls on your head the first time you walk by. "Hmm... maybe I'll try jumping over it." No sooner than a second after you jump over it, it detaches and comes after you.
Eryi's Action certainly isn't a game for everyone. However, those of us that find joy in memorizing patterns and failing hundreds of times (I died 550 times over the course of the game. Thank you infinite lives!) will fall in love with this charming little game from indie developer XTAL Sword.

This game introduces a lot of really good ideas but ultimately falls apart after it impliments them. Example: Weapons essentially autoupgrade per kill thus giving it more damage or an explosive passive or something. Pretty cool right? The Room is a critically acclaimed puzzle game where you try to open boxes, trust me you will want to play it.
Now the description is probably not the best thing ever, but it's how I see the game. So the game is split into chapters where each time you try to open something, which takes you to different rooms.
The story is pretty much not existent, but it doesn't matter.  Maybe it's my fault that I missed something, but from what I gather you find a box which belongs to a scientist who found out about a new energy source. (Probably got the entire plot wrong).
The gameplay consists of you trying to open a series of complex boxes each containing locks which you have to solve puzzles to unlock. Each of the safes have more complex mechanisms and get's more complex as the game goes on.
The game was ported from mobile to PC and the gameplay is pretty much you dragging around a mouse to look around the boxes and zooming in to find a clue or something that will help you open the box.
The game also gives you an eye piece which helps you see things you can see with the regular vision. It let's you see fingerprints and through some objects.
The puzzles are very well designed, it ranges from really simple to pretty difficult. I only had to go to a guide once in the entire game, so if you're a seasoned puzzle gamer, you shouldn't have much trouble.
The soundtrack is also really good, it helps to build tension so much, that at one point I actually thought something sinister was hidden in the boxes.
The gameplay on the other hand I felt wasn't done all that well. I had trouble getting to the part of the box I want as the mouse controls don't really work all that well. But it's just a minor gripe I had with this game.
The game took me 2 hours to finish and I had a lot of fun with it and I highly suggest you pick it up at full price and you will not be disappointed.
Final Words:
Overall I have not much bad to say The Room is one of the best puzzles games ever made and I cannot wait for Part 2 to come to steam

One of the best open world games you can get your hands on.
This should be among the top titles like GTA, but it doesn't have multiplayer, which makes it harder for it to compete.
That being said, the game has a ♥♥♥♥♥on of replayability, i've found myself playing this game for 6.5 hours in one sitting without even noticing the time, doing all kinds of sidemissions and stuff, not even focussing on the main story yet, which is really awesome as well.
Combat is focused on melee combat which works really, really well. There's guns too, but in (Sleeping Dogs') Hong Kong you won't come across any unless you mess with really bad people (or cops).
This feels very realistic and good, melee combat gives you a heavy sense of impact and by unlocking certain skills and using certain moves you can make every melee encounter feel just as cool as the first.
(E.g grabbing, rushing, countering, throwing, using environment etc according to who you're facing).
With that being said, having a gun gives you a feeling of power.
You really do feel like you should be careful with it because if you start slinging it around the local PD will do everything to hand your♥♥♥♥♥to you personally. It feels as if you'd have a gun on you in a real streetfight, for a backup measure if♥♥♥♥♥♥really hits the fan.
The graphics are great (even to this date stuff looks really nice), framerate is smooth and the environment looks really cool with alleys and stuff to rush through or fight in. (I normally don't like asian settings in games for some reason).
The driving works really well, there's a lot of grip if you pick the right speed and if you do it right, you can rush through a densely populated Hong Kong at will. You can drift (not for long distances though, mainly for cornering), ram (seems unrealistic but it's fun) and even jump from your vehicle to another. Heck, just sitting on a bike and holding your handbrake while pinning the throttle to do a quick U turn whilst standing still feels and looks amazing thanks to the cool camera angle.
The camera angles are generally good throughout the game (good meaning they're not annoying or bad in any way), but you'll occasionally have them act up in tight spaces, although this isn't common.
Overall the game is amazing, a really underrated gem.

As I said, if you are a fan of action 2D scrollers then you will be replaying this game a lot, either you will die a lot and need to replay the game while getting better or you will ace it and will keep augmenting the difficulty setting. This is why I think this game is above average, it has that old school ruthlessness that Japanese developers love to keep alive, if you are a challenge lover then you’ll be right at home at Normal (or harder), but if you like to actually make some progress through the many mini bosses and bosses without seeing your mech exploding countless times then Easy is the place to be, and I feel no shame in that since it is "old school kind of easy”… god bless Japanese quality standards.

Even on Easy it was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥being able to finish the first level without a single scratch, that’s an achievement that took me around 20min to get… after that I started my Normal run and got to half of the game, I was happy enough with that and decided to move on to another game.

A nice little idea spoiled by poor netcode at this stage in development. Most rounds will be dominated by a single player who is effectively immune to damage and capable of scoring one-hit kills in melee from ten to fifteen feet in range, and can warp through other players. For a game with such a strong emphasis on close combat, the disparity between melee hit-detection/collision-detection and the sharp (though unresponsive) gunplay is unforgiveable.
I'd hope they can resolve this, but with the history of melee in arena multiplayer games, I find myself without optimism.
As for the gunplay... Weapons make the faintest, most boring noises, sometimes seeming almost completely silent in battle, removing any sense of impact, or any real clue of your own fire-rate. A stylised game like this needs intense audio - but the music is dull and the sense of whether you're doing/taking damage simply isn't there.
Meanwhile the amount of damage required to actually finish a player off seems significantly too high for the style of gameplay on offer - or perhaps it's simply the lack of damage feedback and poor hit-detection making it seem that way?

This is a good game, not a great one but good nonetheless because it lays the foundations of a series that can only improve to become a masterpiece.
I actually felt like I had broken into someone's house and I was trying to open up a safe full of money. The game has a dark and somewhat eerie soundtrack, mixed with background  noises such as the floor cracking or doors closing. But at the same time it is a very relaxing atmosphere, and when I was stuck I just sat in front of my screen, turning the camera around this complicated box, appreciating its complexity and smart mechanics.
Speaking of complexity, the game is not that hard. Yes you can get stuck at times but certainly not for as long as you would in a game like Myst. So don't expect any tortuous conundrum as most of the puzzle is quite self-explanatory. It's mostly a matter of accurate observation and looking for details in every corner. Some riddles appear several times throughout the game, which to me felt like the developpers lacked the ambition to replace them with new ones.
But in the end I appreciated the whole experience, and you can tell the devs have been through a lot of thinking to create these mechanical boxes full of surprises. Hopefully they will keep exploring this idea in a future release and make it really complicated this time.

Has some good points, evokes the classic SNES gameplay.  The game style itself lends itself strongly to a homage of Cybernator.
And this is where the good points end, the gameplay is too reminisent of Cybernator, which I would not count against it if the controls were good, they are not.
The dash mechanic in the game is very short and does not have a dedicated button to engage on it's own.  This is a minor point  compared to a more glaring one is that your forward momentium is NOT preserved when jumping in the middle of a dash.
you can aim your main weapon to pretty much any angle you need, but it's tied to your movement and is held ONLY when firing, not a great setup when trying to setup a shot.
while another minor point, I feel it's still worth mentioning that if you get too close to an enemy, the game defaults to a melee attack against said enemy, which is fine until you're trying to prioritize something further away.  Given the style of play feels like it'd be better just not being there.
Jumpjets in a game are always welcome to see.  Again though, makes no sense if I can't dash and feather them for an extended glide at a good speed!
As someone who enjoyed the original Cybernator game back in the days of the SNES, I cannot recommend it to others as it just feels like the game was gutted of some of the more critical controls that made that game so fun to play. If you came  here with it's description stating that it evokes the older games like Cybernator and Metal Warriors, you are better off not getting this game. It's definitely cheap and not a big loss if you don't enjoy it.

Hearkening back to the SNES mecha platformer Metal Warriors, Gigantic Army is a side-scrolling action fest in which you must pilot your heavily-armored stomper mech into the heart of an alien world, blasting endless biomechanical baddies, blowing up enormous warmachines, and blocking, running, and leaping your way out of danger. This is not exactly the most inspired of concepts, but the execution here is intelligent and crisp, with intuitive aiming and strafing mechanics that make for a much more skill-focused game than you might expect.
Carrying the old-school action theme even further, each level is timed. You can (and really should) pick up Timer extension power ups along the way, along with health and damage boosters, but even so, between the enemy forces and ticking timer, you're gonna die more than a few times. Completing a stage merely gives you a tiny health boost, not a full heal, so it's strongly recommended you not let any items pass. You only get three continues per game, an absolutely archaic system to include in a game released in 2014, but it fits well enough and feels natural. Stranger still, while the story blurbs you receive between levels are painfully low-budget, the actual story and writing they throw at you is honestly pretty enjoyable. Regardless, Gigantic Army is a game that'll hit you with a few Game Overs before you manage to take out the final challenge (particularly on the brutal higher difficulties), but you'll enjoy every boss pattern learned and inch of progress acquired. If you're a fan of the old-school, this one's been whipped up just for you.

Most Classic RPG experiance in an MMO that ive had in a while. its its pretty rare these days where you start off as an actual  normal adventurer and get quests from an adventurers guild. these days most mmos are just replica of "you are a chosen one! now go fight evil" sorta thing.
The combat system is about the same as the standard good old formula, has som pretty animations for combat as well. The Gear and weapons have a nice aesthetic feeling to them and they get the look of the gear right as well, going from begginners gear to higher level gear, it actually matches what it looks like in comparison to the level. no flashy beginners gear. to bad that there is no costume slots so you can use the image of old gear, but most of them look great to begin with.
A great part of the class mechanics is that once you reach lvl15 on your first class, you can choose to pick up any other class and conintue with that, of course starting from level one again. but if you dont want to do this you can always start a new character, since they give a generous amount of character slots per world (at least after the ifrst month of paid sub).
The Story is quite typical of a final fantasy game, chocka block full of characters and plot. since i play most games while listening to something,  i usually dont pay much attention to what the npc's say and just follow quest obj, but this has probably been one of only 10 or so games that i dont do that.
Animations, Graphics and Design of Final Fantasy 14 are quite good, if you look around you realise that every npc, wheteher they be friend or enemy, has a ton of idle animations and animations while being interacted with. for me who uses a pretty low end pc (basically what the minimum it states, maybe a bit lower) its still looks quite beautiful.
The Environment and world itself is quite expansive,though it is section off into different regions. For example Thanalan (name of whole region) -> split into North, South East, e.t.c
There is thankfully no game breaking pay to win gear. though there is gear that you can by with real money, its aesthetic stuff like mounts and costumes. basically all you can by with real money is -> The game itself + paid DLC ( which so far is only heavensward), the sub needed to play and aesthetic stuff like premium dyes, mounts, nostalgic costumes and little pets that will follow you around.
Also if you happen to be a japanophile like me you can hav Jap audio with english sub. just saying, but theres nothing wrong with the english voice actors, they're acutally pretty good.
i wished that they would add more voices to the cutscenes and general talking to npcs, because so far only important mission cutscenes have voice.
maybe no sub fee or a lower one, its pretty heavy on my wallet since i play alot. hahaha

If you like MMOs play this, if you don't like MMOs then you haven't played this one long enough. ffxiv is getting bigger and better than any other mmo and if you want to invest in a game with a fruitful future ahead of it, then this is the one.
I've yet to play an mmorpg with a storyline as good as this, the game is considered to have a storyline that competes amongst even their own well-known non mmo games. Combat is sharp, fluid, and the combos work well; especially when you're decently leveled and don't have peasant abilities. The class/crafting system is also outstanding, and adds tenfolds of gameplay that's worth investing in (if you're worried about leveling said crafting/fighting class, then you'll be relieved to hear that exp bonus' are awarded the greater the level between your current class vs your highest).
Some interesting aspects about the world and storyline to consider:
-The entire planet begins to recognise your character as you gain levels and further yourself, random NPCs will know who you are and its generally pretty cool to come across games that do that.
-Story is of  high standard, there isn't much voice acting in the beginning, but once you start accessing the non-3-year-old content you'll realise SE has been putting even more effort into their story quests.
-Not just the main story either, each class and job comes with their own unique storyline which also progresses your abilities, these get real intense, probably better than the main story in the short run.

I played Final Fantasy 11 online for years. Many years like almost ten. I have to say this Game is a newer well implemented version of it that somehow lacks the experiance of the original ff mmo. I really wished the devolopers had added a few more varied classes, a lot more voiced content, and good lord is group voice chat really to much to ask for with a paid sub game? Honestly though i have my gripes it is a wonderful mmo. The crafting is actually pretty fun and it don't take months to reach simple goals like ff11 did. The combat is by far the largest improvement, with abilities that make sense and timers that make sense(ff11 had abilities with two hour cooldowns). the graphics are pretty and are extremely consistant. Its almost like finding an extinct animal alive to find a glitch in this game. The content is varied and entertaining, but there is still quite a few go here kill 10 of these type quests, honestly it's like milking a cow for a half hour sometimes. Meeting people can be tough especially if your kinda gung ho to do what you want, but for the most part the community is very friendly. Rarely you will run into a serious♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on any mmo and no game is the exception. I play with my wife and we like to run the quests or dungeons together, while playing these events if you do not enter with enough players to fill the requirements other players that queud for the same dungeon will be presented the option to join. The dungeons are well crafted fun and can be challenging, but the community at large is very very very unforgiving for mistakes, even from first time runners. The community almost demands you watch video and read guides on the dungeons before you run them, wich can ruin the fun of figuring out the dungeon and diminish the experiance of victory. I have a blast playing even though i've made next to no "friends" in my time on (seriously i have like two besides my wife) but there are always groups looking to recruit. These groups run the gamut from being awesome community groups to being groups that try to manipulate you and get you to willingly contribute your hard earned resources to the group, then kicking you out of the group for not being elite enough or "invested" enough. Overall ARR is a well crafted mmo adventure with a fair amount of content and a lot of fun to be had.     8/10

This game is very well-rounded, and an excellent source of entertainment if you get bored, can't find the motivation to start up a more complex game like Europa Universalis or Kerbal Space Program, and just want to smash something fast.
That's after you beat the campaign of course, which is fun in of itself. There are three main modes a single person would be interested in, and the same for multiplayer. There's War, Obstacle Course, Time Trial, and Skeeboulder. The singleplayer campaign consists entirely of War games throughout all the maps and five different 'ages', Sparta, (characterized by orange and black clay-jar carvings as an art style) the Middle Ages, (reminds me of ancient tapestries) the Renaissance, (with both roman architecture and a lot of marble) Baroque France, (very blue, very fancy) and Spain. (a very dark and gruesome Spain, however)
I still pop in almost every day to play a few rounds of obstacle course, and while the campaign won't last forever there's plenty there to play for quite some time.

Rock of Ages has the kind of base concept you'd hear and say, "hmm, that'd make a fun flash game".
As you can probably tell, this isn't a flash game.
You guide your rolling stone around a winding course and hit the enemy gate until it dies. But you have a gate and the enemy has a Brian Jones! But you can both place down defences after your Ian Stewards have been smashed! And then you can use your leftover currency to buy better Mick Jaggers!
It's fun, it's as slow or fast paced as you want it be, and it has a challenging difficulty curve.
The cutscenes in story are silly little gags to the layman, and chock-a-block with jokes for the history nerds. The Rock of Ages is called the Rock of AGES for a reason!
I'd heartily recommend this game for a romp with your friends too. Strangely enough, latency lags both players, even when they're playing with their own individual courses. I thought the core design of war mode would have countered that.
Good game, I like it a whole bunch, pick it up when you need to fill some time.

remains fun despite its problems, and makes for some great local competitive play. The campaign gets annoying at times because of the time constraints with defense building, but is quirky and funny enough that it ultimately remains worth the time. If you're looking for something unlike what you've played before, it's time to let Rock of Ages rock your world.
