This is the first game since LIMBO that I have played that I could describe as truly, undeniably great. This game has literally everything that a game needs to have.
It has a compelling story. Some might think it too vague, but it tells you more than enough to keep you motivated and push you forward through the game, but leaves plenty of things to your imagination - a quality that I think many writers underestimate.
It is visually stunning. Seriously, this is the most gorgeous game that I have ever seen. The visuals don't need me to tell you how great they are. Just look at them.
Finally, and some would say most importantly, gameplay. I don't actually know how common this particular type of gameplay is, or if there are any other games that have used it (aside from possibly Bastion, which I will be buying as soon as I finish writing this review). But either way, its execution in this game is flawless. I loved the process of mastering the function combinations and figuring out what worked best, and that unlocking the stories behind the functions themselves encouraged you to use them in different ways and combinations. I also love the fact that the game never feels like the outcome is the result of anything aside from your skill level. I wouldn't call this a puzzle game by any means, but it definitely presents you with problems at times that require a less than direct solution.
TL;DR, this game is perfect, and you should buy it. Don't even wait for a Steam sale. Just buy it now. It's worth it.

Sound design is rather mediocore with the exception of minions who, although repetative, always help cheer up the mood of sometimes gloomy and uninteresting areas. Definitely one of the best puzzle games I've played in a long while.
The puzzles are one of The Room's strongest points, as they should be; while I've had trouble with games like Myst and escape-the-room type games in the past, The Room's design seems to avoid all of those problems. Rather than traipsing across an entire world looking for clues, you always have the option to view every relevant element of the current chapter's puzzle box simply by zooming out, a detail which, given various memory problems I have, was much appreciated. The Room also relies more on observation than pre-known knowledge; for example, many other puzzle games I've played required a basic understanding of Morse Code, ciphers, confusing mathematics, and/or specific logic problems. However, all of the puzzles in The Room (save, perhaps, one in the beginning, which gives you a visual guide anyway) can be solved through observation of the object in question, and there are no drastic leaps of logic in how to solve things.
The Room's tone is also quite strong, though the story doesn't quite catch up. The use of atmospheric lighting and eerie sound design (which gets eerier the closer you are to solving important puzzles) gives a feeling that we're going much further down the rabbit-hole than we probably should, and letters from the creator of the various puzzle boxes give a bit of backstory; however, at the end of the day, the story has little relevance to the actual solving of the puzzles, and the ending doesn't really wrap anything up. This is a small annoyance, however, as the gameplay & visual elements of The Room are strong enough to support the strange plotline.
Though it's obvious that The Room was originally developed for some kind of touchscreen medium, the controls are still very tactile and fun to use with just a computer mouse, and the updated, more detailed graphics are a nice addition in return. There are a few elements that do act up a little bit (notably a dial in Chapter Four that must be used several times, and a turning mechanic on a puzzle in Chapter 5), but in those cases there are certain movements that make them much more consistent, and the hiccups are few and far between.
I feel that The Room was of a good length for the price I payed (as I finished it in just under two hours, spread across two days), though at the same time I am left wanting more. Luckily there are a few sequels out there to scratch that particular itch!

The colors making the room grow colder, the drawn out faces of people in quiet desperation eating away at you patients. But wait! It affects a lot more! You’re now faced with growing dilemmas, pressures, conspiracies, and the ever tightening time constraints, superior reviews, and unscrupulous propositions threatening your very family!
…Well some games have different advantages. Very few would actually sharpen your senses, test your resolve, and show you how and where the collective mindset ends every time. As a girl and non-Starcraft player, I tried playing this to see if it would:
1) manage to hold my interest;
2) teach me more about Starcraft in an entertaining manner.
It didn't.
I lasted 30 minutes before utter boredom took over and I decided enough was enough.
The game does try to accommodate and ease in non-Starcraft people with an introductory video at the start. However, it doesn't tell you much - just a general overview of Starcraft's goals, and how Korean Starcraft players are the best in the world. Nothing is said about game tactics, skills involved, what exactly about Starcraft has made the game so popular, etc etc.
As the story progresses, you can click on certain gaming jargon (e.g. "brood wars", "GG", "PC bang", etc) within the story text, to see their explanation in a glossary. I stopped bothering with this after a while as it got tedious.
The story itself was really humdrum - you are a foreigner who's come to Korea to join a Starcraft tourney. You are filled with self-doubt and apprehension, since as a non-Korean you are already at a disadvantage. And so on. The usual. You know.
You keep clicking
until you have to make a choice. Choices are usually about what you would do in a Starcraft game against an opponent.
Other story characters include: the expert player who's modest & forgiving; the hardened girl gamer with an undiscovered soft side; the cold-hearted trash-talking villain...
The game isn't badly-made with regards to production, but plotwise it's just so very predictable and stereotypical, with your usual cookie cutter characters.
It also failed to make me understand or
understand more about Starcraft. I thought I could learn more about either player psychology, the obsessive cult-like training experience, battle mechanics, common strategies, etc, but I did not. The game is too focused on delivering its plot for this to happen effectively or in a manner that is coherent or engaging for a non-Starcraft person.
I'd rather have gone to Wikipedia or some other gaming website and read up about Starcraft there.

The art is visually appealing and the story is written well. The only thing that is lacks is quality of life improvements that can be found in other visual novels, such as an auto-advance text option and a gallery for unique CGs found through playing. I hope the makers can include these in their future VN works.

I REALLY enjoyed this game. There should be a sequel or at least an expansion pack!!
Pros:
- It's such a unique concept
- The music is really awesome
- The game makes me laugh
- There is a ton of replayability because of the different game modes, as well as possible defenses you can experiment with in the campaign mode.
- The artwork is really cool
- The sound FX crack me up
- Gameplay mechanics are really good
- Great level design
- Controls are easy
- TRICK JUMPS!!!!
Cons:
- Obstacle course mode is way too easy
- Enemy rock AI needs to have difficulty levels and be improved (this is the main reason why obstacle course mode is way too easy)
- There's a bug that screws up camera/controls after many relaunches in time trial mode leading to needing to restart the level again from the time trial menu <-- this is minor
- Finding yourself in the time trial universal scores list for each level is difficult <-- this is minor
- Catapults are a bit OP and/or some units take up too many squares, which sort of forces the player to stick to finding a pinch point and creating a blockade of towers with catapults behind them on harder maps because each of these only takes up 1 square <-- This can make the game a little bit monotonous, but on the flip side it may encourage more experimentation with different defenses on another playthrough so I'm 50/50 on this one.
All in all though this game is seriously awesome, quirky and heavily addictive fun that will see you finishing it in only a few sittings, so I wholeheartedly recommend it!!!

A Very Interesting and enticing game. It gave me the same sensation I got when playing Halo: Reach, but without feeling derivative. The likeness of sensations was akin to the similar feeling given between C.o.D. and Titanfall; though vastly different in mechanics, the pace and personality seem to place both in the same sub-genre of shooter.
While many of the subsidiary parts of the game appear as though they were taken from various popular bandwagons, this is only skin-deep. Blockish shapes and crafting imply Minecraft; bloom, particle effect styling, vivid colour, and map design smack of Halo: Reach; looming, powerful titans reek of Titanfall; and a reward system for kills even evokes thoughts of C.o.D. 6. However, among metaphorical covers of books, this is a dust jacket on a hardback. And, like with many literal dust jackets, the fanciful mainstream picture it portrays serves as a ruse to lure people from the mainstream. The hardcore casual-gamers and fanatics of the bandwagon are its target solely in advertising. Its aims at A) the kinds of people who game all day, but only play games GameStop has had window cut-outs for, and other games like it, or B) the kinds of people who bandwagon Minecraft so hard they think sinuosity-less geometry is more revolutionary than a 1790s Frenchman.
Now that we’ve covered what this game isn’t, let’s talk about what it is. This game is a fast paced third person shooter with a balanced leveling system that takes the “grind” out of grinding –which only leaves the “ing”. While this is bad wordplay, its excellent gameplay; there is no tedium trying to power up your gun or rank up your armor, no playing 15 minutes of a match before earning something more useful than a UAV, and no angry obsession with getting the higher K/D (well it doesn’t induce it for those who don’t normally have it), just pure dynamic gun-play. Like in Hotline Miami, dying is near unnoticeable as you can plunge right back into the action seconds after death, and like in TF2 a decent size death streak early game doesn’t feel like a set-in-stone “gg” for the match. Whereas C.o.D. rewards garnered from kills feel like giving the winning team an even bigger edge, the rewards for kills in Minimum feel more balanced, and are very fluidly gained and lost temporarily mixing up gameplay more than giving team advantage. The crafting system tries really hard to sound like Minecraft in all of its descriptions, but really the out of match crafting is just a well-paced (unlike C.o.D.) unlock system, and in match crafting is just a cleverly disguised skill-tree/upgrade system based on collecting two types of materials that drop from dead bodies like bolts do from Ratchet & Clank.
The pseudo “Titanfall rip-off” gametype, titan, is the main game mode, and the most pleasingly surprising part of the dust jacket. The titans are autonomous, and respawn in alternating waves with resource gathering (which powers up your team’s titan in the next titan wave). Not only this, but the Titans are interested in only two things 1) killing the enemy team’s titan, and 2) brute-force getting past map-based defenses to destroy the enemy core. Now here’s the plot twist. This objective-based game mode style is the same as League of Legends, but in a faster, less tactic-focused cartographically, shooter format. The game mode is much simpler than League’s version of it, yet this seems like an apt adaptation for the genre and pace of the game. You are to the titans what minions are to players in League, but with an additional neutral-team of sub-minions (four-legged rectangular creatures called creepers –I mean creeps) that players grind to power up their titans. Its League dynamic with roles jumbled up.
Teams try to progress further into enemy territory with every respawn while the two team’s minions attack both the larger entities and minions from the other team. The grinding to power up the large entities still exists, and is still fulfilled by the player grinding easily killed herds of enemies. It takes the dynamic of player and minion, and divides it up to accommodate the game’s genre and sub-genre. You still power up your character (with a better balance retention in 1v1 encounters) by killing enemies, the “more powerful the enemy you kill, the more power you gain” still applies, the core objective of teams fighting past turrets (and walls) to destroy the enemy core while aided by smaller/weaker allies still exists, and the many choices of character build based in a per-match system is carried through, but it doesn’t let any of it get in the way. The grinding creatures that are smaller than the player are neutral and don’t attack players, which keeps the combat PvP focused rather than worrying about fighting the creeps as well as making the grinding competitive as both teams try to kill the same creatures –again keeping the focus on outplaying the other players not AI. The grinding of the creeps powers up your titan as well as you, and does so via automatic stat increases, so your upgrading process is kept mostly separate from tipping the scales in objective progress; the better you grind the better your team can progress through to objectives, but that’s as far as your thoughts need go on the subject. Your titan being the only one to agro enemy walls, turrets (map turrets not mini turrets deployed by players), and titans means you don’t have you have breathing room to deal with the enemy players. Similarly, your titan being the only one capable of fighting map defenses, as well as it being solely focused on doing so, means that you don’t have to worry about whether or not you need to go for the objectives/map defenses in lieu of your incompetent teammates –at most you have to attack the titan so it doesn’t get to far into your territory. Lastly, titans killing the enemy core being the only way to win ensures that the dynamic of winning doesn’t live and die with your K/D, but playing strategically still doesn’t get in the way of the focus of competing against enemy players in the unique grind & gun gameplay so much as it does compliment it.
The summation of these things gives a game that feels both distinct and original, yet induces a mood when gaming perhaps not felt since games like Unreal Tournament 4, Halo: Reach (please don’t try to tell me Halo 4 exists -it’s like New Jersey, or Crocs, in that nothing so abhorrent could be real), and Quake III Arena. It paces upgrades well, the unlock system is priced (with in-game currency) excellently, and it has enough variety both when upgrading by loadout and by in-match-progression to offer accommodate many play styles (that feel noticeably different rather than different but same feeling as between different Borderlands guns). As far as titan mode goes, the strategic progression toward achieving objectives feels complimentary to the fast pace death-match happening around it, while allowing individuals to prioritize approach from a League style mindset or a Reach style mindset with equal impact on the team’s collective winning or losing. Keeping in mind this game is in early access and will likely see a lot more additions to the weapons, armor, and other upgrades/loadout choices, this game is well worth the buy. In terms of bugs, developer dedication, and regular (meaningful) updates I’d say this is one early access I think would be safe to support by buying now rather than waiting till “release”, and even in its current state it seems worth it for $5 (on sale). If you liked Reach, or fast paced shooters, I recommend this game.

Let's start with the first thing.  This is NOT it's own game.  It's DLC for Overlord.  Why it's listed as it's own game?  Probably because it was put up on steam before DLC was really a big thing.  I don't know.
So why the negative review?  Well let's start that I played this while playing the base game of Overlord.  I played it at the same time and the game really feels like that's the intended use case.  There's a number of additional "Abyss" levels that the player can go through.  5 of them.  Each have their own story and each has a play on the bosses faced in the real game, with an all new final boss.
There's at least one or two good levels in here.  I particularly liked the level that dealt with everything being a play.   It's an interesting twist, and I really liked a number of things done in that level.  The down side, well the other four levels really didn't fill me with the same enjoyment.   A few of them were annoying, and overall, I felt this is underwhelming.   The last level is insultingly short, simplistic, and tedious all at the same time.  An impressive feat.
Now the bigger issue that I think everyone should take with this.  This is DOUBLE the price of the base game currently, and definitely not worth that and the same price as the sequel.
I enjoyed Overlord.  I actually liked it a lot, but when I was doing things for Raising hell, I felt let down.  It wasn't a horrible experience, it just was more of the same, and while I really liked Overlord, the changes in Raising Hell, felt like they were there to differentiate itself from the base game, and failed at that.
It didn't help that a lot of the levels felt overly padded and uninteresting.  When the game had an interesting idea, it kind of built on it.  There also was a decent amount of interaction with the world.  In the DLC, it felt stale and desolate.  And annoying.  There's at least two puzzles I can think of (the lawn mowing and the sheeps) that was just annoying rather long after the interesting part of the puzzle was gone.
Will you hate this DLC?  No.  But it's just not worth your money.  There's a sequel to the original game that is likely worth you money more than this.  It's not that it's bad, it's just unneeded and lackluster.   For me, that means I can't recommend it.

The Room:
Summary:
6.5 out of 10
The puzzles are okay, but the perspective ones were the most difficult. There is no replay value once you complete the game.
Full disclosure:
I recommended this game, because it feels like a good puzzle game for those who are interested in puzzle games. However, it isn't a puzzle game where you will be racking your head for answers or answering trival knowledge questions. Everything you need, is right infront of you.
Story:
Prepare for some reading! This story line has heavy asian influences with the whole five elements and yin yan balance idea. A ton of pagan lore and demonic rituals thrown into the mix and you have a sort of mildly interesting plot. It isn't going to hold your attention for that long.
Gameplay:
The mechanics are simple. Your mouse controls your perspective and there is a lens that changes what you are see on screen. From there, it is trying to figure out the puzzles. I have a few complaints, namely very tedious tasks: turning keys, pulling out shelves, and other things.
The puzzles themselves are fairly straight forward. Hints to solving them:
1. Look at everything closely. Something silly will stand out and you will need to click on it.
2. Remember or write down numbers or patterns. They will not change on different play throughs.
3. On a perspective puzzle, find the right angle then start moving things around. Eventually things will work out.
So, these tips should get you straight through the game.
Get this game if you want an entry into the puzzle game genre. Avoid this game if you want a challenging puzzle game or you don't like puzzle games.
God Bless, and thank you for this interesting game.

Sleeping Dogs: DE edition is why steam needs more review options than either yes/no -  Sleeping Dogs is a game that I would give a neutral review on,  the gameplay has varied amount of issues and bugs but also occasionally is great fun to play.  Sleeping Dogs is the epitome of take two steps forward and three steps backwards, hopefully SE will decide on making a sequel and address many of the issues that keep Sleeping Dogs from being a masterpiece.
+Great Graphics
+Great setting and story
+Good fighting mechanics
+Plenty of action sequences
+Lots of side missions
+Good voice actors
-Poor racing missions, especially bike races
-Questionable vehicle handling
-Many bugs and occasional crashes
-Poor gunplay
-Frustrating missions
-Useless weapons especially guns
There are many questionable design flaws in Sleeping Dogs which really don't help the game, such as several highly useless abilities like access police weapons from the trunks of police cars, alls this does is immediately start a police chase, not that the guns will help you since they'll disappear if you interact with the world - yes, you heard that currently since SE constantly defend the fact that this is a melee based game, they state that guns are a 'power-up' but that doesn't explain why if I use a health shrine or open a box, or do anything other than shoot the gun will mysteriously disappear - this renders all the DLC that have bonus weapons completely useless.
Hong Kong looks great - plenty of eye candy all around but even so, SE fails to go beyond that - the character customization is limited, clothing is limited with few giving XP or special boosts.   Car customization is non-existant which is a shame and doesn't really make that much sense since a large portion of content revolves around illegal street racing, which brings up another major issue - the racing is exceptionally poor, the car races are 100% based on picking the correct car for the race, its as simple as that - whilst the bike racing is mind blowing bad, your rival racers seem to ride ungodly powerful bikes that go significantly faster, have insanely perfect handling around tight spaces and have godly acceleration, the only chances the player has to win the bike races is to have the best bikes and to drive the race with perfection, no crashes, no drift errors - as your rivals will slow down at certain parts allowing you to get in front, and then catch just as quickly.
In closing,  whilst I'm giving this a recommedation, this game does have its issues so I would rather give it a mixed review rather than a purely postive one.   I would say this game is worth a purchase if on sale or cheap but be aware of potential issues.

Sleeping Dogs was, is and always will be one of my favorite games. Before I review, note that the description is lying. It doesn't include all availaible DLC's. But it does include two major ones.
So you're probably wondering whether Sleeping Dogs has anything to do with sleeping dogs. Nope. Just like Watch_Dogs has nothing to do with watching dogs. It might be a tad boring that way. Just a tad. You play as an undercover cop named Wei Shen who's job and goal is to take down the notorious Triad Sun On Yee gang in Hong Kong. The story plays out really well and characters have good voice acting and are memorable.
If you haven't played the original (which is unfortunately not available anymore on PC) you wouldn't notice the difference in graphics. The only two noticeable changes I saw is the lighting and amount of people on the streets; which already makes for a much more fun experience as it makes Hong Kong feel much more alive. There are some minor annoyances but nothing game breaking. Cars and motorcycles pinball off of walls and other cars and sometimes combos and counters don't register. But it doesn't happen often. I very highly recommend this game as it delivers unique combat on foot and in cars. Which reminds me....to those of you patiently waiting for Arkham Knight, this will fill the whole for a bit as you can unlock (basically) the Chinese Batmobile. It will gain upgrades as you do more missions with it.
That's the end of my review. This paragraph is for those curious to gain knowledge past playing the game. Sleeping Dogs is based on true events. How true? That I don't know but I do know this. The fictious Sun On Yee gang is based on a real Triad gang called the Sun Yee On. And the 18K is based on the Sun Yee On's real arch rivals the 14K. Sun Yee On was founded in 1919 by a man named Heung Chin and currently has around 55,000 members around the world; which is supposedly the highest count among the Triads. The Triads control extortion, drug trafficking, gambling and prostitution. Which is basically everything you encounter in the game. Their favored weapon of choice is the cleaver; which you see plenty of in the game as well. The Triads do not give any mercy to traitors and rats. They do indeed torture their victims before killing them. The term 'red pole' is also a real term used and is actually not a huge deal within their structure. 'Red poles' are enforcers; just one step up from being regular members. Before you were even in the Sun On Yee you were considered a 'Blue Lantern' which is the uninitiated. The initiated and regular members are considered '49ers'.
The characters you see in the game are based off of actual people; but the names were changed to protect them. There is also a reason why Wei Shen came from San Francisco. The Triads were really noticed by the US in 1977 due to the "Golden Dragon Massacre". The attack resulted in 5 deaths and 11 wounded. 2 of which were tourists and the other 9 weren't gang members either. This event led to the creation of the 'San Francisco Asian Gang Task Force'.
People usually tend to think that videogames aren't educational and they teach you absolutely nothing. This is....the definitive way to prove those people wrong AHAHA....I'm sorry I couldn't resist. Now go enjoy being a sleeping dog for (San's) sake!

Gameplay -
Almost every single match in this game offers a unique experience. With dozens of gods already out and more coming out on a regular basis, countless different item combinations, several different gamemodes, and the varying playerbase, every game offers an enjoyable and new experience. While the skill curve and meta-game knowledge might seem intimidating to newer players, you can pick it all up in time and it gets extremely addictive once you get the hang of it. Overall, this is one of the easiest games to dump hundreds of hours into in a short period of time.
Playerbase -
In my opinion, this is one of the weaker aspects of this game, but there is a very simple solution. I'm going to be straightforward and say that going into the solo queue is more frustrating than anything, due to the sheer amount of salty players and feeders; however, there are a few different remedies for this. The first and easiest is just to party up with a few friends, and you really only need two to play a round of Joust (my personal favorite gamemode). Of course you'll need up to 5 people including yourself if you intend on playing a 5-man gamemode. The other way to avoid the solo queue is to just suck it up until you meet some decent human beings so you can party with them, and this is always useful regardless, as I have countless people in my friends list that I can party up with in a pinch.
Developer Support -
While there is an ongoing joke in the community about how Hi-Rez is basically the devil, they really do give this game everything they have, and while it is easy to hate them after they nerf your favorite god or release a broken new one, they do great work on this game with regular patches and events.
Micro-transactions -
This game perfectly embodies how I think microtransactions should be used. First of all, you can play this game entirely free and not miss out on anything, but if you're into cosmetics like I am, prepare to have an empty wallet. This game has skins galore, and personally when I start playing a new god it's just customary to buy the best skin available to me. Other than cosmetics, there are boosters that can increase your flow of in-game currency (which gives no in-game advantages), and the Ultimate God Pack, which I'll now elaborate on. The Ultimate God Pack is in my opinion the best use of your money if you can afford it, this will unlock every current and future god, and while they can all be unlocked without paying a cent out of your pocket, it does allow more gameplay variety from the start.
Balance -
While there are without a doubt problems from time to time, this game is pretty well balanced for what it is. I'm not going to say that it's perfect, but Hi-Rez does actively try to balance the game. While the occasional Loki main can drive even the most seasoned player to the brink of insanity, patches are constantly being released to make the game a more fun and fair experience.
Summary -
Overall, SMITE is an amazing game. It differs from the typical MOBA and does a fantastic job at it, and while it does have pretty minor problems, the overall experience is something you will not regret. I always try to find time to squeeze a few matches into my day, this game truly is a gem.

I've been playing FFXIV for about two years now. I do enjoy the game, the depth, the story, and the overall design. However, in this review, I'll try to be objective about this while I break it down into categories:
Leveling Process
+ The leveling process is very straight-forward for your first playthrough. The story lends itself well to the story and the progression is at a pace that one would expect from Final Fantasy.
+ Easing into your job/class. The way the skills are introduced is very intuitive. You start out with a basic rotation or a basic idea of the job and it steadily grows and becomes more complex.
+/- Dungeon difficulty. The difficulty of the dungeons, pre-50, doesn't exactly increase. The bosses are all pretty straight-forward until you get to Dzaemal's Darkhold where it introduces a new mechanic into it. All of the pre-50 dungeons are pretty easy. Some of the 50 dungeons have their own unique mechanic that you need to adjust to and the 60 dungeons follow the same trend.
Crafting
+ The Crafting system is pretty in-depth. You need to know your stats and how they affect your final product. You also need to manage your CP and skill usage to get an HQ product.
- The crafting system is somewhat convoluted in that you need to level almost every other crafting class to get any good mileage out of it.
+ Crafting classes rely on gathering classes for materials. Gathering classes rely on crafting classes for equipment. Very nice touch.
Gathering
+ The gathering system, while monotonously boring after a while, is an important part of the crafting system.
- Fishing is absolutely terrible. Fishing only really affects Culinarian (CUL) and Alchemist (ALC). The Fishing system is awful because whereas other gathering classes can simply open a node, see what's available, see their gathering and HQ chance, and collect what they came for, FSH can only throw a line into the water and pray.
+ Unspoiled Nodes are pretty awesome.
- There is no ingame system to track unspoiled nodes. You need to write it down or use a third party tool.
Combat Classes
+ Each combat class has its own unique place. Although BLM and SMN are both mages, they both bring radically different tools to the table.
+ Each combat class is completely viable in endgame dungeons and trials.
- Customizing a combat class is borderline impossible. To start off, no endgame gear has any Materia slots unless you craft it. Crafting combat class gear is a waste of time since, even with Materia, it doesn't compare to Tomestone equipment. The only source of customizing used to be from the 2.0+ Relic quests. However, Animus weapons have been introduced and those do not currently have a customizing option.
+ Cross class skills incentivize leveling other classes and trying them out.
+ Several classes synergize with each other (NIN Vulnerability and DRG Crit buff, WHM Medica  II and SCH Succor, etc)
PvE
+ Lots of dungeons. Lots, and lots of dungeons. You'll have to unlock nearly every dungeon to use the Roulette. Same goes for Trials with certain exceptions (EX Primals)
- Of the lots of dungeons, you'll typically only ever run 2-3 for a prolonged period of time and only as part of a daily or grinding from Tomestones.
+ Dungeons have varying mechanics to deal with.
+ Trials, depending on which ones, have simple mechanics to very hard mechanics.
- Drops. During the leveling process (1-49), dungeons drop equipment for their respective level range. This is the main source of equipment. At 50, you'll probably invest into the Allagan gear which renders all lvl 50 dungeon drops useless. Once again, during the leveling process (51/53-59), dungeon drops are the main source of equipment. However, at lvl 60, there's no real reason to use any of the drops aside from an accessory here or there. Most endgame dungeon drops are useless.
Endgame
+ There are a lot of things to do to keep you busy. Leveling alts, crafting, gathering, catching up on relic quests, challenges and logs, etc.
- Once you do get a lot of things finished, the game sort of loses its luster. I have all but 3-4 combat classes at 60 in Alex gear. I have all Gatherers to 60, all but 3 Crafters to 60, and honestly I struggle to find a reason to log in.
+ For a focused build (IE - Crit based, DET based, etc), it keeps you interested to balance which equips to get and to figure out stat weights for your class.
Glamour and other stuff
+ Finding Glamours is awesome. Pulling off your preferred look is awesome. You can be a schoolgirl with a huge Axe, a Xena-like Paladin, etc. The possibilities are really amazing.
+/- Retainers. Retainers are how you put items on the market. This mechanic is working and isn't difficult to use. Retainers also serve as your bank/warehouse. For that purpose, they don't have a lot of inventory space. Each Retainer has 175 slots and, honestly, from stocking up crafting/gathering mats and glamours, as well as extra gear I've collected to finish leveling alts, I've maxed out 5 Retainers.
+ Retainer Ventures are awesome. They're able to go gather mats you don't want to. They're also able to get drop-only mats at a far faster pace than you can (I'm looking at you, Dhalmel Hide).
+ Side quests are entertaining and often rewarding. Some side quests can offer equipment, items, minions, mounts, and more.
+ The community is pretty nice but has its exceptions. it's not hard to meet people or make friends and you'll occassionally run into the one bad apple during an instance.
Final words: I wouldn't say the game is bad. The game has pretty nice graphics, the story, if you can get into it, is very interesting and makes you wonder what's going to happen next. The gameplay is nice, the array of options are nice. Overall, I'd say the game is definitely worth the investment if you are into Final Fantasy games and want a nice community.

I have never liked mmorpg's in general though i have tried a few like WoW, Guild Wars 2, and some F2P titles. I thought the pacing and grinding was awful, i could never get past lvl 30 because by then I was too bored. This game however is something else. I'm a lvl 54 paladin by now. Here's why: there's a very captivating storyline, the gameplay mechanics are awesome (although the global cooldown might be a bit slow for some), the pacing is brilliant; you level quickly due to the main scenario quests and a thing called dungeon roulette (the game throws you in a random dungeon for an exp reward).
Perhaps the most important thing (for me at least) since I never got to the endgame of an MMO before: the community is extremely helpful for new players, be it the guild you're in or the randomly selected partymembers with which you have to clear a dungeon. People were always ready to help out.
There's also a lot of nostalgia-bombing for fans of Final Fantasy, but you absolutely don't have to have played the games beforehand.
Overall I recommend this game for newer MMORPG players as well as older players.

If you're looking for a fast, energetic, action packed shooter with a huge amount of potential then this is the game for you!
I bought this game because I thought the trailer made it look pretty awesome and boy was I right. However this game is still being built, THERE'S A LOT OF THINGS THAT NEED TO BE FIXED. There's also a lot of cool features that we don't have access to yet, with the promise of "Coming Soon" (such as being able to level up your gun) Even with the bare game I still love the look and the play of the game. For some reason I like the simplicity of shape based maps and players! (it still looks awesome and I feel it's easier to run on my rig)
The game modes are really cool (Team Deathmatch, Titan, and Horde, a survival Co-op type game mode against enemies/dinos) My favorite being "Titan" where you must get your Titan to the other side of the map whilist enemies trying to stop yours and progress theirs. If the Titans are destroyed you must battle it out for materials which come from "Crystal Spiders" or "Creeps" a bug like creature that just runs around spawn areas, in order to get your titan up and moving again. There's also a golden creep that gives your titan 10 points of power. The power is how strong your titan hits the other? or how much damage it can take? All I know is that the more points that your titan has, the better. The gamemode's very fast paced and the matches last a fairly long time if the teams are even, around 30 mins max. Even though the match lasts so long, I never find myself getting board due to the amount of things/objectives to focus on during the match. If everything is pulled off correctly your team will achieve victory through your titan smashing the enemie's core crystal.
The weapons are amazing, you can either run around like a ninja or rain down on enemies with your machine gun. Other weapons include, snipers, mini guns, machine guns, shotguns, light sabers, and much more crazy stuff to come. However if you want some extra awesome stuff you've gotta pay for it, and it's quite expensive. You can buy either cool special looking weapons or armour each with their own interesting effects and attributes (for example, a green light saber with the ablility to heal yourself and others around you).
I feel they need to balance the sword more though because of how fast people can get near you and slice you in half(There are amours and Techniques to contradict this!) Each time you get a kill you can pick up a crystal that will upgrade your weapon (you can also get these crystals from friendly/enemies destroyed sentrys) and if you get more than a few crystals then you're maxed out and it makes your gun freaking godlike. It makes other players have to team up against you in order to kill you which is a cool addition to teamwork within gamemodes. Aside from working with your team to get rid of pesky enemies, you can run and jump quite smoothly in game allowing you to avoid gun fire and secure the kill. Last but not least I'd like to say a tad about armour and equipment. Armour can be bought throught the match with materials collected, different armour gives you different abilitys and new armour can be bought with points from playing matches. You may upgrade each peice of armour the same as weapons except armour upgrades don't go away when you die and you may only upgrade armour 3 times to max them out. Equipment can also help a bunch wheather it be a well placed gernade or sentry. You may unlock more equipment simply by unlocking and crafting with aquired points from matches.
I've had a decent amount of server difficulties. Sometimes I'll play a whole match and get a good amount of kills and then at the end it'll say "You've been disconnected" or something as the match score board is up which is really frustrating to a guy that likes to stack up his kills and wins. It'll also kick me sometimes at random times in the match saying "Lost connection to host". Another bummer is that I don't get any xp when this happens so no leveling up.... I don't know if this is happening to anyone else though. It hasn't happened to me to many times but due to the fact that it has happened leaves me cringing towards the end of each match.

I've NEVER experienced problems with queueing for a lobby, the longest I've EVER had to wait was about 1 minute. This game is well worth the $10 ($5 until Sept. 17) it's decreased to. Minimum is a third-person arena based shooter with a minimalist art style and solid gameplay. As of the time of this writing (9/12/2014) I can say that the gameplay is rock solid while the content is yet to be fully fleshed out. I'll try to keep this review from repeating anything you can learn on the store page and stick to the technical details.
Netcode:
The netcode it superb. Hit-detection is client-side, so if you shot something, it *really* is shot. No lag shields here. In fact, rarely have I ever encountered the ill effects of lag at all. Also, VOIP is integrated and works flawlessly.
Gameplay:
Rock. Solid. Simple as that. Weapon choices are balanced, a variety of armor pieces make for significant customization tailored to your playstyle, and three gameplay modes means you'll have a tough time getting bored. As a side note, I can see this becoming one of the classic 'must have' LAN games.
Graphics:
The graphical fidelity of this game is suprisingly high, given the art style. Yet, even though I am running the game on a potato, I am still able to get 60-80 FPS by cranking down the visual options. If you have a decent system, expect to be wowed. If not, have no fear as you can still enjoy the game. Also, FOV slider in the options menu! Huzzah!
Input:
Minimum is set up by default as a standard WASD shooter, but has all of the options for controller play as well. If you happen to need the extra help, aim assist is available. Also, completely rebindable keys.
Tutorial:
A quick and sensible tutorial teaches you everything you need to know without extensive drawn out voice-overs or millions of text boxes. All of the core mechanics are covered.
Content:
Minimum is missing content. As you move through the UI, be prepared to see "Coming Soon!" rather often. You'll be waiting on Ranked Games, being able to host a dedicated server, making upgrades to deployables or structures, and Steam Workshop for user generated content.
F2P Trappings/In-game Purchases:
This is in part due to the title's development history. Originally intended as a F2P title, the game changed hands mid-cycle. The current developers chose to release the title as a one time paid model, but the trappings of the F2P history can still be found. There is an ingame store, albeit only for cosmetic items.
As with all good games, Minimum's core mechanics are easy to learn and difficult to master. Clearly this is a game made by gamers for gamers. The developers are constantly in touch with the player base and I expect they will follow up on everything they say they will.  Although essentially a multiplayer only game (there are bots, but it's not the same) the addition of dedicated servers means that even if the game goes belly up you'll still be able to play with your friends.
If you are particularly jaded, wait to see that all of the promises are fulfilled by the developers. Otherwise, I heartily recommend Minimum to anyone.

As you can see I haven't said that much unlike my more recent and well fledged reviews. I am trying to improve my reviews and by having this one shorter than my most recent one was something done deliberately. This is a very short story so I don't want to spoil anything. And to me the right ambience and mood that you dive yourself into while playing a game, is the most important thing. This game has it. During the whole 15 minutes I loved the feeling I got from this narrative. This dark story that someone decided to tell us. If you are a fan of dark subjects and thrillers and any other mysterious genres of video games, check this out. Papers, Please is the ultimate paperwork experience with a surprising amount of backstory and pressure from all angles. Who knew that looking through peoples forged documents could be so entertaining. Will you be the loyal worker that obeys what you are told? Will you will be the one who helps overthrow the government? Or will you wait in prison with a set execution time… Either way, I recommend this game for the unique gameplay, a challenging experience, and nice story.

Papers, Please is one of my favourite indie-games. It manages to do two things best: It gives you meaningful choices and extraordinary gameplay. If you like games that do that, or if you're interested in both of these concepts, read on. Otherwise, this game might not be for you.
The choices that you make in your tiny booth at the border affect the whole country (Arstotzka), plus every individual person. If you let terrorists pass, suicide bombings might occur. If you let people pass, who are persecuted in their country, they might be allowed to live on. You might support the current regime, you might choose to overthrow it, you might decide to just put up a little trouble, or you might just ♥♥♥♥ it up on the fourth day because you were to slow.
You have to judge people fast and while it's a bit overwheling in the beginning, it get's more easy and exciting over time. You train yourself to search for the relevant infos quickly: "Was this passport given out in East Grestin? Isn't East Grestin in Kolechia and not in Impor? Ha, this passport 's gotta be forged!". I've played the game for over 20 hours, it doesn't get boring. I found this particularly impressive, because I spent less time with Borderlands, though it is visually more appealing.
This game is not beautiful, it is not charming and it is, overall, not very rewarding. But it is a damn witty piece of art.

Sadly not starring Tommy Wiseau, The Room is nonetheless an excellent puzzle game, if ultimately a little short (My steam account shows 2 hours played; I'd say it was something like 2 and a half hours?). There's a series of four or five consecutive puzzles that revolve around cracking into a peculiar box, and hints at a dark mystery behind it all.
The hint system is nice, in that it offers a less direct alternative to just looking up the next step on a walkthrough. I avoided hints and spoilers as much as possible, but in the few instances I did use them, I could see that hints start vague, and hone in on the specific issue as the player repeatedly fails to interact with the right parts of the puzzle.
The game is challenging without being unfair, the graphics are good, and there's a dash of narrative hinting at a dark backstory. Honestly, if this game were the same calibur but much longer, I would be shouting its name from the rooftops. Rest assured that, at the very least, while it might have a short playtime, the time spent playing will be a very solid puzzle experience.

Great game if you like solving problems and engineering.  You don't need to be a math nerd to figure everyhting out, but if you are you can build some beautiful things.
The fun of this game comes from designing your own plans and layouts that are good and then making them better.  It isn't like you just click a "build a factory" button.  You have to think about how it all works together, solving logistics problems like supply and demand, transportation of materials, throughput and expandability.  If you think you have a perfect factory, you could always be making more.
Factorio is the most well-built games I've seen.  If something isn't working the way you want it to, it's always because you're doing something wrong and need to fix it.  I haven't seen any bugs my whole time playing this game, and the creators like to be a part of the community.  They listen to a lot of feedback, give news of what they are working on (with gifs and everything!) and have great support for modders.  The official modding API gets updated often whenever somebody suggests a new feature on the forums.

It is also brilliantly written and designed, with story intertwined with the ability system, and in a small way even the soundtrack with the keyboard input in a unique way. The storyline is sad and universal although set in a world seldom seen in any art form. You play a solitary human being in a world gone mad, a singer without a voice, locked in strange conversation with a sword she is carrying. The story unravels at a good pace in the ten or so hours it takes to finish the game. It is not often you see mastery at every level of game design especially that each part of the game alone would hold up by itself. Do yourself a favour and buy Transistor along with the soundtrack (by Darren Korb, with Ashley Barrett's vocals ).
Seriously, if you like good games, they don't get better than this.

Bought this game because I was fan of Bastion.
If you can buy it while there is sales then sure, go for it. Otherwise I would really suggest thinking about it.
Pros:
+ Beautiful world (it felt "artistic")
(Lots of beautiful scenes, could really imagine making wallpapers from them)
+ Good music
+ Narrator
+ Skill upgrade system
(We all know that feeling when we get new skill in game but it does not feel right for us or it is just really weak. In transistor even these skills can be used. You can upgrade your primary skills (using skills you do not use) or use them as passive bonuses (for example - extra damage, areal damage, shield, temporary clones and so on...)
+ Death penalty
(This is really good.  In transistor when you lose all your hp one of your skills (which you have equiped) gets discarded and you continue fighting with full hp, BUT you cant use this skill for set ammount of "checkpoints" (forgot the name, but basically small platforms in which you can customise your skills, if you die you need to discover 2-3 of them to get this skill back). In the meantime you can replace your discarded skill with other one. It makes players to experiment with most optimal skill set)
Cons:
- Fighting system
(This is some kind of mix Bastion style of combat + turn base game. But action games aspect is a lot, lot weaker. Most of your encounters with enemy starts with position yourself in good place, activating ability which allows you to set limited count of steps (example - I go here, use this skill on enemy 3 times then retreat) and then you execute it. After that you usually cant use any skill at all (if you havent used 1 skill as upgrade, then you can use that all the time), so you just try to survive 4-5seconds and repeat. There is no use for fighting in "real "time" because most of the time enemies are faster and hit pretty hard and most of your attacks takes a lot time to charge, so they just dodge it)
- Story, ending
(Wont spoil it, but it just didnt feel interesting. I barely had any attachment for our main hero and her sword or world at all. One of few elements I liked were the terminals in the game in which you get small info about world or get chance to vote about something, but the rest of story was... Just meh. Ending was dissapointing, maybe I didnt get the message which game developers wanted to deliver, but right now by emotional impact this ending could be compared to COD but without any kind of accomplishemnt)
- Limiters
(Limiters in transistor = Idols in bastion. You activate them to get bonus xp. In this way you can get more challenging enemies which make game more interesting and increase gameplay time. BUT, there is always but, limiters felt or I should better say were "unfair". I played this game 1 time and started new game+ so i had bunch of them. But I really could justify using only 2 of them (which gave in total 4%xp boost). Do you really think it is fair getting only 2-4%xp boost for activating limiter which increase enemies damage 2 times or give shield for their "cells" (you defeat enemy, he drops cell, if you dont destroy it fast enought the enemy will respawn back).  Yes limiters make encounters more challening, but as wrote before fighting system wasnt really that good)
Transistor isn't a bad game, but if you hoped for a fast pace action game with good story then you will feel dissapointed. Characters felt weak (or at least not interesting), story - meh, combat slow.  But otherwise it is beautiful game with great music.
If I had bought it for full price I would feel dissapointed but Summer Sales take care of that.

Supergiant games already blew me away with the story of Bastion, but now, they've just out-done themselves.
Transistor is an amazingly beautiful story, told expertly through it's amazing gameplay, amazing voice acting, and unique visual style.
Transistor tells the story of Red, a young singer who is loved by many in the futuristic city of Cloudbank. One night, a strange group of people known only as The Camerata, attack Red at one of her performances, she loses her voice and her only hope of getting it back is a strange sword known only as The Transistor. And through there, you embark on one of the greatest stories ever told in a video game.
Red is definitely one of my favborite video game characters, next to The Kid from Bastion.
Lets talk about the soundtrack, the soundtrack is one the most beautiful, majestic, and romantic ever composed in a video game. Period.
The gameplay is well crafted and expertly executed. Not ONCE did I ever get bored by the gameplay in this game.
The world is in this game is fantastic, it is masterfully artistic, rich with world-building, and in many ways it is a character of it's own. I never wanted to leave the world of Transistor.
All in all, Transistor was an amazingly mind-blowing experience. If anyone you ever meet says video games aren't art, or story is not an important element of gaming, show them Transistor.
My rating: 10/10

I have never liked mmorpg's in general though i have tried a few like WoW, Guild Wars 2, and some F2P titles. I thought the pacing and grinding was awful, i could never get past lvl 30 because by then I was too bored. This game however is something else. I'm a lvl 54 paladin by now. Here's why: there's a very captivating storyline, the gameplay mechanics are awesome (although the global cooldown might be a bit slow for some), the pacing is brilliant; you level quickly due to the main scenario quests and a thing called dungeon roulette (the game throws you in a random dungeon for an exp reward).
Perhaps the most important thing (for me at least) since I never got to the endgame of an MMO before: the community is extremely helpful for new players, be it the guild you're in or the randomly selected partymembers with which you have to clear a dungeon. People were always ready to help out.
There's also a lot of nostalgia-bombing for fans of Final Fantasy, but you absolutely don't have to have played the games beforehand.
Overall I recommend this game for newer MMORPG players as well as older players.

I wasn't initially that interested in this game, but I fancied something a little different to what I usually play and it was a cheap alpha version of a new indie game.  After playing it a few times, I have to say that it is incredibly addictive.  And don't worry about it being in alpha, this is probably the most stable alpha I've ever played.  It is only in alpha because it is currently lacking a few of the game's final features, such as the lack of a tutorial.
When you first start playing you only have access to the basic
type plague that has no special advantages but also no specific disadvantage either, an ideal place to start.  If you can wipe out humanity on Normal difficulty or above, you unlock the next type of plage, the
+ one of 25 genetic modification codes that can apply additional attributes to your plague at the start of a new game.  Then if you can beat
on Normal or above you unlock the next type of plague + another genetic modification code etc. etc. until you have unlocked all plauge types and genetic codes giving you the ultimate in flexibility.
There are four difficulty modes, Easy, Normal, Brutal and Extra Brutal (these might not be the actual names but you get the idea) and these relate to the simulation of humanity, which is incredibly realistic.  At Normal difficulty, you have a fairly good representation of the real world: 65% of people wash their hands and when a new illness is detected a cure is researched at a fairly realistic rate which is dependent upon the severity of your plague.  Brutal and above get substatially harder and reflect a global population that is way more vigilent than that of the real world.
This simulation of the world's human and animal population lies at the heart of Plague Inc's attraction.  I guarantee that you will think a lot more about how you can prevent the spread of illness after you have had your first couple of "successes".  It is really quite scary to see how easily a virus with the right characterists could wipe out the human race.  And make no mistake about the level of realism here; school teachers have used the game to teach children about the spread of illness and the author of the game, James Vaughan, was even invited to the CDC to discuss the simulation.  They are apparently quite interested in using this model as a way to educate the masses.  James himself has stated that he put in quite a lot of research to develop the game.
You have a number of options available to slow the speed of cure development:  At the molecular level, your plague can mutate rapidly and try to outpace the scientists, you can develop a highly complex genetic structure which will require lots of research to understand and you can develop resistance to drugs and different environments / climates.
For a more direct approach you can develop a certain combinations of symptoms and trasmission characteristics.  For example, you can mimic swine flu to mislead scientists or you can develop a combination of highly infectious symptoms, slowing development by forcing researchers to take rigorous precations.  Or you can just simply infuse the virus with a quick kill mechanic or two, like total organ failure for example, to try and dispense with the population before they have the time to combat it.  Careful though, if the disease kills quicker than it infects, it will kill off all of it's hosts before it spreads to the entire population.  There are many more facets to the simulation too which affect both the speed at which your illness spreads, and the speed of the cure development.  There are various combinations of a number of factors, including whether infected countries are rich, poor, arid, humid, hot, cold, rural or urban.
In terms of difficulty, I initially found it quite hard to defeat humanity on normal difficulty.  However, after a few attempts, I developed varous strategies that worked depending on where the disease started out and it eventually became quite easy to win, even without any genetic modificatoin codes, which is why this game scares me so much.  On brutal, I believe you will need the assistance of one or more of the genetic modifications.  It is worth playing for though, as you unlock various "cheat" modes if you manage to win the game on brutal or above for every type of plauge available.
This game really does deserve attention, not just because it is so addictive, but also because it will educate us, and hopefully decrease the chances of this ever actually happening.

A quick game that will keep you on the edge of your seat the whole time. This is a horror game but there are no jumpscares, however the whole time you will be creeped out because of the atmosphere, the ambience (I actually took my headphones off mid-way because I was getting so creeped out, but looking up a video of this and re-living the very end, the ambience just gets so intense and horrifying.), and of course the story as it unfolds to the very end. Personally I think a game like this is what most horror games should be like and should become, instead of the usual jumpscares and scary abomination chasing you throughout the whole game, this game uses constant ambience that builds up over time, the environment, and the horrific story that really has you thinking about a lot of things once you're done. For me personally the story was a little hard to understand at first since I didn't know what to really expect or completely make of the notes I was picking up, so I had to do some research and watch a video to clarify what I thought happened and what the story was, and for the most part I was correct in my assumptions. Interpret the story as you will and it may affect others differently, but nontheless it is a slow, creepy and eventually gruesome story that just hits you at the very end, and will have you thinking about some things. Not for the young, the faint of heart, or the easily triggered.
Pros:
+A quick game to download and play in one sitting, <30 minutes.
+A unique horror game that does not utilise or even need jumpscares to creep you out
+A story that will keep you wondering and thinking about subjects even after completing the game
+Simple, yet beautiful lighting and pixel graphics (if pixel is your thing)
Cons:
-Backtracking
-VERY slow walking

Minimum made a good progress during the months of Early Access. The developers added new maps, cool things to craft and new game modes. The overall multiplayer stability is much better now. Matchmaking is not perfected yet - there is no server browser and no lobby system and sometimes, I have to wait more than 2 minutes to join a game. But this is manageable compared to the gameplay experience you get.
Titan mode is the heart of the game, it combines old school deathmatch and MOBA focused gameplay, but you can also play classic team deathmatch or the cooperative horde mode against the AI. The gameplay is fast and dynamic, you have to put some time into the game to get more experienced. Your weapon gets more effective with every kill, so there is definitely some snowball effect here, but the better is the feeling when you get your first killstreak. Don't underestimate the importance of crafting and customization. Finding the right set of armor can be the key to dominate a match.
Last but not least, the minimalist art style makes the game fresh and unique. You won't find many textures but the effects are great, the sound is powerful and the maps are very well designed.

This is one of many games of the realy 2000's that was just truly astonishing. This game is a classic hack n slash, which brings you to the 1930's, in the shoes of a Dhampir named Rayne, the sexy heroine in the game, who travels from Louisiana, Argentina and Germany, eliminating bizzare vampires and monsters for the Brimstone Society. Under all this, she is searching for her father, which more unfolds about that in the sequel.
This game brings brilliant, fast paced and accurate gameplay with lots of gore, guns and different attacks. Each act (three all up) bring you different strains of monsters with their own back story, each act holds their own little story, everything begins to unfold by end Act II and all Act III.
I have read that a lot of people dislike this game, what ever reason that is, I think that is bogus, because this game just bring so many cool things to the table. One of the many cool things is a boss battle, in giant, armored robots firing rockets and grenades.
For me I have to say that this game has aged well, and somewhat has a cult following. The games alone spawned a trilogy of movies (terrible) and comic books.
This game has a lot of back story behind it, on the surface there may not be much, but some research later and its got it's own whole universe!
Now to the only bad thing:
Windows backwards compatibility is truely amazing, sure it may come with some prices on some titles and this game has one. The game runs at a full 60 fps despite the games' cutscenes were designed to render at 30 frames, so them running at 60 frames, they go too quick and dialogue is cut off, its a famous issue for the game, so what you would need to do is get a program to cap the frame rate. Some people get random crashes and stuff like that, but I never got any. A simple google search and you will find alot of solved threads regarding making Bloodrayne run as good as possible on newer systems.
So, SUMMARY:
This game is a true classic, worth the cheap price, a game that has aged well, has fast paced action, a decent story along with a sexy heroine. The game does require some tinkering in order to make it run properly on newer windows machines, but once done you're in for a real nostalgic experience.
Hope my review has helped.
Cheers.

Man, this is a hard one to write... On paper, Transistor is pretty much the perfect game. I mean, just read that short and sweet description: "Discover the world of Transistor, a sci-fi-themed action RPG from the creators of Bastion." More of that Supergiant goodness? Yes, please. Bastion is a phenomenal action RPG, one I recommend without reservation.  Transistor has so many of the same winning elements. It's gorgeous, both visually and aurally. You have to piece the deceptively dark story together from text and audio snippets, guided by the everpresent velvet voice of Logan Cunningham. So far, so good.
This brings us to the meat of the game, the "action RPG". Yeah... not quite. Bastion was an action RPG, 100%. Transistor is a real-time-action-with-pause RPG, and it never quite clicked for me. Reflex-heavy bullet dodging uses one part of my brain, and chin-stroking positional tactics another; switching between the two every 15 seconds felt like a disconcerting hybrid of Ikaruga and Chess. Much like Brutal Legend, I felt like I was playing it wrong much of the time.
On top of that, the customizable attacks. Again, a great feature on paper, but in practice it meant I was constantly changing my abilities as new options unlocked and was never able to get any muscle memory going. Sure, learning new systems/mechanics is truly the most enjoyable part of any game, but c'mon. Give me some plateaus so I can wipe off the sweat and enjoy the view, don't make it a 100% vertical climb. That being said, by the end of the game things were feeling a lot better. Over the course of the game some mini challenge rooms are gradually unlocked, which give you a specific challenge and a limited set of preconfigured attacks. They force you to really come to grips with how to synergize these abilities.
I'd probably enjoy the "game" part of Transistor a lot more in Recursion mode (their name for New Game +), but as much as I enjoyed the world and the story I don't feel the need to experience it twice.
So there you have it. Gorgeous game, with a combat system that some will probably love to bits but I found to be mostly a struggle. Recommended, but just barely.

They really improved this game- and I love that I can choose to play the same character on PC or PS4 depending on which I'd rather be on at the moment (unrelated to the PC version, but the controls work very well on PS4).
It has a bit of a slow pace, and of course it's an MMO so there's grinding involved- but the game looks good, is easy to use and unlike FFXI you can solo your way through anything even if you're not a great player, while also making it easy and rewarding to group up both for dungeons and world events.
It has pretty much every feature you'd expect for a modern MMO, an involving story, variety to do, and it has likely the best online community of the AAA group.
You won't feel any adrenaline playing this game, but if you're looking for something relaxing it's perfect. Need a break from enemies? There's entire classes devoted to gathering and crafting you can switch to on the fly (one character can have every single class, almost like specs in another game with no respec cost). There's many mini games, even an entire zone dedicated solely to mini games (the Gold Saucer behaves much like the one in FFVII).
Gathering professions are considerably more involving than other games; and even fishing's enjoyable (though, a bit limited- take in small doses).
The game looks and sounds nice, but some of the voice acting is... questionable. Also, there's still a sub fee.
That said- for a mainstream MMO it's one of the best, and I'm hard pressed to think of one that has the same general appeal for the f2p. Sides, a month of gameplay for an hour's work at minimum wage, or two starbucks coffees, has never seemed unreasonable to me.

You can't hunt almost any animals without spending money or earning a lot of the in-game currency, you can't get new weapons without spending money, you can't get get ammo without spending money or earning a large amount of the in-game currency, and you can't get almost any (if any) other equipment without spending real money.  And missions, what seem to be the main way of earning in-game currency, are incredibly limited in what you can actually do without spending money on the game.  It even claims to be multiplayer, but you can't host that to do with friends without spending money on the game either.  I wasn't even able to participate in their Halloween event without buying some form of weapon and/or ammo.  If the developers decide they actually care about their players instead of milking as much money as possible I'd gladly come back to the game, but not until then.

When I was able to play it, however, I was really surprised at just how good it looks. Comparable to modern-day MMO graphics, BloodRayne is a brutal hack and slasher that is surprisingly more like a dungeon crawler than you would expect. The gameplay is very repetative, but that doesnt stop it being fun, and I was very impressed with the real-time removal of limbs. The writing and voice acting so far is supurb, really nailing the genre without cheesing it up, and I'm eager to play more.
This game is difficult, however, so you'll need to take certain situations very seriously, namely water. That's right, the only major source of my death so far has been environmental hazards - there are point where you're forced to make your way through flooded areas, which steadily drains your health, and if you're indoors then jumping doesn't help much. This game also features old-school style saving - no quicksaves, only saving at area transitions, which can be quite a chunk of gameplay, especially if you die after a boss. Enemies are generally inconsiquential, unless you're forced to fight an extended number than you can't drain life from, or you encounter a bug that makes them invunerable.
All in all, this is a surprisingly good game. Don't let its age or "sexiness" fool you, Rayne is a take-control badass that I'd like to see more of in the games industry.

This is a combined review for the main game AND the Raising hell expansion pack.
Overlord is a great game where you basically play a parody version of Lord of the Rings, where you are an Overlord that looks a lot like Sauron and you have to use your minions, ie orcs/goblins or whatever to go and kill humans, halfflings, dwarves and elves.
It's a very clever take on the genre, the humour and story added a great deal to the experience for me.  I wont spoil the story but having played the game through a second time I got all the little bits and pieces of hidden things going on, so it's more in depth than just running around and killing things.
The expansion pack blends seemlessly with the game, if you have both DO INSTALL Raising Hell straight away, as you can do the missions from it in amongst the missions from the original game, I highly recommend that.
The game mechanic of using your minions to attack your opponents, and pick up power ups etc works well, but sometimes their pathfinding is a bit average.
Overall, very funny and fun, only negatives are your minions not always obeying commands and some of the expansion levels use new mechanics that don't work well at all..(when you have to 'mow the grass' go online to get some hints, it will save you from smashing your computer).
Don't let the negatives turn you away though.

Before we start I'd want you to know that this a browsergame is older than most steam accounts that gave it a "not recommend" with two lines of text. From a time where browsergames were actual games and not build around the currency you can acquire through spending money. Unlike today where the game itself is just an UI to get you to spend money as much as possible as often as possible for every feature you could possibly monetize (like most browserbased / mobilebased games nowadays on steam and elsewhere).
The definition of "Pay To Win" (P2W) varies from person to person but I'd like to focus on these points in particular:
Q:
1. Is the currency exclusive to paying players?
2. Do the obtainable features / items / etc. through the currency give a player an absolute advantage over other players?
3. Does it split the community?
A:
1. No. The currency ("Mushrooms") can be obtain by simply playing the game. Though it is RNG-based you receive enough to get you through without feeling pressured to spend money to get things done.
2. The features linked to the currency are mainly skip waiting times (PvP), energy (Adventure/Dungeons), refresh vendor stock. Which are hardly considered absolute advantages in my humble opinion.
3. No, there are no areas or features exclusive to the currency or paying players. Everyone gets his face smashed in.
The gameplay itself is more of a hero manager with minimal interaction (browsergame restriction) and best experienced for yourself to give this game your own critic.
If you decide to give this game a try, fill your waiting times by reading the webcomic this browsergame is based on and enjoy the ride.
This review serves mainly as assurance for the wary.

Man, this is a hard one to write... On paper, Transistor is pretty much the perfect game. I mean, just read that short and sweet description: "Discover the world of Transistor, a sci-fi-themed action RPG from the creators of Bastion." More of that Supergiant goodness? Yes, please. Bastion is a phenomenal action RPG, one I recommend without reservation.  Transistor has so many of the same winning elements. It's gorgeous, both visually and aurally. You have to piece the deceptively dark story together from text and audio snippets, guided by the everpresent velvet voice of Logan Cunningham. So far, so good.
This brings us to the meat of the game, the "action RPG". Yeah... not quite. Bastion was an action RPG, 100%. Transistor is a real-time-action-with-pause RPG, and it never quite clicked for me. Reflex-heavy bullet dodging uses one part of my brain, and chin-stroking positional tactics another; switching between the two every 15 seconds felt like a disconcerting hybrid of Ikaruga and Chess. Much like Brutal Legend, I felt like I was playing it wrong much of the time.
On top of that, the customizable attacks. Again, a great feature on paper, but in practice it meant I was constantly changing my abilities as new options unlocked and was never able to get any muscle memory going. Sure, learning new systems/mechanics is truly the most enjoyable part of any game, but c'mon. Give me some plateaus so I can wipe off the sweat and enjoy the view, don't make it a 100% vertical climb. That being said, by the end of the game things were feeling a lot better. Over the course of the game some mini challenge rooms are gradually unlocked, which give you a specific challenge and a limited set of preconfigured attacks. They force you to really come to grips with how to synergize these abilities.
I'd probably enjoy the "game" part of Transistor a lot more in Recursion mode (their name for New Game +), but as much as I enjoyed the world and the story I don't feel the need to experience it twice.
So there you have it. Gorgeous game, with a combat system that some will probably love to bits but I found to be mostly a struggle. Recommended, but just barely.
