To me, this paragraph is describing another game entirely. It's one case of marketing that I could argue negatively affected my impression, and eventual review, of a game. I did create a review several years back but I've returned after several years to make it informational and useful to you, the reader. So, let's begin.
Overlord is a quirky cartoonish game sure, but a dark twisted fantasy adventure where you get to be really evil? I disagree. It’s true that people who do evil deeds don’t feel evil or in the wrong when they’re doing them. But...well...let's talk about the story. In the game, you're setup as some sort of evil Overlord, tasked with bringing darkness and ruin to the world along with the help of your minions. So, you go out into the world and destroy people who are more evil than you and bring peace….and prosperity….to the land. Ok, that's one way it ends. The other way the story ends is that you create a land ruled by fear and your power's corruption and devastation of the lands. But all it does is affect the ending cutscene, not the game itself. Well, it doesn't affect it that much. I really don't like games that set me up to think that my in-game actions will affect the world when all it really does is affect the end cutscene.
This game doesn't really let you be an evil overlord during the course of play. Part of which is to be blamed on the more comedic, cutesy tones present throughout the story. You can’t just randomly kill people if you wish, only in special circumstances. While you can set fire to wheat fields, slaughter sheep and destroy all the kegs of beer you can see, they just regrow back as soon as you leave. I get that it needs to be that way for gameplay reasons but it’s hard to feel evil when you know what you’re doing isn’t really harming anyone. If anything, I just feel more like a destroyer of boxes than a ruler of all that is dark and evil. I can’t even make children cry at the sight of me! I mean, c'mon. What is this...
All that said, it does make for a decent time as more of a comedic/light fantasy story than a dark tale of power & corruption. Characters are two dimensional and stereotypical but the interactions can be somewhat amusing at times. Especially between the Overlord and the town citizens. All typical fantasy creatures can be found here. Drunken Dwarves, Ethereal Elves, Portly Halflings, Dumb Trolls and more are in this world, serving the part they play in most any other fantasy genre. You get to see a decent variety of locations too. But there wasn't much that surprised me.
You control up to 100 minions and an unnamed overlord at the same time. The overlord gets a melee attack chain and the use of spells but he should generally stay out of the fight. Otherwise, you'll wind up running out of health and mana extremely fast. So, you'll be playing most of the game through your four types of minions:
It’s a decent variety of minions but the game lacks in tactical decision making. Just send swarms of minions at your enemies and recall if you notice a big telegraphed attack coming. That’s really about the sum of the combat. Most of the time you’ll be losing minions because the controls didn't respond or you didn't see a hazard in time. That or they become stuck on doing whatever activity you "assigned" them or in the terrain. The sweeping function doesn't help matters either as it has the same issues. It’s more tiresome than enjoyable to deal with these controls when multiple types of hazards/enemies are present in a level. One last thing: I was fighting the camera more than I felt necessary for a 3rd person game which doesn't help the already frustrating gameplay. You have very limited control over it.
I never did get a chance to experience multiplayer because the servers were shutdown after Overlord II was released. You can play online through Hamachi but the community has no doubt suffered. There is a split-screen mode though, that’s rather unusual for a PC-centric title. Graphics settings are solid. Resolution options, AA slider, V-Sync, Texture/Debris/View distance sliders are here as well. FOV is missing but you probably won’t need it. Audio sliders are present as well and it supports up to 8.1 speaker systems which is nice. Mouse and Keyboard function well enough but I think controller is the preferred control scheme. Even with a controller, the game feels like it’s fighting me the entire time. The game is getting on to be 8 years old now and it is rather disappointing that the framerate doesn't stay consistent. I noticed even on my current machine that it would fluctuate between 50-60 fps during the first level. I don't think it's enough to be a deal breaker but I wonder how bad it would be to play some of the later levels again.
It’s not worth it. Half of it is challenge levels with a minor amount of story attached and the other half of it is maps for the now non-functioning multiplayer. Unless you really enjoy the mechanics of controlling your minions and want to challenge yourself to a new level of frustration, this expansion is a pass. Oh and keep in mind that the original game won’t launch if the expansion is installed. Not a big deal but something I should mention here.
I don’t recommend Overlord or Overlord: Raising Hell. While there are glimpses of really fun gameplay, it eventually gets worse over time. Frustration set in long before the game ended and there’s a constant sense of repetition and
that plagues the latter half. It just becomes a long grind. Between that and the quirky controls/minion behavior, it leaves a lot to be desired. Additionally, there is a ton of backtracking. The story itself is...ok. Its not awful but its not very memorable either. It seems at odds with itself on whether you're a good guy or bad guy. Outside of smacking minions around, destroying some buildings and killing a few people, you don’t really feel like a true Overlord to me. You just feel like an anti-hero who's a jerk when all I'm doing is defeating corrupted heroes, saving the townspeople from starvation and being a generally good guy. It's a decent enough 3rd person "RTS" game but I think it could have been much better given more attention to its gameplay.

I love this game! I actually haven't come across any bad glitches. The music is relaxing, and the gameplay is fun/challenging.
Not to mention the cubs are super cute and it's easy to get attached to them.
TIPS:
-Don't leave prey at the den. It may seem really efficient, but it'll just attract eagles and other unwanted predators.
-Before you go and mark trees/hunt, feed your cubs. You might get caught up fighting off predators or hunters, which takes time. By the time you come back, your cubs could be starving.
-Fight off rival females as soon as they come close. Even if they don't look close to the den, while you're out hunting, they could get to your cubs before you do.
-Character upgrades are important. Without them, it'll take longer to kill predators. (Example: two eagles are attacking you. While you slowly fight one of them, the other eagle kills a cub.)
-Crouching to hunt is pretty much useless. It's faster to just chase the prey.
-Keep prey piles a little while away from the den. This way, you can always have prey to give your cubs. Refill it when it gets low.
-Stay in target mode at all times. It'll alert you when predators/prey are near.
-Moose are scary. Stay away from moose. (RIP Fern and Pine... ;-;)
My remaining cub, Stone, forever hates moose for killing his siblings. xD
Anyways, this game is worth the $14.99! I recommend it.

Very solid FPS with old-school arcade-style gameplay: rack up a kill streak to get extra points. But those points are also XP for an RPG-elements system, which I also love in my FPS games. There are three different paths to choose from: Ranger, a long-range rifle-based class, Gunslinger, the midrange pistoleer, and Trapper, a close-range shotgunner.
The game's story is also excellent, and worth a replay in New Game+ mode. The new game+ lets you keep all your abilities, but it also turns on extra loading screen hints - ones that explain more of the story now that they don't have to worry about spoilers.
One unique detail I liked about this game was that it has a frame story. You're not playing the events as they occur, you're playing the events as they are retold by your character. Both Silas' inclinations and the people he tells his stories to can affect the story, and with it the area and enemies around you.
Solid 10/10 singleplayer FPS. If you still aren't sure, try the demo and play the first level. If you like FPS games and/or great stories, I doubt you'll regret it.

So yeah, game is worth, even with no story or just some background story, and it is kinda short, but hey, you can't expect 20+ hours of gameplay from this type of game. Also, there is no reason to play this game again (you know, puzzles are identical, nothing will change), but if you just want to work out your brain, you can play it once per year or so :) But yeah, it will not be that magical like for the first time :) Those machines and mechanisms are truly amazing. Yeah, you start with "only" one safe. But it is not just some random safe. It's like 5 puzzles in another 5 puzzles builted in safe (or table and box later in the game). If you are looking for Bastion 2, this is not it. Sorry. A lot of the design decisions are similar, but the combat system could not be more different, it's much more linear (you can't advance without killing all enemies, can't backtrack, and the number of fights you can skip are countable using fingers), and the wonderful narrator character has been replaced by one that's merely passable.
That said, the game is pretty good if you're willing to accept it for what it is: Its own game.
* The combat system has good depth (even if some abilities are woefully over/underpowered compared to the rest, and important hints are only displayed once in a way that you can easily miss them).
* The story is ok (though you're left to fill in a lot of blanks on your own). It borrows a lot of cues from Bastion on presentation.
* It has an equivalent of Bastion's Gods that lets you scale up the difficulty to whatever level you want at any save point (in fact I like this game's selection better than Bastion's, since it doesn't favor some weapons over others the same way).
* New Game + keeps the difficulty scaling and your leveling going from the same point it was at the end of the game (good thing since the story is shorter), as if there were no interruption.
* The way the lore unlocking is implemented encourages you to try out every ability in all three possible slots, which is a plus in my opinion.
* It is pretty and has good music.
Combat is a mix of real-time and turn-based, with the time between your "turns" scaling with how much you did during the last turn (though attacking without going into turn mode is a valid strategy and a few abilities are always available). It veers wildly between frantic, fun, methodical, tedious and everywhere inbetween, depending on the enemies and your skill loadout; but usually hovers near "frantic and fun". Instead of Bastion's variety of balanced weapons, you mix an match abilities an upgrades. Some are blatantly better than others but there's certainly no "one good build".
A really good game to waste some free time on!

I definitely would recommend playing this, especially if you liked Bastion.  The gameplay is similar to any turn-based combat game.  I definitely found the combat satisfying.  You plan out what attacks and combos you want to do on your turn, then Red acts them out immediately.  You then go on cooldown for about 5s, then can make another attack. During this cooldown time, you are vulnerable and have to dodge whatever you can. If you "die" you lose an ability until you re-load it by going through checkpoints.
The story was not as intneresting or in your face like Bastion's was.  I would say story wise, Transistor seems more thought out but the delivery was not my favorite.
The characters were actually really cool! The atmosphere is abundant throughout the entire game, and there are even little "screensaver" type places ("Backdoor") to hang out.
As a busy person, this game fits in quite well with my schedule. You can pick it up and play for a little while, or you can dive in for a couple hours and plow through a bunch of content.  Usually the pacing feels great if I can actually finish a game (which I did).
I beat the game in around 14 hours, the extra gameplay time was from when I previously picked up the game (a year or so ago) and played through a couple chapters and then just stopped playing.  It does seem there is some replayable content in the way of "Recursion mode" which seems to generate random battles for you to fight. The battle system was interesting, but I am definitely overloaded with games to play so I will probably not be stopping in to do a couple battles any time soon.
All in all, I'd give this game a solid 10/14.

In this game you control minions which do your♥♥♥♥♥kicking for you as you take on tasks which generally involve making your way through enemies or pathing your minions through a certain route to either kill enemies or collect objects.

I call it an attempted pickman clone because it IS. Basically you have colored minions that help you fight enemies and collect objects around the world. that's pickman in a nutshell, only pickman is at least fun in the sense that it controls better and you're fairly quick to get your multicolored friends and start adventuring. In this game i felt like i was getting my minions at a crawl and i didn't feel like i was really adventuring. each level had so much linearity to it that there were only occasionally branches in level design which led to chests for your minions to break open and that's about it. The Good:
- Unique narrative experience as far as video games go.
- Collectables worth seeking out for those interested in American West history

- Priced appropriately for content provided (If you can grab at a super discount, it's well worth it).
The Bad:
- Limited voice talent, with narrator filling in for most of the cast.
- Most of the number based mechanics feel fuzzy/soft, especially during shootouts.
- Fairly short story mode.
- Small arsenal of weapons.
- Little gameplay variety. Action setpieces and shootouts make up your experience. Few shake-ups to the standard run n gun gameplay.
The Ugly:
- If you're into Western games, this, Gun and Red Dead are pretty much it right now.
Recommend To: Western game fans who have already thoroughly enjoyed Red Dead Redemption. Fans of run and gun or shooting gallery games. Fans of games that stray away from traditional narrative storytelling. Anyone with $4 to spare and a few hours to kill when this game routinely makes the rounds on Steam sales.

Smite
a MOBA, but I use that very loosely. Smite is a MOBA in the sense that Conquest fits most people's perception of what a MOBA is today. Smite isn't a MOBA in every other situation, and for most people that play this game Smite technically isn't a MOBA (when compared to the big contenders). It has been stated by an official Hi-Rez employee (somewhere out there on the internet. I will try to find the source) that Arena has the highest player population out of any game mode. While it may sound like Arena would fit the theme of a MOBA (multiplayer online battle arena), it doesn't when using League and DOTA's definition as a comparative. So if you have never played Smite before, it's best you ignore the MOBA label for now.
Smite is fairly inclusive of what kinds of players it attracts. For the traditional MOBA players there is the Conquest game mode. It doesn't flat out copy League or DOTA game play; rather, it emulates it to a degree. It is actually, in my humble opinion, much more of a simplified version of those two games. Those who don't care for the kinds of games that League and DOTA are shouldn't be discouraged as there are 5 other game modes to choose from as well as a Match of the Day mode, all distinct from each other. Arena in particular is as divergent from Conquest as can be because it is, in a nutshell, Team Deathmatch with the inclusion of minions and a "scoreboard" that starts at 300 tickets and decreases by the amount of god kills, minion kills, or minions that walk into the enemy portal. The average match time differs between game modes as well. Someone who wants a short and sweet mode can play Arena, which averages about 15 minutes. Someone who prefers longer, more drawn out games can play Conquest, which averages about 30 to 50 minutes. The other modes fall in between these averages.
Smite is advertised as free-to-play and it means it. Nothing in Smite can be purchased to gain an advantage over another player; all purchasable content in Smite is purely cosmetic, or in the case of the god pack, gives you all gods and future releases for a one-time purchase of $30. The god pack regularly goes on sale as well, but many people have bought all the gods simply off of the favor they earned throughout the course of playing the game.
Hi-Rez
concerning the e-sports scene that exist currently. Namely there has been an abundance of shady e-sports organizations backing teams and, in the end, not paying the players anything relatively sustainable. A
is the accusation that Zapman, owner of and ADC for Eager, used the money to pay off his student loans and
or anyone else laboring for Eager. Starting with Season 5, Hi-Rez will properly invest money into the e-sports scene. This is a fantastic step in the right direction for increasing interest in Smite e-sports.
As shown on the
, members of Hi-Rez sometimes interact with the Smite community, either by banter or by addressing concerns with the game. Most Hi-Rez employees are on Twitter doing the exact same thing. The lead designer also
on a Tumblr he created to do just that.
Lore isn't a huge facet of Smite but it does exist. As of this review there are 9 pantheons in the game: Greek, Roman, Hindu, Mayan, Egyptian, Chinese, Japanese, Norse, and Celtic. All of the maps have a certain pantheon theme to them, and gods often have abilities and in-game voice lines related to their mythological background. It does not impact gameplay in any form. It is just a nice detail for people who enjoy mythology of any kind.
Toxicity in a competitive game is a given. Smite does not deviate from the stereotype. Chances are you will receive BM often during your play time. While I don't condone toxicity, it shouldn't discourage anyone from playing the game. There are countermeasures to this: the in-game mute button and the report feature. Lots of people take the report feature for granted though. Just because the report feature exists does not mean you will get toxic players instantly banned. The best thing one can do is write a thoughtful description in the box provided when you report someone. Write down any incriminating evidence, including what was said or timestamps if someone was intentionally feeding/trolling. The more you attach to your report, the more likely Hi-Rez will issue a ban. On the bright side, when someone you reported does have action taken against them, there will be a notification in-game telling you so. It does not include in-game usernames.
When new gods are released, often times they are either over-powered or under-powered and nothing in between, which can become a
frustrating norm. The same may be said about items. Patches are typically implemented on a bi-weekly schedule, meaning it can take weeks for a god to potentially receive balance changes. Over-powered gods tend to be balanced sooner than under-powered gods, which may also prove frustrating for some, depending on what kinds of gods one enjoys. Simply put, balance isn't Smite's strong suit, and for some could ruin their experience.
Since there are so many game modes, each game mode doesn't have as many players queuing as it could. A great example is Ranked Conquest - it is very easy to play with and play against the same people you saw in the last match simply because the player base is quite low.

on how matchmaking works. At its core, it "looks for similar MMR values, similar levels, and wants to make sure the highest MMR isn’t too far away from the lowest MMR value." Sounds great, right? Well, it "also has to make sure players don’t wait too long and parties of 4 or 5." As the queue timer increases, "the qualifications for what is considered a good match becomes more and more relaxed until a match is found." Since the population for game modes are much smaller than they could be due to the split player base, chances are your queue timers will be long and your games won't be very balanced. This can lead to some frustrating matches where there is a clear imbalance in skill level,
. The only way to combat this is either to remove some game modes, or find a way to create a larger player base.
New players will have a difficult time getting into Smite due to the sheer amounts of smurfs and the lack of tutorials and resources readily available in the game. The latter is being improved upon by the in-game "Learn" tab. Hopefully it will encourage more players to play Conquest, which I believe is its main goal. There is no way to prevent smurfing.

I was not expecting to like Patrician IV as much as I did. The first historical trading sim I tried was Port Royale 2, and I found it plenty enjoyable to sail the Carribbean and snap up goods to offload for a profit. Patrician III does the same thing across Northern Europe, but it was a little too involved and challenging for my tastes. I assumed IV would be similarly complex, but to my surprise it was far more my speed than any of the others I've played.
Like its predecessors, Patrician IV places you in the finely-tailored boots of an aspiring merchant in the Hanseatic League. Starting with a single ship and counting house, your goal is to make your fortune across the many ports of Northern Europe and Scandinavia. Each city produces four or five goods from a list of about twenty, but consumes all at varying rates. To that end, they require traders like you to ferry goods around to supply towns and help them grow, and make a tidy profit while you're at it.
The basic trading is probably the best of its kind, thanks to some clever quality-of-life improvements. Buying and selling is done on a slider between your convoys or warehouses and the town, allowing you to quickly and easily pick exactly the right amount to give or take. A helpful four-dot display also shows you the effect of your trade on the city's overall supply, which is important because good trades for the city improve your reputation with them. In just an hour or two routes will start to become obvious to you, and you'll be zipping around the sealanes loading and unloading your wares.
Reputation in the many ports grants you access to construction options, allowing you to build your own industries and move on to selling your own goods at market. Your farms and workshops will produce goods for you to trade at much greater margins, thus expanding your operations across many cities. This phase of the game is helped by a very comprehensive trade route editor, which lets you specify which goods to load, unload, or trade at every port on the route, right down to specific quantities and price points. It's an elegant system that will see your profits soaring almost immediately.
There's plenty more to do in the many buildings found at each port. You can make business deals and loans, go on patrols and hunt pirates, or even woo a spouse. These secondary activities aren't as complex as they were in Patrician III but still add welcome variety to your trading adventures. Additionally there are endgame goals like being elected mayor and completing major projects for your cities as before, so there will always be more to do no matter how great your company grows.
Patrician III had all this and more, but it was hidden behind some steep learning curves and unintuitive designs. I'm happy to say IV is a major improvement on this point, mainly by having an extremely useful campaign questline to follow. These missions will ease you into every aspect of the game by giving clear instructions and context, and then leaving you to work out the execution. I've found much more success in this outing thanks to this, along with the clearer messages and polished user interface.
The cost of this accessibility is shallower gameplay than in III, but pulling back from such a deep well is not such a bad thing. Overall, IV feels just right to me, a perfect balance of complexity and fun. The graphics also help with the inviting feel, though fans of the previous crisp pixel cities may be disappointed. I love the soft colors and simple models of the new engine though, and the sound design completes the gentle, inviting ambiance that relaxing sims thrive on. Patrician IV managed to surprise me by shooting to the top of my sim list, and I'm looking forward to many more hours with it.

240 hours I have spent of what I think is the best mmo made thus far. This game is amazing for many more reasons than I am allowed to type down in this review. So instead, let me just give you my top 5 reasons as to why I think this game is amazing.
5. fluint animation and amazing graphics
Most mmos put all there money into gameplay and story writing. Not that theres anything wrong with that, but this leads to lack of visual presentation. Take wow for example. How long has it been out? Longer than most mmos. Has it updated its visual quality since its release? No. It looks the same as its always been. Now take a look at ff14. What do you see? 60fps gold encrusted in gorgeous platinum grade textures. And the best part is square knew they didn't have to try. ff11's looks are on par with wow. So why did they try? Because they care.
4. no limits on how many classes you can have
In the beginning, you choose your one main class. However, when you complete the level 15 quest from your guild, you are free to take on as many other guilds as you like. There is no need to make a second character unless you REALY want to. Square did this because they knew that it would have been tedious to have many characters under one profile due to class limitations. With just one character, you can suit the needs of all roles. Wether it be tank, healer, or damage dealer.
3. NON-elitest community
How many times have you been kicked from a raid in wow because you had the "wrong" armor on, or you put your attribute points in the "wrong" spot. True there is an optimal way to play ff14, as there always is with video games, but if you dont have a perfectly specced, perfectly outfitted, GOD among charcters... nobody cares. You can shove all of your black mage attribute points into strength, you can equip robes and a wooden sword as a gladiator, you can ignore your skill hotbar as a monk... and nobody cares. No matter your level, attributes, euipment, and mmo skills in general, you will never be dismissed from a game provided that you are respectful and you at least try to do your job. ff14 has the best community of all mmos ive ever seen.
2. amount of dlc
Just about every mmo gets there largest sum of profit from dlc. The temptation of new classes, races, side quests, main quests, and the increase of your max level is hard to ignore. Now, how much dlc does ff14 have? Take a guess. On second thought don't. I know you would have guessed wrong anyway. The amount of dlc for ff14, as of now, is... 1. That's it. Just heavensward. Other than that, the base game has everything else. Now don't take it the wrong way. this game has plenty of content. In fact, almost all races, classes, side quests, and main quests are added in the main game via PATCHES. I mean, what other mmo does that? Just giving you free stuff because you own the base game? can't think of any? Me neither. It's pretty clear that square cares more about the communitie's satisfaction than their profits in the making. thanks square.
1. are you ready fo this... IT'S CROSS-CONSOLE!
Yup. You heard me. The pc and ps4 ports of ff14 share the same servers. Servers that are filled with over 5 MILLION happy customers accross the world, and accross different platforms, The ps3 verson of the game is a minor exception, considering that heavensward almost broke the system because it was not built for such content. so its obvious why ps3 needs its own exclusive serverse. But other than that, YAY FOR CROSS-CONSOLE!
ff14 is by far the best mmo I have ever played. Even without the 1 dlc that is out right now, you can still enjoy this game for hundreds upon hundreds of hours without getting bored. Infact, you can almost be certain that square will patch in new content to keep you playing.
All in all, i recomend this for those who like rpgs, mmos, final fantasy, and any other square related rpgs.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is an excelent blend of story and fast paced shooting gallery. You play as Silas Greaves, feared bounty hunter of the wild west. Everything start and ends in a saloon, where Silas tells his stories to a few other characters that narrate the whole game. You PLAY the stories while Silas gets more and more drunk, creating an amazing experience of unexpected 4th wall breaks and silly scenarios.
From a technical standpoint, it's a pretty well done shooter. There is nothing that would stand out as bad, maybe apart form the lack of a FOV slider. You can choose beween 3 different skill trees as you progress through the game, but you are not limited by just one. If you are good enough, at the end of the game you will reach the end of all of them. The weapon selection is rather small, offering you 3 different pistols, two variants of rifles and two variants of shotguns, but that doesn't hinder the game at all. Gameplay is very swift, giving you the ability to slow down the time in "concentration" (basically bullet time), which helps you in tough situations. I recommend playing on the hardest difficulty right from the getgo, because you can break the game quite quickly if you are good enough, as for each subsequet kill you get an xp modifier thats stacks really quickly with the right perks.
Other aspect of the game are the showdowns. They are short and require quite a bit of practise to get used to. There is also a complete gamemode around them, which is always welcome.
If you like western setting, you won't be dissapointed. This game has one of the best voiceacting I've ever heard and it really pulls you in as you are shooting your way through dozens of outlaws. Graphics are stylised into sort of a comics feeling, with black outlines and yellow-ish tint to the colours, which still looks very good to this day.
When you see it on a discount, get it, you won't be dissapointed

Gunslinger was a suprise to me. I was raised watching shows like the lone ranger, so I was used to the cowboy scene. I hadn't really looked into the video game realm of cowboys beforehand but a friend recommended the game to me. I have always loved story games so I took a look and wil never be the same. I have never played a game that did a better job of making you feel like you were realy intertwined in a situation of such insanity and wildness. Every shot you take in this game feels satisfying. If you love cowboys or satisfaction this game is for you.

As an avid fan of westerns and the "cowboy culture", this game truly felt like a playable western movie. Built upon a story of revenge, you play as a bounty hunter hellbent on completing his personal quest, letting nothing stand in his way. The story is very interestingly narrated by the main character, from his recount in a saloon in 1910. Gameplay-wise, the shooting might feel very bland to some, but to me, the constant fire your character endures and the bullet-time feature makes you feel like a master gunslinger. The dueling mechanic is very challenging, but welcome. You can even take the "easy" route and be remembered as a coward, but where's the fun in that? The different guns feel vastly different, and the shotgun feels extremely powerful, and when an enemy comes after you with one, you feel as though you are in genuine danger. While the game tells it's own story, it follows in the footsteps of games like Assassin's Creed where the characters face their demises and real world events happen as they did in history. The collectables in the game also feel rewarding, as each gives you a short summary on the characters, places, and events mentioned in the levels. While the game may be short (I finished the game in roughly four and a half hours on hard difficulty), the game offers a lot of replayability with the New Game+ feature as well as the side challenges you can complete. Overall, I reccomend this game to any fan of the "Old West", westerns, shooters, and anyone looking for some fun.

Assumingly the designers set out to create a simulation style game that highlights the tough existence that cougars deal with everyday.  What they ended up created is a thin non-descript forest that is almost devoid of any life.
Controls feel like the cougar is walking in molasses and the physics strips away from the realism every time a situation brings it to the forefront.  Combat lacks nuance while the cougar life goals of raising cubs are even less detailed.

OVERVIEW
You start off by picking the colour of your cougar, with a surprisingly large amount of choices. Then, you find yourself in the world. There are lots of plants and trees, and the world has lots to explore. First, you get to find a mate and mate with it (blurred out). Then, you can pick one of many den sites, where you will have cubs. Once you have cubs, you will need to hunt food for you and them, protect them, mark your territory, and move dens when angry males get too near. The cubs will inherit colours from you and the mate, which is a nice touch.
PROS
-The world is detailed and has a wide variety of foliage, flowers, trees, and rocks, as well as rivers, cliffs, and bridges
-You have lots of choice - lots of mates, dens, food, and colours available
-Lots of gameplay elements - mating, cubs, hunting, dens, protecting, fighting, exploring, marking territory, etc
CONS
-The graphic quality is not amazing. However, you get used to it and it doesn't affect the enjoyability of the game!

I can sort of recogonize certain areas, but the map isn't good and a lot of it is very similar. That's how it would be in the wild, but for actual gameplay it's pretty bad.

You create your own strategies, play your own game and get completely unique animals every time you boot up a game. There is a lot of interesting (and patient) gameplay involved in this game.

- Membership, involves license to hunt all animals
- Firearms
- Clothing
- Callers, lures
- Dogs
- Equipment
- Ammunition, to an extent. As a member, you get 3 free replenishable packs of ammunition, but if you want more ammo, you have to buy it.
There is also an in-game, free currency you can earn to purchase some items, including ammo, scents, and other things.

This game is not for everyone (even though it probably should be). Short summary opinion is at the end for those that want to skip reading a longer opinion.
The quests in this game are much more diverse than in many other MMO games. They range from investigation style quests, to NPC interaction quests, to your cookie cutter fetch and kill quests and more. Some require you to run dungeons and other require you to take part in mini raid style battles on the world map (you dont need a party to participate in these).
It needs to be understood that this game is extremely heavy on storyline content to the point that some may feel like they are reading an interactive book rather than playing an MMO. This means quite a bit of single player questing and even single player instanced battles as part of many questlines. For some this may be a source of irritation but for people that are familiar with the Final Fantasy brand, this is an amazing chance to become engrossed in the realm of Eorzea.
If you are planning on playing this MMORPG just to skip every dialogue and run to every quest mark, you will probably start feeling either annoyed or confused at what is going on with the quests and frustration may result from that. This is because the main story quests play a large part in character progression in terms of unlocking areas but they are also very detail oriented in terms of conveying a personal story to the player rather than simply grinding out exp to level up.
The storylines, both main and side, reflect some of the best writing to come out of a Final Fantasy game in a very long time and you can very easily forget you are even playing an MMO at times.
There is a rather large drawback however, depending on your point of view...  This game demands that it's players EARN practically everything.
You are NOT given a mount for free when you hit a certain level, you have to meet certain conditions to earn the right to ride a mount or stick with cheap taxi mounts until you do.
You are NOT given access to your full ability tree as you level up and instead must take part in quests / storyline unique to your class in order to earn additional abilities and even a job class unique to your base class.
You are NOT given access to dungeons in the game until you either follow the main story quests to the point they are unlocked for story reasons or until you find the side quests that unlock them for story reasons.

Note: I haven't played the others in the series, so I'll be reviewing it without that comparison.
Anyways, COJ: Gunslinger is a very competent FPS. Not quite an amazing 10/10 thrill ride, but close. It actually reminded me a lot of Bulletstorm in terms of combat mechanics, which is a great thing. But it's not just a strict shooter, It also has a few skill trees you can fill out to build up your character in different ways. The levels are also pretty great considering how good this game looks and that it released last gen. The trend towards the end of the gen was smaller levels and better graphics, but somehow Techland managed to keep the scale large and the presentation top notch. Some levels achieve the mini-sandbox feel of Far Cry 1 and the Crysis series' levels.
So, that's basically the game, there's a fun and slightly Tarentino-esque storyline that is sort of throwaway, since it mostly serves to just set up the action. Although there's lots of great references to western genre tropes. And there is a nice bit near the end that has deeper implications for the player character. On the whole though, this is a game that doesn't require much thought to untangle its narrative.
Overall, I would gladly give this an 8/10. It is a bit short and the levels have unused paths that make me think the missions were going to be longer originally. But it is still a great game, and probably the best FPS set in the wild west.

This review is a post-release review. Scroll down for my views during the EAC.
Having returned to the game and given it a few more tries after it came out of Early Access I can definitely say I would not recommend this game as a purchase at the current moment.
As mentioned in my EAC review, this game has a whole lot of potential, but that alone is not enough to warrant paying for this game.
Balance issues still exist. Devs and 'regulars' of the community continue to insist that weapons like the Giantkiller and other sword varients are easily counterable. The problem is their view of their own game is pretty short sighted.
The devs view so far concerning items/balance has been their damage outputs and offensive capabilities of armor and weapons. While that's needed, Minimum is one of those games where any slight change to your potential movement translate to HUGE advantages in combat.
Items like Icarus Pants, swords, shotguns, and berserker pants all have the ability to completely spiral a game out of control.
On top of balance issues, my main concern has been that most of the items are hidden behind a grind system. Bought the autosniper because you thought it was cool but it turned out to be severly lacking in damage? Guess you're stick with it until you unlock it after grinding your next level.
There are interesting cosmetic items available to buy (which are a way of unlocking some weapons without leveling) but it feels like just an attempt at squeezing the last few dollars out of the last few dedicated groups of players.
The devs have spoken regarding this, and they're actually considering making items tradeable/sellable in the market and plan to give them unique modifiers. If that doesn't give you a hint of "pay to win" then I don't what will besides having to straight up buy each weapon.
I initially bought this game in hopes of supporting a great idea from a great dev in the hope the dev would learn from their mistakes. I made this decision even with the knowledge that they were planning to add cash shops and weapon unlocks.
Seeing how the game is developing, with half-baked changes and silly cash grabs instead of real content and consumer-friendly updates, I unfortunately cannot recommend this game to anyone.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Does Minimum have potential? Yes. Is it worth buying at this point? Absolutely not.
I was initially on edge about buying this game (especially early access, which I've decided not to do anymore) but seeing that Human Head Studios, the creators of the Rune series, was making it I decided to make the jump and support them.
The game is pretty unbalanced, but this can be forgiven as it is early access and it seems the devs are pretty active at updating the game. The art style is hit or miss, personally I love it but I am sure a lot of people will not like it.
The game has a lot of potential, but other than that it's filled with a lot of balance issues.
The biggest issue in my opinion is you need to play many games to farm resources and unlock schematics. This wouldn't be an issue if it were for cosmetic items, but to place all weapons, armor, and items under this catagory is a problem. The idea of crafting your items on the fly is a great one, and opens up a lot of posibilities and variation as every item significantly affects your character's abilities and sometimes even your allies.
To force players to grind out those items puts you at a pretty clear disadvantage if you don't have the time to do so or you buy items that are not currently in the meta.
This isn't a free to play game (hell even F2P games like Dota 2 don't do this kind of thing) and shouldn't be treated as such. Until the system is changed, I can't recommend this game to anyone who takes competition seriously.

Smite
a MOBA, but I use that very loosely. Smite is a MOBA in the sense that Conquest fits most people's perception of what a MOBA is today. Smite isn't a MOBA in every other situation, and for most people that play this game Smite technically isn't a MOBA (when compared to the big contenders). It has been stated by an official Hi-Rez employee (somewhere out there on the internet. I will try to find the source) that Arena has the highest player population out of any game mode. While it may sound like Arena would fit the theme of a MOBA (multiplayer online battle arena), it doesn't when using League and DOTA's definition as a comparative. So if you have never played Smite before, it's best you ignore the MOBA label for now.
Smite is fairly inclusive of what kinds of players it attracts. For the traditional MOBA players there is the Conquest game mode. It doesn't flat out copy League or DOTA game play; rather, it emulates it to a degree. It is actually, in my humble opinion, much more of a simplified version of those two games. Those who don't care for the kinds of games that League and DOTA are shouldn't be discouraged as there are 5 other game modes to choose from as well as a Match of the Day mode, all distinct from each other. Arena in particular is as divergent from Conquest as can be because it is, in a nutshell, Team Deathmatch with the inclusion of minions and a "scoreboard" that starts at 300 tickets and decreases by the amount of god kills, minion kills, or minions that walk into the enemy portal. The average match time differs between game modes as well. Someone who wants a short and sweet mode can play Arena, which averages about 15 minutes. Someone who prefers longer, more drawn out games can play Conquest, which averages about 30 to 50 minutes. The other modes fall in between these averages.
Smite is advertised as free-to-play and it means it. Nothing in Smite can be purchased to gain an advantage over another player; all purchasable content in Smite is purely cosmetic, or in the case of the god pack, gives you all gods and future releases for a one-time purchase of $30. The god pack regularly goes on sale as well, but many people have bought all the gods simply off of the favor they earned throughout the course of playing the game.
Hi-Rez
concerning the e-sports scene that exist currently. Namely there has been an abundance of shady e-sports organizations backing teams and, in the end, not paying the players anything relatively sustainable. A
is the accusation that Zapman, owner of and ADC for Eager, used the money to pay off his student loans and
or anyone else laboring for Eager. Starting with Season 5, Hi-Rez will properly invest money into the e-sports scene. This is a fantastic step in the right direction for increasing interest in Smite e-sports.
As shown on the
, members of Hi-Rez sometimes interact with the Smite community, either by banter or by addressing concerns with the game. Most Hi-Rez employees are on Twitter doing the exact same thing. The lead designer also
on a Tumblr he created to do just that.
Lore isn't a huge facet of Smite but it does exist. As of this review there are 9 pantheons in the game: Greek, Roman, Hindu, Mayan, Egyptian, Chinese, Japanese, Norse, and Celtic. All of the maps have a certain pantheon theme to them, and gods often have abilities and in-game voice lines related to their mythological background. It does not impact gameplay in any form. It is just a nice detail for people who enjoy mythology of any kind.
Toxicity in a competitive game is a given. Smite does not deviate from the stereotype. Chances are you will receive BM often during your play time. While I don't condone toxicity, it shouldn't discourage anyone from playing the game. There are countermeasures to this: the in-game mute button and the report feature. Lots of people take the report feature for granted though. Just because the report feature exists does not mean you will get toxic players instantly banned. The best thing one can do is write a thoughtful description in the box provided when you report someone. Write down any incriminating evidence, including what was said or timestamps if someone was intentionally feeding/trolling. The more you attach to your report, the more likely Hi-Rez will issue a ban. On the bright side, when someone you reported does have action taken against them, there will be a notification in-game telling you so. It does not include in-game usernames.
When new gods are released, often times they are either over-powered or under-powered and nothing in between, which can become a
frustrating norm. The same may be said about items. Patches are typically implemented on a bi-weekly schedule, meaning it can take weeks for a god to potentially receive balance changes. Over-powered gods tend to be balanced sooner than under-powered gods, which may also prove frustrating for some, depending on what kinds of gods one enjoys. Simply put, balance isn't Smite's strong suit, and for some could ruin their experience.
Since there are so many game modes, each game mode doesn't have as many players queuing as it could. A great example is Ranked Conquest - it is very easy to play with and play against the same people you saw in the last match simply because the player base is quite low.
Hi-Rez
on how matchmaking works. At its core, it "looks for similar MMR values, similar levels, and wants to make sure the highest MMR isn’t too far away from the lowest MMR value." Sounds great, right? Well, it "also has to make sure players don’t wait too long and parties of 4 or 5." As the queue timer increases, "the qualifications for what is considered a good match becomes more and more relaxed until a match is found." Since the population for game modes are much smaller than they could be due to the split player base, chances are your queue timers will be long and your games won't be very balanced. This can lead to some frustrating matches where there is a clear imbalance in skill level,
. The only way to combat this is either to remove some game modes, or find a way to create a larger player base.
New players will have a difficult time getting into Smite due to the sheer amounts of smurfs and the lack of tutorials and resources readily available in the game. The latter is being improved upon by the in-game "Learn" tab. Hopefully it will encourage more players to play Conquest, which I believe is its main goal. There is no way to prevent smurfing.

I played the majority of my time before the Steam release with about 650+ hours total.
I love Smite.
Graphics: Not mindblowing visually but that's a good thing it turns out. A 3rd person MOBA needs to be simple and avoid unnecessary nonsense all over the screen. Still can get hectic but graphics are simple, fitting, and tasteful.
Sound: Awesome. The sounds themselves and the voice actors are great. Lot of character and passion put into the music, voice actors, ability sounds, etc. Everything is unique.
UI: Over the years the improvements have made some really good changes. Customizable and simple.
Control: Super smooth. Every character has their own "feel" and "pace". Movements and abilities are fluid. Customizable.
Gameplay: Quite a few modes in which almost all have their own meta. Sometimes it feels like a different game from mode to mode. Hi-Rez includes a "game of the day" type mode with special rules that resets each day as well as adventures with even more elaborate configurations.
Gods (Champions/Heros): Every single one is unique. Visuals, audio, gameplay, they are all their own beast 100%. 90+ Gods to play. The ultimate pack which unlocks all gods current and future is such an insane value even if you dont play long-term you'd be a fool not to shell out the $30 for it. Also most skins are awesome!
Community: This one is almost subjective. Some people are hyper-sensitive. It's a competitive internet game, you'll find ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s just like anywhere else, but I've met a lot of very cool fun people and group with them regularly.
Matchmaking: Can't really say I've seen a big issue in PUG matchmaking. Be advised I don't play ranked, but when was the last game everyone posted praising the matchmaking system?
Balance: Tends to wax and wane a little bit. Be aware that a lot of the balance whiners are more than likely referring to ranked conquest only. Lucas Pope has quckly become for me a dev who is the king of simple games that get really hard as you go. Papers Please at first seems like a really boring game at first. You sit at the border of two ficticious countries, deciding who can get in and who can't. The fun comes from the unique controls and the hidden storylines that emerge as you play.
The gameplay is simple throughout the whole game but gets increasingly difficult as you play. You are in charge of the Grestin Checkpoint of Arstotzka. You do this by clicking and dragging the many items you are in charge of. Your first day is very easy: only let people with Arstotzka passports in, everyone else must be denied. Of course you could let anyone in with a dock in pay. You can let anyone in on the second day as long as their passports aren't expired. The whole point of the game is to follow the rules. It's easy to look at them in the first page of your handbook, but making sure all the conditions for entry, especially in the later part of the game, is difficult.
As far as those hidden storylines go, you are also in charge of getting paid enough money to feed and warm your family. There's also some people who want you do do things that might be unsavory to the dilligent border officer, from accepting bribes to be let in without a passport, to corrupt governments and a rebelious cult. All these elements mix together to add up to over ten different endings. It is possible to get through the whole game without getting a paper check wrong, you can do so poorly that you starve your family to death, you can help corrupt people, or have them taken care of. The choice is yours...
In short, the satisfying and simple controls to a complicated and dynamic pixel world make for a fun and stressful game.

Two years ago I was detained on my way into America. I was taken away from the line, seperated from my passport and dumped in a bleak empty room filled with lines of chairs and people in various states of distress. Nobody told me what was happening. Occasionally an agent would appear at the back of the room and give passports to some of the people waiting, who left quickly and quietly. At one point an elderly man went up to the desk and begged to be let through, to be met with ice-cold condescension.
After about half an hour I was called through into the back room. There I was told to sit down in front of a man called Keane, on a desk filled with papers. Keane never looked at me. He asked where I was going and why I was going there. When I said I was visiting my girlfriend he leered and asked me if it was "true love". When I asked him whether I'd been pulled out of the line for a reason or if it was a random check, he told me it "wasn't random". When I asked him if I would make my flight in 20 minutes, he told me that it depended how fast I could run.
Eventually Keane gave me my passport back and told me to "lift my heels up". I missed my flight by minutes. I waited for an hour for the next flight and then another hour on the plane for it to take off.
This game made me feel sorry for Keane.
10/10, would feel empathy against my will again

Disclosure: I marked “received this product for free” because I obtained it through a giveaway.
Admittedly, Angel Express isn't the type of game I typically play these days.  It is a cute anime style sidescrolling racing platformer created by Japanese doujin developer EasyGameStation.  Several of their games are on Steam (notably Chantelise and Recettear) but were published by a different publisher (Carpe Fulgur rather than Rockin' Android).  Strangely, the developer on the store page is currently listed as Easy Game Station instead of EasyGameStation which probably makes the game harder to find for EasyGameStation fans.  Anyway, I'm a fan of platformers so I decided to give it a shot.
The player takes the role of a messenger girl on her quest to become an Express Angel.  It's fairly light on story, but what's there can be humorous at times.  You race through each stage as fast as you can maneuvering around obstacles and sometimes competing with other messengers.  After you beat the game, additional stages and branching paths open up.  If you want to reach the final ending you'll be required to beat the same stages multiple times.  They're pretty short though and mostly easy once you get the hang of everything.
Each stage has an objective.  There is some variation but most of the time it will be to beat the stage within a time limit or to win a race against one or several messengers.  Not unlike Mario Kart, there are plenty of items that can be used to your advantage.  Some are offensive, some defensive, and others are speed related.  The main character can be customized.  You can select her outfit color, dash style, and class (once additional classes are unlocked).  The class bonuses are small, but one of the ones I found was very helpful for traversing the stages.
All of my playtime was spent in the single player campaign. It appears the game features local and online multiplayer, but I have can't say how well it works as I had no way to test it out.  If it works, I imagine it would be quite fun.  I encountered several bugs while playing single player, so it wouldn't surprise me if there are some issues with multiplayer.  There wasn't anything severe enough to prevent me from completing the game, but the game crashing on start the first time I opened it felt like a harbinger of things to come. I found a few minor bugs and one reproducible crash bug which fortunately wasn't connected to the actual gameplay.  I imagine it all would be quite easy to fix, but the fact that it hasn't been fixed gives the game a sloppy feeling.
Despite a few issues, I enjoyed my time with the single player campaign. It took me approximately five hours to do a blind completion on normal mode. TL;DR - It's an adorable sidescrolling racer that's a throwback to charming Japanese-made Playstation and Dreamcast games visually. With cute-but-chunky 3D visuals, bright & colorful textures and stylized background art, it particularly recalls games like Klonoa or Threads of Fate. If you were worried about controls or something, don't be. This may be simple but its well made. Angel Express is just a fun, simple little game. And its a pretty unique spin on the platformer. If you like the looks of it, and enjoy games like Klonoa, don't hesitate to pick this up!
What is this? - Angel Express plays like a hybrid platformer and "kart" racer. You can jump, double jump and use a dash if you've built up enough juice to use it in your special bar. The heroine generally feels pretty good to control: she's speedy enough, responsive, collides with the environment correctly, stops well, has a good jump & double jump, and a good bounce off of targets. So with a solid feel under its belt but just a small group of core game mechanics, the Pickups are where some gameplay depth is served up... though its still a pretty simple, pick-up-and-play type of game overall.
You race through a stage 3 times (for laps), picking up gems and items from treasure chests, while avoiding traps and enemies (or stomping them/using items to clear them out of your way). The levels are even destructible to a certain extent, so watch where you're throwing those bombs ;) Every area has two unique tracks, except for the last area at the end of your run. There, you'll find just one track, and you'll have to fight a boss. Angel Express also features a world map with branching paths that opens up after you complete your first playthrough too; more on that in a bit.
How is it? - There's a nice selection of levels with varied themes, a cute little story (told through short asides between stages), and multiple stage types. Some are straightforward "just beat the level before the timer runs down"-style challenges. Others may change things up with environmental effects such as adding fog to decreases visibility. Several stages pit you against your rival. Some pit you against multiple opponents, and then there are the bosses. The boss fights are not always races; you'll have to do battle with some of them by avoiding attack patterns, gathering treasure chests and then unloading items onto the boss.
The progression is a little weird, as you don't have free reign on the World Map. You'll be run through 4 stage courses straight to a quickie end. Then you continue that game, and head down the world map again, this time taking different branches throughout your runs to see more stages and endings. Its kind of like Outrun, how that game would start in the same area and then give you different end points depending on which forks you took throughout the race? That's how Angel Express' World Map works.
Any downsides? - The momentum makes it hard to slow down and actually land on 1-block platforms while racing, and the collision tends to get messy in VS races when colliding with other players, and also on certain traps/items - namely, the spinners. I also saw slowdown whenever there were more than 2 messengers running. Heck, there'd be random, minimal, slowdown during those 2-player races too, but its far worse in 3 or 4-player. Its like playing the whole stage in bullet time... which is actually pretty okay. It just made it easier to react to, and appreciate, all the chaos going on during those stages, honestly. Any little annoyances don't really equal frustration or even difficulty; you shouldn't have to retry a stage more than once or twice to actually get through any of them, and the punishment for losing is... getting to try again. This may surprise you, but this cheerful & colorful adorable game isn't big on punishing the player :P
Wrap up - That's really all there is to it. Fun races and challenge types, with a good little chunk of levels to play through, plus the ability to make your own. This won't be clogging up your backlog; you'll actually be able to get through this in a few hours, but it'll all be enjoyable. This is bright and cheery, with cute music and characters, and a solid, charming script (honestly, there's far fewer misspelled words than I ever would've expected. Good work, devs!). This is the kind of game not a lot of people make anymore, and when you pick this up, you'll be reminded of how sad that is. This game is a gem for fans of instantly fun arcadey action and pure positivity.
------
Notes about the Level Creator: It's pretty good. Its kind of like a basic Mario Maker; you scroll through the stage and drag and drop elements  from a menu -- your tiles, blocks, traps, gems, enemies, etc. -- onto the grid to make your level. It's pretty intuitive. The only thing that's weird to me is that there's no "instant test" option; so you have to Save it out, then leave Edit, then go to Time Trial, THEN select your "Edit Stages" and pick it there to try it out.

Game Background:
This is a 2D platformer time attack game where the main goal most of the time is to finish the set course within the given time. You finish the course by getting to the end goal on the rightmost part of the stage and completing the required number of laps.  Along the stages there are monsters and obstacles which will try to hinder your progress.  There are many tools that you can collect to help you clear a stage. Some of its effects include destroying walls (bomb), make you run faster (carrot) , make you invulnerable and smack any monster you go into (cake) and many more.
Sometimes during the adventure, there are other AI players you will encounter, for this type of challenge you need not only to clear the course within the time limit, but also make sure that you have higher points than them, otherwise you can't proceed to the next stage.
Story:
The world the main character lives in has seen a rise of monster population in recent years. Because of that, the letter delivery industry is having a hard time to their job. To combat this, they begun hiring messengers, girls who can see spirits, to deliver all kinds of letters to any location. Because of the aid of spirits, they have little trouble passing through monsters.
The main character (which you can name whatever you like) is a girl who aims to get the mythical title "Express Angel", although the circumstances to get this title is somewhat unclear. Along the way, she will overcome various obstacles, and meet friendly(?) rivals, and who knows, she might actually get the mythical title.
What I like:
Basically this game is fun. I like platformers myself so... anyway this game is fun because of the time mechanic, it's like you're already playing a speedrun for every round.  The controls are smooth too, even by using the default keyboard layout I didn't have any problems during in-game. This game can also run on any toaster due to its low requirements (my current PC is still a toaster, but I'm upgrading soon lol.) The graphics are 3D, not too realistic but the world itself is full of bright colors. The characters are modeled after the "Chibi" style (or SD or etc.) The game also has story cutscenes which are alright. The humor reminds me of Gurumin, where the narrative pokes fun at the setting itself. Most of the in-game stages are well made.
What I don't like:
There are few issues about the game. The ability to change keyboard controls is not present, even though I tried my best to look for it on the game folder, or in-game. If there is a way without relying to 3rd party software please do inform me. So if you are not familiar with Japanese style keyboard game layout (arrow keys + Z key), then you might need to play this with a Steam controller or any other gamepad (I'll try my arcade stick next)
Overall:
If you happen to like platformers and racing against time, then this game is for you.  The stages are interesting and the game is easy to pickup. Although having the ability to change the keyboard controls would be better, if you have a gamepad then you can play this with no problem.

A new action game by EasyGameStation, the studio behind Recettear and Chantelise. With such a pedigree, there's a lot to live up to!
It's a sidescrolling race/combat game, similar to Speedrunners, Rush Bros., or Sonic Rivals. It's score-based, you earn points for getting hits on monsters and other players, by collecting goodies, or by crossing the finish line first, and you lose points for dying or falling behind. Each type of gem you pick up slightly increases your speed, acceleration, or defense, depending on its type.
The translation is by Rockin' Android (instead of Carpe Fulgar), and for the most part is competent, albeit not as gut-bustingly entertaining as Recettear. There's the obligatory typo in the first cutscene, but I haven't seen any other errors yet. The kerning is all messed up, but doujin games always tend to be like this. You're only allowed five letters to name your character with, and there's no default character name, but I suppose that's only mildly annoying. There's a "newletter" you can read after every stage, which contains gameplay tips and a novelization of Chantelise (although the character's names have been relocalized for, I assume, licensing reasons).
The music is good, although the invincibility item throws off your groove with every use, resetting the stage’s music. There isn’t any annoying voice acting.
I’m happy with my purchase, overall. I’ll rate this game a $7.49 out of $9.99, which makes it a steal at just about any sale price.

The negative reviews are almost all from cheapskates that wanted a 100% free game, or the handful who hate memberships.
This is easily the best hunting sim I have ever played.  Its beautiful, the maps are huge and there are many of them with another being added very soon.  The animal behavior is excellent.  Probably the best "enemy" AI that I have seen in any game.  There is a wide variety of weapons to choose from.
The leveling system does a great job of progression.  It really makes you feel like you are getting better as a hunter.  For example, the more tracks you read, the more information you can get about the animal you are tracking and the more accurate that information becomes.
The community is fantastic.  It isn't a huge community, but there are always multiplayer games open, and those games are often hosted by higher ranked players who open their games to share the resources they have invested.  Treestands, fast-travel tents, bear and hog feeders, goose and duck setups etc.  There is also a lot to be said about the comraderie of MP games.  Its always nice to get positive feedback from someone when you harvest a nice scoring animal.
For me, the best part of theHunter are the competitions and missions.  Competitions usually last just a couple of days.  There are cosmetic trophies and often in game currency rewards for placing in the top 3.  The missions and competitions add just a little bit of focus to your hunts.  Gives you a sense of purpose rather than just wandering around looking for animals to shoot (not that this isn't fun by itself).
theHunter is among my favorite games of all time.  I have never bothered to write a review before, but I don't want people to miss the opportunity to play this fantastic game after being put off by reviews.  You can definately spend some money to enhance your playing experience, but beyond getting a membership to be able to hunt all the animals, its not necessary to spend a lot of money.

Sleeping Dogs is a superb open world action game that will make you feel like the star of a kung fu movie.
Sleeping Dogs is one of my favorite open world games ever, I played it so much when it originally released and I was surprised how great the game actually was. All of the environments in Definitive Edition look beautiful especially when running on higher settings. The gun combat isn't bad but it's not really anything special, where Sleeping Dogs really shines is with the hand to hand combat. The fighting mechanics feel great and throughout the game you learn new fighting techniques to add to your arsenal. There are also several different environment takedowns you can preform that are brutal as they are awesome. Sleeping Dogs also allows you to free run and preform stunts all over Hong Kong. Where Sleeping Dogs took me by surprise the most is its story. In Sleeping Dogs you play as Wei Shen, a undercover cop tasked to infiltrate the Triads. The story is well written and all of the characters are intriguing. The story takes lots of twists and turns, is mostly action packed, and makes it harder for Wei to decide if he is more of a cop or more of a Triad as it progresses. Unlike other point-and-click games where you would just click randomly everywhere on the screen to see what activates, this game was different and much smarter. Two years ago I was detained on my way into America. I was taken away from the line, seperated from my passport and dumped in a bleak empty room filled with lines of chairs and people in various states of distress. Nobody told me what was happening. Occasionally an agent would appear at the back of the room and give passports to some of the people waiting, who left quickly and quietly. At one point an elderly man went up to the desk and begged to be let through, to be met with ice-cold condescension.
After about half an hour I was called through into the back room. There I was told to sit down in front of a man called Keane, on a desk filled with papers. Keane never looked at me. He asked where I was going and why I was going there. When I said I was visiting my girlfriend he leered and asked me if it was "true love". When I asked him whether I'd been pulled out of the line for a reason or if it was a random check, he told me it "wasn't random". When I asked him if I would make my flight in 20 minutes, he told me that it depended how fast I could run.
Eventually Keane gave me my passport back and told me to "lift my heels up". I missed my flight by minutes. I waited for an hour for the next flight and then another hour on the plane for it to take off.
This game made me feel sorry for Keane.

I've played WoW on and off for years, and I've also played Guild Wars and Guild Wars 2, and dabbled with WildStar and numerous other MMOs. After all my expierenes with MMOs, Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn is my favorite, and it's the game that made me stop playing WoW.
The first thing you'll notice when you launch the game is just how gorgeous the world of Eorzea is. Gameplay wise, the combat is interactive enough; it may not be as involved as a game like WildStar, but you're constantly using skills and dodging attacks which makes it very entertaining. The main story is interesting, and is full of likeable characters. The voice acting is pretty good for the most part, I haven't encountered anything that really stood out as bad like a Jill sandwhich.
As much as I do love this game, I still have some criticism (since after all, nothing is perfect). The most glaring issue is the slow pacing players will encounter at the start. It can easily turn new players off of the game as they will be bombarded with meaningless "go there, talk to person X, go back to quest giver, get reward" type quests, and getting those out of the way before you get to the combat is pretty boring (though you do have the option to skip those and go straight to the combat quests right away).
The ability to have access to every class in the game on a single character removes the need for alts, and is neccessary for the job system within the game. Jobs are essentially advancements of a class, and require class A (the class that is being advanced) to be level 30, while having a specific class, class B, be at level 15. This allows you to have new abilities, and access to job specific quests form levels 30-50 (60 with the Heavensward expansion), each with their own story, much like the class quests that you'd encounter from levels 1-30. The only gripe I have with the ability to change classes on your character, is the lack of quests in the game. Since you'll eventually run out of quests to do to get XP, you'll end up doing the same dungeons, FATEs, and levequests repeatedly, which can get dull.
Overall this is a great game, and well worth the subscription price in my opinion (there are two subscription models available: Standard $15 a month with no restrictions, and the Entry level for $13 a month which limits you to one character per world). It's a good game for Final Fantasy fans and non fans alike, though fans of the series will probably get a bit more enjoyment out of it due to the bits of (non-intrusive) fanservice sprinkled in.

Ok, I played the game for about an hour or so, and I must say I had a fun time. I really liked both Shelters, and Wolf Quest. Until today I didn't even know Untamed : LOAC existed. Because it was cheaper than usual I decided to buy it.
So, what are my views?
The graphics are quite nice, my laptop is not very good, so I couldn't completely enjoy it for I had to turn it to fastest. It kinda reminds me of lif graphics, lif has better water though xD
The gameplay....I'd say it's Shelter and WQ brought together, which is a good thing. You have to find a mate, find a den, give birth to your cubs, name them, protect them from predators and other mountain lions, feed them. Hunting is pretty fun, though on easy mode it seems a little too easy.
Protecting our cubs isn't neccessarily the easiest thing in the world, for sometimes they like to wander off, away from the den. I also don't like that when you get attacked by a wolf, your character drops the cub, which makes it impossible to run away. In that moment you're forced to stay and fight the wolf/wolf pack. To me, dropping the cub/pup against our will is one of the most annoying things in such games. I also don't like that if you have a den on that big mountain, and you fall, it takes forever to come back to the top. I went hunting once, I killed a prey that I can't run with, most of my cubs starved.
If you like sand-box and survival games, and you're a big cat lover, then i highly recommend it.
What else can I say? Give you some tips perhaps?
1. Look out for wolves, hunters, and the crazy male that attacks you to eliminate your offspring,
2. You don't need to look out for the cubs, as long as you're absolutely sure that no predator is near enough to smell them. The oly problem then is that you might have to carry them one by one a long way.
3. If the vultures, gathering and eating your prey, are a big problem to you, then I recommend putting your kills underneath your den "roof". They can't reach it there.
4. Attack while carrying a big prey and rushing to get it to your cubs. It will make it faster.
I'd really like to play a good big cat sim. This isn't it yet. Maybe one day it will be, but it currently feels way too poorly put together and just not at the quality I'd hoped for.

Minimum is a great concept of a game with several positive traits. Its art style is fantastic, as is its music, the amount of blueprints for crafting is good, and the gameplay is pretty fluid.  Three things concern me at this point.  I left Loadout to play this game believing it had greater potential.  I still believer that.  However, I didn't realize certain things I missed from that other game.  The first thing is player population.  This will inevitably go up in time, but it's still pretty disapointing how long I have to wait for a good match to start in game.  Secondly, why is there no ADS (aim down sights) in this game? That seems pretty moronic.  It's too easy to kill people, and your skill doesn't get differentiated from anybody else's as a result.  I have seen there to be an ADS mechanic with snipers which is good, but i believe it should be extended to all weapons.  Lastly, I believe the game needs to add a dodge mechanic pronto.  That's one of the reasons swords are so OP at this point.  If a person has great map knowledge, you're at a severe disadvantage if you're a sword user.  Dodging would help immensely, as well as to escape gunfire.  Things like more maps are obviously going to be added which is why I'm not including them, but the issues such as ADS and dodging are a core issue with the game, which may not get fixed.  Loadout, whether you're a direct competitor or not, will blow this game out of the water with player population if you don't.  Likewise, this game can steal alot of that game's thunder with some careful tweaking.

well, I like the game, however I think it's a bit too hard even on casual and normal, there aren't always enought dna points available to accomplish world domination. this game should actually "start small" in a more specific way. When you choose your starting nation, you should be able to manipulate how the plague affects the local area before attempting to expand. ALso detection of the plague should depend on what it does.
