A great alternative to other MOBAs if you're looking for something that changes the formula enough to spice it up, while still staying true to its roots. There are plently of interesting characters to choose from, which are all based on mythological gods/figures (which can be pretty interesting in its own right, seeing the team's interpretation of said figures), and I feel Hi-Rez has done a great job of keeping each of the gods feeling quite unique so that you never really feel like any are too similar to other gods (something League has been guilty of recently, though it's still my favorite MOBA for other reasons). The main place it gets points of League, though, is in the variety of game modes available. There's the traditional 5v5, there's a 3v3, a 5v5 with 2 lanes that leads to a more chaotic game with less jungle focus, a 4v4 siege mode, a 5v5 arena mode that can be fun if you don't have much time, an ARAM mode, and a final limited game mode that change out daily.
Additionally, the Ultimate God Pack is a great ♥♥♥♥ing deal to anyone planning on spending any real amount of time playing. For $30, you get every god currently available and every god that will ever be released. Not a bad deal at all, and it allows you to use the in-game currency you acquire for other things, like skins.
My only real complaint with the game is that most of my friends from League refuse to pick up Smite, so I'm mostly left queuing with randos. Which does limit the fun of a team-based game a bit. I've seen a lot of complaints about the toxicity of the community, but it doens't seem any worse than other MOBA's communities in my experience. It could be that I don't play ranked much, and also tend to avoid the generic/classic 5v5 mode because it's not as fun to me. I feel like people are more relaxed on other game modes too.

Sleeping Dogs is a superb open world action game that will make you feel like the star of a kung fu movie.
Sleeping Dogs is one of my favorite open world games ever, I played it so much when it originally released and I was surprised how great the game actually was. All of the environments in Definitive Edition look beautiful especially when running on higher settings. The gun combat isn't bad but it's not really anything special, where Sleeping Dogs really shines is with the hand to hand combat. The fighting mechanics feel great and throughout the game you learn new fighting techniques to add to your arsenal. There are also several different environment takedowns you can preform that are brutal as they are awesome. Sleeping Dogs also allows you to free run and preform stunts all over Hong Kong. Where Sleeping Dogs took me by surprise the most is its story. In Sleeping Dogs you play as Wei Shen, a undercover cop tasked to infiltrate the Triads. The story is well written and all of the characters are intriguing. The story takes lots of twists and turns, is mostly action packed, and makes it harder for Wei to decide if he is more of a cop or more of a Triad as it progresses. Wei Shen is a fantastic protagonist, he is just a truely bad♥♥♥♥♥character, one of my favorite video game protagonists of all time for sure. While I'm at it I might as well say that all of the other main characters are great and well voiced too. There is always something to do in Sleeping Dogs; you can go do a mission for the Triads, do a police mission, help a stranger in need, participate in a race, participate in a fighting tournament, bet on a♥♥♥♥♥♥fight, go on a date, take out rival gangs, learn new fighting moves from the dojo, explore the world to find lock boxes, plus lots more and everything else you could expect from a open world sandbox action game. So in closing, Sleeping Dogs is a amazing game filled with action, narrative, and variety that I highly recommend to anyone who is even just a little interested in the game, it should pleasantly surprise you as it did to me. Sleeping Dogs is a hidden gem among open world games and one of the best open world games I have ever played.

WHAT'S IN THE CORNER!? WHAT IS THAT BEHIND THE CHEST OF DRAWERS!? WHAT IS IT!? I CAN SEE BLOOD. WHAT'S BEHIND THE CHEST OF DRAWERS?
A decent mood piece/short story with a bit of a twist and a genuinely unsettling atmosphere, this "game" nevertheless suffers a little from rather amateurish design decisions.
Developer take note: if the entire purpose of your creation is to tell a story and deliver an eerie experience, you do not need to insert keypad puzzles. The moment a gamer finds a convenient "I changed the code" note pinned to the wall, their eyeballs tend to roll so hard they're in danger of popping out. Leaving multiple notes like this is likely to result in blindness.
As such, I would have preferred to read a little more or explore a little further than be forced to backtrack to enter a code... repeatedly. Especially when said code was deliberately easy to figure out; it felt like I was killing time, rather than progressing.
Nevertheless, the art style was good. The odd, pixelated textures on everything coupled with the gloomy lighting and dust sprites left it all feeling hazy and dreamlike, and I was genuinely hesitant to take those last few steps to reach the ending.

i'll start off by saying transistor is a wonderful game. i'll get a little more detailed but in case you don't wanna do a whole lot of reading:

-the game replays well, which makes up for the length imo
-the music. THE MUSIC. THE MUSIC!

9/10
alright so: the story in Transistor does not come out at first, you have to dig for it. the city of Cloudbank is enigmatic and as you progress, you discover terminals that help you learn about the city, and functions that teach you about its citizens. interaction is the main way you'll learn more about the city and your companion, the Transistor.
in addition, the music is SO important to the plot. listening to the music will help you understand the nature of cloudbank and the relationship between Red and the voice of the Transistor.
the battle style consists of turn-based combat. the "functions" i've been mentioning are abilities you collect through the game. the functions are all malleable; you can make any of them passive abilities, upgrades to other functions, or active functions. the amount of options for builds keep the combat fresh.
the length of the game at first concerned me, but it is really replayable and i loved doing my two runs. i'll probably start another soon.
on a closing note, i gotta say i really enjoyed the Transistor as a companion. the dialogue felt natural and it even calmed me down at some aspects of the game. the Transistor reacts to almost everything you do. if you backtrack for something you missed, it will say "Hey, where are you going?" or something along those lines. it reacts to whatever you read on the terminals. i thought it was a lovely touch and just adds to the whole experience.
the game is good. play it twice if you're mad about the story, it'll help.

For a build-up game that's in its 3.5th installment, I would have expected more.
The game concept is nice, but whoever was in charge of designing the game control mechanisms should be fired! Automatic trade is tedious to manage:
- an '(un)load everything BUT' option is still missing (as with earlier versions);
- trying to select a destination city with the mouse repeatedly results in the program switching it with another one, or simply nothing being selected at all;
- cities can only be added or deleted completely, not just the destination changed;
- and to top it all off, the game keeps arbitrarily changing certain settings of trade routes back to its own defaults, WHILE THE TRADE ROUTE IS BEING USED!
Specifically, this means that loading your ship from your storehouse in a city will occasionally get changed to buying from the city instead. Quite a big deal when you wonder why your funds aren't getting ahead for hours.
The counting house manager seems to sometimes just forget to do his job, as was the problem before with Patrician II.
Also, when quantities get really large, the default trading amount is increased - which is good for manual handling, but it sometimes seems to prevent the manager further from executing any orders, e.g. when lump trades change the average trading price and he consequently doesn't act at all. Although I'm not quite sure if these two might not just be same problem after all.
The overall game flow suffers from bad priorities for messages. Various events are lumped together as 'task accomplished', without specifying what it is exactly: a returned loan you gave, or a mission you took on.
To know for sure, you have to check the history list - where you then have to delete and confirm every single item of e.g. returned loans to keep the list clean.
Other times, your advisor/uncle - or worse, a competitor from one of the many cities - just pops up and delivers a spoken message while you were just trying to micro-manage some part of the game. You can usually just ignore the competitors, but as far as I can tell, the advisor-uncle only says everything once.
I probably forgot about 4-5 things that annoyed me like hell too.
As I was saying: The person(s) responsible for this mess should be fired.
Anyway, if all that doesn't bother you, the game is somewhat more charming than its predecessors.
Further on the plus side, the uncle's tutorial tips don't try to micro-manage your game. He only shows up at major milestones and you are free to act in between as you wish.
I will probably spend a bit more time with this game when I'm bored. But I'm not going to get addicted or look forward to playing on, like I could have.

I've played WoW on and off for years, and I've also played Guild Wars and Guild Wars 2, and dabbled with WildStar and numerous other MMOs. After all my expierenes with MMOs, Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn is my favorite, and it's the game that made me stop playing WoW.
The first thing you'll notice when you launch the game is just how gorgeous the world of Eorzea is. Gameplay wise, the combat is interactive enough; it may not be as involved as a game like WildStar, but you're constantly using skills and dodging attacks which makes it very entertaining. The main story is interesting, and is full of likeable characters. The voice acting is pretty good for the most part, I haven't encountered anything that really stood out as bad like a Jill sandwhich.
As much as I do love this game, I still have some criticism (since after all, nothing is perfect). The most glaring issue is the slow pacing players will encounter at the start. It can easily turn new players off of the game as they will be bombarded with meaningless "go there, talk to person X, go back to quest giver, get reward" type quests, and getting those out of the way before you get to the combat is pretty boring (though you do have the option to skip those and go straight to the combat quests right away).
The ability to have access to every class in the game on a single character removes the need for alts, and is neccessary for the job system within the game. Jobs are essentially advancements of a class, and require class A (the class that is being advanced) to be level 30, while having a specific class, class B, be at level 15. This allows you to have new abilities, and access to job specific quests form levels 30-50 (60 with the Heavensward expansion), each with their own story, much like the class quests that you'd encounter from levels 1-30. The only gripe I have with the ability to change classes on your character, is the lack of quests in the game. Since you'll eventually run out of quests to do to get XP, you'll end up doing the same dungeons, FATEs, and levequests repeatedly, which can get dull.
Overall this is a great game, and well worth the subscription price in my opinion (there are two subscription models available: Standard $15 a month with no restrictions, and the Entry level for $13 a month which limits you to one character per world). It's a good game for Final Fantasy fans and non fans alike, though fans of the series will probably get a bit more enjoyment out of it due to the bits of (non-intrusive) fanservice sprinkled in.

Patrician IV is a trading strategy game based (loosely) on the historical period of the Hanseatic League. It has been a board game and Patrician I was released about a decade ago. If you are a fan of strategy games, then you have probaby already heard of (and have) the original version. If you haven't heard of it, think of the strategic map view of Medieval Total War, but with the activity done by ships, not the armies.
Essentially this is the same as the orginal. The graphics and sound are slightly better, but this doesn't impact gameplay. One improvement is a 'rating bar' against items in each market to show demand - this makes it much easier to make money without a running a spreadsheet alongside the game. The automatic buy/sell through your warehouses has been changed from the original, but splitting the buying from the selling on different tabs has made it fiddlier to manage your administrators. A better tutorial is included for new players.
I played the original version of Patrician for hundreds of hours and the lack of major changes means that I'm expecting to get hooked again. So, for experienced players, this is worth the upgrade fee during Steam sales whilst new players should enjoy this even at full price.

Alright, so I have played Smite for a little bit of time now and have come to some sounds pros and cons when it comes to Hi-Rez (the game's developers) and Smite itself. This review is somewhat biased because I am a huge fan of the game, but I think my dedication to it gives me some grounds to say what is good and what is bad about it.
*PROS*
-Smite's community is thriving and thanks to multi-queue, getting into a game is now faster than ever.
-Smite's 3rd person camera positioning makes it one of the MOST immersive MOBA experiences out there.
-The gods in the game are easy to understand (most of the time) and their abilities are fairly diverse.
-There are only 5 consistent game modes to chose from and the maps are the same every time, but each game feels fresh and a Mode of the Day offers up an interesting look at a new way to play.
-There are regular updates to the game and new gods are being added constantly.
-The grind for new gods and skins is satisfying and rewarding enough to make you want to keep playing.
There are plenty of other things I could say about the game that I believe are done well, but the ones above are the most prevalent ones that I have come across since I started playing. Now, the cons are not meant to discourage you from playing the game, but are just there as a way to prepare you for some possible frustration in the future!
*CONS*
-No matter how good your computer or internet is, Smite will still crash for no apparent reason. This is only on occasion and normally will not ruin an entire game.
-Smite can feel like a chore at times, especially trying to get all the First Win of the Day gold and that's why I recommend playing with friends.
-In the current meta, early game seems to be very important and, all too often, a deciding factor for a game. Hi-Rez has been working on fixing this, but still nothing has really changed.
-Hi-Rez also has a lot of kinks to still work out in the game and their servers go down at some of the most inconvenient times.
*CONCLUSION*
Smite is certainly a game for the MOBA lover and will have you hooked from the tutorial! It's immersive gameplay and interesting gods offer a wide variety of games and outcomes. The grind will keep you coming back for more and friends will certainly keep you into the game for longer. Hi-Rez has given a lot of love to this game and with it's commuity being as strong as it is, I know Smite will be around for a long time.

For those waiting for GTA V or a similar open world type game, Sleeping Dogs fills the gap suitably. The structure of the game is no surprise for any GTA player, or if you have played the previous True Crime games, with the only major difference here is that the game's combat is based on a Batman-style melee approach, which is suitably fun once you get the hang of it and identify the various moves. It does get a bit repetative towards the end of the main mission set, but that's common with most open world games; there's also a good deal of completionist gathering one can go after. However, elements like the story itself are somewhat lackluster - you can get an idea where the story is heading early on, and there's not much redeeming or vile about any of the characters.
The Definition Edition includes two packs of DLC, both adding another 2-3 hr each of gameplay. The second one, Year of the Snake, feels like a good single movie in terms of plot (attempting to stop a cult bombing the city), while the first one has fun elements of movies like Big Trouble in Little China in it.
The only issue that I have against the game is a lack of technical updates from the publisher, which many have commented on the forums. In my case, I had started the game, and during that time had to update a completely separate hardware driver for a camera device, among other things. This caused the game to be inoperable. Only until I was at a point that I had replaced the camera with a different one, did the game then work fine. As one of the few troubleshooting tips they have given has been to disconnect all USB devices which have worked for some but not all, this might create a technical problem for you.

Verdict: Skip this one. Play the sequel if you want to try this franchise out. You're not missing anything story or gameplay wise. This is like the beta for that game. And everything you didn't like about the core game is worse in the DLC.
This needed more work and more commitment. Its like the game was afraid to really let you be an evil Overlord. It feels like a rushed production. They threw together the broad sketch of what an Overlord is but didn't really flesh things out. You'll end up running around doing lots of errands either for the people or your adviser.
You can't even sit on your throne.
That said, the minions are a fairly well realized bit of gameplay. Point and click and they'll run out attacking your enemies, destroying stuff, pillaging towns. The four types of minions give you some variety for tactical play but honestly you don't need it.
Big minuses.
1) No minimap or other navigation. You have no way of figuring out how to get anywhere except through raw memorization. You'll even occasionally get directions like "go east" when there's absolutely no way of knowing which way east is (you can't see the sun and nothing indicates a cardinal direction)
2) Can't sit on throne.
3) The "evil/eviler" karma meter system sounds good on paper but in practice it works a lot like a standard karma meter. Thanks to their non committal premise, the villagers are actually happy when you conquer them because the people in charge before were worse. If you want your villagers to fear you, you actually have to go back through their town on a separate "YOU'RE SUPPOSED TO HATE ME!" rampage.
4) Cheesy tepid humor. It kind of reminds me of the style of humor you get in Fable 3 but weaker.
5) Game undermines the experience of being an Overlord. When you're at the castle you're constantly being nagged by your adviser and mistress to go back into the field to do some overlording. Aside from using the portal to jump to different maps there's almost no point in visiting your stronghold.
EDIT: So this review got voted down 4 times. I wonder why? Who is defending this incredibly mediocre game? What have I said about the game that is untrue? I really mean it when I say "Try the sequel instead". The sequel really is much better than this. It fixes a lot of my gripes about this game and generally fleshes everything out, making it more robust.
In the sequel, instead of this game's karma system where you choose between acting like a good guy who is a little naughty and acting like a bad guy, you get to choose between being a tyrant and a marauder. The second game mostly gets things right. Try that one. Don't waste your time with this one. The plot is very thin in these games and playing the first one will do almost nothing to help you appreciate the second. The one or two plot points from the first game that are relevant in the second one are sufficiently explained in the sequel.

Papers, Please is a unique (as far as I know), highly enjoyable border control simulation, a claim which will probably only make sense once you've started playing.
The mission thrust upon you is to man a fictional border and, using the evidence in front of you and the instructions given to you each morning when you turn up, to decide who to let through into glorious Arstotzka. Getting it right means you earn a living, getting it wrong gets you reprimanded and eventually penalised, which makes the various attempts to corrupt you even more appealing as you struggle to progress from the bottom-grade residence they've assigned you and your family, whilst you try and keep them fed, watered and medicated.
Part memory game, part puzzle, this point and click misadventure balances the need to do a job thrust upon you, whose demands change daily, with the need to look after your loved ones and, perish the thought, yourself. Sounds easy, right? Do your job well and climb the ladder, if only the requirements of your job were not quite so demanding and the clock didn't tick around just that little bit too fast every day as the pressure slowly (and then not so slowly) mounts.
If you only like your games slick and shooty this might not be the one for you, but I believe everyone should try this at least once if only for the music and fantastic deadpan humour, with the very basic graphics ensuring this will run on a wide range of machines (it ran on my old laptop, and that barely coped with streaming video day-to-day). If you're on a notebook, I'd probably try playing with a mouse, as when it gets frantic playing on a touchpad can be quite frustrating.
Completely recommended.

It changes every day, and there are scripted events, so you kind of play for the events in each day, and they're pretty fun to see too. The interactive-ness of the game kind of leaves the interpretation of the game's message and overall story to you, allowing you to look at the smaller scale stuff in a bigger picture, putting emphasis on whatever, which is really well done and has some feel of a book. This game feels really nice, and is really well executed and has a lot of care.
I know what you may be thinking, "Games revolving around gimmicks are lame and have no fun beyond the first 15 minutes!", and you're right, but this game is one of the few that goes for a mature feel, appealing to an adult audience with an adult topics, with an interesting take on the gimmick genre (one with gameplay alone giving a really strong tone to the game), which was a risky move on their part but really nice to play. Get it, and you'll enjoy it.

Individual Conclusions:
Story: 4/10 (Mediocre)
The game is 2.5-3 hours AT BEST and that should be an automatic warning sign. The story felt kind of rushed or just made on bullet points. Random nobody goes to South Korea to get good and is constantly depressed? Check. Random nobody is our PC? Check. PC finds multiple high-profile eSport gamers and gets noticed? Check. PC impresses them, despite getting SQUASHED at least 3 times IN THE SAME DAY BY 3 DIFFERENT PEOPLE? Check. PC gets high-profile person X to leave their team? Check. The story just hits bullet point after bullet point and it sucks, because it hides some interesting issues and nuances with eSports and professional gaming. (e.g.: Accel, AKA: Anime-Chill-Bro, mentions that his Brood War team was forcibly disbanded by sponsors not paying and the players couldn't pool enough dosh together to sue for damages.)
Characters: 3/10 (Bad)
Accel is an emotionless walking male cliche. Jett is the hothead ♥♥♥♥♥ that hates life. Mach (the PC) is the "I regret every decision I ever make" idiot. Stunt is the brat with an ego that could rival the Milky Way Galaxy for size. Rega is the emotionless walking anonymous cliche. Bolt is basically Shadow The Edgehog, except eSports. It just hits cliched character after cliched character that make you wanna slam your head on the desk when you talk to them. Multiple times, while playing, I asked myself "Now, WHO THE HELL ARE THESE PEOPLE? We met them in PC Bangs and all of a sudden, we're acting like we're soul mates? WHAT?!"
Art: 6/10 (Fine)
Artwork's fine. Nothing to write home about. Each character has a max of 4-5 poses each.
Suspension of Disbelief Held: 3/10 (Bad)
So, let me get this straight. There are 3 HIGH-TIER PROFESSIONAL PLAYERS (Accel, Jett, AND Bolt) conveniently hanging out in the exact same PC Bang, that you just so happen to wander into (after probably passing at least 3-5 others) and they just randomly make time to talk to Mach, the random nobody? AND Jett just so happens to be bailing on her team, wanting to start one with Mach, besides only knowing him/her no more than a week?...I don't buy it.
Gameplay: N/A (No Rating)
There is none. It's a visual novel, you expected something to do besides stare at the same anime poses for 3 hours?
Overall Rating: 5/10 (Average)
Play it once and you'll likely forget about it after. Potentially entertaining with some prophetic allusions to eSports nuances and issues, but the characters are cliched, stupid, and forgettable. Not awful, but could have been more.

The story is very self contained, and while the subject matter, esports, may appear daunting to those unfamiliar with the scene it actually works seamlessly in the style of a Rocky tale, the underdog trying to make it in a competitive world and the struggles they face and the expectations versus reality of it all as they find their own place.
Admittedly the story may be a tad predictable as goals, hurdles and antagonists are introduced early on, but while the plot may not break new ground in terms of story telling that is in no way am issue, if you are looking for a story more concerned wtih twist reveals you wont find that here, but if you are looking for a story with a genuine love for its subject matter and more concerned with the journey than the destination this is definitely a must.
The technical values are nothing out of this world, they serve as a medium to tell the story and they do so sufficiently well, no mini games clogging up the pace of the story either, which for me is always a plus when it comes to visual novels, nice art, backgrounds and expressions all work well with the story.
Over all a really interesting game to play through and one I would definitely like to see more of in the future.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger does everything right, except make a fun game.
A lot of the assests used to make this are fantastic. The art style is cell-shaded which works perfectly for the graphic novel feel they were going for. I find cell-shaded graphics overused but it works well here. Colors are vibrant and enemies are easy to see; they don't mush with the background like in a lot of other FPSes. The campaign has a solid story, told in the past tense in the first person by a rambling narrator. It opens up lots of unique elements like enemies/environmental objects popping in as he 'remembers' different parts of the story. The whole aesthetic has this superb Spaghetti Western feel, very much in the vein of Sergio Leone. They nailed the look of the comical Western Villain and Hero. Sound design is great as is much of the voice acting, if not a bit hammy. All of the classic Western environment will be featured from sleepy towns, the back woods, trains, and mountain passes.
So why is this not recommended? Because the gameplay is boring as hell. It's a standard CoD FPS. Regenerating health bars, cover shooting mechanics, extremely scripted gameplay with "YOU ARE LEAVING THE MISSION AREA" prompts, instant deaths from falling 2 feet 'cus it's not in the mission, and invisible walls as far as the eye can't see.
At least with CoD you have weapon variety - here it's just pistol, shotgun, and rifle. Oh sure there are
different pistols and shotguns, but that's still all you get. Instead of grenades you've given dynamite but it's the same thing. End bosses end up being bullet sponges.
It has a few mechanics to try and differentiate it but it's just not enough. There's a 'draw' mini-game that metaphorically means lining up 2 circles on top of 2 targets at the same time, you can evade lethal bullet on a cooldown through a QTE, and there's a bullet time feature similar to Max Payne. It's not enough. I was bored after the first level and it never got better. Blissfully the campaign is short at 4 hours. The only thing that kept me going was the narration, but I still wouldn't recommend it even with that.

I've spent most of my time on the 'Rise of a Dynasty' DLC, 17.9 Hours to be exact, since the DLC loads separately even though it uses or check the base games files. I know very well what the DLC does and does not include, and I will not be factoring features of the DLC in this review.
Patrician is a great nautical trading game. You buy low, travel to another city, and sell high. As you gain more money, you buy more ships so you can carry more goods. Then you can start a second Convoy(a team of ships basically), and assign it a route. A route tells the ships which cities to go to and what order to do it. You can tell them what they should buy and what they should sell in that particular city. And they'll do all that without any more input from you, and they'll be earning you money in no time.
You can even start producing goods yourself, and have dedicated ships to deliver it to another city either to sell high, or give it to another goods producer you own so they can make more complicated, and therefore more valuable goods to sell. You gain favor in a city by selling them goods that they are low on, which makes them like you more. Once they're happy enough with you, you can start buying buildings in their city, and producing goods unique to them.
You can also take up Contracts/Missions/Whatever at the Pub. This ranges from delivering a certain amount of a specific good, or even hunting down a specific pirate or rival.
One thing it's starts losing quality on is sea based combat. Most of the time, you'll just want to let the fighting resolve automatically rather than take control yourself, since it's rather boring. Once you start getting more well known in the game, your ships will be attacked by pirates more often, and sometimes not even towards you specifically. Sometimes they'll park their boats outside a cities port, attacking anyone who comes or goes. Most of the time, if you lose, they'll just take a large amount of your goods, and sometimes a ship, and let your convoy go. To counter this, you can assign specialized boats with armor and weapons to fight, protect, and even scare off pirates on occasion. You can even put cannons on your merchant boats, however, this subtracts from overall storage space, but it's worth it if a specific convoy gets attacked a lot. Sometimes though, they're just a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ and you'll have to send your own specialized combat convoy to take them out permanently, since no one else will do it.
There's a lot of trading to do in this game, and the DLC will add quite a bit more. I'll need to write up a review for 'Rise of a Dynasty' too, but later.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys trading games,

Plague, Oh Plague.
Wow, where to start.
Gameplay, lets start with the basic gameplay features and where you start on your path to total Global Life Extiction.
I hear that there is a free tablet version of this game. I do not own that as I don't have a tablet and I am writing this review based solely on the version here on steam. My game play is accurate for the time I have spent in game.
You are given some simple plague samples to mutate into what you would have as your Choice for human destruction. Then you are given a map where you pick your location and a lucky soul stumbles upon your not so big of a deal at this point infection. A few moments into the game and you are given mutation points. (This is where things get fun) You are then able to mutate your Virus, Bacteria, Legion, and many other types of infections into what you want based on what types of effects it will have on its host as well as what types of climates and global regions your infection best thrives in. After infection the population as much as possible, then choosing the time to flip the switch is crucial as you see the population suddenly plumet and the world panic as all forms of transportation go on lock down and all borders for all countries are sealed. Suddenly you are not the micro organism on your own planet as what you see as a paridise prison planet! ....."Ring Around the Rosies, Pocket full of Posies, ashes, ashes, we all fall down."
Intense game play, wih in detailed mutaion structuring and simulation like responses from wrold organizations. Plague Inc, I feel, Bring a fresh and awesome take on a great idea for a global simulation. Fantasic job everyone hands down a great game and a well worth time investment. 9/10
The only thing I would change is the fact that there isn't anything added to the game that we wouldn't predict, there are some funny twerks here and there but for the most part the game play is always the same... spread infections like mad, and then flip the switch and kill everyone. The simply key to the game is learning how to spread each infection correctly and knowing when to kill off the world. If you don't infect all the countries before you start killing everyone you won't win.... and untill you figure this out you probably won't win very often unless you are lucky. After that the game is easy... even in the hardest most. It only took me a game or 2 to figure out that I could burn through levels by setting it to the fastest setting and mutating infections like mad then mutate and kill everyone once all countries have at least 10k infections. Of course the obvious logic is slowing killing them off as the last people get infected so the countries that have the smallest amount of infections don't have all the infect people die and then they are a safe country again.
All in all great game and I very much enjoyed the time I spent playing it. I hope they update it more as I am sure that will bring me back to it.

Give this game a try!

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I think this game is very interesting and engaging, I've had a lot of fun playing it. That being said, there is room for improvment. The menu screen looks like it was made by someone in Paint, the music to go with it is ridiculous as well as all the text. There are typos - such as the word Territory, and the menu style overall makes the game look very unprofessional.  Character upgrades are located in the strangest sub-menu, the soundtrack is jarring, there's too much noise too often. One of my largest issues is if a female cougar enters your area and begins to attack you cannot kill it, if you're trying to move cubs to a safer location it will attack again and again. It would  be less annoying  if marking your tree prevented this, but it doesn't. It would still be annoying because the trees that line your territory are nowhere near your territoy. I think it would improve the game if the map was a little more logical, and for such an expansive map there are very few dens. I don't know the mechanics of the game, but I think it would feel much more open world if there were more den opportunities, even if they weren't marked on the map. There are hint interfaces that pop up while you're playing at inconvenient times, like when you're tracking prey, they're also blurry and full of huge yellow text which really takes you out of it.
I think the animations are fine, and I like the fighting style. Shelter 2 is another game I play that is similar but it was taken in a more artistic direction, and has a little more development. I still enjoy this game, I just wish that it wasn't quite so sloppy. A few simple changes would make the game a lot more enjoyable.

If your the type of person that's into Proper animal simulation games. It's nothing like those crappy Ipad games you find that claim to be an animal simulation but is clearly not. untamed life a cougar is quite a realistic Cougar simulation. The graphics are good, and have improved alot since when it first came out. You play the role of a female cougar, which you get to pick out of quite a few colors. You start out in search of a mate. This is the only time that the males are Friendly to the female. Infact on my first try I sat and watched several males fight eachother over the right to mate with the female cougar. Once the strongest male won, I allowed him to do the 'Deed'. After falling pregnant, i started searching for a den to give birth in, catching prey and avoiding hunters along the way. When i found a place i liked, I give birth to 3 cubs. They were small and slow, but adorable. I left them at the den to search for food and to mark my territory to keep rival females at bay. We stayed there, until a male had learnt of our whereabouts. And so i had to lead my cubs to safety, otherwise that male would kill them. My cubs are now on the second stage of life. They are still spotted but are able to keep up with mum. The female you begin with isn't that strong or able to run for a longer period of time. That's where the stats come in. You can gain stats and use those stats to unlock abilities. Like Longer health, Stamina and even Quicker acceleration. I've also recently found out that the cubs have genetics from both of the parent's. So the parent's colors affect the cubs colors. Each animal reacts differently to your approach. A deer will flee, a Male deer, will also flee, but if attacked he will kick. A bison,Moose and Horse will warn you by either shaking their heads or scraping their hoof along the ground. If you get too close they attack, instead of other games where npc's automatically attack the second your in range. Predators though will attack you when in range. Specially wolves. Bears and foxes, i've caught them stalking my cubs. Eagles attack both mum and cubs. I've caught them swooping down on my cubs, i just manage to get there in time and the eagle hobbles along on the ground trying to take off. Not all of the human NPC's are alone.. That's right, some of them have backup.
Pro's
Realistic Animal behaviour. (For both Cougar's and npc's.)
Realistic Cougar and animal Sounds.
Quite Realistic Animations.
Different Life stages for cubs. I've only witnessed 2 so far. Barely walking stage (Maybe a week or 2. Has Spots), And Cub stage(Has Spots, and can keep up with mum.) But from the website, i've seen a slightly older cub with no spots.
Upgradable Cougar. (Stats)
Plenty of prey to hunt and dangers to face to keep you on your toes.
Game not easy, (Even on easy.) Prey is sometimes hard to Stalk and catch in normal mode. That's what Target mode is for (T)
Cubs play with eachother.
Day and Night cycle.
The Game World is beautifully detailed.
Con's
Foggy. It's too foggy so you can't always see where your going.
You can get swarmed by a lot of predators. I was attacking humans as i ended up bumping into them, since the fog made it hard to see a few feet in front of you. When i had Told my cubs to stay, and focused on the humans, a bear came out of nowhere, and attacked 1 of my cubs, then the dogs decided it would be fun to join in to. I had 1 cub left. So i had no choice to maul everyone who provoked my wrath and then reloaded my save.
No weather. (Though that's probably coming in later.)
Seasons. There's no seasons. It's always spring. I wonder what it'll be like in winter. How hard it would be to survive if prey numbers dropped.
Having to shift constantly between target mode to normal mode after each fight. As when attacking in normal mode it's hard to keep sight of your prey. If in Target mode it automatically locks on for you which makes it easier. But because i'm the type of person that likes there character to be fully zoomed in, i have to keep constantly scrolling after exiting out of target mode. Though it's not a big deal as i'm getting used to it.
Killed prey despawns too quickly. At the newborn stage, i left the cubs at the den since they are far too slow to keep up with mum at that age. Well there was no food near home so i travelled for awhile. When i caught a deer, i dragged it back home only to get a few feet away from my den and have it poof. My poor cubs were starving by this time. Maybe have it where prey that have been killed have a longer time to despawn.
Things i'd hope the developer will consider is random litter numbers. Each time you always have 3 cubs. I think it would add alittle suspense to the whole "oh i wonder how many cubs i'll have this time" kind of thing.
Other than those the game is fun to play. This game is to show you all the things a cougar must face to raise offspring and survive. And it pulls it off.

Simplistic, time consuming and strangly addictive.
The concept of the game is simple, you're a trader in the Hansiatic leauge, and you have too expand your trade empire. How? By selling and buying a number of diffrant goods, all from Hemp, bricks, pelts, salt, wine and much more. The whole game is built around supply and demand, you buy goods were its cheap, often were the goods in question is produced, for example logs and mead from Stockholm or wine and wool from Colonge. These goods you will then need to deliver all across the Baltic sea and the northen Atlantic. After a few hours you might have enough money and respect in one of the cities to start producing your own goods, maybe you will start a grain farm in Lübeck and have it delivered to Riga and Malmö. The trading is very very simple to learn but hard to master, you will trade by sending trading ships into diffrant towns ( or if you have a counting house in the city you can sell goods from your local storage) and then sell any goods that you have on the boat. You can avoid all the micro management later in the game by setting up basic trading route running along maybe three towns. You can with this system have a boat sail from Stockholm with a bit of logs and hemp, and then have it sold in London were you then pick up wool and iron, you can then inturn sell these goods in Oslo were you pick up Salt and bricks that you take back to Stockholm and restart the route.
The Combat in the game is quite small, you can turn into a pirate and harrass your compeditors, but also you will need to defend your own ships from organised pirates that sail all over the Baltic sea, the battles will have you control a max of three ships as you order them what kind of ammunition you want them to fire and what ship you want them to target. But this really does not effect the main gameplay that is trading, Later in the game you will also be able to become mayor in a town, this enabling you to construct certain buildings and increasing the size of the town.
With all this put together there are still some flaws in the design of the game, at times it can seem too micro heavy to handle and often you end up unable to handle the changes to the trade, you sometimes lack an overview over what effects your income outcome and how you can change it, the tempo of the game might also scare away anyone who is not willing to put a sizeable ammount of time into it.
Despite this I find this game to be extreamly addictive, this is not for the large cool battles or the huge cool citites you can construct, but because I can have an impact on the flow of trade around the whole region, I can utterly destroy the price on hemp or spice, and ruin my enemies chances on a market on that specific ware. This can enable me to buy up the market and then I can sell it to a very high price instead, the effects of your trade matters and you can have an complete blast seeing how your trade empire grows month after month. 7/10 for one of the best medival trading simulators out there, it will challange you to be effective in your trade, and plan out a strategy for how you will become the most popular and richest trader in the Baltic Sea.

Fast-paced arcade first person shooter with an interesting narrative.
The character is Silas Greaves, a legendary ex-bounty hunter, who is telling his story of vengeance to a bunch of crowds in a bar. You play as Silas as told in the recollection of his story, hunting infamous outlaws in the old West while fulfilling his quest of finding the man who murdered his brothers.
Storytelling is nice, with Silas' commenting on your misdeed and the crowd interrupting Silas' story in the middle of action. Characters banters is often funny and the lines are very well-written. As Silas' memory is hazy, the levels you're playing in will occassionally change as you progress through his story - like sudden change of routes or enemies appearing out of nowhere. This is all done in a really smooth flow without disturbing the fast-paced action, although in Story mode sometimes it's difficult to focus on the narration as the combat takes a lot of your concentration.
The game itself plays as arcade FPS with a combo meter. You can also level up Silas to unlock more skills according to each of his class' proficiency (there are three class available: Gunslinger, Ranger/Sniper, and Trapper/Shotgunner). There is a duel combat mode at the end of each level where you face classic old West infamous like Dalton brothers and Sundance Kid. It also has a cool bullet time mechanics which is activated either with a button, when your health is low, and/or when you can move faster than your opponent in duel.
Speed is really emphasized. From shootout to duel, you need to move your hand fast to sweep down your opponents. This is especially true in the Arcade mode where you need to combine fast playstyle with flexible weapon swapping to build the combo as high as 50. AI opponent is smart enough that their moves can be unpredictable - you need to think and move fast to not lose the combo meter. Shootout can be very amusingly chaotic and how well you fare depends on your concentration (the game even has a tip about not panicking).
I finished the Story mode in 9 hours, but for the completionist in me Arcade mode and Duel mode provides more challenge to be tackled. There is also a New Game+ in the Story. I can firmly say that Call of Juarez Gunslinger is an excellent, fun old West FPS.

Alright, so I have played Smite for a little bit of time now and have come to some sounds pros and cons when it comes to Hi-Rez (the game's developers) and Smite itself. This review is somewhat biased because I am a huge fan of the game, but I think my dedication to it gives me some grounds to say what is good and what is bad about it.
*PROS*
-Smite's community is thriving and thanks to multi-queue, getting into a game is now faster than ever.
-Smite's 3rd person camera positioning makes it one of the MOST immersive MOBA experiences out there.
-The gods in the game are easy to understand (most of the time) and their abilities are fairly diverse.
-There are only 5 consistent game modes to chose from and the maps are the same every time, but each game feels fresh and a Mode of the Day offers up an interesting look at a new way to play.
-There are regular updates to the game and new gods are being added constantly.
-The grind for new gods and skins is satisfying and rewarding enough to make you want to keep playing.
There are plenty of other things I could say about the game that I believe are done well, but the ones above are the most prevalent ones that I have come across since I started playing. Now, the cons are not meant to discourage you from playing the game, but are just there as a way to prepare you for some possible frustration in the future!
*CONS*
-No matter how good your computer or internet is, Smite will still crash for no apparent reason. This is only on occasion and normally will not ruin an entire game.
-Smite can feel like a chore at times, especially trying to get all the First Win of the Day gold and that's why I recommend playing with friends.
-In the current meta, early game seems to be very important and, all too often, a deciding factor for a game. Hi-Rez has been working on fixing this, but still nothing has really changed.
-Hi-Rez also has a lot of kinks to still work out in the game and their servers go down at some of the most inconvenient times.
*CONCLUSION*
Smite is certainly a game for the MOBA lover and will have you hooked from the tutorial! It's immersive gameplay and interesting gods offer a wide variety of games and outcomes. The grind will keep you coming back for more and friends will certainly keep you into the game for longer. Hi-Rez has given a lot of love to this game and with it's commuity being as strong as it is, I know Smite will be around for a long time.

Sleeping Dogs was originally released on August 13, 2012 for Xbox 360, PS3, and PC. It was recently released on Xbox One and PS4 as well. It was developed by United Front Games and published by Square Enix. It received a 9 out of 10 on Steam, 4 out of 5 on Metacritic and an 8.5 out of 10 on IGN.
While most people consider Sleeping Dogs a GTA knock off set in Hong Kong, I would argue that perception is false. While the initial concept is the same, an open world crime game, the basic mechanics of Sleeping Dogs sets it apart. These mechanics include cop/triad alliances, a focus on melee combat, and a Max Payne esque bullet time when sliding over objects during gun play.
Because of the great implementation of the aforementioned mechanics, the smaller size of the open world compared to similar releases such as GTA and Watch_Dogs, still provides a fantastic experience.
The story in follows an ex San Francisco cop that has been thrown back into the world of the Triads in modern day Hong Kong. While the story may seem cliche at first, if you give it some time you will find a rewarding plot line to follow.
The Definitive Edition includes six downloadable content packages for your consumption, and with the current holiday sale on Steam, is well worth the additional cost.

Sleeping Dogs grabs the best aspects from many famous franchises and mashes them into a surprisingly cohesive whole.
Usual GTA brand of sandbox comes in a very detailed asian island flair to explore, boasting some very interesting cultural references that are unique to this title; Arkham style combat which relies on timing and countering, as well as some combination attacks (which can be upgraded as you find specific collectibles); the usual free running stuff for some parkour tricks (although in a somewhat limited manner); and a very polished gunplay mechanic which includes Max Payne-ish bullet time. Oh, also, completely absurd car physic (this is a plus in my book).
The game plays very well and pulling counters, slow-mo headshots, and driving enemies off the road (amongst others) are all incredibly satisfying. Counters and environmental kills can get quite brutal and gory, which is nice and makes the combat feel weighty and significant most of the time.
“Character Progression”, if you would call it that, is present through a few different “meters” you level up; leveling up gives you points to spend on certain perks. You can choose your way but you will likely end up with (almost) everything. However, the amount of experience you get for these meters is still not particularly well balanced, a problem the original also had.
Integrated DLC is very interesting but some open up at somewhat weird times. “Death by a Thousand Cuts” opens up
soon and can frustrate; “Shaolin Showdown” also seems somewhat random. The “Zodiac Tournament” (which deserves special mention for being a
piece of DLC done right) also opens up too soon, but it's worth going in an taking a peek just to see what's in store for you. It's great. Everything else works really well. I particularly liked the SWAT DLC being broken into several missions that gradually open up as you progress in the story; it definitely helped in keeping the variety up.
A few words about the story: I personally really liked it. While far from the most original thing, it was very well written and delivered.
Many games try to get the player attached to its characters but, at least personally, they mostly fail. I simply find it very hard to care or to empathize. So I was very surprised to find myself deeply engaged with the characters of this world. Wiston, Peggy, Uncle Po, Ricky, Conroy, Jackie. They all mattered and played their part, but it goes beyond. The character arch of Jackie, how Conroy’s attitude towards you shifts through the whole game. It’s not a moment’s difference, it’s everything that happens. How the game takes the time to make you do menial tasks for Peggy. Everything builds up.
I’ve bought and played this game at around 2014 December. I had a few minor visual glitches every now and again but nothing even close to game breaking. Even though this version is somewhat infamous for running poorly, it ran pretty well for me. There are also plenty of graphics options to tweak in case you want to sacrifice some bells and whistles for stability. I would recommend trying your best to get World Density (or whatever it’s called - it’s under advanced graphical settings) to the max though; it had a significant difference in the feel of the environment for me.
One of my favorite games of the 7th generation. It takes the best parts of many worlds and combines them into a really solid whole. Combat is fun, the story is engaging and the world is alive and interesting to be in. DLC implementation is really well done. Definitely recommended.
Managed to 100% the main game in roughly 43 hours (in-game time), but I had already done it before on the PS3, so I knew my way around.
Regarding the extra DLC chapters: I've only done about an hour of the "Nightmare In North Point" chapter. It's OK at best. There are some good jokes, but I was not particularly taken by it. The vibrancy of the world is replaced by a really heavy handed blue-filter which makes everything look the same. The new enemies are not particularly interesting to fight. It definitely wasn't my cup of tea, and it honestly sucked a bit of hype for the other chapter (Year of The Snake), which I haven't even played and for all I know could be way better.
Moral of the story here is that I get that sometimes people want more, but sometimes leaving that desire unfulfilled is what keeps us coming back. I'm shelving this game for the time being; it just seems like it has given me enough. One day I will feel like playing this again (because it really is a great game overall) and then maybe I'll get those extra chapters done.

This game is free to play if you don't want to be play the game itself. If you'd rather walk around the world moving more slowly than a bike without wheels and not actually do anything, don't spend a penny. If you want to actually test the game's central mechanics, you need to buy one of the "starter" packs. These packs aren't actually starter packs, but monthly subscriptions that you need to keep buying into in order to continue playing the game. I am not opposed to the concept of buying games. I've bought many games, some of them good, some of them bad. However, none of them pretended to be a free-to-play game and locked off the core features of the game. Other common game practices are also missing, like being able to change video quality from the game's pause menu instead of from the launcher / main menu.
I downloaded this game with a friend to see what all the negative fuss was about, and now I understand. The community for this game acts as though paying for functionality for a free-to-play game is typical. There are fantastic free-to-play titles that allow for progression, or even being able to play the base game at all, without spending any amount of money at all. These games understand what the term "free-to-play" means. This game is pay-to-win in that you can't even access the mechanic the game is centered around. Had this been advertised as a forest walking simulator with the ability to fire a non-lethal weapon, maybe I could understand how functionality is behind a paywall. However, the game is called "theHunter" and is labeled as free-to-play, yet you can't do any hunting without paying a minimum of $15.

Okay, where do I start with this?? I am going to start out saying that this will be my first lengthy review about any game in my Library. Why?? Because I feel like this game is NOT getting fair feedback looking at the overall reviews. Even when you read the Posotive Reviews of this game, NO ONE sheds light into what this game is AND why they rated it a Positive. And I hope that this review will ease your mind into actually giving this game a try, and finding out for yourself that the reviews either consist of .....
1. People who does not have a job as of yet, want to play the best hunting game around, but can not afford this.
2. Trolls just hating on the game because of the Free to Play aspect of this game and NOT the overall game itself
3. People that has a COMPLETE wrong mindset of the Pay to Play factor and NEVER even tried to pay to play the game
and that I will go into bigger detail about those factors and why the review score is Mostly Negative because of those 3 points. In the process, I will also clarify a few things for anyone reading this review, and I hope you stick around to read it all. I promise it will be worth while, and that it will change your mind towards things to actually give this game a shot. Because, I was just like you (The Reader) at the start of it all, and also just like you (The Reader) my reaction to this game, the reviews and the Pay to Play factor just drove me away from this game COMPLETELY. When in the end, all that was needed to enjoy this game to full, was $49.99. How is that for Pay to Play??
Okay, now for the actuall review.
I will go as far as to say that this is the best hunting sim I have ever played, even though I was sceptical at the start because of the whole Pay to Play aspect of the game. At the time I HATED this game because it was Free to Play, but I cant even shoot anything in the game, because everytime I want to shoot, it tells me I need a license for this and license for that. I just got mad, and at the moment I felt like this game is the biggest pile of crap I have EVER played. Who even plays a crap game like this AND pours money into it?? What is this, another World of Warcraft??
Till one day, I just felt like wasting money, and decided to waste money onto this game, because why not?? I went to the store page of this game's Launcher, and I went to purchase a Membership. Looking at the options I had, I decided to go with the Trailrunner Subscription ($49.99), which gives me a 12 month (Year) Membership to shoot what I want, where I want AND to ease me into the game, I got 9 extra Weapons to start off my game AND 35 other items to accompany me. Ranging from scopes for my 9 Weapons, Cammo, Lures, Backpack and much more usefull items.
Eager to start out the game AND still keeping in mind that there is still MUCH MORE to purchase in the game store than what I got with my Subscription, I started a new game, and made due with what I had for the time being. The game started up and the hunt was on. With my lure at hand and my trusty .300 (Gotten from Trailrunner Subscription) I was determine to shoot some Deer.
I set out with my trusty HunterMate, and I started learning the game and what goes for what. My first encounter was a Turkey. I went to the location of the Turkey call, and saw the tracks. My HunterMate told me in which direction the Turkey has fled, and I just follow along the path. The path led me through the Forest and Swampland areas, and I was soon greated with a Deer Grunt Call in the distance. It was at that moment I paused in my tracks. I took a crouching position, I got my Lure ready, and I called the Deer in. Sitting in the bush, looking left and right past the trees, through the bushes I am trying to find the Deer AND be as quite and low profile as I can get .... at the same time worrying about a stupid Turkey ....
I saw the Deer peeking he's head over the scrubs infront of me, I bring up my .300 to scope .... I line up my shot and I just let it go. The Deer fell on the spot and I jumped with joy. I went to collect the Deer and I was happy with what I got. I went back to the tracks of the Turkey, and continued my journey.
Its been a year later, and what was once a piece of crap game to waste money on, is now the best game I ever wasted money on. Funny how that works right?? Its also been a year later, and I only spend $49.99 on this game since then. Yes, you read that right. After one whole year, the Trailrunner Subscription for $49.99 was AND is all you need to enjoy this game to the fullest. I now renewed my Subscription for another year which is now $34.99. I used the other $15 and I bought myself more Lures to use on for the other animals, and I still only use my weapons and equipment I got from my Trailrunner pack. NEVER bought anything extra than what I got for spending $49.99 on this game.
If you have sticked with me up until now in my review, I am sure you are now more convinced to actually try this game out INSTEAD of just looking at the Pay to Play factor and relying on the Review System of Steam.
In general, all you EVER need to play this game is the Trailrunner Subscription. NOTHING more and NOTHING less. The other items you can purchase is just for better convinience and a better overall gameplay to make your life easier. In truth, the Weapons and Items you get in the Trailrunner Subsciption is MORE than enough to play this game to fullest of experience.

3. A lot of Game Reserves to choose from
4. Each Game Reserve has its own Game and Hunting tactics to adapt
5. Overall very good hunting experience
6. New Game Reserves was added (with Game) and is still being added (with Game)
7. The game offers a level up system for each Weapon and Animal the more you use your Weapon and Track an Animal
8. The game offers multiplayer where you can hunt with your friends
Cons.

2. Devs does not seem to listen to its already small community to improve on overall user experience
3. The controlls are kind of clunky and stiff, but you get use to it
Putting it all together to sum it up. Purchase the Trailrunner Subscription ($49.99) and try this game out for yourself. Do NOT purchase the other subscriptions as you will not enjoy the game to the fullest, and they dont offer you as much gain as the Trailrunner Subscription does. Thats all you will EVER spend on this game in your life, and as you play the game, you will soon relise that you gave the game a unnecessary hard time BECAUSE of the overall Steam Review AND the fact that it is Pay to Play.

just thought I'd say hi and get some important things out of the way for those that are looking to get this game. For those wanting to get theHunter, know this; it is a Hunting SIMULATOR. This is NOT like Cabela's Big Game Hunter where you can just stroll up to a deer and shoot it point blank in the face without it spooking. YOU HAVE TO PLAY THIS GAME AS IF YOU WERE HUNTING IRL, which is why I recommend to AT LEAST learn the basics of hunting before even starting this game if you have NO hunting experience whatsoever. If you choose to ignore me, you'll find the game boring and give it a crappy rating, just like what all of the other inexperienced players have already done, hence why the rating is very poor. Other than that, for anyone with hunting experience, such as myself and a few other friends, we can say as a whole that theHunter is very entertaining to play for someone with hunting experience. My only complaint with the game is the Collision Avoidance and Pathfinding for the animal AI, including Scent Hounds and Retrievers. The thing is: there practically isn't any collision avoidance or pathfinding. For example, I've had several times of where I've been tracking/chasing a game animal, only to find it stuck in a bunch of trees, simply because its AI had no collision avoidance/pathfinding programmed into the code to dodge the issue. Same thing for the Scent Hounds/Retrievers: I've had moments of where I'll be walking through the forest or up a hill, and my Scent Hound will get stuck in a bunch of trees or on a rock, simply because its AI had no collision avoidance/pathfinding programmed into the code.

There aren't many games out there, where the point of the game is to traid and to do some capitalistic♥♥♥♥♥♥ One of them is definitely Patrician IV. I've been playing the game for some time now and I think it is time to say something about it.
These games can be boring sometimes, and this or similar kinds of gameplay, are usually part of some bigger game. But the thrill is not in the gameplay, it is in the role that you are playing. In this particular game you take the role of a merchant in medieval times on the Baltic sea. Your goal is to be the biggest merchant of them all. And as far as the story goes that's about it. So, as you can see, there isn't much of a story. But there is a lot of trading to do and you have to industrialize your production of goods and trading roots.
For the gameplay I can say it is simple as far as handling it goes. You don't have any trouble trying to figure out how to do things around there. The mechanics of demand and supply are realistic and you can quickly overproduce or oversupply a market of a city that you came to trade in. So in that way you have to be careful that you always keep them a bit short on supplies.
There is one thing that is in this game and has to be mentioned separately, and that is the naval battles. You can have naval battles with pirates or you competitors, but these battles are not big ones which is little bit disappointing. You can only have fights 3 on 3. Never the less, it is a welcome change in the monotone playing experience.
I am enjoying playing this game, but I think that those who like more action will be bored. That's why I am giving the game 6/10, and I gave it a rating that high just because, I like to play it once in a while when I feel that this capitalistic world is not the best decision that humanity has made.

Sleeping Dogs was originally released on August 13, 2012 for Xbox 360, PS3, and PC. It was recently released on Xbox One and PS4 as well. It was developed by United Front Games and published by Square Enix. It received a 9 out of 10 on Steam, 4 out of 5 on Metacritic and an 8.5 out of 10 on IGN.
While most people consider Sleeping Dogs a GTA knock off set in Hong Kong, I would argue that perception is false. While the initial concept is the same, an open world crime game, the basic mechanics of Sleeping Dogs sets it apart. These mechanics include cop/triad alliances, a focus on melee combat, and a Max Payne esque bullet time when sliding over objects during gun play.
Because of the great implementation of the aforementioned mechanics, the smaller size of the open world compared to similar releases such as GTA and Watch_Dogs, still provides a fantastic experience.
The story in follows an ex San Francisco cop that has been thrown back into the world of the Triads in modern day Hong Kong. While the story may seem cliche at first, if you give it some time you will find a rewarding plot line to follow.
The Definitive Edition includes six downloadable content packages for your consumption, and with the current holiday sale on Steam, is well worth the additional cost.

Sleeping Dogs grabs the best aspects from many famous franchises and mashes them into a surprisingly cohesive whole.
Usual GTA brand of sandbox comes in a very detailed asian island flair to explore, boasting some very interesting cultural references that are unique to this title; Arkham style combat which relies on timing and countering, as well as some combination attacks (which can be upgraded as you find specific collectibles); the usual free running stuff for some parkour tricks (although in a somewhat limited manner); and a very polished gunplay mechanic which includes Max Payne-ish bullet time. Oh, also, completely absurd car physic (this is a plus in my book).
The game plays very well and pulling counters, slow-mo headshots, and driving enemies off the road (amongst others) are all incredibly satisfying. Counters and environmental kills can get quite brutal and gory, which is nice and makes the combat feel weighty and significant most of the time.
“Character Progression”, if you would call it that, is present through a few different “meters” you level up; leveling up gives you points to spend on certain perks. You can choose your way but you will likely end up with (almost) everything. However, the amount of experience you get for these meters is still not particularly well balanced, a problem the original also had.
Integrated DLC is very interesting but some open up at somewhat weird times. “Death by a Thousand Cuts” opens up
soon and can frustrate; “Shaolin Showdown” also seems somewhat random. The “Zodiac Tournament” (which deserves special mention for being a
piece of DLC done right) also opens up too soon, but it's worth going in an taking a peek just to see what's in store for you. It's great. Everything else works really well. I particularly liked the SWAT DLC being broken into several missions that gradually open up as you progress in the story; it definitely helped in keeping the variety up.
A few words about the story: I personally really liked it. While far from the most original thing, it was very well written and delivered.
Many games try to get the player attached to its characters but, at least personally, they mostly fail. I simply find it very hard to care or to empathize. So I was very surprised to find myself deeply engaged with the characters of this world. Wiston, Peggy, Uncle Po, Ricky, Conroy, Jackie. They all mattered and played their part, but it goes beyond. The character arch of Jackie, how Conroy’s attitude towards you shifts through the whole game. It’s not a moment’s difference, it’s everything that happens. How the game takes the time to make you do menial tasks for Peggy. Everything builds up.
I’ve bought and played this game at around 2014 December. I had a few minor visual glitches every now and again but nothing even close to game breaking. Even though this version is somewhat infamous for running poorly, it ran pretty well for me. There are also plenty of graphics options to tweak in case you want to sacrifice some bells and whistles for stability. I would recommend trying your best to get World Density (or whatever it’s called - it’s under advanced graphical settings) to the max though; it had a significant difference in the feel of the environment for me.
One of my favorite games of the 7th generation. It takes the best parts of many worlds and combines them into a really solid whole. Combat is fun, the story is engaging and the world is alive and interesting to be in. DLC implementation is really well done. Definitely recommended.
Managed to 100% the main game in roughly 43 hours (in-game time), but I had already done it before on the PS3, so I knew my way around.
Regarding the extra DLC chapters: I've only done about an hour of the "Nightmare In North Point" chapter. It's OK at best. There are some good jokes, but I was not particularly taken by it. The vibrancy of the world is replaced by a really heavy handed blue-filter which makes everything look the same. The new enemies are not particularly interesting to fight. It definitely wasn't my cup of tea, and it honestly sucked a bit of hype for the other chapter (Year of The Snake), which I haven't even played and for all I know could be way better.
Moral of the story here is that I get that sometimes people want more, but sometimes leaving that desire unfulfilled is what keeps us coming back. I'm shelving this game for the time being; it just seems like it has given me enough. One day I will feel like playing this again (because it really is a great game overall) and then maybe I'll get those extra chapters done.

Something that struck me about "Papers, Please" is that it isn't a fun game. It's a paperwork simulator that feels unrewarding and almost painful, but for a good reason. Everything about this game adds to the story from the dreary atmosphere to the sympathetic characters, and it's this context that turns the dull mechanics into something truly tense and deep.
Possibly the most appealing aspect are the choices you make. The ones you make are both big and small, but you only ever have a few seconds to decide on something that could change the lives of the people you meet. Okay, where do I start with this?? I am going to start out saying that this will be my first lengthy review about any game in my Library. Why?? And I hope that this review will ease your mind into actually giving this game a try, and finding out for yourself that the reviews either consist of .....
1. People who does not have a job as of yet, want to play the best hunting game around, but can not afford this.

3. People that has a COMPLETE wrong mindset of the Pay to Play factor and NEVER even tried to pay to play the game
