In the process, I will also clarify a few things for anyone reading this review, and I hope you stick around to read it all. I promise it will be worth while, and that it will change your mind towards things to actually give this game a shot. Because, I was just like you (The Reader) at the start of it all, and also just like you (The Reader) my reaction to this game, the reviews and the Pay to Play factor just drove me away from this game COMPLETELY. When in the end, all that was needed to enjoy this game to full, was $49.99. How is that for Pay to Play??
Okay, now for the actuall review.
I will go as far as to say that this is the best hunting sim I have ever played, even though I was sceptical at the start because of the whole Pay to Play aspect of the game. At the time I HATED this game because it was Free to Play, but I cant even shoot anything in the game, because everytime I want to shoot, it tells me I need a license for this and license for that. I just got mad, and at the moment I felt like this game is the biggest pile of crap I have EVER played. Who even plays a crap game like this AND pours money into it?? What is this, another World of Warcraft??
Till one day, I just felt like wasting money, and decided to waste money onto this game, because why not?? I went to the store page of this game's Launcher, and I went to purchase a Membership. Looking at the options I had, I decided to go with the Trailrunner Subscription ($49.99), which gives me a 12 month (Year) Membership to shoot what I want, where I want AND to ease me into the game, I got 9 extra Weapons to start off my game AND 35 other items to accompany me. Ranging from scopes for my 9 Weapons, Cammo, Lures, Backpack and much more usefull items.
Eager to start out the game AND still keeping in mind that there is still MUCH MORE to purchase in the game store than what I got with my Subscription, I started a new game, and made due with what I had for the time being. The game started up and the hunt was on. With my lure at hand and my trusty .300 (Gotten from Trailrunner Subscription) I was determine to shoot some Deer.
I set out with my trusty HunterMate, and I started learning the game and what goes for what. My first encounter was a Turkey. I went to the location of the Turkey call, and saw the tracks. My HunterMate told me in which direction the Turkey has fled, and I just follow along the path. The path led me through the Forest and Swampland areas, and I was soon greated with a Deer Grunt Call in the distance. It was at that moment I paused in my tracks. I took a crouching position, I got my Lure ready, and I called the Deer in. Sitting in the bush, looking left and right past the trees, through the bushes I am trying to find the Deer AND be as quite and low profile as I can get .... at the same time worrying about a stupid Turkey ....
I saw the Deer peeking he's head over the scrubs infront of me, I bring up my .300 to scope .... I line up my shot and I just let it go. The Deer fell on the spot and I jumped with joy. I went to collect the Deer and I was happy with what I got. I went back to the tracks of the Turkey, and continued my journey.
Its been a year later, and what was once a piece of crap game to waste money on, is now the best game I ever wasted money on. Funny how that works right?? Its also been a year later, and I only spend $49.99 on this game since then. Yes, you read that right. After one whole year, the Trailrunner Subscription for $49.99 was AND is all you need to enjoy this game to the fullest. I now renewed my Subscription for another year which is now $34.99. I used the other $15 and I bought myself more Lures to use on for the other animals, and I still only use my weapons and equipment I got from my Trailrunner pack. NEVER bought anything extra than what I got for spending $49.99 on this game.
If you have sticked with me up until now in my review, I am sure you are now more convinced to actually try this game out INSTEAD of just looking at the Pay to Play factor and relying on the Review System of Steam.
In general, all you EVER need to play this game is the Trailrunner Subscription. NOTHING more and NOTHING less. The other items you can purchase is just for better convinience and a better overall gameplay to make your life easier. In truth, the Weapons and Items you get in the Trailrunner Subsciption is MORE than enough to play this game to fullest of experience.

just thought I'd say hi and get some important things out of the way for those that are looking to get this game. For those wanting to get theHunter, know this; it is a Hunting SIMULATOR. This is NOT like Cabela's Big Game Hunter where you can just stroll up to a deer and shoot it point blank in the face without it spooking. YOU HAVE TO PLAY THIS GAME AS IF YOU WERE HUNTING IRL, which is why I recommend to AT LEAST learn the basics of hunting before even starting this game if you have NO hunting experience whatsoever. If you choose to ignore me, you'll find the game boring and give it a crappy rating, just like what all of the other inexperienced players have already done, hence why the rating is very poor. Other than that, for anyone with hunting experience, such as myself and a few other friends, we can say as a whole that theHunter is very entertaining to play for someone with hunting experience. My only complaint with the game is the Collision Avoidance and Pathfinding for the animal AI, including Scent Hounds and Retrievers. The thing is: there practically isn't any collision avoidance or pathfinding. For example, I've had several times of where I've been tracking/chasing a game animal, only to find it stuck in a bunch of trees, simply because its AI had no collision avoidance/pathfinding programmed into the code to dodge the issue. Same thing for the Scent Hounds/Retrievers: I've had moments of where I'll be walking through the forest or up a hill, and my Scent Hound will get stuck in a bunch of trees or on a rock, simply because its AI had no collision avoidance/pathfinding programmed into the code.

Patrician IV, henceforth known as "Patty IV's" is in something of a niche genre, in that it is a Renaissance trading  simulator set around the Hanseatic League in Northern Europe. Doesn't sound like the most riveting game now, but when I rephrase that as TIME TRAVELLING DOSH SIMULATOR 1420 EDITION it starts to sound ♥♥♥♥♥ing dank. The difficulties in the true sandbox mode work pretty well too, they basically make more bad things happen the higher difficulty you select, like pirates stealing your♥♥♥♥♥♥or bad winters freezing ports over as well as ramping up the costs of production, so that in order to maintain a decent profit margin you actually have to spread your goods out intelligently. I'm writing this as a review of both Overlord and the expansion, Raising Hell. Honestly, I don't feel Overlord is complete without Raising Hell, since it adds new unique magic items, one of which is almost a must have: the Sword of Life-Stealing.
I wouldn't say Overlord: RH is a great game. It barely merits "good". But, some of the wit made me chuckle, the combat felt somwhat satisfying, and the crafting tied it together. The minion controls were in a word, awkward. They don't control well, and it basicaly devolves into mobbing enemies or sticking your minions on guard duty.
The tactic I found that works the best is once you have the Sword of Life-Stealing and Arcanium armor with +75% or better health regeneration you're basically unkillable. While this does detract from the difficulty, it also makes the game less exhasperating to play.
But do you truly get to be an "evil overlord"? No. if they'd made the main character a knight, gave you binery moral choices that allowed you be to a "chivalrous knight" or a "black knight", and made all your minions squires instead, the game wouldn't be very different. Is the idea sort of amusing as the backdrop for the gameplay? Sure.
Recommended if you want to take a break from all the other third person action games.

How to properly spend money and play this game:
1. Buy the 3 month bundle or whole year subscription, it comes with a bundle of weapons and items that get you started.  All animals are unlocked, all maps are unlocked.
2. Learn how to activate missions, and complete the missions for $gM, you can buy certain items from the store using $gM.
3. Participate in competitions, 1st place = 75 $eM, 2nd place = 50 $eM, 3rd = 25 $eM.  Some competitions have higher prizes up to 150 $eM.
4. use $gM and $eM you earned to buy more weapons, clothes, or whatever.
In the end you only spent between $10 to $40, for a high quality hunting game.  Whereas if you don't know how to spend money, you will spend more than $100 to get started.
Also please don't write reviews for games if you only played for like 5 minutes.  It makes you look like a chimpanzee trying to tell humans how to build a pyramid.  (P.S. my record shows 0 hours because I just added the game to steam recently, I have 300-400 hours in the actual game account).
My review conclusion: I do recommend this game.  You will have more fun figuring out how to play it properly rather than expecting to have the fun handed to you.

You might have played tower defense games like Kingdom Rush.  You might have played reverse tower defense games like Anomaly: Warzone Earth.  But have you played one that has both?  That's what Rock of Ages is about.
In each level, you control a boulder and the objective is to knock down the enemy's gates by repeatedly running your rock into it.  The problem is that to get there, not only do you have to navigate your boulder through a winding course in a physics-based game, the enemy is continuously setting up devices to block your way such as catapults and elephants with stone towers on their backs.  If your rock is damaged enough, it loses mass and will do less damage to the gate and if it's damaged even more, it can eventually break apart.  Not only that, but you have your own gate and the enemy has his own boulder.  So now you have a tower defense game, reverse tower defense game, and a racing game all packaged up into one as you and your opponent are trying to outdo each other in defenses while trying to destroy each other's gates as fast as possible.
This was a surprisingly fun game with many unique levels and ideas that gets even better with the fact that it has not only online multiplayer but local as well.  It also helps that the campaign story has a great sense of humor.

The Room is a point and click mystery/puzzle game that is reminiscent of Myst but with less mobility. The entire game takes place in a room if you could imagine that, and sometimes branches off into (spoilers)
I bought this game on sale for $1.29 USD and I think it was well worth that price. The game takes about 2-3 hours to complete and $5 is pushing it. (I generally like the idea of 1 dollar per hour played, but there are exceptions)
Overall the graphics in The Room are done rather well. The cutscenes are a tad choppy, but it honestly just gave me more of that classic Myst vibe. The graphics are good for what they need to accomplish, and I have no complaints here.
The game opens at a comfortable ear piercing volume, which is always a favorite of mine. It's games like these that make me glad that I take my headset off when launching a brand new game. After you turn the volume all the way down to 1 or 2, you can begin the game without destroying your hearing. As far as music goes, there isn't a lot. What little music there is definitely is mysterious, but there seems to be times where the developers didn't know what direction they wanted to go in. The classic horror violin sounds start coming in, but the game isn't doing anything to creep me out, so it seems out of place when it drones on and on like a jumpscare is going to happen, when you know it isn't.
Beyond the music, the clacks and clicks of the various mechanisms you're unravelling are all done rather well. Gears turning, cogs winding and keys unlocking all make you feel like you're actually accomplishing something.
The Room's gameplay is basically a series of puzzles with a light storyline attached. It revolves around I believe 4-5 or so objects that have components that open, close, shift and reveal new parts to solve. There are 5 chapters, with each chapter taking around 20-35 minutes average.
The entirety of The Room is played with your mouse. You left click, right click and turn with the mouse. While this wouldn't be a bad thing, I do wish that maybe they had allocated one or two keys to do some of the interacting. There were plenty of times where I would try to get to something and I either slide right past it or I zoom in to the wrong thing. It was annoying, but not gamebreaking. Other times, the game wants you to zoom in to look closer at something. There's nothing wrong with that, but sometimes it wants you to zoom in twice or three times, which is annoying as hell. You see what you need to do and you're trying to grab at it, but it won't slide or press and it makes you think you're wrong, when in reality all you had to do was zoom in once more.
Speaking of knowing the answer, that was one of the biggest issues I had in this game. There were a ton of times where I go "oh I know what I need to do", but then have to comb the entire object trying to find where exactly this one hole or cog is. I actually got frustrated enough to ask for a hint and it told me what to do but not where to go. Maybe I'm nitpicking, maybe that's just part of the fun. But it's just annoying when I have to thoroughly inspect a box with many of the same looking shapes for one particular one. I don't think I'd raise such a fuss about this mechanic if the developers didn't do what they did at the end. Towards the end of the game, you're solving things as usual, but once a new part of the table opens up, the camera immediately pans to the part you need to be that rather than letting you find it. And to be honest, I enjoyed that much more. It left me wishing that had happened the entire game.
Overall, I would give The Room a 7.5/10. It was a lot of fun tinkering with different parts to try to solve the mystery of the various boxes, tables and machinery. There were a few improvements that I think could have made it fantastic. I would honestly be willing to give it an 8/10 if the base price were reduced to 3 dollars or less.

This is a very fun and highly addicting game. However, it isn't the game for everyone. It'll only appeal to people who can appreciate complicated economy systems and a lot of strategic planning with repetitious maintenance requirements. The game is all about economic growth. You buy low and sell high, over and over again, which would seem boring after a short period if it weren't for the automated trade convoys and various other automated options for accumulating wealth.  Players can rent houses, produce goods, hire an accountant to manage foreign affairs, sell captured ships, trade between cities or even entire oceans--there are a multitude of methods for achieving your financial goals, but money isn't the only motivation. Players can also achieve reputable statuses within cities, and even achieve diplomatic ranks which allow for the player to control a city's development even further. To most this may all seem rather boring, but if you're like me, it may just be worth the investment.

This game had potential, it could have been so much more interesting and fun. A lot of the game is spent killing floating parasites, running through uninteresting levels where you have to locate and kill dozens of nazi generals and generic soldiers along with some terrible platforming sections...There is barely any storyline, the gameplay get's repetitive quickly, most of the boss fights are too easy except the last one which can be frustratingly hard...I played this game on Windows 7 and I got quite a few error messages every time I started the game along with not being able to view the very first and last cutscene.
It's a nice game, reminds me of childhood. Plus, it works on Windows 10, even on 1920x1080 with a few tricks.

First of all, the game requires a 3rd-party patch to get the controller support into a somewhat usable state and fix the cutscene audio getting cut off at the end. Voice acting is still terrible on all characters, though.
The game gets tedious quickly. There are a few main sections, each of which is a seemingly endless sequence of levels that are pretty much all the same. Even the objectives never really change; usually it's "kill the officers". Sure, tha Nazis have an evil plan and all that, but... that doesn't add anything. It never felt like a story.
Occasionally, the path to progress is hidden; I frequently checked a walkthrough on how to proceed which is a main source of negative score on a game. The game is not encouraging trial-and-error or exploration in areas that have bottomless pits or a lot of environmental damage, since a death requires a restart of the level from the beginning.
For that reason, and because the bossfights are tedious to no end, I also preferred to check the walkthrough for them so I could do it correctly. Regardless, I was unable to kill the final boss (Beliar) despite checking walkthroughs -- they just keep shooting at him, but there aren't enough weapons around and he grows quickly in my playthrough, so that never worked. Blades don't seem to do anything, and there is no way to recharge blood rage -- so all attempts ended with me being unable to do anything.

FIrst time playing the game, missed it in the ps2 days but always wanted to try it. The game for me didnt work right after installing, had some problems with windows 7 but was easy to fix. WIll try to help other interested in playing the game,
First change your rayne.exe compatibility mode to windows98/me in (Steam\steamapps\common\BloodRayne), then copy steam.dll into the folder. Now to fix the framerate and video skipping you need a program to lock the games framerate to 30 in game, i used Dxtory but if you already have a program that can do the same thing it will be fine. All thats left now is to fix the resolution. Steam\steamapps\common\BloodRayne\system folder go to rayne.ini edit with notepad and find gamePIXY, gamePIXX edit to your needs and have fun.
Now the game itself is very fun and fast paced, the combat is very much hack and slash with some shooting. The voice acting is B movie goodness which you will like or hate. The downside to the game is the story is just there, but not very well told. It seems like the story almost skips around, but for the most part the gameplay will keep you interested.

Note: this is a review for both the original game as well as the expansion, as steam seems to think they are one and the same.
Be Evil!  That's the supposed attraction of Overlord, an interesting hybrid of tactical strategy, action RPG and adventure game, all wrapped in a purely satirical shell.  However, how evil you actually get to be is rather low, being either murderous evil or the evil version of “nice by accident”.  In either case being evil isn't really the attraction of the game, as much as it is about the parodic fun the game pokes at all things fantasy.
Which is good, because the battle system is unwieldy, the stages are sometimes a bit too long, and in the middle of the game the expectation of lifeforce to imbue into your weapons and armor vs the amount you actually have results in a near grinding halt of the gameplay as you grind away in your dungeon on beetles and their ilk.  Clearly the game has some problems, not the least being the somewhat obtuse Hell stages of the Raising Hell DLC.
But it's all ok!  Though those problems can be felt, they are helped along by a silly, interesting, goofy tale that really ends up being about revenge, sin, and what it really means to be evil . . . as well as by some fairly pretty graphics, even seven years past the game's release.
For anyone that enjoys a silly tale of fantasy parody and ordering goblin/gremlin-like minions to kill things, this is a game best picked up.  Though if you can find this game, it's DLC and the second game on sale in the Overlord Complete Pack, I'd suggest that even more. ;)

Most are very enjoyable. Some take a but of time to figure out the objective but that doesn't take away from their playability. This is a good but not required add-on to Overlord. If you're deciding between the two, get the Raissing Hell for the extra content.

How to properly spend money and play this game:
1. Buy the 3 month bundle or whole year subscription, it comes with a bundle of weapons and items that get you started.  All animals are unlocked, all maps are unlocked.
2. Learn how to activate missions, and complete the missions for $gM, you can buy certain items from the store using $gM.
3. Participate in competitions, 1st place = 75 $eM, 2nd place = 50 $eM, 3rd = 25 $eM.  Some competitions have higher prizes up to 150 $eM.
4. use $gM and $eM you earned to buy more weapons, clothes, or whatever.
In the end you only spent between $10 to $40, for a high quality hunting game.  Whereas if you don't know how to spend money, you will spend more than $100 to get started.
Also please don't write reviews for games if you only played for like 5 minutes.  It makes you look like a chimpanzee trying to tell humans how to build a pyramid.  (P.S. my record shows 0 hours because I just added the game to steam recently, I have 300-400 hours in the actual game account).
My review conclusion: I do recommend this game.  You will have more fun figuring out how to play it properly rather than expecting to have the fun handed to you.

I highly reccomend buying a membership (you dont have to buy the bundle if its too expensive) and buy em$ for items in the store. You can wait for items to go on sale or get them right away. For begginers I reccomend the snakebite bow, the .300 rifle, and at least one treestand or blind. Maybe some callers if you have a hard time finding animals. Camo is optional but reccomended if you do alot of hunting outside blinds or stands. As long as you have the weapons, you could even use other peoples setups on Multiplayer.
TLDR; Try the game as a guest, if you like the gameplay get a membership and buy EM$. Get a bow and a good rifle, rest is up to you. This is a game where you need to stalk and call your prey in, dont expect to just see animals everywhere if you run around and shoot guns. Overall I highly reccomend this game.

This game is like someone threw Monty Python, Tower Defence, and Marble Madness in a blender, turned it on high for a few minutes, arranged it into a delicious dessert, and sprinkled some history on top for flavor enhancement. Honestly, how can you go wrong with a game in which you control a gigantic boulder (of varying shapes and sizes - I must say the fist is my favorite), and use it to shatter your opponent's gate? Even better, you get to squash their defenseless, flailing forms immediately afterwards to an immensely satisfying whoopie cushion sound.
If that is not enough to satisfy, there are also trained war bovines, elephants, and mammoths for you to use and abuse in the defense of your fortress. There are also elephant-launching airships..  If you are like me, you may derive much more pleasure from their strategic placement to troll your enemies, whether they be human players (yes, this game has online multiplayer) or historical figureheads.
Highly Recommend for some hard core laughter.

I was a little reluctant to buy this as I can play Pandemic 2 for free as an online Flash game, but I'm glad I DID buy it!  Although it's Early Access, the main single-player campaign is fully playable and I've encountered no serious bugs at all (multiplayer and new single-player missions are now being worked on for later addition).  The game has taken care of all the irritations of the online Pandemic (where Madagascar would slam shut its borders as soon as anyone merely stubbed their toe, meaning game over), diseases can cross borders via birds and insects even when border controls are closed and there are more factors to meddle with in the hope of being evil and spreading your new disease before anyone has chance to notice and work on a cure.  Additionally, successful completions of the game unlock new bonus traits you can collect and use to develop your own mutations and improve your chances of winning.
The developers have made an excellent job of the game and I'm glad they brought it from app to PC.

Before I start my review of this product, I would like to mention that this is one of my first gaming experiences on the PC and this game has won me over. At the time of reviewing this, I have put in 90 or so minutes into the game so you could consider this a first impressions review.
Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition is a revamp of Sleeping Dogs with improved graphics. Wei Shen finds himself at ends when he gets in too deep with the gangs of Hong Kong as you work undercover for the police to infiltrate the Sun On Yee gang.
Rating/Topic
Let's start at the graphics, which is a selling point for the definitive edition. The game looks amazing and the city of Hong Kong has a feeling of immersion like nothing I have played before. The graphics are great and they do live up to the marketing of the definitive edition. Overall, this department is solid.
My second topic is the controls for keyboard and mouse. I really am not a fan of them, but I don't like KB&M for most third person games either. I guess they are okay if you are good with a keyboard and mouse in third person games, but I found it to be a much better experience on the Xbox One controller. The game recognized the controller immediately and I was very satisfied without needing to change any of the default controls. The KB&M controls aren't as stellar as the graphics, but they are decent. I recommend a controller to get the best experience for this game.

The storyline is a modern masterpiece. I have played only 90 minutes, yet I can say that the story has excellent pacing and makes you think about your actions. I went in playing the game like GTA, but every car you steal and every rival thug you beat up alters your opinion and immerses you into the game like nothing I have experienced. I can't emphasize how enjoyable it is to play this game. After a session of gaming, I sit back as if I am Wei Sheng and contemplate my actions like the game is real life. Overall, the story is amazing and is a huge selling point of this game.
The combat is simple enough for me as someone who does not play fighting games, I found the combat sequences to be at a good middle ground for difficulty. The camera shakes as you slam someone against the wall and you can feel each hit you put on your opponent. The AI is great and thugs will be less likely to attack you when you push one of their face's into a fan or smash someone against a telephone booth. This game is great at immersing you into every aspect of the game. In all, the combat is just as solid as the graphics and storyline.
+ The soundtrack fits the theme very well
+ Traffic and NPC's are very realistic, a must for a game set in one of the biggest cities in the world
- Driving feels a bit clunky
+/- Little to no gun combat, which could be a plus or minus depending on how you feel
+ Definitive Edition includes all DLC's
+/- Okay optimization, got a stable 60 FPS on high @ 1920x1080 on an OEM GTX 760, which gets 4-5 frames per second lower than a normal 760. Quick pro tip here, running this game on the Extreme preset enabled will turn on high SSAA & FXAA, which will eat up your FPS without providing much visual difference. Best to use a custom preset and switch to high FXAA and medium SSAA.
Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition lives up to it's claim of improved graphics and delivers a very enjoyable gaming experience, but the keyboard and mouse experience is not the best. I recommend a controller, and be weary that the Extreme graphic preset enables high super sampling anti-aliasing which will eat up FPS, I recommend using a custom setup and use medium SSAA and high FXAA if you have a mid-tier graphics card such as the 270X or 760.
I would happily recommend this to anyone who has enjoyed games such as GTA, Assassin's Creed, Watch Dogs or any of the Batman games. It isn't the most recent title, but the definitive edition includes all the DLC's and the updated graphics are on par with 2014 releases. My overall rating for this game is a very sold 9/10.

is a frenzied, artistic action game that, though it is marred by slight technical difficulties, still provides an enjoyable alternative to the standard action-sandbox.
' greatest strength comes from its presentation. The developers implemented the game's open-world replica of Hong Kong painstakingly with striking visuals and smartly interconnected layouts, which help the player see this beautifully-realized city from all angles. The characters' presentations are also done in an effective manner. The effort put into the story of the main character especially pays off, as gamers can easily identify with the upbringing and struggles that drive development of protagonist Wei Shen as he searches to define himself between connections with the Hong Kong Police and the gang Sun On Yee. Wei is joined by a cast of secondary characters that would generally fall into the category of "stereotypical", but fortunately most have some extraordinary developments or twists that keep them from becoming stale or predictable.
Comparisons between
and the
series are commonplace. However, such claims made in an attempt to denigrate
is, at best, ignorant. Martial arts motifs play a significant role in the design of the gameplay here, composing the greatest difference between this and GTA. The player lacks the GTA-standard arsenal of weapons to carry around as combat is largely focused on hand-to-hand combat. Though some later levels heavily feature guns, players will largely find themseleves using combos and counters to dispatch foes. Other mechanics, ranging from a unique on-the-road hijack system to genre-standard slow-motion sequences further reinforce the kung-fu movie feel that the game is going for.
suffers from an array of technical malfunctions and limitations. The game in general works appropriately (no issues with rendering or framerate), though on rare occasion it crashed with no warning. Because the game generates cutscenes and scripted actions in the real game environment (i.e. instead of cutscenes being full video, the background of the scene is a continuation of what is going on with NPCs in the open world), unintended consequences often result. These consequences range from the hilarious (two characters showing indifference after being run over during a cutscene) to the catastrophic (being stuck behind an invisible wall after a scripted event, requiring reset). Getting stuck is moreso an issue with platforming in this game, as it attempts to emulate
's parkour system, only to provide an unrefined version, leaving many instances of floating above objets or glitching around walls where one shouldn't be. Finally, the overreliance on the counter mechanism during combat makes it difficult to fight off groups of enemies as the game cannot handle many targets to counter at once. This proves especially troublesome during the beginning of the game, when Wei is too weak to take most attacks and must abuse the counter, leading to some unfair situations. This becomes less of an issue as he grows stronger in the game.
In spite of this variety of issues the game faces, it was never enough to outweigh the positive experience that playing this game provided. It offers a lengthy primary campaign, bolstered by sidequests, completion goals and simple-yet-fun minigames. The
provides a significant amount of bonus missions and accessories to effectively bolster the length of the game after beating the main game. Additionally, it provides two scenarios seperate from the main game to play, which are both worthwhile in their own right. Though the final result of the game faced faulty implementation due to what the game was trying to accomplish, it still succeeds in providing a more visually-enthralling, narrative driven experience than is normal for action sandbox titles, and is a worthy game in any collection.

Overlord has you take the role of the almighty Overlord, an evil presence who is set to rule over the land.
You begin the game, a newly awakened dark force – tasked with rebuilding your dark tower. You raise an army of minions, terrorize the local population and craft your own armour and weapons. You can even customize your dark tower, which is a nice touch. The narrative and environment are very reminiscent of Middle-Earth, in the sense of a twisted parody where you play as Sauron. The setting is very light-hearted and comical, despite playing the villain in a Tolkien-esque world. The graphics aren’t exactly stellar and there are issues with pop-in, but it does a nice job of portraying the theme of the overall experience. It’s similar to World of Warcraft’s style of softly lit and stylized environments and characters.
Although you are a dark and powerful Overlord, you start off fairly weak, which is where your minions come in. Like Pikmin, you need to gather a force of followers who can aid you in your quest. You need a certain amount of minions to perform specific tasks for you - such as moving obstacles, pulling levers and of course, combat. They can also access smaller areas otherwise inaccessible, revealing secrets and other goodies. There are also various colours which specialize further. Brown minions, for example, are your standard fighting force, whilst red minions are your ranged attackers; greens are your stealth attackers and blues are your healers.
Overlord plays like a very old game; now, I do not mean this in a negative sense – not dated or “retro” – I’m referring more to the game design and ideology. Although there is a main thread to follow, you’re not held by the hand from point A to point B, you are encouraged to explore and find things for yourself. The world is rather large and full of secrets and puzzles, which need actual work and thoughtfulness to find. It makes a very refreshing experience compared to more modern games full of set pieces and elaborately staged corridors.
The controls are very well done, both with keyboard & mouse and a controller; although camera control is limited with a controller. You control your Overlord as you would expect, attacking and using magic but you can also control your minions directly as a horde, allowing finer control, such as sweeping them through inaccessible areas. You are also able to set guard points, sending your minions to station there until you recall them; this allows you to set your fire throwing reds at the back, set up an ambush with the greens etc. It’s nice how much control you have.
The game lasted me roughly 25 hours, which felt very well paced. Some games feel too long, others too short. This game fits neither of these categories.
I highly recommend this game, as I thoroughly enjoyed my experience with it.

I'm not sure why I'd even bother to write a review for this one, because you already know if you want it. Either you're intrigued by the concept, curious just how they can manage to make such a boring idea into compelling action, or you're instantly repelled by the premise, and rightfully so. This is about as indie as indie games get, and also as brilliant as they get. It takes such a simple thing, and wraps it up in politics, real-world parallels, and perhaps even some genuine feels to make you feel more invested in the fate of a fictional immigration officer than you ever would about a generic grimacing action hero.
But drama and intelligence aside, it's also surprisingly fun, with a very smooth difficulty curve that makes you feel your own skills improving just enough to meet the game's increasing demands. It even comes with some bonus high score modes that you could conceivably see yourself playing. It tells an interesting, branching story through simple means while also somehow managing to make boring real life work into entertainment I want more of. This is pretty much the epitome of why I love the indie game market despite all its warts.

There's really nothing here that qualifies as horror, a game, or even a story, really, despite the tags and description.
I don't know what standards other reviewers have, but the atmosphere is lacking. Graphics aside, the sound bytes are okay at best, but the "suspense" is artificially created by making walking almost painfully slow. On top of that, the constant backtracking to the single puzzle solving device reminds you constantly that you are not part of a fluid narrative.
After reading one of two of the first ntoes and hearing one of the occasional sound byes, the message is clear. There's no real surprises to be found. To be fair, the final reveal isn't exactly obvious, but it is ultimately pointless, as it adds nothing to the experience.
The subject matter is dark, but the notes are written with such a heavy handed amorrality that even Ayn Rand wouldn't take it seriously. It loses the sense of humanity that would make it truly disturbing. It's as subtle as being hit in the face with a ham and about as interesting.
The game feels like the creator's sole intent is to delight in his ability to hint at dark things. Big deal. There are writers out there who could take this premise and write something truly gut wrenching. This? This is nothing.
To call Fingerbones an "interactive story" is a cop-out. It's half of a short story artificially extended with slow movement and backtracking.
It's free, so at least it only cost me some time.

Beautiful, inspired game... bitter sweet and just the right length

Weird.
Okay, so the plot and the game exist in two different universes, apparently.
There's some weird logic about the city being taken over by machines, and it's never really explained why it was a good idea or where that idea evolved from. Maybe it's somewhere in the screeds of text you can optionally-read.
Sometimes I think Supergiant subscribe to the anime school of plot design, where you hide behind a mask of "it's zen" and "ooh spooky" to obscure your complete lack of story-telling ability - or plotholes.
No concrete world is provided, leaving the game feeling both emotionally and cognitively ungrounded.
Which is bad, because, for the first 30 minutes of gameplay I had no idea why I should be playing this game. Because that's how long it takes for the number of attack options and combinations to reach a point where they're fascinating, and by that time you've mastered the game mechanics, which're poorly spelled-out (there is, for example, no indicator that your health bar is what it is - you have to work that out through visual observation over time).
By the end of the game you realise Oh, that's what I was fighting for. But by that point...
There's an anime director who got asked a question "why are there all these deep motifs in anime" at a local convention. He answered, "because that sells". I kind of feel like Supergiant did that here, leaning a bit too heavily on the "it's spooky because you don't know" without going into specifics.
Feeling ungrounded is only spooky if it comes from a juxtaposition of feeling grounded in *something* in the first place.
But, the gameplay, is great. It's a disappointment that you never get to fight the major "uber-process" that you catch fleeting glimpses of - felt like a bit of a tease on Super's part - and the end boss was stupidly easy, once you put together a decent combo.
But the rest of it is worth it.
The graphics, yes, they're great. There's a lot of polish on the gameplay itself, which the company clearly spent a lot of time on. It's a mechanic that normally doesn't grab me - turn-based combat - but it works here.
The music? Yes, good, though I don't quite get the love that others have for it. It was also very ambient, and emotionless.
One final note, and that is that shoehorning in a new-game-plus mode into a heavily (albiet ambient and amorphous) story-oriented game and launching into that immediately after it's finished is very akin to a TV channel playing an advertisement for next week's show just as the credits roll. It's disorientating, and it completely negates the feeling of a completed story. That's not what you want. It works in more lightweight games, but I believe it was a mistake here to dwell on it. A minor but crucial moment.

As someone who went into the game without doing any research except reading the "Overwhelmingly Positive" consensus by other reviews, I was pleasantly surprised by what I found. I hadn't played Bastion and I'm not the biggest RPG fan, but turn-based combat fascinates me, and Transistor introduced a refreshing twist to this style of gameplay.
Transistor is an action RPG whose combat involves a mix of RTS and turn-based fighting. You can choose to play the game straight and try to defeat all the enemies without a chance to stop and think, or you can press the spacebar to plan a "Turn()", which effectively pauses the game and gives you time to strategize. During your turn, you have the opportunity to move around the battlefield and use your abilities to blast enemies apart. Between battles, you use "Access Points" to customize your active and passive abilities and limiters. Only four active abilities can be equipped at a time, but the game allows the player to combine abilities to strengthen them. Limiters are unlocked as you progress, and are used to make the game harder, with the benefit of leveling up faster. Progression through the game is extremely linear, but the ability combinations and limiters can be used to fight the way you want, the principle on which the gameplay seems to be based.
Disclaimer: I'm not going into details (read other reviews for those).
The story is well-written, the characters are kept to a minimum, the dialogue even feels right... essentially, it's kept to a level that's not too hard to understand. Replaying the game will give you a better grasp of everything if you didn't understand the first time. Unfortunately, the game is rather short and doesn't allow itself much time for fleshing out the characters we know; even character bios aren't exactly 100% satisfying (although they are intruiging as good short reads). I'd have liked to understood the main characters better, but I'm not complaining with what I have.
10/10 in this department, as everyone else agrees. It's hard to find a game that looks and sounds as beautiful as Transistor. The art style is consistently fitting and amazing throughout the game's few-hour stay. Darren Korb did a spectactular job on the soundtrack and the voice acting is great (as well as Red's singing). I really can't find a fault with this aspect of the game.

First and foremost, I want to start by saying that it's okay to dislike things about classic games, it's okay to not like them and it's okay to pull them up on things that just plain suck. I'm going to be writing a completely honest review from my point of view and honestly, BloodRayne isn't at all a bad game, but that doesn't mean it's directly good or flawless.
Now, onto the review!
: Developed by Terminal Reality and published by Majesco, BloodRayne was originally released on the  PlayStation 2, Xbox and GameCube in 2002, only being ported over to PC a year later. BloodRayne is an action hack and slash video game and the first game in the series that goes to follow the storyline that inspired a series of films and self-contained comic books.
: The game begins in 1933, in a place where people seem to believe in vampires, in Mortton, Louisiana, as Rayne's first mission with the Brimstone Society, along with Mynce, her mentor. They are sent there to investigate an outbreak of an unidentified disease in the area.
Brimstone Society-a top secret fraternity that hunts down and destroys supernatural threats; are here to recruit Rayne. However, the other member does not want a Dhampir with the Brimstone society, regardless of the fact that she is only half-vampire and has fewer weaknesses, as the Society is trying to rid the world of Vampires (and presumably people with Vampire blood in them). Eventually they agree to recruit Rayne, and leave her a necklace with their symbol on it (Hence the BloodRayne game symbol).
Rayne must face off against Juergen Wulf, the leader of Gegengheist Gruppe (Counter-Ghost Group, abbreviated G.G.G.), which aims to bring Hitler into power through the use of occult artifacts, including reassembling the remains of Beliar.
: Honestly, it's utterly rubbish, and to get to this initially if you're running an operating system higher than windows 98, you will need to play around with game files. Which in of itself is annoying and finicky enough.
Control menus, option menus? Nah, you don't need an easy way to find these, not only that, but it's really clunky all around - even for the time, it's rather crappy.
: Pretty decent for the time, also a bit blocky compared to others released the same year but still quite enjoyable.
: I'll start with the things that I really enjoyed, what stands out the most to me are the enemies. Like Doom, it has unique designs and ideas for its enemies, something that wasn't common at the time and it's wonderful.
Along with them being quite a challenge, the fact that weapons and ammo are so scarce really make the importance of not wasting it prominent. Topped with the unusual mechanics of BloodRyane it allows it to pull some pretty decent stunts like having a survivor behind mountains of stuff in hiding - Making Rayne have to dive through a cracked wall and bust them out to safety.
Now, considering that you spend most of your time going from one place to another, killing one thing after another and going to another place to kill another thing.. You need to make killing, story and levels engaging enough for this to keep the player entertained, and while I do enjoy it a lot of the time, both level design and killing fall flat in doing so.
Levels felt recycled, empty and too spaced out even later on in the game. Animations and killing as well. The first few kills are incredibly satisfying but after about half an hour, it already looses its appeal with its un-changing nature and don't even get me started on voice acting/sound effects such as draining blood.
Actually, now that I mention it, we might as well touch on voices and sounds. Now while the sassy one-liners spat from our heroine are actually quite entertaining, it's generally voiced in such a monotone way and it's fairly disappointing to say the least because it could be so much more.
Basic biological creatures have literally one sound when draining them, and so does Rayne, which to be frank it sounds like they hired a porn star just for that part of the voice acting - Not that it is entirely a bad thing, but some variations would have been nice.
: Crunch time. It's either a love or a hate. Now, I love me a good hack and slash, but this is so poorly done. Between reused animations, voice clips and the utterly uninspired surroundings, it's really a let down for what the game has to fully offer. It kind of shrouds over how good it -could- be.
Shinobi released in 2002 was an example of a much better made Hack and slash.
Considering it's a PC port and has been added to steam, one would think and hope that it would be optimised to run semi-efficiently on a modern computer, but not only has it not being integrated with steam, it cannot cope on newer operating systems and even as a hoarder/collector of trading cards, the fact they were added before making it playable for steam users and windows 7(and up) users is completely ridiculous.
So, in it's present condition, I can't recommend it, not on steam anyway - Honestly it's best to just go buy it off GOG(Good Old Games, for those that aren't aware of this wonderful place) as they have at least optimised it to run better on modern machines.

A solid Western aesthetic, coupled with a graphic novel look to many of the cut scenes, creates a game that initially draws you into the storyline quite successfully. But once you are over the look and feel of the game, you are left with an extremely simplistic shooter that only provides a handful of weapon choices and some rather straightforward enemies with little in the way of tactical ability beyond a shoot - duck for cover - shoot scenario. Playing on Normal difficuly, as someone who almost never plays FPS games I still found it to be quite easy.
An added dimension is brought to the gunplay through the "Concentration" mechanic, essentially a few seconds of slow motion allowing you to target multiple enemies, and the "Sense of Death", which lets you sometimes "feel" the moment a shot might kill you. In those situations you are given a 50-50 chance to avoid the oncoming bullet, also in slow motion. A few RPG elements have been added, allowing you to customise (I use the term loosely) your game experience around the style of shooter you want to play - short range six gun (or two pistols) ; long range ; and close combat. The handful of options available for each "class" are really quite generic and do not allow for more than being able to carry extra ammo or providing the ability to zoom in further with your sights.
However, the most intriguing part of the game is its "Duel" system, which puts you in a quickdraw style shootout against a fellow gunslinger (in the tradition typical of the film Western). In the "Duel", the simple controls are definitely a positive because it leaves you feeling less like a gamer, and more like someone actually participating in a gunfight at High Noon because everything comes down to your aim, character's hand positioning, and your own reflexes. Unfortunately, in the Story Mode, you only really see one of these Duels in each game stage, and so it seems as though more could have been made of it.  Ultimately, after about an hour of gameplay I was already tired of Gunslinger, and so I cannot recommend it.

What can I say? Sure its short, but the story is great, the voice acting is amazing, the gameplay is fun, and the style of graphics they use suits the grittyness of the game well. Its a first-person shooter with QTE's thrown in, but the game also lets you add skill points here and there that unlock things like faster reloading, or more focus when doing bullet time aiming. Personally I think this game is a hidden gem, and is worth taking a look at  if youre wanting some serious gunslinging.

A game that requires you to teleport from one area to another to talk to an NPC and deliver an item. 100 hours later, still only halfway through the story. If you are interested in playing with friends who have this game, you must finish out 346 main scenario quests, and 112 Heavensward quests. They are relatively simple quests with some decent dialogue, but at 458 quests, the tediousness of running from one area to another sets in. This does not include class quests, which range from another 50 to 100, and sub jobs, crafting jobs, gathering jobs, which delve out even more quests required to complete. Your level of fun-factor will be on whether you think a story-line of 500 quests is actually worth doing in order to experience that coveted "end-game content" of hunting for relics.
Thankfully there is a pretty decent matchmaking system which helps with knocking out the dungeon/leveling content. They got the mechanics down for partying really well; it's a shame a lot of the game is designed to waste your time teleporting back and forth to areas already discovered. This wouldn't be so bad if these quests were not required, but it just drags the game down when you're playing a massively open world with a highly linear storyline.

Note: My actual playtime is around 3 full weeks as of writing which isn't counted by Steam.

Okay, so I don't have the countless thousands of hours play-time like some of the FFXIV veterans in these reviews, but I can say this is without a doubt the most fun MMO experience I've had. I never knew how much fun I could have inside a Final Fantasy themed MMO. It has a very fantasy vibe, that arguably a lot of the later titles lack in.
The story-driven narrative has been what has sold me on it. It's more personal to the player as it involves only the player and his or her quest across Eorzea. Even the dungeons have some form of purpose to them within the story, and aren't just the sure-fire way of hitting the level cap faster.
The classes - Oh god, the class/job system in this game is like every altoholic's dream. Remember how in most MMO's you had to start a new character if you wanted to start a new class? This game deals with it perfectly. The idea is that you start with one class in the game (that also determines where you start), and after completing your class-specific guild quests, and progressing a short ways though the game, you are given the option to choose another class. You can level this as a secondary class which at a certain level will allow you to take up a job which is formed from a combination of two classes.
It doesnt stop there though. You are allowed to level every class in the game and every job in the game. It actually baffles me how other games haven't thought of this idea. For example, I started this game as an archer because eventually I wanted to unlock the Bard job. After a while I felt I wanted something a lot more damage heavy, turning to the Black Mage as what I wanted. After leveling the two required classes for the Black Mage, it allowed me to unlock it, and I loved how easy it was to make a switch. I feel as if it's because the game has you learn two classes first and then on becoming a Black Mage etc. You already know how to play the job because of the experience of levelling the classes.
All in all, I think that this game is one of the best of it's genre. It takes everything that was "revolutionary" about World of Warcraft in 2005 and brings it into this generation of gaming, making everything even more fluid and refined. I will admit there are signs of grinds sometimes, especially when you blindly follow the main quest without attempting any of the side quests. However, it's the sheer fact this game is so big, and has even more content with it's expansion, a number of players that is slowly climbing up to Blizzard's numbers, so, the demand is there. I can't really think of a good way to close this because I still have so much more to do in Eorzea so, I will leave you with this:
Did you know you can also play this whole game with a controller?!
10/10 would play with or without friends.

I'm blown away by this game and everything that comes with it. The visuals, audio, gameplay, writing, events, community,  and merchandise are all top-notch. It even has controller support and is cross-platform; something you nearly never see done well, especially in MMORPGs.
Every sidequest has a unique story with meaningful dialogue, and the game is full of cutscenes if you like believable worlds. For those of you who just want to get to the gameplay, everything can be skipped and viewed at another time. If you end up loving the game, there are free desktop/mobile wallpapers and ringtones; as well as tons of high quality merchandise.
There is a subscription fee to pay of course, the cheapest being £7.69/€10.99/$12.99 for 30 days. The basic subscription only allows 1 character per server, but this doesn't matter as characters are not limited in what they can learn. It is entirely possible to max out every class on one character if you have the patience.
There is nothing negative I can say about this game, it's perfect in my eyes. Download the demo and give it a shot, it might not be for everyone but it certainly does it for me.
Oh, and if you still aren't sure; go look at some game art, listen to the soundtrack and watch some gameplay. The passion of the team behind this game speaks for itself.

Now, now, where to begin with?
To put it simply, this game is like a big budget cult B-movie, if that makes any sense!
I had played it back in the day in the first Xbox and I was unsure if I would still like it, however replaying it was quite a satisfying experience, so sit back and let me explain:
--- What is good about this game:
- It contains and blends many many elements from other successful games and does that quite well, namely it has elements from:
Max Payne: graphics and eternal night atmosphere are similar, there is a slow motion mode here as well, named Dilated Perception and even the game's name has the same pun (max payne/max pain, bloodrayne/blood rain). To top it all, there's also a level where you have to escape from fires & explosions, much like in a Max Payne level!
Return to Castle Wolfenstein (and the Raiders of the Lost Ark Indiana Jones movie): the game is filled with classic power hungry Nazis who seek supernatural relics, as well as zombies, vampires and other monsters, you couldn't ask for more! You can feel the rottenness in the air everywhere! (the spiders of the initial levels even reminded me of Dead Space's necromorphs at times)
Devil May Cry: similar gameplay, where you wield both a close range sword-like weapon (dual blades in this case) and a long range type weapon, namely pistols, rifles and rocket launchers!
You also get to jump quite high, which is great, since you avoid much platforming and feel like a true vampire. In fact, Rayne's single jump is of the same length, if not a bit greater, as Dante's double jump!
- The atmosphere and music are quite good, despite their age, you have your classic zombie/vampire/third reich horror setting, where the dawn of the day is almost nonexistent. However, since it's an action game and Rayne is quite unstoppable, it's not as scary as, say, the Resident Evil or Dead Space games, where your movements are more confined (though there is a level where a horde of worm-like zombies chase you and you are weaponless and can only run, that was quite a tense and scary moment).
- The heroine of the game, Rayne, is a really hot and kickass redhead, pretty much the female half-vampire equivalent of Blade and she kills/dismembers every enemy with quite some style and as a matter of fact she also swears a lot! You'll hear the F-word and B-words (both male and female one) quite some times and towards the end she even shows the middle finger! Not even the God of War games, despite their gore and violence, have so much swearing! She also, like Max Payne, speaks many witty and cheesy lines!
Sucking Blood from various enemies is quite cool as well and as is the Blood Rage mode, which is your typical limited time Berserker/God mode, where you are almost invincible for a short period of time... and dismember every poor enemy in your way!
In a particular level you even get to drive a Mech suit, felt really cool too!
- The old fashioned cheats system the game enables you to input, where among them existed a cheat that enlarged the female characters' breasts (!) and another that showed how the main character would look like if all the weapons she carried were on her body! There's even a hidden thank you message cheat!
- Violence, decapitations, dismemberments, swearing, buckets of blood sprayed everywhere... oh, did I mention violence?
--- What is bad about this game:
- It feels too much like a true B-movie (or B-game, if you want) at times and the graphics are quite dated for our day.
- The gameplay is a bit restricted and you pretty much end up doing the same and the same after a certain point, but I cannot totally blame it, since even Max Payne (or other great 3rd person games) had quite a bit of repetitiveness, but I never saw anyone complain!
The slowmotion ability is not as good as Max Payne's however, as it's infinite and it doesn't really add superspeed to your movements, alas just the ability to see everything slower and move accordingly at your pace, but it gets too slow and boring to use most of the time.
The game's blades are also limited in their attacks (unlike the long range weapons which have some variety at least) and end up quite boring too to use (except from a stealth fatality attack which dismembers unaware enemies from behind and is quite cool, but rare).
- While Rayne is almost unstoppable (a lot thanks to being able to blood-suck dry almost any enemy, except bosses of course), in the limited occasions where you lose you have to start the whole level from the beginning, as there are no checkpoints or a free save system. That made the game quite frustrating.
- The initial swamp levels are a bit misleading about the game's entertainment factor, as I've heard of people dropping the game because of them. Just have some patience, when the Nazis enter the scene, the fun begins!
All in all, that said, I wholeheartedly recommend the game for cult B-movie lovers: it's dated, cheesy and filled with swearing and gratouitous violence, what's not to like??!

Fingerbones is a short, story-driven horror based around a social issue which isn't discussed anywhere else in videogames.
While the graphics may be simplistic, interactive objects found in the world are still obvious enough to find: The result is that they don't take focus from the narrative.
Its ‘Good design 101’, and it’s something that’s often flawed or completely missing from free to play games.
The sound direction does the job at complimenting the narrative, and at times left me with a real sense of dread (Whoah, whodathought?)
No mind-blowingly difficult puzzles to solve, but then again the focus is narrative. If the puzzles were difficult enough to pause the narrative then the game would fall flat.
Overall it’s a solid little story, complimented by some smart design choices.

As someone who played Starcraft (all 'cept for Legacy of the Void), and someone who plays Go (well sort of I mean I'm hardly above 20 kyu), and an avid lover of VNs in general this game should have been right up my alley, and it's certainly worth your time, but the ending cuts off at a, well, not at a cliffhanger but at a point where one who's read up to this point might certianly want to know what happens next for these people.
You get introduced to five pro gamers, each with their own distinct personality.  Now, I wouldn't go so far as to say they're all well-developed, but hey I for one care about them!  To end the story this quickly feels like the authors plan for a sequel locked behind a pay wall!  >:)
The tale tries to compare Starcraft 2 to Go (Baduk/Weiqi).  Perhaps that would help younger players respect that old and celebrated game, but I feel that the two games aren't similar enough for the comparison to stick...  Or maybe that's just some grumbling akin to old vs new.
Either way, stop reading this review and start reading this VN now!

One of the best games I've played so far ~

+ Impressive graphics; particularly well done are the exterior urban environments
+ Suberb voice-acting
+ Gorgeous weather effects; you can even see steam rising from the pavement after a fresh rain
+ Melee fighting mechanics are satisfying and intuitive
+ Vehicles are well-designed, of sufficient variety, and handle well; the racing missions in this game (not something I'm usually a fan of) are extremely entertaining
+ Freerunning/Parkour (whatever you want to call it) system is simple enough that it adds to the game, but doesn't come off as frustrating
+ The story is engrossing and well-written; not necessarily anything original in content, and there are no significant surprises, but it is delivered so well that you will be very invested with the characters and their relationships (the character developement, too, is very, very  well done)
+ Variety of outfit customization, including several cheeky cameos from other popular franchises
- There are lots of cookie-cutter NPC models
- Plot is linear, in that your choices will not affect the outcome
- Firearm mechanics are easily this game's weakest point; they are clunky and poorly-implemented

This was a very enjoyable game to play. I mean, let's be honest. who hasn't ever wanted to be a cowboy once or twice? The story is excellent and sticks very well to the theme of "Unreliable narrator." I also caught the star wars reference somewhere. The controls are fluid and when you die it tends to be through your own doing rather than the game's. It isn't without flaws, however. Don't get this game expecting great boss fights, as they tend to revolve around one of two formulas, either "Press Q and spam your gun" or "DYNAMITE". I beat literally every boss in the game by either using concentration to freeze him in time and empty my guns of bullets into his head, or by emptying my pockets of dynamite in his general vicinity. And the duels... Oh the duels! Ironically the only duel I got first try was the Butch Cassidy/Sundance fight at the end of the story. The controls for dueling are impossible to wrangle at times, and half the time I didn't know what I was doing. However as you only got to these towards the end of each level they aren't as bad as people make them out to be. They are a neat idea on paper, but the game would be better without. Like Despicible Me sequals. Aside from this, however, it is an excellent story-driven, almost arcade-like shooter which makes you feel like an action hero when you enter a room and within three seconds everyone is dead. I would recomend this as a neat addition to any cowboy fan's library. I just wish it was a fair bit longer, as I finished it in about four days.

This is a review for the expansion: Raising Hell. For a review of the original Overlord, please reference my steam review at
Raising Hell's storyline takes place after the events in the original Overlord. Abyss Gates are spotted in each of the lands that you have previously explored and present a twisted, more hellish version of each area. The seven sins of hell come to mind when playing through these areas. Your goal is to go to each Abyss and take control of it. You will also find moulds in these zones to create new and interesting equipment.
The unique armor and weapons added in Raising Hell present new abilities that otherwise would not be available to you; however, the new equipment is woefully underpowered. If you already have a full set of upgraded Arcanium gear, you're better off ignoring these new items.
Although the expansion adds much appreciated content to an already outstanding game, it does little to nothing to fix the flaws of the original. Trying to control your minions to solve some of the new puzzles can be frustrating. In particular, there is one puzzle that you must sweep your minions left and right to mow a lawn. Don't complete it fast enough and you have to start over. Nothing tells you that you failed due to time so you could end up like me looking it up online to figure out what I am supposed to do. This happened about two or three times for me. Guidance isn't exactly clear on some of the puzzles.
If you enjoyed the original, this game will be well worth your money. If you are unsure of buying both Raising Hell and the original Overlord in one go, do not fret. Your saved game on Steam of the original will transfer over into the Steam expansion so you can enjoy the content at your leisure.

This isn't just a good game, it's an immersive and emotionally involving game about paperwork of all things. This is currently my number one pick for proof of games as art. I've never played a game that used the actual gameplay to evoke emotions and thought. I own games that exist solely to be both fun and art, such as To the Moon and Proun, but this is the only one that uses the unique aspects of video games to tell its story and build its world.
Also, real life experience as a paper pusher makes this game a lot easier than many people suggest.

You're working in the booth one day, and you receive a note.
The note tells you that there's a serial killer in line today, and that he's killed a man's son.
That man is line behind him.
The note implores you to let this killer into the country, so that the man can find him and take revenge for his son.
Or, you can detain the killer and have him taken by the police.
However, on top of all this, you have a sick family at home. Your own son is very ill and you need money for food and medicine. You could be seriously penalized for letting EITHER of these men through if they don't have proper paperwork.
Hell, do you even know if the man will be able to CATCH this killer? What if he fails? You'll have let a murderer walk freely into the country.
You have to make a decision quickly because any time you waste means less money for your family.
This is the kind of scenario you deal with in this game. At first it feels like just the bleak observational game where you just look at paperwork and allow/deny access. But as the game goes on, you'll be presented with these moral quandries that really test you. Any decision you make, be it morally good or bad, saintly or selfish, could have a range of consequences. Which winds up making the game incredibly curious and makes you want to keep going to see what happens.

Fingerbones was one of those games that just...wasn't scary. The game's creator tried to set a unsettling atmosphere, and if it wasn't for the minecraft-grade graphics ruining it, he could've achieved that goal. However it's hard to feel unsettled by just ambient music and blocky textures. Sure, it's a free game, but to get your audience really scared, you have to have them be absorbed into the world. The graphic level of this game doesn't nearly set that world up.
Also, as for the story setting a creepy tone, have you ever watched a film, and within the first few minutes you managed to predict the rest of the whole film? By the time you read the second note on the first floor, you've already figured out what happened, which removed the creep factor because now you know what to expect.
Fingerbones was a good start, and I feel with a few more games under his belt, the creator could make something really special.

is a round based inspection game, where you play as immigration inspector.
You play as immigration inspector to earn the livelihood for your family. At the end of each round you will get your daily salary - if your daily salary is too low and your reserves are too low, then you have to option whether your family will get no food and/or no heating. Your salary will get lowered, when you do mistakes during your inspection and you let somebody past who is not authorized to cross the border. Mistakes means, that you haven't asked the immigrant why his passport says that he is female but he looks male or you haven't followed the order that immigrants from a certain country won't be past, because of threat of terrorism. You've got your twin shooters, your shotgun, a mouth full of tar and a belly full of lead that you can heal just by thinking about it. Add in a combo meter and you've got Call of Juarez: Gunslinger.
Guided by the guttural tones of your roguish and absolutely lying through his teeth protagonist
you head through a series of deliberately poorly told flashbacks as he regales his fairly captive audience with tales of how brilliant he is as he totally took down a succession of entire posses and gangs, with nary the sight of hyperbole.
The tales are all fairly simple. Silas Greaves is a simple man, he only really wants the one thing: to shoot a man dead. One man in particular, but he's not too picky.
So you head through a nice stream, barn, train, or some other Western scenery, and shoot as many ironsides in their iron-sides as humanly possible. More often than not butting heads with one of the many old West dime novel legends: the Dalton brothers, Jesse James, Billy the Kid, even Doc Holloway gets a mention. There's collectable  playing cards with their full stories and this was all a labour of love.
Shooting all those red bandana clad bandits in itself is a fairly fun affair. Now the mechanics themselves are what you'd expect: you've got your regenerating health, grenades, tactical squat, generous aim-assist and a short-ranged sprint. It's every FPS game ever.
Where it sets itself apart is that it's an arcade game in an effective disguise. You build up combos, extend them, multiply, divide, BODMAS, and use every weapon, skill and and destructible teacup and barrel of dynamite in the environment to keep it going. Never dropping it for the best points, and buying an absolutely ridiculous amount of skills that can completely change playstyles.
String headshots and reload automatically with the tap of a button with one weapon set, completely obliterate bosses or snipe out entire settlements with instant headshots with another. It's varied and it's worth messing with. Games short enough that it's not much of an investment, either.
Game knows it's got a good thing going, too, because you've got a couple of additional modes that are either entirely arcade, a good 10 maps to ravage through, or an endurance test through a bunch of the ingame and fabricated duels.
And much like the tales with which it pays homage to, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger rides off into the sunset, with nothing bad to say about it behind its back.
It's absolutely worth playing, to anyone with even the barest hint of interest in FPS games. This one has earned its reputation.

I really love this game. I'm going to be going to school for infectious diseases so I'm kind of biased when it comes to this genre but I really do believe others will find it as fun as I do. This version is a lot more complex than the free online Flash game (I'm not sure whether or not it's made by the same people though) that has the same concept. If you liked the Flash version then you'll love this. The Flash one, however, get's kind of boring once you've beaten it the first time but Plague Inc: Evolved allows you to unlock items and options that increase the depth of your gameplay. By doing this, even after you've killed all of humanity once, there is still tons left in the game for players to want to come back to. Unlike the Flash version, you won't get bored after your first time winning as there will still be so much more to expreience. Instead of giving you all the options right at the beginning like the Flash version, you actually have to work for things in Plague Inc: Evolved. So far I've played around 36 minutes, which on the Flash version would have been long enough for me to beat the entire game, but with Plague Inc: Evolved 36 minutes is only enough to expreience the very beginning. I think one of the other really important features of this game is that, although you don't need to have a high end PC to play it on its highest settings, it still looks beautiful. If this is the kind of game you're into (puzzle, statagey, infetious diseases) or you enjoyed the online Flash version then I highly recommend buying Plague Inc: Evolved... you won't be disappointed. It's well worth the $15.

Gameplay is an interesting combination of an action fighting game with the great ability to go into a freeze time tactical turn planning mode, though because of how good the Turn()-bursts are the forced real time while waiting for the Turn() to recharge can feel not as fun. Powers are handled in a pretty novel way, with each having an active effect, a upgrade to an active power effect, and a passive slot effect, thus allowing for a wide variety of combinations of how to use the many powers you unlock throughout a playthrough. The main story is about maybe 12 hours of gameplay, with some side challenge modes, and an offered "recursive" new game plus mode, to give you more time to try out all the powers you might not have had a good chance to tinker with in a first playthrough.
