Let’s start with the story. Much like in Bastion, exposition is the name of the game. You play as a silent protagonist in an empty, broken and breaking world, trying to figure out what caused all this via narration, various news terminals scattered across the city of Cloudbank, and the function details. Much like in Bastion, of the defining features is the unique narration element, with the dude trapped inside the transistor sword-thing that you carry around compensating for the protagonist's silence. Unfortunately, unlike Bastion, the narrator is boring as♥♥♥♥♥♥ and the exposition feels half-baked at best. None of Cloudbank seems captivating or remotely interesting and even if it is, you'll never be hearing it from sword guy, as most of their cheesy lines alternate between professing his love for Red for the umpteenth time, and his hatred and distraught towards the process, the Camarada, and the destruction of Cloudbank. Unlike Rucks (the narrator in Bastion), sword dude never fleshes out the world in any meaningful manner, just namedrop after namedrop of locations that never tie into the story. The most fleshing out that any location ever got in Transistor was the pizza place, with a grand total of two mentions on separate occasions, now I know that they sell flatbread. Woo. Nevertheless, while you may disagree with my saying that the narrator's lines are boring, I'll provide an objective critique: the narration is less reactive than Bastion's, and not reactive enough to be engaging.
Three-fourths into the story, you enter a room filled with enemies mulling about, upon attacking one, they all swarm you and sword dude suggests you make a quick escape. I had other plans in mind, and proceeded to wipe out all of the enemies, hoping for an interesting remark, and what happened when I cleared out all of the enemies? Nada. Zilch. Sword dude was busy thinking about the flatbread. To make matters worse, sword dude then says 'See ya, ladies' as I walk out. THERE ARE NO LADIES; I KILLED THEM ALL. This lack of reactive narration is prevalent throughout the entire experience. One of my favorited aspects of Bastion was the abundance of lines in the game and all of the minor details that the narrator would comment on, as though they were actually a real person, narrating my game in real time. In Transistor, I felt as though sword dude was just reading out generic exclamations from a script. 'Whoa, here we go, let's do this, look at that, that was rough,' seriously? Are we sure you aren't the new announcer for Forza?
I think that this all stems from the fact that Cloudbank isn't an interesting setting in the first place and is both visually and thematically homogenous. The art-style, although very polished, in no way exotic, striking or unique. None of the areas were memorable, and this feeling of 'sameness' was only strengthened by the lack of any sort of world map that was present in Bastion. I have no idea how far away Fairview is from Highrise, because I can't travel there directly due to the game's linearity; I don't know how large the areas are, because I can't explore them completely them as individual areas, the areas
very small,l because you spend less than half an hour walking through each one, and honestly, they all look the same. Even the isometric perspective that worked very well for Bastion feels cluttered in Transistor, full of very abstract buildings and objects that make for a rather jumbled landscape that all add to the unpleasant labyrinthine quality almost all of the areas have.  Cloudbank lacks culture of any kind, and where I was fascinated by both the Ura and the Caelondian in Bastion, all of their traditions, their way of life, their attitudes, none of the banal information given to you about Cloudbank is connected to anything else, it's just 'this is a pizza place, this a pool, this a storage facility.' Not once did the town ever feel magical, or sci-fi-esque, it was just a bland setting and a bustling town sans the bustle.
The story itself is rather terrible. For starter's it's much less interesting and engaging than Bastion's, due to the fact that you spend 90% of the game clueless as to what's going on, and are then bombarded with information in the last twenty or so minutes of the game. Even then, the story is extremely convoluted and poorly put together, there are numerous glaring holes in the story and many things go either unexplained and are really poorly strung together. Bastion had several minute details that were left up to the fans to decide, but not
, how did the Process originally begin? Who was it created by? Who created the Transistor? Some moments feel like a very far stretch, including the fact that a one-in-a-million chance Transistor corruption caused Red's voice to be stolen. Seriously? Although sword dude never stops reminding you that the Camarata took your voice, the game never really explains how, as though embarrassed by its half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt at justification for Red's silence. Bastion did this much better by just never bringing it up and the narrator speaking for Zia and Zulf via indirect dialogue. For all we know, the Kid may well be able to speak, he just doesn't want to, but in Transistor, sword dude just wouldn't shut up about Red shutting up. Only after reading through the Steam Story Guide did I gain
understanding of the story. Writers, if your readers need a strategy guide to understand your narrative, you’ve done something wrong.
Combat alternates between the enemies being frozen still and providing no challenge at all as you wail on them, and the inverse, where you helplessly walk around the combat zone with no shield, dodge, or retaliation method waiting for your 'freeze time' button to recharge. Two words: not fun.
Transistor's combat system isn't sure as to whether it wants to be action-y or strategy turned-based-y. It fails to do both and ends up being repetitive and frustrating. The only challenge/threat during combat is trying not to die while you helplessly walk around the map and wait for your time-freeze to recharge. Trying to use the abilities in real-time is frustrating due to the long animations, the inability to chain attacks into combos, and the clunky aiming, essentially forcing you into usage of Turn().
Then there are the bugs. Despite the fact that I finished this game almost a year after its initial release, there are STILL numerous visual glitches with the Turn() system that can force you to restart and combat encounter if you've got all the limiters turned on. Even without the glitches, I found that the Turn() tell-tales were often entirely wrong and generally useless. Attacks would be blocked when they were supposed to hit, or hit when they were supposedly blocked, trajectories on the haircuts and Load() mines were always off, seeing how much damage an AOE ability would do to every unit affected isn't possible and trying to effectively calculate damage to enemies with any chaining / splitting abilities was far beyond the Transistor's capabilities.
TL;DR:
3/10.
*You can enable these skills later on, but they're not very effective and cost memory that could better spent on increasing your offensive capabilities),

Sleeping Dogs is a nice blend of several different game genres, and while none of them are anything new or groundbreaking, everything generally played well. The original (non-definitive) version is one of the few games I have 100% completion on in my steam library.
Since you can read up on pretty much any review for the actual game, I thought I'd focus on what's new for this re-release.
The biggest improvement probably went into how the dlc was handled. Every single dlc (with the exception of the top dog booster packs) is now included, and rather than just dumping them all on you at once, they were all was integrated into the game a little better, unlocking a few pieces from each as you progress through the story. While some of the changes are minor, like a new vendor in the night market who sells some of the dlc costumes, they actually went back and tweaked a few of them to flow better. For example, the "Shaolin Showdown" side mission is no longer an endless arena where you fight until you die, but now has you running to several locations fighting smaller groups of enemies, eventually climaxing into one of the largest melee fights in the entire game. The Swat dlc missions were also changed into individual "Cop missions" that feel like they have a little more variety now and unlock over time instead of all at once. In fact, almost every mission got some sort of small tweak to it. However, Nightmare in North Point and Year of the Snake are still separate standalone stories that don't take your progress in the main story into account (though they both still unlock a few bonus items for the story when completed).
The graphics also got a bit of an upgrade, though it's not immediately obvious because the original PC game was already a big improvement over the 360/ps3 versions. Mostly, everything now has even higher-resolution textures, and there are some new effects like fog in the streets, remodeled skin and hair for most characters that looks great in cutscenes, more dense vehicle and pedestrian traffic, and some new outdoor effects. In particular, the new rain effect (and the puddles it leaves on the street) looks fantastic.
If you never played Sleeping Dogs, you really owe it to yourself to pick up this re-release, as it fixes some of the flaws of the original and includes all the dlc. However, if you already played the original and most of its dlc, you should probably skip this. Improvements and dlc aside, there is no new content (mission or story-wise) whatsoever.

I haven't written a review before and this was the game that inspired me to do so. In a lot of ways it wasn't exactly what I was expecting; it was so much more. The first time I sat down to play it the story and immersion kept me playing it for hours. I didn't want to stop for any reason; I was loath to even go to the bathroom because I thought it would ruin the experience and flow that I was feeling with the game. The game explains very little directly outright and at first I was annoyed by this. But over time I realized that working out both the combat and equipment system as well as the story myself was so much more rewarding and interesting. For me it was a perfect mix of a BioShock-like story and immersion with a very customizable Final Fantasy VII-esque equipment system and a relatively unique combat system. But the best part of this game is that none of these factors are independent. In order to uncover more of the story you need to use your abilities and limiters in different combinations and ways that you otherwise wouldn't think to. In a way you take the role of detective, being told very little but able to find out almost the whole mystery. This also opens up unique ways to play as well. I discovered an awesome CC build that I used for a while because one of the tests in the Backroom forced me to use abilities I hadn't really wanted to but I realized it allowed me to lock down most enemies for a long time.
Gameplay: 9/10
Visual and Audio: 10/10
Story: 10/10
Overall: 9.5/10
Buy it, because I want to see what else Supergiant Games can do.

BloodRayne is truely a nostalgic classic for me and I have to say, I still enjoy this title even after 12 years of my initial first playthrough. It has many flaws, but above all these, it has a swift and amusing gameplay, great heroine constantly throwing out black humor quotes and the "cutting system" (you can literally cut any imaginable little piece of body, like a quarter of face or piece of fingers. Or you can slice and dice the bad guys like a bread into a thousand of segments - what a highly sophisticated technology for such an old game! :-D ) of enemies can be really strangely satisfying.
To solve crashes, go to your Steam directory
and in the folder, right click on rayne.exe and set it's compatibility mode to Windows 98/ME. Also, be sure to check you have disabled the DPI scaling (it is in the same tab as the compatibility setting). This solved all the crashes for me and I haven't got a single crash in 4 hour playthrough.
For low resolution solution, launch the Bloodrayne first and after entering the menu, starting a new game, go through the first cutscenes and then quit the game. After that, go to your Steam directory
and in the folder, open rayne.ini - In the .ini file, search for these two gamePIXY= gamePIXX= and after the "=", type your desired resolution (for example gamePIXY=1440 gamePIXX=2560). I run the game in 2560x1440 without any problem.
And finally, to solve the sound clipping issue, install MSI Afterburner. The clipping is caused by the fact that the game is designed to run on 30 FPS max and newer computers run it on higher FPS - that is causing the problem. So you have to lock/cap your FPS to 30. To do that, install MSI Afterburner and load it. Wait until a RivaTuner icon shows in your system tray and after that, right click on it, select Show and set your FPS limit in the interface to 30 FPS. Remember to always turn Afterburner on if you want to play BloodRayne.
Hope this will help to enjoy this great classic! Cheers!

is a round based inspection game, where you play as immigration inspector.
You play as immigration inspector to earn the livelihood for your family. At the end of each round you will get your daily salary - if your daily salary is too low and your reserves are too low, then you have to option whether your family will get no food and/or no heating. Your salary will get lowered, when you do mistakes during your inspection and you let somebody past who is not authorized to cross the border. Your family will get sick and yes; they will die, when you do to much mistakes at your work. Mistakes means, that you haven't asked the immigrant why his passport says that he is female but he looks male or you haven't followed the order that immigrants from a certain country won't be past, because of threat of terrorism. After certain days and enough money you can upgrade your booth to work more efficient. Over the time there will be scripted events where you have to make moral decisions. These decisions will influence the story. The final goal is to help or to infiltrate the country you are working for - and yes; it has multiple ends! ^^

I don't usually expect much from expansion packs anymore...these days games have been victimized by lackluster 'DLC' that adds a few things that would have fit right in with the base game. Maybe a new weapon or two, or a minor quest line.
But Raising Hell is one of those rare extras that does just what it claims to do...expands the game, and it does it beautifully. It picks up right where the original game left off, and opens up a new epilogue that not only continues the story of our dastardly overlord, but does so with all the excitement and humor that was inherent in the base game. It also sets the story up for the sequel, if that matters to you.
Raising hell adds 5 unique dungeons with the supporting quests, each with their own little suprises and gimmicks. All of them are fun, though the last one could have been longer. It also adds 5 "unique" pieces of gear, each with their own special bonuses; however, they seem fairly weak compared to the end game equipment of the base game.

Funny and evil in all of the right ways, humorous voice acting and enjoyable music.
There aren't many reasons to play through Overlord twice and the multiplayer isn't too great, but there is good reason to invest your time doing everything in the single player game.

The original Overlord supplies hours of stupid, mindless fun using hordes of minions to do your bidding. The Raising Hell expansion is pretty much a full on stand-alone game which supplies even more hours of stupid, mindless fun. My biggest gripe with the game is the lack of direction. There is no mini-map or waypoints. Even a directional arrow would have been a welcome addition. Instead, most of the time, I just ended up wandering aimlessly until I found a new objective. The controller support is great for everything except camera positioning--which makes playing with one much more frustrating than it should be.
The gameplay feels original and unique over more traditional action/adventure types. The concept never gets stale, but getting lost really took a toll on my patience meter making the game much longer than it needed to be. I never thought I'd put so many hours into it, but it's just so damn fun. It's hard not to recommend.

Easy, by far, the single Best MMORPG I have played in all my 24 gamer years.
Final Fantasy XIV The Realm Reborn has it all: Graphics, Characters, Community, Story, Gameplay, Soundtrack, Feelings and Magic.
FFXIV ARR takes almost every other title of the final fantasy franchise and brings back characters, places, songs and tales of older games, adapting them into the universe of Eorzea. Nostalgia is abundant and strikes at you at every single angle possible.
The game shines in its gorgeous and well detailed ambientation, with complex landscapes, ranging from the forested marshy shrouds of Gridania, the deserted regions of Ul'dah, the coastal rocky beaches of Limsa Lominsa, and the snowy tundras of Coerthas, among many other special areas and dungeons.
With simple, yet clean and fairly realistic characters, highly detailed, unusually practical and realistic fashionable clothing and armor, the game taps into tradition and class, yet polished originality, giving it it's own feel and grace.
The gameplay, yet slow at first, speeds up and grows to a tactical complexity that can be barelly seen in other MMOs, revealing a feeling of growth that can only be compared to the best MMOs to have ever existed. With the classes and jobs being fully interchangeable in a single character, having access to the entire cast of fun just multiplies the experience many times fold. And behold, everything in this strophe applies to crafting classes as well, the best crafting ever created by the way!
Despite everything else being enough to create a game, more is required to create a RPG, and that is a universe, story, lore, and characters. FF14 brings you to a world of conflict, of post apocaliptic scale, in which its people is trying to rebuild their lives after a scorching inferno has blazed their homes and beloved ones. In an aparent peace, evil forces are working behind the scenes to ruin everything once again, and it is up to you and a special cast of characters, that will follow you through most of the story, to put a stop to it. Simple and cliche, but well done, polished and personal. The animations of cutscenes, the voiced cutscenes, the personalities, the characters... All of them will bring you into the game, feel the game, feel the world.
All it takes to for simple ingredients to become HQ master pieces.
And what else helps to create that feeling other than music? The soundtrack is fantastic, and if you have ever played any Final Fantasy game before, you will recognize at least a few of the tracks.
Adding to the MMO experience, the community has proven to be mostly extremelly polite, funny and with RPing tendencies. A grace bestowed by the subscription system and the game's warmth, for sure.
As for how this game feels... It feels like Magic. Like that first MMORPG you have played when young, when that feeling of wonderment overwhelmed your senses, when you forgot your life into a new found joyful experience.
My 200 hours in a month and 48 hours in 4 days are there to attest to that.
An outstanding experience, worth every single coin, and every single second invested on it.
I could not recommend anything else.

After the disaster that was Call of Juarez: The Cartel, I thought that this series is gone for good. It would be difficult for a game to redeem itself after a game like The Cartel. I was very surprised when they announced yet another game and this time around, they went back to the roots, with the game set in the Wild West.
Gunslinger is one of the most fun FPS games I have played. The last western FPS game I played was way back in 2005 called Outlaws. Great game, but western games never caught my attention since. Gunslinger looked very interesting, and when Humble Bundle offered this game for $1 as a part of Humble Ubisoft Bundle, there was no reason to not pick it up.
The story is told in the form of flashbacks, as recalled by the main character Silas Green during his days as a bounty hunter, to a group of patrons at a bar. This has allowed for some creative gameplay techniques, because at times, the story is questioned by the patrons, and the game rewinds as the narrative changes.As the story is told, the environment also changes in real time to reflect the details being recounted.
You get to fight against historical figures in the campaign, such as Billy the Kid etc., as Silas recalls his encounters with them. Silas does not let the truth get in the way of a good story, and it leads to some funny dialogue.
I felt the reason this game is so entertaining is because the developers did not take the story too seriously. It felt as if they wanted to create a game that was fun to play, first and foremost. It s weird weird saying that because you would think fun gameplay would the main motive behind all games, but I don't often get the impression when playing modern AAA games.
Shooting is so satisfying in this game. There are three classes of weapons, revolvers, rifles and shotguns. Based on your preference, you can pick any weapon to specialize. There is an RPG aspect to this. The selection is limited, but the shooting is excellent. I personally liked the rifle and revolvers the most. It is possible to dual wield revolvers, and its a lot of fun to dual wield in bullet time mode.
Speaking of which, bullet time works as a combination of slow motion time and x-ray vision. Using this is a lot of fun, they did not try to innovate on this too much by adding QTEs (which do exist), they kept it fairly simple, and as a result, when it is activated in a tough situation, it is very useful, while being stylish.
A note about QTEs in the game, I don't mind the way they are implemented. The game prompts the player to press a button in some situations, but it can be ignored. The game does not punish the player for not engaging in QTEs, for the most part. Ideally, I would like for them to not exist at all, but as it stands, its not as bad as Battlefield 3.
I have not used shotguns a whole lot, but when I did, they have a lot of impact, and fun to use, unlike the last game I played - Spec Ops: The Line.
Enemies range from natives to other outlaws, and the combat is always entertaining and frantic.
The developers did a fantastic job with the atmosphere. The art style has a comic book feel to it, reminds of the cel-shaded game, XIII. The intros to some of the characters are very well done, and this is one of those games where I did not mind watching the cut scenes. The visuals are beautiful. Its not all set in a desert, you travel through ghost towns, lush green forests, swamps, canyons etc. The level design is beautiful. For the most part every chapter has its own setting, and they are expertly created.
Audio deserves a special mention here. Voice acting, music, gunshots, and  atmospheric sounds are excellent. The term immersion is overused in gaming media, but that perfectly describes the audio. It captures the Wild West theme perfectly and adds to the immersion.
However, all is not perfect with the game. There is one aspect I did not enjoy, and that is the duels. The mechanics are vague, and although the game does try to educate the player on how the system works, I still had trouble getting used to it. The part that I hated the most about the duels is how the reticle does not obey player input. It feels as if the input lag is increased, and the dip is decreased. I found this system to be very irritating and unnecessary. I hope they scrap this feature in future titles.

Yes, this is a game your should purchase if you like point-and-click puzzlers in the "Myst" vein.
The situation?  In the middle of a room is a giant puzzle box.  Your mission is to figure out all of the puzzles as you work from the outside in.  Image that as you choose one "layer" of puzzles that layer strips away to reveal yet another "layer" of puzzles on the box.
The game is well made, the graphics are very good, and it is, without question, worth the time that you spend.
An intriguing part of the game -- because you are only dealing with the box, chances are that you won't miss any key elements or pieces in the environment.  This is always something that I get frustrated with in a point-and-click puzzler -- if you don't pay close enough attention to the pixels you miss something.  There are no other rooms and there are no other puzzles except the box.  Therefore, you can't miss much.
However, that being said, being limited only to the box this makes the puzzles somewhat easier to solve.  The puzzles are straightforward, requre only a modicum of intellectual effort, and aren't very complex.
All in all, I solved this game quickly -- about five hours.  That's a good Sunday afternoon for me -- as a casual gamer I have to take my time when I can get it.  For five dollars, this game is an excellent distraction.  From a behavioral standpoint, you have to put in about the right amount of effort for a reward.  This keeps the player intrigued in the puzzles without losing momentum and becoming frustrated.
Would I buy it again?  Yes.  As with all point-and-click puzzles, the replay value is low.  I can still, for example, remember the solution to Infocom games that I played thirty + years ago.  But it is interesting, you will enjoy it, and for a while you will embrace the escape from your career, your family, your life, and soul-crushing student loan debt.
Buy it, yes.

No no. No no no no. No. No no. No no no no no. No no no no no no no no no, no no no. No no no no. No no.
No.
This game isn't good any way you try to spin it. Even the ol' "for its time" argument simply doesn't hold water. Even at a $1.99 price point, it's just not worth taking the risk of seeing if it'll even run on your system (which from what I've gathered from the forums is a crap-shoot.)
BloodRayne simply offers no gameplay worth engaging with. At all. Everything about this game boils down to, "Flail around and hope things happen." Your melee attacks have no sense of impact and you're never quite sure you're actually hitting things or not.  There's no way to actually stick to a target either, so you're quite literally flailing at enemies and seeing if things worked or not. It's about as effective as MMO combat. You have very little, if any control over ranged combat. Rayne just kinda runs around holding guns, aiming them every which way and shooting, and from my experience in the game's Normal mode, even if shots do connect, it can take as many as 4-5 shotgun blasts (and even more rounds from smaller arms) to actually drop an enemy...that is if she's actually aiming properly.
The platforming is also smooshy and unresponsive. Rayne is supposed to lock herself onto small catwalks or power lines and "tightrope" across them, but more often than not, you'll miss those jumps or she'll "animation" through them for some reason and fall through.
Even as a curiosity, just don't! This isn't a "so bad it's good," like a lot of games can be. This is just bad, broken, not funn, boring bad.

SC2VN is a light visual novel that follows your fictitious character “Mach” and his/her experience moving to Korea in an attempt to hit it big in the Star Craft 2 esports scene. From the beginning of the novel Mach is seen battling with her recent loss in a tournament qualifier and second thoughts about moving to Korea.
Obviously there are two barriers to entry: knowledge of Korean terms and knowledge of Star Craft/esports terms. Thankfully the game has you covered on both fronts. A glossary unlocks as you read that defines advanced terminology. Additionally there is also a short introduction to what Star Craft 2 is, narrated by one of the best casters Sean “Day[9]” Plott”.
Being experienced with video games and esports the glossary was not more than a handy reminder. It will definitely be useful to the uninitiated. Though, even I found some Korean terms, not contained in the glossary, that I did not know.
This isn’t just a text document with attractive art and effects (there are some entertaining though minor effects)—there are some choices to be made. Do you choose to make an aggressive maneuver or defensive? Do you ask a character an emotional question? The options are entertaining, but happen so occasionally it left me wanting.
Overall, it’s an entertaining visual novel that had me itching to continue the story whenever I put it down. More than that, it has me wanting to get back to playing Star Craft 2 despite my horrid performance.
If you’re new to visual novels, this is an excellent place to start.
If you’re unaware of esports, this is a great place to learn.
If you’re unknowledgeable of Star Craft (2), this is a great place to pick it up.

Sleeping Dogs is an open world 3rd person game set in Hong Kong. You play as Wei Shen an undercover cop trying to take the Triads out from within.
Gameplay:
The gameplay you could say is a lot like Grand Theft Auto and Saints Row. One of the big differences is Sleeping Dogs relies more on hand to hand combat than gunplay. The game flows really well and the combat is really good. Fighting is a lot of fun with the many different combos you pick up along the way.
The gunplay is also a lot of fun with different weapons. The gunplay is also very well made and flows much better in Sleeping Dogs than in GTA, GTA can be clunky at times but this doesn’t happen in Sleeping Dogs.

Parkour is also a very fun thing in Sleeping Dogs. Running through the market and leaping in-between buildings is a lot of fun.  Although this is a lot of fun, you don’t seem to parkour that often. Shooting can also be combined with parkour when you vault over an object and aim at an enemy the time will slow down for a bit, this is also the same in cars.
Cars can be hard to drive. The camera angle will sometimes switch to a stupid angle and this can cause you to crash.  Except from that the driving is fun, especially in a chase.
Graphics:
The graphics are really good in the Definitive Edition. Hong Kong is a really busy city and it shows. A lot of the locations are gritty and run down. When it rains it makes the city look even better and the rain and water looks really good.
Story:
Sleeping Dogs in my opinion has a very well done story. It shows how Wei Shen is struggling not to get attached to anyone in the Triads and be a police officer. I will not speak any more about the story since I don’t want to spoil it.

Glee is the word that comes to mind when I think of this game. Two words would be "gleefully mischievous." Imps and goblins usually annoy me - like the sidekick in The Darkness II - but these little fellows manage to be endearing.
Anyway, this game has its tongue firmly pressed to its cheek, in a good way.
It parodies LOTR - except you are playing as pseudo-Sauron, sweeping your minions across halfling villages and elven forests with an evil grin on your face.
You (the Overlord) are slow and lumbering, but your minions - whom you can guide with an invisible hand or more precisely assign tasks to - are fast and fluid.
It's sort of open world - open enough to let you revisit previous (respawning) locations to replenish your gold and Souls.
Negatives: Lots of backtracking. No way to sprint or speed up your Overlord character. And no mini-map of any kind. These three problems are a big no-no in an open world game.
Still, I'm early in the game and I am really enjoying it.

Easy, by far, the single Best MMORPG I have played in all my 24 gamer years.
Final Fantasy XIV The Realm Reborn has it all: Graphics, Characters, Community, Story, Gameplay, Soundtrack, Feelings and Magic.
FFXIV ARR takes almost every other title of the final fantasy franchise and brings back characters, places, songs and tales of older games, adapting them into the universe of Eorzea. Nostalgia is abundant and strikes at you at every single angle possible.
The game shines in its gorgeous and well detailed ambientation, with complex landscapes, ranging from the forested marshy shrouds of Gridania, the deserted regions of Ul'dah, the coastal rocky beaches of Limsa Lominsa, and the snowy tundras of Coerthas, among many other special areas and dungeons.
With simple, yet clean and fairly realistic characters, highly detailed, unusually practical and realistic fashionable clothing and armor, the game taps into tradition and class, yet polished originality, giving it it's own feel and grace.
The gameplay, yet slow at first, speeds up and grows to a tactical complexity that can be barelly seen in other MMOs, revealing a feeling of growth that can only be compared to the best MMOs to have ever existed. With the classes and jobs being fully interchangeable in a single character, having access to the entire cast of fun just multiplies the experience many times fold. And behold, everything in this strophe applies to crafting classes as well, the best crafting ever created by the way!
Despite everything else being enough to create a game, more is required to create a RPG, and that is a universe, story, lore, and characters. FF14 brings you to a world of conflict, of post apocaliptic scale, in which its people is trying to rebuild their lives after a scorching inferno has blazed their homes and beloved ones. In an aparent peace, evil forces are working behind the scenes to ruin everything once again, and it is up to you and a special cast of characters, that will follow you through most of the story, to put a stop to it. Simple and cliche, but well done, polished and personal. The animations of cutscenes, the voiced cutscenes, the personalities, the characters... All of them will bring you into the game, feel the game, feel the world.
All it takes to for simple ingredients to become HQ master pieces.
And what else helps to create that feeling other than music? The soundtrack is fantastic, and if you have ever played any Final Fantasy game before, you will recognize at least a few of the tracks.
Adding to the MMO experience, the community has proven to be mostly extremelly polite, funny and with RPing tendencies. A grace bestowed by the subscription system and the game's warmth, for sure.
As for how this game feels... It feels like Magic. Like that first MMORPG you have played when young, when that feeling of wonderment overwhelmed your senses, when you forgot your life into a new found joyful experience.
My 200 hours in a month and 48 hours in 4 days are there to attest to that.
An outstanding experience, worth every single coin, and every single second invested on it.
I could not recommend anything else.

The main balance complain seems to be over the katanas, but as of now, there have been plenty of counters and a variety of loadouts that have been able to take on katana users no sweat.  The simplest solution is to backpedal and shoot.  You can also craft armors that give you melee defense, higher speed, or higher jump to easily avoid katana users.  As for ambushes? Well, that's kinda what they are good at, so watch your back!

The most unique and quirky game I've ever played, and likely ever made.
Made by a team in my home country (Go Chile!), Rock of Ages is an odd hybrid between a bowling racer and tower defense. The game is a sort of duel between you and an opponent (either human or AI-controlled) in which you each throw boulders down a track toward your doors. Between rolls, money you earned from rolling your boulder can be spent on tower-like constructions to slow down, weaken and hopefully destroy your opponents boulder.
The game features a huge amount of very fun maps, to the point of which it could've been a full game without the tower defense aspect. The humor is, as said by others, Monty Python-esque, with 2D paper-like animations for characters. The campaign takes you through much of history, with plenty of genuinely funny cutscenes!
This is honestly a game I cannot recommend highly enough. It's quirky, sure, but the humor alone is worth the $10. Good luck, and first downhill wins!

Rolling giant boulders downhill smashing all that stands in their way ought to be immensely fun. Somehow, it isn't here. They've done this weird vs. approach where you and an opponent throw boulders down the slope at each other's gates, first one smashed loses, and that's good enough for an arcade game. Along the way you smash dwellings, inhabitants, and similar bric-a-brac to get money, which buys you fortifications you can use to defend your gates against your opponent's rock.
Problem is, the fortifications don't actually do much of anything to deter an incoming boulder—maybe they would if you had time to lay out defenses strategically, but because everything takes place in real time you're never given the chance to build your defenses with any kind of deliberation. So with the vast majority of the game's mechanics going un- or underused, it becomes a mad rush to launch your boulder first. Which quickly becomes less than interesting. It's entirely possible that the available defenses become more useful and engaging to play with in later levels, but the game doesn't hold my interest long enough to get at them.
Which is really too bad. The art and sound design are unreservedly fantastic, with this great whimsical Terry Gilliam Python-era animation thing happening. I just wish the game was as much fun to play as it is to look at.
If you haven't done it yet, play this game.

Let me summarize by saying  I love ADOM but am not sure if it's for you, I 'll explain. No game has ever had me fist pump, yell with glee, scream in terror, or pout with discouragement as this game. That's what makes it great, it's a game that inspires very strong emotions, and that's why I love it. Upsides are there are tons of artifacts I've only seen once then never again, or not at all, making exploration very exciting, you never know if you'll find some new epic gear you've never seen before each playthrough. Now the downside, this is a roguelike, you expect it to be hard. You want it to be hard. You want to lose a character you loved, come back and kill that SOB with your next guy with flaming fires of avenging RAGE! That you can do, and it feels great, but early game is really, really tough. Specifically there are creatures which with one hit can poison you, stun you, confuse, or paralyse you, any of these status affects almost always end up in instant deaths. And first times through you won't know, hey don't get close to that guy or you'll die, in 1 hit. You're just hitting everything else like normal then pop, game over. The game guides I have found are terrible at explaining hey if you see this type of creature stay away, there's no list like that anywhere I have found. I learned by trial and error which was extremely frustrating. But once you get past that nonsense, the middle and late game is fantastic with enourmous depth. Artstyle and music are also wonderful. If you like rouguelikes this is one you definetly should buy, no question, just know what you're getting into.

Hi,
I first played the game back in Grade 10, back in 2004 (13 years ago) and thoroughly enjoyed the ASCII game back then. So, imagine my surprise when it got a successful launch of Indiegogo; I'd have joined onto that investment opportunity, but well, ADOM had faded from my mind by that point and wasn't actually looking for it. However, these days, I'm happy I didn't get on it, as I throughly regret purchasing ADOM Deluxe.
When I first bought ADOM Deluxe, it had like 50% of the promised features on day one. Then, the developer went on a very long hiatus, holding up the development team, and we had no content updates for over a year and a half. I gave up on the game, sometime around June of 2017, of ever seeing an actual update to ADOM. Fast forward 6 months, and I found out that ADOM finally got a slew of major updates. So, I redownloaded the game to try it out.
Honestly, I should have just left ADOM on steam collecting dust. The interface changes are terrible; hell in the character creation screen, most of the text pops out of the interface boxes... a sign that things weren't going to be good. Created a new character, and most of the controls I've learned to use from the old ASCII build and the build I played back in Dec of 2016, are all changed. The interface and controls has been changed and not for the better. Being that the game forces you to know a ton of information, just to make it playable, forcing players to relearn a brand new interface and keybindings is too much.
Honestly, I'd suggest everyone to stick to the free, ASCII build. It was a pretty good game then, and it is now too, but you have to really dig to find it, and these days I have better things to do that relearn everything from scratch. If you want to support Thomas, then buy the game. But, if you want to play the game, don't bother with the Deluxe edition.
I'd stick around and offer advice on how to fix things, but honestly, the last time I tried to do that, the toxic community and the hostile development team, ate me alive. And watch, as they do so again!
tl;dr = Excellent game, just don't bother with the Deluxe edition; its just not worth it.

SC2VN is an emotional rollercoaster. Anyone who has tried to play any game at a competitive level will be able to relate, though most people won't have experienced circumstances like those in the story. The beautiful artwork and flawless music tie everything together to make a unique experience.
In SC2VN you follow the adventures of Mach, foreign trash extraordinaire, as he takes a probably misguided trip to South Korea to determine, once and for all, whether or not he can go pro. A couple fortuitous meetings in the local PC bang- a cyber-cafe of sorts, to make a really poor analogy- get him into much more than he bargained for.
There are two things to keep in mind: first, SC2VN is free. All it asks is your time (approximately three or four hours of it), and I think it's worth the price. The characters aren't the most complex, most of them seeming fairly archetypal, but they're fun to hang out with and have nice dialogue, anecdotes and backstory tidbits. The antagonist didn't strike me as being very realistic, though, even compared to the protagonists. However, the rollicking, fourth wall-breaking extra material unlocked after finishing the story gives a bit of justification for his... intensity.
Second, note that as far as I can tell (after one playthrough) the VN is completely on rails. There's a couple choices that affect dialogue (maybe a few more than I give it credit for, come to think of it), but none of them do much. Further,
Finally (big spoiler coming up), a certain set of options is fake.
I found this unacceptable. If you ask me, it's the VN's single great failing- though if one isn't bothered by the story's overall lack of choice this statement is high praise, considering what else could have gone wrong.
All in all, while SC2VN is much more something one reads than plays, its wonderful atmosphere and fun, inspiring story more than make up for its shortcomings.
"Strive to win, Mach. Not to not lose."

In all seriousness, SC2VN is a decent little VN that's also available for the grand old price of zero dollars. I enjoyed my time in it and I didn't waste any money so why the negative review?
Because this game raised 8000$ on Kickstarter to deliver a VN that can be finished in around 3 hours that's completely 100% linear. Two choices in the game lead to a bad end and every other choice has almost no bearing on the story. The two choices take place during the SC2 battles where you select your strategy, and the game often has these "battles" that seem to be a sort of minigame (You get a popup regarding the known info of your opponent and his strategies) but they're literally SC2 screenshots with a single choice in the middle. Two of these choices don't matter and the other two have a possibility of a game over. The very final battle of the game was hyped up in the story with a lot of the characters giving you tips, info and advice to use against your opponent. I thought it was gonna be a multiple choice strateg-a-thon and took notes so I can remember all the info.
In the end, there was absolutely no choice whatsoever in the game's ultimate clash, contrary to nearly every main match up to that point. The game ends just as you become a full fledged pro gamer. (ie when you think it's about to get good)
That disappointment was the final motivation to write this review.The game promised so much more during kickstarter, it was almost gonna be
but it delivers on not a single promise:
1. Game will be finished in 6 months: Failed. It took 2 years
2. Game will have romance options: Failed. No romance options exist
3. Game will have multiple paths: Failed. It's an absolutely linear story
4. Game will allow you to choose training partners: Failed. There is no choice in the storyline. There are no "stats" to train.
5. Game will allow you to choose which team house to train in: Failed. There is only one team house and it's simply a backdrop to an end-of-game scene
6. Game will allow you to enter online amatuer tournaments to test your character's skill: Failed. There are no tournaments in the game.
There's no reason in 2015 to take 8000$ and deliver what is essentially a free fan made game made in a free VN engine.
Katawa Shoujo was made with literally Zero dollars by a bunch of autists on ♥♥♥♥♥ and each of that game's multiple paths is longer and deeper in every way than SC2VN's single one.
So really, the best thing I can say about this game is: It's free and a decent waste of a couple of hours.

Players will idle in your spawn (which there is no penalty for) and spawn kill you with the 1 hit kill level 5 plasma cannon, over and over again. When they said “We want to work with you guys - the Steam Early Access community - to make Minimum the best, most player-focused game on Steam," they truly meant it and still do. In contrast to other online shooters, the idea of crafting weapons in the order you wish to is one aspect that sets Minimum apart from others, but this is just one of many aspects that do this. All in all the game is spectacular so far and has me actively engaged and thoroughly happy.

Firstly, most of my playtime is on the non-steam version.
If you're looking for mindless action, this game is not for you. While there is a combat system, it's not what makes this game shine. We're here for the factories (hence the name).
You start life in Factorio on an endless planet rich with natural ressources and wildlife. There is but one thing to do: Exploit or kill all the things!
From a man with a pickaxe surrounded by untamed nature sprouts an industrial revolution directed by your own ingenuity and limited only by how creative and dedicated you are. You'll automate your mines. You'll automate production. Before long, you will be surrounded not by trees but by conveyor belts, transporting your goods through the massive factory that is now your home.
But enough with the prose. The initial manual labour is somewhat reminiscient of Minecraft, but it goes far beyond that.  The main aspect of the game is automating and upgrading a factory. It's all about finding efficient ways to route your items, placing components in the right position and working out how many machines you need making iron gears to supply the next level of fabrication. You can spend hours optimizing tiny components to save space or ressources
Graphics are kept simple (though the devs have promised HD textures) and gameplay is isometric. Using WASD instead of mouse controls is unusual for this and takes some getting used to, but once you're there it's simple enough.
The game performs quite well for medium factories, though in large multiplayer setups, lag will eventually become an issue. Each update of the game improves this, but when you go fully insane and start producing items in the millions, you will experience slowdown. However, unless you plan to play with dozens of people or you feel like one can never have enough expensive things, you're unlikely to ever see the FPS drop below 30. I never did and my PC is not the strongest.
Small bugfixes are regular and new content is added in larger chunks every few months.
The only issue is the combat. The controls are not ideally suited for clustered and dense combat, and in the late game the sheer number of enemies can make it a hassle to secure more ground. Enemies can be toned down in the settings, but for now they have unique drops that are needed to craft endgame items. This issue will supposedly be addressed in a future update though.
TL;DR: This game is definitely worth the price and can provide hundreds of hours of entertainment with simple gameplay that is nonetheless a constant source of puzzle and frustration (in a good way).

I really enjoy classic Roguelike games, and have played everything from Rogue proper to Moria, Angband, Nethack, Zangband, Cthband, TOME, and more.  I though that ADOM would be another success in that line of games that I would really embrace, and was really looking forward to playing it.
And there are a lot of things that ADOM does well, such as a better graphics presentation than anything else not-named TOME or some character building options and decisions.  You also have the major keys you want to press that bring up various screens on the side of the UI so you can use hotkeys like every Roguelike player has had to do or you can just click and play that way.  Good job on those, ADOM!
I also enjoy the additions of leveling up with skills, training, the sign you were born under, and more, and the character design has more teeth to it than a lot of other games in the genre.
There are a few qualms that I have though.  Most Roguelikes are hard, that's the point.  They are designed to be a challenge, and no less so with ADOM, especially in the early game. I give ADOM mad props for being tough too.  But where it errs is pushing that to design decisons that make the game require extensive foreknowledge or heavy subsequent plays to have a shot at winning.  I'll give you two examples of that in a moment.  But that is not a normal Roguelike tactic. I can pick up, and win at, Angband without reading the entire wikia first and five or six walkthroughs and watching YouTube videos.  Sure, I will get better as I play more, which is true of other games, but Angband and friends always played fair with you, even when it was playing hard.  I won Angband without scumming.  I never came close to beating Moria.  I almost beat Zangband, but lost in the final battle.  You get the idea.
ADOM doesn't play fair.  It has design decisions that force you to know about ahead of time and plan for.
Here are two examples, one early, and one later:
Early Example - In the first town, there are two mutually exclusive quests that you could come across by talking with one of two people there, and the first one you talk to gives that quest.  Since you have a quest coming into that town to talk to as many people in the first town as you can, you are talking to them anyways, as there is an in-game incentive to complete that quest.  But one of two quests gives you a prize thats good for some characters and not others, and vice versa.  I took the wrong quest becuase I didn't know that the town had two quests that are mutually exclusive, and they don't even need to be.  Both create seperate dungeons and characters, and you certainly could do them both.  Without knowing the rewards ahead of time, you miss out on a major quest reward early.
Middle Game Example - There is a dungeon in the game called the pyramid that you cannot get to until you're of a high enough level.  I entered it when I arrived in the vicinity with my Halfling Duelist and was told I didn't have an invite.  Then around level 14 I found a papyrus and read it, and I was invited for a challenge at the pyramid. Now's that's totally fine up until now.  You have dungeons that open up later pretty often in lots of RPGs, including Roguelikes such as Zangband.  I finished my dungeon delve of this 12 level dungon and then by the time I had finished I had reached level 17, and then I stepped out, dropped off some of my extra gear at this oasis I found, and then went to the pyramid.  But I couldn't enter it.  Why not?  I still had the papyrus with me.  So I looked it up on the Wikia.  And this is a major and very important dungeon to complete because the ruler has two major guaranteed artifacts you really want to snag.  And the issue was that you can only enter it from levels 13-16.  I was too high to do that challenge.  I saw that one of the items, a special armor, is one that is perfect for my class, and really helps you survive long term, and I missed out.
That's ADOM.  Design decisions have been made about the game but have not been communicated to you as a player.  The papyrus that invited me to the pyramid didn't say that I couldn't arrive after level 16 and it was a limited time offer.  The quest in the first city never said that if I accepted it I couldn't do another quest instead.
So the result is a game that appears, with the investment of a few hours, to be a sturdy entry into the Roguelike genre, but the more I delve into it, the more I realize that this is not a game that plays fair with me as a player.  And why would I want to continue to play that sort of game after already investing more than 20 hours into it?
This could have been a game I would easily have seen myself with 100+ hours.  But there are these horrible design choices that don't respect me as a player or give me the agency to change them in the game.  That's a major philosophical issue that I hope the game cleans up.  And if it does, and becomes more player friendly with inforamtion in the game, or changing up some of those design decisions, then I would certianly be open to revisiting this review and the game itself.  But that's not today.  And it's likely not tomorrow either.
It's okay to be hard.  It's not okay to hide information that makes the game harder.

I've been playing ADOM for 15 years, and I still love it. One of my favorite roguelikes. This version has the best art I've seen from any roguelike -- and it isn't just pretty, it's actually super functional, as I'm better able to tell monsters apart with the art than I am with the ASCII. (But if you want to play it old school, ASCII is still an option.)
Keeps getting updates, which is sweet. Lots of variation in classes and races, so there's always some new way to try to go about things.
Also, you can play without perma-death -- that's actually the default -- which is great, bc I get confused and die to stupid things a lot otherwise :D
If you're real lost, the wiki is a great resource.

ADOM is the truest roguelike there is. It feels like playing a solo game of Dungeons & Dragons with a supercomputer as a DM. There's a lot of room to be clever in every situation, but at the same time, you live and die by the whims of fate. This review assumes you're OK with that, as it's a basic premise of all roguelikes. If you aren't sure, you can download a free version of the game from their site and try it out.
+
- tons of strategies, treasures, and interactions to discover
+
- it might take dying once or twice, but the game teaches you how best to survive
+
- graphics, animations, and sounds are lovingly made and engrossing, while the story and NPC dialogue keeps you feeling like your heroism is meaningful
+
- the stuff being added to the game is actually outpacing the rate I can discover it
-
- lots of keybindings combined with a "learn by dying" approach can be offputting to new players
-
- I've won twice in four years of playing. I have a level 49 wizard on track for a special "ultra ending", but can't work up the courage to actually take the plunge with him yet, which leads me to...
-
- one mistaken keypress or unnoticed enemy can cost you a character, which can be stressful
-
- these used to kill your character, but now the game saves frequent backups for you, so it's hardly a setback
ADOM's a pretty incredible game that can pull you back even after it kills your luckiest character. Don't let the equal-sized pro/con list fool you - I wholeheartedly recommend this game. It's seriously one of a kind.

This was the first visual novel game I've ever played. Before I played this game I had a generally negative view of VNs. However, I also played starcraft and playing a VN that was about something I enjoyed also allowed me to give this game a chance.
The story is overall, very well crafted and thought out. Character development is good, and the game avoids useless sideplots and instead takes interesting paths in developing the main plot and the characters along the way. No character is wasted, or simply exists to fill some hole in the story. Each and everyone of them has a purpose and represents the many different backgrounds that Starcraft players come from.
It also reveals the amount of hardwork and drama that goes on in the professional esports scene. It's not all glamour and fun. There's hardwork involved, and just as much luck and fate as well. Some make it, but many do not. Overall one gets to see that it is a serious industry with serious people with serious dreams no lesser than your own. They have many of the same challenges that we face, like disapproving family, stiff competition, self-doubt, and uncertain futures. But it also shows us that with hardwork and supportive friends anything is possible.
I had fun playing this VN and I definitely learned alot. It also renewed my love for Starcraft and I can't wait to increase my own understanding and skills in the game. I highly encourage those who love esports to give this VN a go!

Factorio pushes all of the right logistical buttons that other games just cannot come close to satisfying. Initially, Factorio appears daunting - a monolith of moving parts. However, dig a bit deeper and dig into the ores in this strange new world. Smelt these ores into plates, and distribute the plates throughout the factory to create different parts and components.
Everything expands at your own pace, quite literally too! It's easy enough to set up basic systems of supply and demand, there's no rush. True mastery arises from layout optimization and scale of factories. Ship resources across large swaths of land using trains if you'd like, or fly resources overheard using drones: the tools are all there once the player advances their research.
Plus, Factorio has excellent multiplayer support. As an aside, a friend of mine now occassionally has dreams of Factorio too, a blessing and a curse of optimization in the dream world.
Very addictive, this game will keep you up for hours after you swear you were going to bed, there is always one more thing to tweak to improve production......

Factorio feeds that part of you that just wants to be efficient. It feeds your need for creativity and problem solving. Factorio is: possibilities.
For a game that's still in development, this is the best money I've ever spent on a game.

A good successor to Transport Tycoon.
It is fun to create your factory/city piece by piece and watch it work endlessly on manufactured parts. Another example that well-designed 2D graphics might be a very good choice even today.
The only thing lacking is some better interaction with the environment. In TT you had at least growing cities according to your supply of transportation services and virtual passengers going to/leaving villages and cities. In factorio there are only semi-ignorant greenpeace local creatures that try to attack your worst polluters and the only option is to either seal them off or exterminate them.
Overall a very good idea with nice graphics, good UI and a "one-more-building-before-bedtime" principle.

The most addictive thing ever made. Forget heroin or other drugs, this is the real one.
It's really something for every type of player. You can do research, you can fight, you can create incredibly complex circuit networks you will never be able to figure out again if you don't play the game for a day or so and you start over again anyway.
10/10 would by again.

Most undying game I ever played

ADOM has been in development since 1994, and wow do you feel it. The idea of a title with complex, emergent gameplay with an evident and long history of development gave me strong Dwarf Fortress vibes.
ADOM is probably one of the more Rogue-like roguelikes you can find on Steam. The game is stuffed with content, including dozens and dozens of ways to meet your demise. If you survive, the game promises many rewards. You can become a king, or achieve godhood. Neither of which I experienced, because in my few hours of the game I simply stumbled into various ways to die within 24 hours.
I had mild frustrations with the controls and UI. Usually the mouse would be sufficient to navigate and find the information I wanted, but sometimes I would find myself confused on why a spell didn't fire correctly or how to perform certain actions. Understandable considering it's history, but that doesn't mean I'm still not a spoiled modern gamer. Evidently the game will be getting an updated rerelease sometime soon, which I expect will resolve some user unfriendliness.
I'd highly recommend this game if you're deep into roguelikes, difficult games, or imaginative adventures. I'd also recommend this title if you missed out on 90s PC gaming and want a little taste of history.

ADOM belongs with Angband and Nethack as one of the definite classic roguelikes. Complex and merciless it demands a lot of failures in order to slowly learn and succeed in eventually winning the game. This version does improve on the original by adding beautiful tile graphics, many ways of easing the game's ruthless difficulty and generally opening it up for everyone besides hardcore roguelike fans.
"The" roguelike as far as I'm concerned. Most if not all pale in comparison to the depth and intricacy that ADOM contains.

I've played many roguelikes over the years. Before ADOM, Angband was my go-to. When ADOM came out I tried it and never went back. While I tried others like Stone Soup they didn't capture my attention like ADOM. The world setting, multiple dungeons, and story line were unlike any other roguelike experience I'd had.
When its crowd funding campaign started I was glad to back it as thanks for all the fun hours I had with the game. Now the tilesets, additional content, and improvements to the game have me playing and learning its secrets again.

ADOM has been worked on for decades, but the current version on Steam is the best ever. The text-only interface has been replaced with a functional and well made graphical interface. But the depth and difficulty which makes the game great is still there.
For me, the best roguelike is Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup. ADOM could well be the best Steam roguelike. Not bad!

Do you..
..enjoy colors? Buy Transistor
..enjoy music? Buy Transistor
..enjoy new game mechanics? Buy Transistor
..enjoy stories? Buy Transistor
..enjoy beautiful environments? Buy Transistor
In short, stop thinking about it and buy Transistor

Before we begin, let us establish something that should be obvious from the game's title, but apparently isn't to some players:
THIS IS NOT BASTION 2
Playing it like it was Bastion 2 can only lead to frustration and disaappointment. To appreciate Transistor, you must approach it respectfully, on its own terms, and not guided by your own expectations, as, really, you should be doing with every game worth talking about.
While it uses some of the same innovative mechanisms that were introduced in Bastion, it is not, nor does it try to be, more of the same - something I admire with Supergiant's production that, apparently, some players of the game find frustration with. They could've easily printed money by making a Bastion 2, but chose to make something original instead. How can you not admire such a departure from the unscrupulous money grab that is sadly becoming the norm in this hobby?
I've likely already gifted you this game if we're on reasonably friendly terms. But for everyone else, allow me to say that, speaking as an experienced gamer, this is my favourite game. It is, in a word, perfection, and those of you who know how critical I can be of these things should know I do not say that lightly. Perfectly harmonized design, art direction, music, writing, everything. The team at Supergiant, earning themselves a place as my personal favourite developers, and in any case an honoured spot on the true A-list, have here created another superbly crafted game that I warmly encourage everyone to try and experience.

Bloodrayne is a third-person, action, hack and slash game that originally came out on October 15, 2002. It's been 11 years since i last played it on the original XBOX. Exploring the levels and meeting all the antagonist and monsters again is really nostalgic. Rayne is the main protagonist in the game. She is a dhampir who is in search of her father; Kaegan. She is later recruited into the Brimstone Society and that is where the game begins.
Story:
The story in Bloodrayne is not complex at all. You and your mentor Mynce from the Brimstone Society are sent to Mortton, Lousiana to investigate a disease that is turning humans into mutates. The unique enemy in this act are called Maraisreqs. Not much happens in this act apart from your first boss fight the Queen of the Underworld and your first meet with Jurgen Wulf (The main antagonist) who is the founder of the G.G.G and is trying to become immortal by acquiring powerful relics scattered across the world. The next act takes place 5 years later in Argentina, Rayne is assigned to eliminate several high ranking G.G.G.(Gegengeist Gruppe) officers before they can get ahold of one of the powerful relics. These officers serve as the mini-boss and bosses of the game. Midway through the act a new enemy type is introduced called Daemites. Act III takes place in Germany. Rayne is assinged a new list of G.G.G targets to eliminate. This act also introduces another enemy type called Feral Vampires. I can't put the rest of this act in words without spoiling major parts of the story.
Gameplay:
The combat system is plain and repetitive but enjoyable; Rayne's primary weapons are her blades which can do up to a 5 meele combo as long as she makes contact with an enemy. Her secondary weapons are guns. There are about 33 different weapons including Pistols, Rifles, Shotguns, SMGs, Assault Rifles, Dynamite and Grenade Launchers) in the game. She has 8 slots for weapons, 3 for light weapons, 3 for heavy weapons, 1 for grenades and 1 for special weapons. Rayne has 3 unique abilities that she can use, one from the start of the game and two you unlock in Argentina. Aura Sense: Targets and destinations will shine bright blue, Dilated Perception: Slow motion, and Extruded View: Allows you to zoom. The game will take you anywhere from 6-8 hours to complete.
Pros:
+ Basic but enjoyable combat.
+ Decent amount of variety.
+ Great level progression.
+ Immersing experience.
+ Rayne's dialogue.
Cons:
- Checkpoint system can be an annoyance at times.
- Graphics are outdated.
- The last few words of all dialogue in cutscenes cuts out. (Fixed by turning V-Sync ON = 30 FPS)
Notes:
"Another man falling to pieces over me." ― Rayne

Before we begin, let us establish something that should be obvious from the game's title, but apparently isn't to some players:
THIS IS NOT BASTION 2
Playing it like it was Bastion 2 can only lead to frustration and disaappointment. To appreciate Transistor, you must approach it respectfully, on its own terms, and not guided by your own expectations, as, really, you should be doing with every game worth talking about.
While it uses some of the same innovative mechanisms that were introduced in Bastion, it is not, nor does it try to be, more of the same - something I admire with Supergiant's production that, apparently, some players of the game find frustration with. They could've easily printed money by making a Bastion 2, but chose to make something original instead. How can you not admire such a departure from the unscrupulous money grab that is sadly becoming the norm in this hobby?
I've likely already gifted you this game if we're on reasonably friendly terms. But for everyone else, allow me to say that, speaking as an experienced gamer, this is my favourite game. It is, in a word, perfection, and those of you who know how critical I can be of these things should know I do not say that lightly. Perfectly harmonized design, art direction, music, writing, everything. The team at Supergiant, earning themselves a place as my personal favourite developers, and in any case an honoured spot on the true A-list, have here created another superbly crafted game that I warmly encourage everyone to try and experience.

I enjoyed this game very much. It is mechanically a unique combination of hack-and-slash with turn based strategy (sort of like a more elaborate version of the VATS mechanic in Fallout 3), which takes a bit of getting used to but is definately worth it. The game has a very detailed and flexible system where the abilities you acquire can either be equipped as attacks or used to passively modify other abilities or your character. It also has a very good story and soundtrack.

Supergiant games have become 1 of my favorite indie game developers. First they made Bastion and now Transistor. They have a good roll going, and I hope that it won't stop.
Transistor is in many ways similar to Bastion. A pretty vague story, everything being narrated by a guy with a golden voice, and taking place in a crumbling world. The gameplay has seen some changes. The combat is much more complex now, and I did find myself enjoying it for the most part. Trying out new attack combinations was refreshing, but sadly I mostly just used the same basic attacks from beginning to end, and just added variations to them. Also I wouldn't mind if there was a bit less combat overall, it was getting a lil bit tedious at times. Transistor also ditches the Hub world from Bastion in favor of a linear structure. This I was not a huge fan of. Seeing your "home" grow was 1 of my favorite things and Bastion, and it's a shame that they took that out.
I also found the story to be intresting, but it just didn't click for me like Bastion did. The ending for example left almost no emotional impact(doesn't mean that it was a BAD ending). It was still a good story though. The music was spot on again, and the voice acting was really good, so no suprises there. Visually the game also looks quite nice. I liked seeing familiar areas change their style over time. You could feel the progression!
The length of the game was something I was a bit disappointed by. Even though Bastion was not exactly a long game either, Transistor ended up being only about 4-5 hours and that includes a lot of exploration and almost all of the challenges. I didn''t mind it much because the game was able to tell it's story just fine in that 4-5 hours, but I did hope for some more side content.Also, it did start to feel a bit repeative towards the end. Ah well...
Overall Transistor is a really good experience, even if it doesn't reach Bastion in that regard. The interesting story and the world will keep you hooked until you see the curtain fall. If you are a fan of these types of games, you should definitely give Transistor a shot.

- story driven by narrator
- 'bastion'-like beach house where you can unlock things through minigames
- Soundtrack is similar
- The general 'feel' of the game is like bastion.
These are all nice things, but felt somewhat repetitive for me.
So to narrow it down:
Pros:
- Story (this can also be a con, depends on what you like)
- Narration (I like it)
- Soundtrack (when you pause the fight to plan things it becomes a sort of melancholic humming, totally adds to the already desperate atmosphere and I like it)
- Gameplay
Cons:
- Story (you have, at not a single point, a complete understand of wtf is going on)
- Low variety of mobs.
- Combat does get repetive at some point
Verdicht:
Good game. For me, it doesn't even compare to bastion, but perhaps if I had played this game first I would have said thesame thing about bastion, instead.

I have played this game off and on over the many years it's been promoted and advertised.
This is a fenced in game riddled with micro transactions that require you to spend money to get new items and gear along with actual Hunting licenses as a Monthly Subscription.
I am not a Fan of the Micro store requiring actual money, but they do offer missions to get consumables through in game currency for hunting contracts. Granted, the game is enjoyable as a Hunting simulator and challenging. But, the game has evolved since I first started playing.
Beta (2009): free to play limited to 10 bullets and Mule dear for hunting only
2012: free to play limited to only Mule dear Hunting only with unlimited ammo

Well worth a few hours of your time, this free Visual Novel is a great peek into the sorts of challenges facing someone looking to become a professional gamer. There's some concessions of realism for the sake of story, but they don't hinder the game in any real way, and I found myself actually interested and even caring for/about the characters.
The interface is clean and responsive, and the medium is put to good use, as there's little things that happen, like interruptions which wouldn't be possible with a non-interactive book. Do note, however, that while you do get to make a few decisions here and there, this is less of a game than an experience, so the emphasis is on telling the tale of Mach and his/her journey. That's standard for many VNs, but it has to be noted, because this is a genre that will be new to many players.
I personally feel it's a better experience with the female protagonist, as then the issues of discrimination and sexism are more relevant, as well as some of the bonds formed between characters feeling more true to life,  but it's not heavy-handed with either player choice. Although fictional, there's quite a bit of historic fact and character traits based off real people included, so, in a way, SC2VN is educational as well.
Recommended for anyone interested in eSports, StarCraft, gaming in general, or just a few hours of reading and enjoyment.

I played a little of ADOM before the resurrection. It's one of the big names that really paved the way for the roguelike genre. ADOM is fairly unique among the other big traditional roguelikes. It's a lot more about story, not satisfied just with fun mechanics under a vague fantasy theme. The presence of the overworld and the interactivity of NPCs offering quests really elevates the RPG elements and immerses the player into the world. Since development was resurrected, the work done has been incredible in taking an already complete experience and modernizing the game, fixing bugs and adding content. The tiles and overall graphics are some of the best among traditional roguelikes (although there are a few menus that still look like an emulated terminal), and the soundtrack is one of my favorites in video games. A lot of work has been put into making the game far more accessible to new players, along with the introduction of more forgiving modes where you can customize the experience or simply play without permadeath.

Cool game, lovely voice work and great graphics. The environments are nice and the combat is fun. However there is one thing that I cannot shake when I play this and it is very irritating. It feels like a poor man's GTA. Driving vehicles is no fun either, mostly because when using a mouse and keyboard, the camera is awkward. Reversing on a bike will spin the camera, but if you manually move the mouse to get a better look as you set off forward, it will still rotate the camera and as such go beyond the forward view - as if it has to complete the entire motion. Why they couldn't of made it so moving the camera view yourself resets the camera spin, I just don't know.
There are are a few other minor annoyances. Sometimes AI will walk into things, which isn't that bad really and many games are guilty of that (ahem Payday 2), but one of my biggest gripes when playing on foot is that there is no toggle for walk and run. Instead, if you want to walk you must rely on holding the free aim button (which is right click by default). However using free aim to walk is evidently not the proper way of doing it because whenever you get near an interactable object that you wish to talk past, your guy will just... sort of strafe past it while trying to get it in focus. Bit daft really that they couldn't simply add a walk toggle button.
Another annoyance? The weird buttons. The game plays brilliantly with mouse and keyboard, but I have no idea why some menus rely solely on pressing Left-CTRL and Right-CTRL and Backspace and Enter. Why couldn't a cursor be implemented? Seems a bit lazy if you ask me.
Overall, of what I've played (among some other very minor bugs which I've decided not to mention here), the game is excellent and well worth the money if you haven't already got the base game. For those who have the original Sleeping Dogs, I wouldn't necessarily say the increase in graphical fidelity and draw distance was worth it... although that is ultimately your decision.
