This game is just amazing beyond words. Everything is fantastic from the superb soundtrack to the story and the characters. I especially loved the vivid world the game offered and it left me satisfied the whole time.

Firstly, most of my playtime is on the non-steam version.
If you're looking for mindless action, this game is not for you. While there is a combat system, it's not what makes this game shine. We're here for the factories (hence the name).
You start life in Factorio on an endless planet rich with natural ressources and wildlife. There is but one thing to do: Exploit or kill all the things!
From a man with a pickaxe surrounded by untamed nature sprouts an industrial revolution directed by your own ingenuity and limited only by how creative and dedicated you are. You'll automate your mines. You'll automate production. Before long, you will be surrounded not by trees but by conveyor belts, transporting your goods through the massive factory that is now your home.
But enough with the prose. The initial manual labour is somewhat reminiscient of Minecraft, but it goes far beyond that.  The main aspect of the game is automating and upgrading a factory. It's all about finding efficient ways to route your items, placing components in the right position and working out how many machines you need making iron gears to supply the next level of fabrication. You can spend hours optimizing tiny components to save space or ressources
Graphics are kept simple (though the devs have promised HD textures) and gameplay is isometric. Using WASD instead of mouse controls is unusual for this and takes some getting used to, but once you're there it's simple enough.
The game performs quite well for medium factories, though in large multiplayer setups, lag will eventually become an issue. Each update of the game improves this, but when you go fully insane and start producing items in the millions, you will experience slowdown. However, unless you plan to play with dozens of people or you feel like one can never have enough expensive things, you're unlikely to ever see the FPS drop below 30. I never did and my PC is not the strongest.
Small bugfixes are regular and new content is added in larger chunks every few months.
The only issue is the combat. The controls are not ideally suited for clustered and dense combat, and in the late game the sheer number of enemies can make it a hassle to secure more ground. Enemies can be toned down in the settings, but for now they have unique drops that are needed to craft endgame items. This issue will supposedly be addressed in a future update though.
TL;DR: This game is definitely worth the price and can provide hundreds of hours of entertainment with simple gameplay that is nonetheless a constant source of puzzle and frustration (in a good way).

This game held my attention harder than almost any other game ever has. Loaded with mystery and discovery, The Room is an excellent example of puzzle gaming done right. The puzzles themselves are interesting, feel good to solve, and use a wide range of different mental skills and mechanics. The story develops nicely through the handful of written notes, and the writing is very effective at communicating information and cranking up the intrigue. It's short, but it feels just the right length for the type of game it is. It's a beautiful game that rewards attention to detail and critical thinking.

I loved The Room.  I solved it in 5 hours, so what I really want now is a sequel.  It was awesome.   I found that the hint level I could access (I never could figure out how to get to hint 2 in any sequence) told me what I already knew, so I did it pretty much on my own.  I'm pretty proud of doing it all without appreciable help.  The graphics are immersive, primarily because the objects look so real that you forget you're not actually touching them.
I really liked the fact that I didn't seem to be falling back on any prior knowledge (or particular puzzle-solving tactics learned from oldies like the Myst series, 7th Guest and 11th Hour) to solve the puzzles.  All the answers were right there; I just had to find them.  If you want a quick fix game, this isn't for you.  But if you want a game that will make you lose track of time and wrench your brain around in your noggin because you just KNOW you saw a coin slot around there somewhere, play The Room.  You won't regret it.

Most obviously, it's the first where EA Canada has really got to grips with Steam, resulting in a mass of changes to the graphics and animation engines. Some are merely cosmetic, and some so subtle as to be almost unnoticeable, but many have a genuine impact on the gameplay.
Less obviously, SC2VN 5 seems to have moved away from the focus on ball control and the defensive game of SC2VN 3 and SC2VN 4, and towards a more dynamic, aggressive and - frankly - exciting style of play. If you played the last two  SC2VNs tired of getting mired in the midfield, bored witless by the slow, methodical pace, then you'll probably find this year’s SC2VN the best since the glory days of SC2VN 2. It's still a game built by people hell-bent on reflecting every aspect of the beautiful game, but this time they’ve remembered that SC2VN can also be fun.
Structurally, it's pretty much identical to FIFA. The single-player campaign remains dominated by Career mode, where you can take either a player or a manager through several seasons, hoping to take your team to league and tournament success, or build a fantastic national and international career.
It's still basically a combination of the old Be a Pro and Be a Manager modes, where you roll through the season playing matches, dodging or accepting loan and transfer requests and getting the odd rollicking for your behaviour on the pitch, and as before, you can choose whether to play matches from the viewpoint of just the one player or play with the whole team. The latter will be most people's choice, but playing in just the one position can be interesting, really making you think about where you need to be and what you need to do to make the most of every opportunity, while creating opportunities for others.
This game is also a First Person Shooter, like Call of Duty, or Counter Strike, even Skyrim with guns. The only downside is that you have too kill a dog to progress, and that is the only flaw with this game. I rate this game a 9/11

Before I start this review two big health warnings. This is an early access game and most of it is not complete. So don't expect a review, but my first impressions. Secondly Plague Inc is a tablet game on Apple and Android, I have only played the PC game.
On the technical side, you don't need a powerful machine to run this game and don't worry about the tablet port side of things, the options menu is better than many full price games. Some things still need to be added like rebindable keys and accessibility options, but these things should be in the final release according to the Ndemic Creations website.
So what is Plague Inc? It is a disease simulator, it lets you play anything from a humble bacteria to a full blown Zombie plague. You infect people, thwart human research efforts, spread across borders and kill people, lots and lots of people. Now this is fun in a dark kind of way, and the game does have lots of multiplayer and social media potential for competitive play. There is great replayability since the game is easy to pickup and yet there are many different strategies to employ. Still I can't give it an unequivocal recommendation for one reason, it does not make sense.
Now I don't mean that zombies or brain worms don't exist, I don't have a problem of with that. It is the breaking of the laws of nature and common sense. How can everyone in the world be infected and never get better till a cure is found? Why do all the mutations in the game make the disease stronger?
If you've ever studied biology you could go on and on about how odd the game model is, but from a gaming perspective it represents a lost opportunity for a really interesting simulation game. What you have instead is a fun, dark, casual, indie game.
My verdict wait for the full game or a steam sale.

I played a little of ADOM before the resurrection. It's one of the big names that really paved the way for the roguelike genre. ADOM is fairly unique among the other big traditional roguelikes. It's a lot more about story, not satisfied just with fun mechanics under a vague fantasy theme. The presence of the overworld and the interactivity of NPCs offering quests really elevates the RPG elements and immerses the player into the world. Since development was resurrected, the work done has been incredible in taking an already complete experience and modernizing the game, fixing bugs and adding content. The tiles and overall graphics are some of the best among traditional roguelikes (although there are a few menus that still look like an emulated terminal), and the soundtrack is one of my favorites in video games. A lot of work has been put into making the game far more accessible to new players, along with the introduction of more forgiving modes where you can customize the experience or simply play without permadeath.
It took me 15 years to beat this game. You might be smart and it might not take you that long, but it's definitely worth the money.
It's my favorite roguelike, so if you like roguelikes this one is good.

It might run well on ciurrent hardware (fonts scale great and look smashigly sharp at 4K!) but make no mistake the engine behind it is purge old-school rouge-like. You can even choose to play in ASCII mode and it has all the requisite litany keyboard shortcuts. Though I must say I'm digging the tile art and UI niceties layered over the classic game engine.
If you're going to try it, give it at least 15 hours or so. Play the tutorial. Ease yourself in. You will be killed. You will be killed in glorious and what sometimes feels like unfair ways. Keep learning nuances and information, and keep trudging through.

Well I do agree that this is probably the best hunter game out there.  If someone disagrees I would love to hear about it so I can buy that game.
However there are a couple reasons I don’t play it any more.
1) The number one reason is that stalking/spotting is impossible.  The game engine only renders animals out to 200-240m or so.  However animal detection range when walking is further than that.  So you can be spotting a wide open valley with binoculars that looks empty and start walking and spook an animal that is outside the render distance so you can’t even see them.  I have a great computer and video card but the 200m limit is fixed.
2) The only way you can try to sneak up on animals is by crouching or crawling.  BUT even turkeys move faster than that.  So you can be following a trail of most animals and you will NEVER be able to catch up to them and the minute you walk, they run.
3) Nickel and diming to death.   Now I know free-to-play is always looking for whales.  Paying $55 used to get you an AAA title with all content.  I am fine paying $55/yr for the Trailrunner pack but you are missing a ton of scents and calls.  Due to the walking issue listed in 1, without scents and calls some animals are extremely difficult to hunt because you can’t stalk them.
4) As an adult I don’t have hours and hours to play.  Sometimes I just have 30-45min and want to have a quick game.  Walking from most lodges and trying to get to a good hunt site and allow the animals to roam nearer to you generally takes longer than 30-45min.  For these short sessions it is more like a walking simulator than a shooting game.
So for the rendering issue, the reduced ability to hunt many species despite paying $55/yr, and the inability to have much fun when you only have 30-60min means that I let my subscription lapse and will not be back.
Too bad because when the animals are around, it is a lot of fun.

SMITE.
Jesus Christ, SMITE. I used to love this game.
Then the community got worse, and the updates started making the balance slowly die.
Hi-Rez are by far the most money-grubbing company I've ever encountered.
There are 90 gods playable, and out of those, 5 are playable from the start. 5. Yes they have some on rotation every week, but that isn't reliable if you want to play one of the other 85 gods.
Do you know how you unlock a god? You either slowly grind for favour (which takes forever), or you buy a £20 pack for all of them.
See that cool Jack O' Lantern skin for Thanatos? You can't buy it with favour (like most skins), and unlike most skins, you can't buy it with expensive gems. You have to roll a RNG chest (a la overwatch but with more cost for less) and there's a CHANCE you MIGHT get it. And if you don't? The event is very short, so you'll want to buy more gems, giving them more money. Lots of skins do this, and lots of other games do this, but with the gods, Hi-Rez is effectively locking their content behind a paywall.
The gameplay is typical MOBA style, but Hi-Rez's balancing team is even stupider than Overwatch's, and at least that game's fun as hell. Every two weeks, expect a wacky balance change nobody asked for and expensive skins that you have to pay to get or pay to have a chance to get, and every month expect a REALLY overpowered god that gets nerfed to hell when the next one comes out so it doesn't steal any spotlight.
The community are the saltiest community I've ever seen, and I've played Overwatch. Instalocking then throwing is ridiculously common, and teams of multiple people can mass report you and get you banned for literally no reason because they felt like it.
In total, SMITE was once fantastic, but it went downhill and I don't think it's getting back up any time soon.
It breaks my heart to give this game a negative review.

Firstly, most of my playtime is on the non-steam version.
If you're looking for mindless action, this game is not for you. While there is a combat system, it's not what makes this game shine. We're here for the factories (hence the name).
You start life in Factorio on an endless planet rich with natural ressources and wildlife. There is but one thing to do: Exploit or kill all the things!
From a man with a pickaxe surrounded by untamed nature sprouts an industrial revolution directed by your own ingenuity and limited only by how creative and dedicated you are. You'll automate your mines. You'll automate production. Before long, you will be surrounded not by trees but by conveyor belts, transporting your goods through the massive factory that is now your home.
But enough with the prose. The initial manual labour is somewhat reminiscient of Minecraft, but it goes far beyond that.  The main aspect of the game is automating and upgrading a factory. It's all about finding efficient ways to route your items, placing components in the right position and working out how many machines you need making iron gears to supply the next level of fabrication. You can spend hours optimizing tiny components to save space or ressources
Graphics are kept simple (though the devs have promised HD textures) and gameplay is isometric. Using WASD instead of mouse controls is unusual for this and takes some getting used to, but once you're there it's simple enough.
The game performs quite well for medium factories, though in large multiplayer setups, lag will eventually become an issue. Each update of the game improves this, but when you go fully insane and start producing items in the millions, you will experience slowdown. However, unless you plan to play with dozens of people or you feel like one can never have enough expensive things, you're unlikely to ever see the FPS drop below 30. I never did and my PC is not the strongest.
Small bugfixes are regular and new content is added in larger chunks every few months.
The only issue is the combat. The controls are not ideally suited for clustered and dense combat, and in the late game the sheer number of enemies can make it a hassle to secure more ground. Enemies can be toned down in the settings, but for now they have unique drops that are needed to craft endgame items. This issue will supposedly be addressed in a future update though.
TL;DR: This game is definitely worth the price and can provide hundreds of hours of entertainment with simple gameplay that is nonetheless a constant source of puzzle and frustration (in a good way).

Rock of Ages is kind of a mix between racing, tower defense, and bowling. You're playing, essentially, as one person building traps to place in the way of your opponent's boulder, then you roll your own boulder down their side until you smash against their gate, while trying not to get destroyed along the way. The story mode starts out pretty easy but turns surprisingly hard at one or two points once you start facing against ballistas and such. The war game mode is the meat of it, and it's a blast.
I did have one or two complaints though. Firstly, the kind of humor in this game can be hit or miss, and for me it was a definite miss. Secondly, the boss segments in the story were by far the most boring parts of the entire game. It's not even clear at first what you're supposed to do, and when you do figure it out it's repetitive and dull, making you wish you could just get back to smashing open gates. Third, I kept running into a bug when resetting levels where the sky view on the war map would get stuck and refused to move until I realized it was detecting the W key as being constantly active; hitting the W key once fixed it, but it was still annoying.
Apart from that, I still haven't found anyone to play multiplayer with, at least through random matching. You'll need a friend or two with the game to make that aspect work.
Still, those minor complaints aside, this is a really fun game. Not one you'll sink tons of hours into, but one you'll have plenty of fun with for a while, and can come back to once in a while to relax while smashing things up with your giant rock.

As for the game play, it still needs some work, but overall this is a lot of fun.  Any projectile weapons you hit the target with (deer, wolves, people) vanish as soon as the target dies.  You can get them back if you run up and hold 'q' in exactly the right spot while chasing them beforehand.  (This should be a "hit," not "hold," or even better you should collect them off the corpse.)  The building system is a little haphazard, but if you misplace a block, you can retrieve it again.  The textures are beautiful, but the render is a little lagged.   The land will look like a golf course, and then the ground cover will appear.  You will spend hours gathering resources, and more hours waiting for those to combine into the next resources.  This is another reason to avoid the official servers unless you are joining with a team who can watch your stuff 24/7.  Basically, you are going to work for what you build.  Unless you can get yourself right to siege and go steal from everyone else.

Normally, I'd say it's the devs' fault, but there's nothing they can do. Ban one account and another pops right up in its place. ADOM has rapidly become my favourite of the major roguelikes: it's been discussed many times so I won't add too much to that other than my personal love for this stems mostly from the feel of the game. You can tell any art that has had time, effort and love pumped into it: it radiates out and feels just great. ADOM is exemplary in game design, has a multitude of options and is, for the most part, fair. With any roguelike game, imagination plays a key part (the main reason I still play in ASCII, although I must say that the tiles on this Steam release are of a very high quality indeed and will please those whol prefer graphics) and therefore the feel of a game can be most personal to the player. ADOM has just enough fluff and detail in-game to really allow the imagination to play: you can bump your way through many of the early dungeons without much thought for this and without some of the classic RPG elements this might get a little dull, but I think Thomas Biskup has gotten the mix of ingredients just perfect.
Great great game, worthy of the status as major roguelike, certainly one of the best RPG games ever made and you could do a lot worse than supporting the developers by purchasing the Steam version, as it enables them to add new content.

I've played this game for just shy of four hundred hours at the time of writing, and I've only beaten it twice. There are still locations, quests, items, monsters, spells and secrets that I've never encountered, and a large number of race/class combinations I've never tried. Given all that, I've no doubt I'll end up playing four hundred more.
A lot of the negatives mentioned by other reviews are completely accurate. Yes, it's an incredibly hard, punishing game. Yes, the mechanics are complex and hard to understand at first, and the keybindings are extensive and take a lot of time to remember. It'll be a long time before you make significant progress, especially if you want to avoid spoilers, and some deaths will be unfair. It is not balanced, nor does it try to be.
And yet, it's one of the deepest, most compelling and replayable games I've ever come across. If you're up for a challenge and willing to put in some time to learn the game, you will be rewarded manyfold. Ultimately, it's one of the best games I've ever played, and though I wouldn't recommend it for everyone, if you like the idea of a game to invest a substantial amount of time into for relatively cheap, this is the game for you.

Transistor, being the second product of Supergiant Games, is naturally quite a lot like Bastion (spiritual successor, not sequel), except with enough changed around that they didn't make the same game twice.  Transistor's combat is much, much better than Bastion's, which was already passable.  Red as a protagonist...  I like her quite a lot.  Her character shows itself in short snippets at a time and it's clear she's silent only because her voice was literally taken from her.  The soundtrack is still good and reminds of certain parts of Bastion's soundtrack, but I wasn't immediately struck by any of the instrumental tracks; there's no In Case of Trouble or Spike in a Rail here, but it's all quite nice regardless, and I'd argue that the vocal tracks are stronger this time around.  Cloudbank is a great setting but I definitely liked Caelondia more.  The color palette feels a lot darker in Cloudbank up until the very end, so it feels like the environments don't quite stand out as much as Bastion's.  But even with that, the art in Transistor is every bit as gorgeous as the art in Bastion and I hope to see a lot more from Jen Zee in the future.
The story's themes are probably the biggest difference between the two games (at least to me) and they're most of the reason I personally like Bastion more even though Transistor is a lot better in a lot of other ways.  But that's undeniably subjective and I'll leave that to you to decide.  Transistor is probably about half as long as Bastion as well, but I don't think it's any shorter than it needed to be.  Long story short, if Bastion was Deus Ex, then Transistor would be Human Revolution; a worthy "sequel" no doubt, but the first is still better (once again, to me).
This game is still absolutely worth your time.  Bastion is as well.  Play both.

Really excellent game.
It's a simple plague simulation game that involves a lot of strategy to try to infect and destroy the world. The infection patterns are quite realistic. To start off, the plagues are fairly simple bacteria, but you unlock crazy plagues (allowing zombies, for example).
Games are pretty quick, running 10-30 minutes from my experience.
You can name your own plague, creating many hilarious phrases to pop up during the game. Stick to singular nouns or proper names and you will get some amazing combinations.
For anyone worried about it being early access, there is more than enough content to keep you busy for a very long time. If the creators hadn't told me it was unfinished, I wouldn't have known. I still look forward to updates (which the developpers are keeping up with), but it's not an incomplete game without them.
On a science note, the only real problem I have with this game is how mutations occur in all the Plague cells at once. In actuality, a mutation would only occur in one instance and then have to spread again from the new patient 0. It makes the "infect everyone then evolve deadly symptoms" tactic to lose some of the magic.

This game is rogue-like. Not rogue-lite. This means it takes no pity on your soul. It means that everything may be going ok and the God of RNG will throw an outlier event at you and one-shot your awesome medium level character just because. That is part of the love-hate I have for this game.
I started playing ADOM approx 15 years ago. It was released 21 years ago on DOS. It is fair to say that this game has replay value and longevity.
With the Steam launch and the NotEye graphics version I find this game to be more approachable as the game provides easier visual clues as to what sort of monsters/items are shown on screen instead of having to remember what is a pink left parenthesis and what is a green at sign.
Overall my score for this game is 4/5 -- I take one away for all the damned one-shots Biskup has reigned down my up-n-coming heros.

10/10 would stumble through half of the wilderness of the Drakalor Chain blinded by mud not realizing I just have to wipe my 'F'ace again.
With more seriousness though, if you're here reading this, I assume you know what a rogue-like (as opposed to a rogue-lite) is, and what that means in terms of a high learning curve and general gameplay difficulty.
I constantly read the Ancardia Wiki (that's the only way I learned about shift+'f'), and I constantly get my rear-end sliced off and handed to me on a plate. Sometimes I forget I have a healing spell or have a wand, sometimes I just die in an early dungeon to falling rocks or fireball traps, and sometimes I make decent progress, let it go to my head and then get in over my head, and get swarmed by things I can't kill. But I keep coming back for more, because that's the kind of masochist I am.
*spoilers*
Someday, I will make it past level 20 before I get into a situation where I'm in over my head.
Someday after that, I will get really lucky and save Khelevaster, but still die in combat a couple floors down when I had an unidentified wand that would have saved my life.
Someday far in the future, I will be a couple steps from godhood, able to put all of ChAoS at my mercy... and then die once again to random rocks falling from the ceiling because I'm low hp from the aftermath.
And perhaps someday, years down the line, I will beat this game. I will sigh, and slump down into a heap... and play again because I still will have only gotten a normal ending.
Because that's the kind of noob and masochist I am, and that's the kind of game this is.
10/10 would die a million times for a one chance at glory again.

I have a certain fondness for puzzle games. Especially ones with an appealing visual aesthetic. So
basically already jumped out at me, specifically because it wooed me with its pretty updated graphics that don’t reflect its mobile origins.
But a puzzle game can’t be measured by its aesthetics alone. No, the puzzles themselves are what we’re here for. And on that front I’m kind of ambivalent towards the title. It reminds me a lot of those old escape-the-room flash games. Specifically of
and
, if you remember those from back in the day. I at least had a lot of fun playing those, but often, you could luck yourself into a solution, while at other times having to make certain leaps in logic that would make the Sierra of the 80’s proud.
The same thing basically applies to
. You’re searching the objects in front of you for solutions to puzzles that the very same objects pose to you. There’s only a handful of items you’re given at any time and if you run out of things to rub them on, it’s time to go down the old-school adventure game route and just double click on anything in the hopes that it triggers something you might have missed. As a result, you can brute force your way through a variety of puzzles with only minimal research.
One instance that immediately springs to mind was a puzzle with two dials, numbered one to five. I had no clue what combination was expected of me, so I just left one dial at one and went through all five options on the second dial. Rinse and repeat by increasing the number on the first dial and just going through all the options on the second one and presto, brute force your way through a puzzle.
Still, there are a handful of solutions that make you feel smart in a way only a puzzle game can make you feel smart. You know, that smug satisfaction you get from doing something completely obvious but being under the impression of being smarter than the developer for figuring it out so quickly. But as a whole, it’s still a bit on the easy side for a puzzle game. It’s nowhere near as hard as
, which I’d still consider the best game of that ilk that I’ve played.
But I can’t give a negative review to a game that I greatly enjoyed playing, even though it barely lasted two and a half hours. I immediately replayed it, because the conglaturations-screen mentioned something about more rooms and I had hoped for some kind of new game+ mode or something, but no, you get five chapters and that’s your lot. Unfortunately, it was referring to the sequels, which means that the story they’ve set up ends on a cliffhanger. And those sequels haven’t made it to PCs yet – if they ever will –  and are only out on mobile devices. But you know what, this has been the first thing in existence that made me buy a mobile game, so it must have done something right.
I still hope they get to port the sequels to PC, but I guess I’ll be happy enough if the third entry gets released on Android some time later, since I don’t have an iOS device. If they do port it though, I hope they don’t include one of their game-breaking bugs in it. There was a puzzle very late in the game that refused to get solved, even though the solution was obvious from just glancing at it. And it had the stupidest reason why it didn’t work: Just because I’ve got a 120Hz monitor and the game runs at the same frame-rate, it broke that puzzle. I had to manually cap the framerate at 60Hz in order to progress, which is really weird behaviour by a game that really has no business tying anything at all to the framerate.
If you’re a fan of puzzle games that don’t need to be completely obscure at all times, I’d say
is worth the investment. Just know that there’s no replay value to be found and that the story – what little there is of one – ends on an unsatisfying cliffhanger.

Dont´t get fooled by an unattractive title or drab gameplay trailers. This game is in fact so much fun!
The core of the game revolves around controlling the boulder around (or better to say down) the map and hitting the enemy gate at the end. Simple right? Actual strategic skill and planning take place very soon, when you are able to build defensive to stop the enemy boulder from hitting your gate (and so do the enemy). There are quite a lot of maps to play, each of them require a bit diffrent style of playing (some of them you need to rush, whereas some of them require careful planning, for example). Now imagine this packed into a satiric story with hillarious art style, animations and historical references and you get extremely enjoyable single player experience.
Now consider everything already mentioned, add another game modes - skee boulder, where you collect points by hitting objects and try to finish faster then your opponent with scoring high multiplier on the target board, or obstacle course, in which you try to get to the end faster avoiding the defensives that AI builds - bring your friend - and prepare to be suprised how much enjoyment will the game give you.
Sure, (almost) nothing is perfect and you will experience some minor bugs (nothing gamechanging, really) or get stucked from to time on the loading screen. Game will get repetitive after some time. But that won´t stop you to come back to laugh over it with your friend or solo.
Worth trying if you are interested in single player, a must-have if you have someone to play with.

Transistor, being the second product of Supergiant Games, is naturally quite a lot like Bastion (spiritual successor, not sequel), except with enough changed around that they didn't make the same game twice.  Transistor's combat is much, much better than Bastion's, which was already passable.  Red as a protagonist...  I like her quite a lot.  Her character shows itself in short snippets at a time and it's clear she's silent only because her voice was literally taken from her.  The soundtrack is still good and reminds of certain parts of Bastion's soundtrack, but I wasn't immediately struck by any of the instrumental tracks; there's no In Case of Trouble or Spike in a Rail here, but it's all quite nice regardless, and I'd argue that the vocal tracks are stronger this time around.  Cloudbank is a great setting but I definitely liked Caelondia more.  The color palette feels a lot darker in Cloudbank up until the very end, so it feels like the environments don't quite stand out as much as Bastion's.  But even with that, the art in Transistor is every bit as gorgeous as the art in Bastion and I hope to see a lot more from Jen Zee in the future.
The story's themes are probably the biggest difference between the two games (at least to me) and they're most of the reason I personally like Bastion more even though Transistor is a lot better in a lot of other ways.  But that's undeniably subjective and I'll leave that to you to decide.  Transistor is probably about half as long as Bastion as well, but I don't think it's any shorter than it needed to be.  Long story short, if Bastion was Deus Ex, then Transistor would be Human Revolution; a worthy "sequel" no doubt, but the first is still better (once again, to me).
This game is still absolutely worth your time.  Bastion is as well.  Play both.

Im sorry but this game is not really good, maybe for 2$ to kill time, but here are some reasons I just dont recommend it:
-It feels too much like a Super Meat Boy clone. The double jump spins just like a certain character in the game, the levels are filled with saws to increase difficulty, and the player is square.
-Speaking of the player, who even is he? The game doesn't really define who he is, for all I know, he is some Tiny Minecraft Wizard ripped out of an iPhone app.
-This game has more achievements than Zup! 1. I hope thats not the selling point.
-Said achievements get in the way of my view. I couldn't see myself or the exit sometimes because it would be completely blocked by 2 or more achievements.
-The Game Expects you to know every level by heart at first glance. Why does the level have to start the second it loads? This is especially a problem because the whole game revolves around going fast, I at least want a "Press jump to continue" preview before just jumping into it.
-The game is too short. Only 90 levels, and the very last one is filler.
-3/4 of the soundtrack are bland and barely differ from eachother, and the 1/4th of it is used during sections where it doesn't fit at all.
-Said music poorly syncs up with the timer.
-Both "Challenge" and "Options" seem locked but theyre not. Seriously, why would you ever have an unlocked option blend into the background? This is especially a problem for newcomers that havent seen how the game ACTUALLY locks things.
-"Challenge" mode is one big "I Wanna" needle game. Fangames for "I Wanna Be The Guy" are meh in themself but the fact that you have to rip them off for another selling point just seemed weak to me.
-There isnt even a level editor. The game seems simple enough for one, and it hurts replayability to not have one. Plus, you went crazy in the challenge levels; is it my turn yet?
-You had to advertise the game on my profile. I know you want to raise attention for it, but that doesn't seem like the way to do it.
Overall, I did not really like this game, and definitely would not recommend it to anyone who wants to play something great. It just... flopped hard.

For anyone worried about it being early access, there is more than enough content to keep you busy for a very long time. If the creators hadn't told me it was unfinished, I wouldn't have known. I still look forward to updates (which the developpers are keeping up with), but it's not an incomplete game without them.
On a science note, the only real problem I have with this game is how mutations occur in all the Plague cells at once. In actuality, a mutation would only occur in one instance and then have to spread again from the new patient 0. It makes the "infect everyone then evolve deadly symptoms" tactic to lose some of the magic.

Rock of Ages is a charming, humorous, and highly original game.
The basic premise is this: you control a boulder rolling across a twisted battlefield of ramps, obstacles, and enemy traps. Your aim is to destroy your opponent's gate.
As you destroy your opponent's defenses, you accumulate money to spend on building upgrades. These upgrades can be either single-use power-ups for your boulder to make it stronger or more deadly. Or, you can spend the money on defenses like elephants, dynamite, and catapults that can knock your opponent's boulder off the map. You get to place these obstacles wherever you want on the map.
So, on one hand RoA is like a wacky driving game, but on the other it is like a tower defense game. The balance between these two is perfect -- it is fast-paced and really executes the central mechanics well.
Where the game really shines is the campaign and art direction inspired by Art History. Each level has you progress from ancient Greece, across Europe and through various artistic styles. In Italy, the levels have a High Renaissance art theme. There is Rococo in France and a Romantic (Goya-inspired) theme in Spain. And each level unlocks a new type of defense (dynamite, flying machines, ). for you to place in your. Perhaps the only issue is difficulty: it may be too easy as the AI is good at placing defenses but not so great at driving its boulder. But if you want more of a challenge there is always the multiplayer or the time trial mode (with scoreboards), so the game does not get old.
Basically, if you like the look of the game from the trailers -- get it! It delivers.

This is one of the most frustrating games I have ever played... ( BUT I LOVE IT ! )
EDIT: July 2015...I bought an Xbox wired controller just for this game, and what a difference! Even makes driving easier and can now fight much better. I strongly recommend playing this game with an XBox controller, wired or wireless if you are set up for it.
There are several  issues that need attention to make this game playable on a PC from a ported console game. Using a keyboard and mouse for some aspects of this game make it difficult to play on PC, driving being on top of the list. If you intend to play on PC, you may want to get a controller because it is quite obvious that this game was intended to be played using a controller. I say this because a keyboard is either 'on' or 'off' and makes things extremely difficult while a controller has some linear movement, keep this in mind.
Playing this game is definitely for the player who has real good keyboard skills and a gamer keyboard and mouse. I am admittedly an older player who loves to play good games and I would like to enjoy this game without this kind of frustration.  Despite this, here is my 'review' of Sleeping Dogs to this point and regardless of my frustration level, will keep it neutral.
PROS:
GRAPHICS: One word, Gorgeous! With the HD texture pack, this game is visually wonderful on screen, and you get a genuine feel of the story and atmosphere. The models and textures are some of the best I have seen for a game of this genre. Up till now, SR3 and SR4 were on top of my list, keeping in mind I said a game of this genre. I would love to be able to re-texture some of the clothes and hope that we will be able to do so some time in the future.
VOICE ACTING: Doesn’t get better then this,  voice overs can make or break a game and in this instance, the characters are believable and and you can sense the personality of each.
MUSIC: Great variety of music and really adds to the atmosphere of the game. It would be great to play the music when out  on foot exploring the sites.
STORYLINE and WRITING: Compelling. I got drawn right into my character's story and what he is doing or trying to do. Frankly, for this reason alone I will try and continue the game. It is rare that I can bond with my character and I have with Wei. Later on you can see him start to change and almost feel the internal conflicts he is having. I know many disagree, but I for one feel that the story and writing are excellent for a game.
ANIMATIONS: WOW! Good stuff here and wonderfully done, fluid and believable, when you pull off a good move in a fight, makes you feel like you really did something. I would like to see a 'walk' option rather then Wei jogging all the time when out exploring, if there is one I haven't found it. There is one pet peeve I have and that is if Wei is wearing an outfit and he is barefoot (wearing the GSP outfit as an example) in a fight, or if he kneels down or is in a move that requires him to bend down, his foot goes into the ground. That is, his toes go into the ground. They don't flex or bend as they should. A small detail. The modelers and animators need to pay more attention to details such as this.
CLOTHING and ACCESSORIES: Personally, I am not one who cares about 'outfits'. But I have to say that this game offers many and all are very well done. The diffuse textures, normals mapping and specular really show on the clothing and are a visual treat in game. I would like to see the ability to breakdown some of these 'set outfits' such as the GSP outfit and use the items separately, that is, have the option to 'mix and match'. An example would be, using the red GSP shorts with a hoody and red tennies. I for one don't care if a clothing item gives me a bonus in a skill or not. That said, the separate clothing items and outfits are excellent. By the Wei?...who ever came up with those boxers? What were you drinking? Those will be the first thing I hope to re texture. I have seen screen shots of some yellow beach shorts but have not found them, it would have been nice to have some shorts for Wei to wear.
DLC clothing: Zodiac Tournament. Once you get through this, you get two outfits, both with good looking shorts especially the Ikoze yellow shorts. Problem is, it is an 'outfit' again, you can't use the shorts by them selves. But the real thing that ticked me off is when wearing both outfits you are barefoot. Fine by me, barefoot is good, but when you walk anywhere you hear the sound of walking in shoes?...what! Spoiled the whole thing for me, what was QC doing?
Then to add for more confusion...and this is actually funny, remember...you're in Hong Kong which used to be a British Commonweatlh so drive on the OTHER side of the road!  To add to the keyboard issue, the camera has a nasty habit of swinging around 180 degrees facing the other direction during your driving or if you swing your car or bike around.In my game, Wei is using the slowest bike available and for a car, Wei is using the Bisai or Smart car equivalent. Why? Least I  can drive them...somewhat. In Saints Row 3, I can drive like no ones concern. I can power slide, take corners and keep most vehicles in SR3 (especially the bikes) under control. The driving commands in this game are almost identical, yet, because they move so fast, the keyboard commands usually amplify the command and it is one crash after another, you have to try and think ahead if possible. If any of you played the first Saints Row (PC) and tried to drive in that game? This is a close second on the list. EDIT: Dumb luck was with me....moving on.
Other minor Cons, this game should have a difficulty level setting. Just for the sake of the story itself, being able to just play the game at a slower and easier pace, and for those hard core folks...let them set it for that. This game was made for console, so the keyboard commands for some moves is complex and can only use a few of them. Not a game breaker, but it is difficult. Having a broken finger on my left had makes the 'Q' key and 'left shift' almost impossible to use, but you can remap some keys. It would be nice to take screen shots without the HUD, I am not aware of a way to do this if there is. Lastly, the GPS is not reliable as far as taking you to the right location during a mission. I have had this happen many times in game already. It took me two hours to figure this out on a side mission 'Cheaters Never Prosper Part 3'  There is a short cut to save time and when you do get there...look for a window. I don't think that qualifys as a 'spoiler'.
CONCLUSION: If you are going to try this on PC, fair warning. Not for the novice player and especially if you have a lack of patient or short tempered. This game is challenging. Despite my various frustrations, I like this game...very much. A visual treat for the eyes, great story and one can easily bond with your character. This game does not work well on a keyboard and mouse and at this point never will. Strictly my opinion. But I will say it is worth the money and I can go even further and say that Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition has a replay value for sure. Is this my favorite game (of this genre)? No, because of the technical issues, SR3 is still on top of my list. I appreciate the hard work and many talents that went into the development of this game, but as usual, most games have a priority for the console market and a conversion or port to PC only makes this game suffer from that process. It is sad that game developers get hung up on the console market as they do and ingnore the PC folks as a last option.
On my scale of 1 to 10....I give this an 8.    A wonderful game, but Wei too many technical glitches. I hope we get to see Wei again.

I got this game during a Steam sale sometime ago for about $5 so I wasn’t really expecting much. Call of Juarez: Gunslinger’s story is one of revenge and a lot of bullets.
A LOT of bullets.
You play Silas Greaves as he makes his way through the west, hunting down the men who killed his brothers and left him for dead and getting into fights with legendary outlaws like Jesse James and Butch Cassidy. Gameplay is your standard shooter. You’re get a pistol, a rifle, a shotgun and some dynamite and earn experience with kills and finding secrets. In my playthrough I decided to use dual pistols and a rifle and dynamite. Didn’t like the way the shotgun handled.
The AI in this game has almost human like accuracy to the point that if you can see an outlaw, they will probably hit you in the first or second shot. There are also special enemies shut as the shotgunners, armored shotgunners and Gatling guns. The boss fights can be separated into two categories: standard gunfights and duels. And this is where I started getting frustrated.
The mechanics of the duel was so INFURIATING to the point I literally stopped playing this game for ~2 years. And as you progressed in the story it would just get more and more complicated until the last one in the game.
Otherwise, the story was great, the music on spot, the voice acting decent, and the environment was so gosh darn beautiful. And the ending satisfying.
There is an arcade mode to the game but I didn’t touch it.
All in all a decent in the middle of the road game. Pick it up at full price if you’re a fan of the series or do what I did and wait until it goes on sale.

I love this game! All the Final Fantasy characters and monsters! You don't need a new character to play a different class/job! The music is amazing! The story quests are easy to track, and put you at the center as the Hero of Light. Everyone is fighting for the same casue, no good vs bad, so you don't have to worry about being in the wrong place and getting smashed by another player.
There is pvp arena's for those who like to. Plenty of things to do, like hunts, treasure maps, the Hildibrand story line, Chocobo racing. Speeking of Chocobo's, you get one early on for a mount, and it doubles as a companion to fight with you.
The Duty finder is helpful to get into instances when your friends or Free Company members are not around. It also looks to other servers to find players, as well as being a cross-platform with the PlayStation version. Thats right, controllers and KB/M playing side by side
Your are rewarded for your total subscription time, no need to pay every month if you don't want to, you still get the rewards when you have meet the amount of days payed (exp. your first 30 days payed earns a reward, you can not play for a year, and when you pay again, you get the 60 days reward. After a few, it starts to take more time between rewards).
Fighting in this game requires you to move to not be hit by mobs attacks. Even as a caster, you must pay attention to what is coming your way, and sometimes it is just a matter of knowing where to stand to get spells off before you have to move again.
Everything in this game looks great, the characters and equipment, mobs and bosses, zones and backdrops, and of course, the cutscenes! Oh and the spells and ability!!
There is even a Limit Break system while in instances. A shared guage that builds up to 3 levels, and the different class groups (exp. casters, healer, tank, dps) have a different limit break. A level 3 healer limit break will raise all dead party members, casters cast meteor. Time it right and save the day!
Crafting, almost forgot crafting! You don't just click a button and wait for a bar to fill. You have skills to use as a crafter. Skill rotation helps determine output quality. Plus quests for your craft, and the gear just for crafting. Some of the crafting gear is also styled around what you are crafting.
Gathering jobs are  miner, botanist, and fisher
Free companies have houses that provide a place to grow crops for cooking or feed for your chocobo, training dummys to practice your rotation, and a few vendors for repairing equipment, buying regents, or just selling junk.
All of these things (and so much more) tie together wonderfully, and give (me at least) a sense of place in the grand scheme of things.
This, compared to one other mmo I played a lot of, is a huge difference. I just didn't feel the other game gave me any drive to "do great things" other than to complete a quest, or run a instance for the fun of it. I never felt like I was part of the Big Picture. Kind of hard to put into words, and maybe I just did not play with the "right" players, and I never made it to end game raids.
Over all, FFXIV is Best MMO I have ever played, and still crave to play!

A basic membership is only around 10 euroes for 3 (I repeat - 3) months.
I'd say that's a fair price (again, it's 3 months).
Included in the 3 months of hunting any animal you want, you
also get access to all reserves and unlimited basic ammo.
You might need to buy a weapon that is meant for the animal
you're hunting, but who doesn't like weapons nowadays ;)
You can also buy one of the packs on Steam or their site which,
besides containing weapons, also have memberships in them.
I hope these 2 cents were any help for you.

Highly recommended, even if puzzle games are not your favourite. The Room is beautiful and elaborate, but not too complicated. You will rarely find yourself stumped for very long over a puzzle, and even if you do, you can use a hint to help you out. This might make the game seem too easy, but there are so many smaller puzzles that constantly move you along onto the next one that you won't notice it. You are presented with various devices that you are trying to open, in order to find out what the cryptic messages, which you've been left, are all about. The design of these devices is brilliant, with a lot of little mechanisms and clockworks that you need to make work, hidden panels you need to uncover and keyholes you need to find keys for. The HD textures, the option to zoom in on various sections and look at them from different angles, and the fact you need to use the movement of your mouse to turn keys and open drawers make the objects you interact with seem real, almost as if they're in front of you, and that makes them strangely inviting, you can't help but want to explore them to uncover their secrets. The game is not very long, and there's not much of a story in it, but it's a great game to spend a few hours with.

Extraordinary game.
This game started as an ASCII roguelike and pretty small, now it is graphical and but not pretty big. It's colossal.
First of all before you start the game you have to understand that the game has kind of a learning curve, there will be a lot of deaths caused by things you did not expect. If you especially hate starting over, the game is not for you. I hate starting over too but not enough to deter me from this masterpiece. There are so many race/class combinations to give you a new kind of game that you are mostly just excited to try again with different tools - if your high elf wizard died early to some trivial door trap, start over with a troll beastfighter. Now you maybe cannot read but hey, the trap that killed the flimsy elf only tickles you. Maybe use those spellbooks you find as missiles now? And if you die again perhaps try a more stealthy approach as a gnomish assassin. You get the idea.
The monster library is endless and the game story is intriguing, I dunno how anyone can have the intelligence and creativity required to make this game happen but I am glad someone did. It's a very complex and unforgiving RPG - to be able to beat the game honestly you will need a lot of time, brains, patience, nerves and also some luck. ADOM is _not for everyone_ but I still recommend if you like RPG's and a BIG challenge. TIP> use the internet for information, there is a good wiki. EXTRA TIP> to make the most out of the game, disable all form of game saving and go for the true ADOM experience.

This is not a review. I am just letting people know to disregard any negative reviews concerning keyboard commands and key bindings.  I just played a bit and used my mouse for the entire session.  There are many key commands if you just want to use a keyboard, but ALL of the keyboard commands are listed right next to the written commands.  You do not have to memorize tons of keyboard commands to play ADOM. There's even floating text windows that appear when you mouse over certain things.
ADOM is now streamlined and very user friendly!  I almost didn't purchase this game because of the negative reviews concerning the multitude of keyboard commands. So if you were on the fence about purchasing this game but was worried about having to memorize many keyboard command, it's not true any longer.  You can use your mouse for "most" of the commands.  I never needed to use the keyboard once...
Just by my brief session with the game, I can assure you that this is a quality game made with a lot of love!  There are many options covering all aspects of the game.  The UI is basic, but again has many options and is also mouse driven.  This game has been steamlined and looks to be one of the best roguelikes I have played.  So far I would recommend this game, but I have not played it long enough to really review it.
So far the game has runs silky smooth on my computer, but crashed when I quit the game.

I really enjoyed SD:DF. Take the mechanics that made the GTA games fun and combine it with an edgy and interesting storyline set in modern day Hong Kong.
Wei Shen is a Chinese-American returning home after many years with a chip on his shoulder regarding the corrupt and powerful triad that messed with his family long ago. The Sun On Yee, the game begins as Wei, now an officer of the law infiltrates the Sun On Yee through an old friend Jackie and the story just continues to build from there.
You are given the ability to roam free in the large city of Hong Kong with side quests litered everywhere. From progresing the Police quest line, to the (main) Triad story there are quests to increase your face (reputation), unlock new cars through street races, street brawls, and many variets there of.
To add additional flavour you can unlock additional skills and attributes depending on how many side quests you have done which can turn you into a martial arts, asskicking, gun welding unstopable machine.
Highly recommend, I played it in small-chunks after work and it kept me thoroughly entertained.

This open world, third person action feels a lot like Saints Row with a more serious note. There's blood and scenarios are merciless.
The game is mainly fought with fists, but guns are available on select missions. Some situations are crazy, specially the bike races - NPCs will ram the flag girl at the start. The rest of the way, they will go crazy on you.
Car physics are not easy to control. Ramming (button) can also be used while going sideways, which could be exploited when racing or driving fast in general. If you think races are difficult, just race later after you have the prototype car - then races can get funny.
Movement is also awkward (I am using a mouse and keyboard setup). Camera angles in any mode (car / bike / foot) is hard to control, and you can't look too far up (which I find weird and sometimes irritating). On foot, turning is not as precise or quick as in other games (or even compared to real life). This can be frustrating in fighting... until you realize that you can use a car or bike to win them. The game is probably programmed more towards using a gamepad.
Soundtrack is good. I only started to get tired of them after more than 30 hours of playing.
Graphics are good, but sometimes can't keep up when driving fast. It only required 50% at 750MHz from my GTX 770, so I think many gamers can play this game.
Sound effects are amazing. It has perfect use of audio positioning and environmental sounds are there. Though, at times, motor boat and water splashing sounds were skipping (not produced) for a few seconds in intervals.
The story is alright, and the story telling is fine. Events can sometimes get weird. You can't grab who you're chasing (even when you're already touching them) until you've reached the end where you'll fight a group or they simply give up; but at the same time, as part of the game rule, you can't be too far away from them (again, in a chase scenario).
This game scored a 5/10 for me, but I'm labeling it as a Recommend for the story telling and overall good fun. The controls is the biggest let-down as I was forced to play with a hard to control character until I finish it. The game has a serious note, but remember that this is a game and better just take full advantage of what you can do to avoid character control, camera and other possible frustrations it could give you.

Not much I can really say about Borderlands that hasn't been said already: it's your standard run-gun-loot FPS with a fun art style, the replay value is high, most of the dialogue aged like milk in the sun, and the game got additional content released over a span of a whopping eight months after its initial release. I can probably make a few (a lot of) jabs at the plot if I want to nitpick, and Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode definitely isn't nice to casual/leisure players, but in all it's a solidly-built game that does its job well and remains fun while doing it. If you don't like replaying things (you can only reach max level by replaying the main story 2-3+ times, depending on which DLC you have), then you'll get about 35 hours total out of the base game (and a solid 20-25 hours atop that with all the DLC).
I'm writing this review in 2017, five years after its release, and I can confirm that the multiplayer scene is still alive as well. As a matter of fact, in the 400+ hours I've spent playing this game, a good half of it comes from joining the games of complete strangers, helping others, sharing loot, and -- to get cheesy for a second -- making friends. Once you feel confident with a character (or even just right off the bat!) I can't recommend trying out the multiplayer enough. By no means is it mandatory (not until UVHM at least, if you're like me and bad at games), but it really changes the way the game plays.

Oh, you were looking for reviews for this game? Then you have come to the wrong place. Oh, you were looking for a recipe for cabbage rolls? Then you've come to the right place!
Ingredients:
1 pound ground chuck 2 eggs, beaten 1 small onion, chopped 2 3/4 tablespoons regular rice, uncooked 1/2 teaspoon salt 1/4 teaspoon pepper 1/4 teaspoon garlic powder 1 large cabbage 1 medium onion, chopped 1/2 cup shortening, melted 1 (1-pound) soup bone 1 (14 1/2-ounce) can whole tomatoes, undrained and chopped 1 (8-ounce) can tomato sauce 1 cup plus 2 1/2 tablespoons firmly packed brown sugar Dash of sour salt.
Step 1
Combine ground chuck, eggs, 1 small chopped onion, rice, salt, pepper, and garlic powder, mixing well. Set aside.
Step 2
Turn cabbage, core side up. Using a sharp knife, make an incision across the base of the outermost leaf. Gently peel away the leaf. Repeat this process until leaves can no longer be removed without tearing.
Step 3
Make additional incisions around the base of the next outermost leaves. Place cabbage, stem side up, in a colander. Pour boiling water over cabbage until leaves can be easily removed. Repeat procedure until all leaves have been removed.
Step 4
Place 1 tablespoon meat mixture in the base of a cabbage leaf. Roll leaf jellyroll fashion until the mid-section is reached. Fold left side of leaf inward, and roll up remaining length of the leaf. Carefully stuff in the open end, using fingertips. Repeat with remaining meat mixture and cabbage leaves.
Step 5
Sauté remaining chopped onion in shortening in a large Dutch oven. Add soup bone and tomatoes; stir gently.
Step 6
Alternate layers of cabbage rolls and tomato sauce over sautéed onion and tomatoes. Do not stir. Add water to cover. Cover and cook over medium heat 30 minutes.
Step 7
Add brown sugar and sour salt; stir gently. Cover and cook over medium heat 1 hour. Uncover and cook 1 hour.
Step 8
Remove cabbage rolls from cooking liquid, and place on a warm serving platter. Serve immediately.

Picked up on impulse based on the aesthetic, alone.
As of right now only Titan mode is available but I don't have any problems with this, Titan mode seems like it would be my favorite even with more play modes available.  Titan mode has 2 teams of players doing battle at the feet of giant Titans.  As the Titans do battle one will die at the hands of the other and begin to march on the fallen Titans base, fighting its way through defensive walls and turret fire.  The team being attacked must focus on killing the Titan before it reaches their base and ends the round.  If both Titans are downed the game switches momentum toward the "creep spawn" phase, where small NPC creatures begin to spawn around the edges of the map.  Kill the creeps to power up your Titan for the next Titan battle, keeping an eye out for the Golden Creep for extra power.
The game starts you out with 6 available loadout slots, and a basic arsenal consisting of a sword, assault rifle, shotgun, sniper rifle, grenade, and deployable turret.  More weapon options open up almost immediately as you begin to play and spend currency earned in game (no pay to unlocks) to unlock and craft new weapons.  Weapons range from Titan killing giant swords to swords that heal your after a kill, to new versions of the sniper rifle and a few launcher weapons.
Once you've chosen your loadout and begin the match there is still some customization and and specialization to consider.  At any time during the match you can hit the M key and open the armor crafting menu.  Each round you start out as a naked block man, completely capable of getting kills and winning the round, only without the bonuses and negative effects that come with the armor sets.  Armor bonuses range from increased Titan damage, ability to double jump, increased run speed, to increased damage and more.  Now that you've entered the match, crafted a piece of armor, and got a kill you can pick up the power orb dropped by the enemy, evolving your weapon and increasing your power until you are killed.  For example, if you are wielding the sword weapon and grab a power up orb, you are now dual wielding swords and look like a bit of a badass.  Power it up further to wield two flame covered swords and strike fear in the hearts of anyone you can sneak up behind.
So, grab a load out, craft your armor, kill the enemy, power up your weapons, and defend your Titan until it's time to creep farm and make the final push on the enemy base!

I probably should have left this review on the original Sleeping Dogs game, but here we go anyways. Probably contains spoilers so consider yourself warned.
\\ Story:
The story is an amazingly tangled mess of triad fighting and personal choices. It is going to break you down inside and i was left a crying mess throughout the game. It should be said that i am very easily attached to, and affected by things. The wedding, where the oh so sad love song always plays before♥♥♥♥♥♥is going down, Uncle Po, and not to forget the most horrible death of them all (to me at least), Jackie.. The last had me bawling my eyes out because the story and character had sucked me in (and i kinda had a minor crush on Edison Chen). Anyhow, the story is solid, A+.
\\ Gameplay and graphics:
The improved graphics are stunning, and almost killed my computer because i was overly confident while choosing the ultra high settings. It was definitely worth the upgrade and it was even more immersive this time around than the first. I sat for eight hours the first day and ten hours the second to finish the game and i've never gotten so sucked into anything before. The vibrant colors and the city itself feels even more realistic now. I love the random encounters with people selling art and birds and whatnot too. And the food looks so amazingly good i just keep drooling every time i look at it.
The only thing that annoyed me was towards the end of the game when the car valet kept saying he was busy and couldnt deliver to you, but apart from that i have nothing negative to say.
Easily one of my favorite games and one of the best i've played so far.

One of the most fun shooters I've played in the past five years, mostly because of its simplicity in combination with a dark but fantasized tale of a bounty hunter looking for vengance and money (with no shortage of slow mo).
To start off, the visual choice the team went for the cutscenes really gives the idea of this being an old story told by an old man, recounting the most significant parts of his adventures. It really gives the feel of, in the terms the game would describe, reading an old dime novel with illustrations to push forward the scenes.
While the story isn't deep or rich, it has quite some twists that can throw you off guard, and the humor of the game you're playing being a story told by our hero shows up in the form of deus ex-machina style paths and ladders showing up out of nowhere, as well as slowdowns in the game itself, or straight up cuts or rewinds midgame as the bounty hunter tries to get his facts straight with the people he's telling the story to.
There are a small handful of characters to be sure, but they all add to the experience with their wit and sarcasm, and are really enjoyable, especially when they accidentally mess with the bounty hunter's story by inputting what they remember.
Gameplay wise, it is a solid 8 out of solid, the aiming doesn't feel obtrusive, and most of the guns can kill the outlaws you fight in one to two shots, unless you're really off and are shooting them in the leg. The Rifle especially feels overpowered at times, until you realize you have to reload it all the time, and then that the standard SHOTGUN has the same range as the six shooter and is FAR more overpowered with just a couple of skills. I would love to elaborate on Concentration and Sense of Death, but all you need to know is the former slows down time and highlights enemies and explosives (while adding an extra point bonus), while the latter allows you the chance to keep from dying by dodging the bullet fired at you, but you have to wait for it to become available again, while the former you have to charge by killing♥♥♥♥♥♥
Yes, sometimes the hitreg feels wonky or even like it screws you over at times, but gunplay is satisfying nonetheless. As for the unique dueling gimmick the game brings, it actually takes a lot of skill, focus, and high reaction time to get quick kills on your enemy while maintaining your honor (by drawing after they draw). At the end the game throws a curveball by pitting you against two others in a Mexican Standoff, but it feels awesome killing guys after drawing second.
Progression in the game is fairly basic, kill things to level up, and kill a lot of things with a really big multiplier and accurate shots to level up an INSANE amount. The game fairly rewards you for doing well, and rewards you EXCESSIVELY for being a god at the game. You can get all the skills by your second playthrough at the earliest though, as the game is really short, but if you are smart with your combos, that proves to not be a problem at all.
There are only 6 guns you'll ever use in the game (8 if you include the insanely powerful Gatling and the "Why is this even here?" sawed off rifle, I am not including dynamite as it's basically just a grenade reskin you can shoot midair), and they all are unique and work differently, having specific purposes for specific situations. The Rifle and Ranger are for long range high damage, with low fire speed, the Shotguns are for close range fights you can end in a single blast, the six shooter and quickshooter are for midrange combat, with balanced preformance and speed over firepower respectively. The sawed off rifle, I just don't get why it exists, but maybe someone can help answer that for me.
The levels will take you places, lots of random but interesting locales, such as a bar, a bank, a speeding train, and even a ghost town filled with (cough) abandoned buildings and fog.
Speaking of fog, it is usually used by developers to help increase the framerate that a game plays at. In this game, it runs at a fast framerate regardless, there was never a jitter or hiccup in the game's frames for the entire time I played, and I'm playing on a subpar desktop. One small issue that was recurring was the Steam Overlay versus the game itself. On occasion, when I'd open Steam Overlay to message a friend, the game would act as if I was clicked out of it. The cursor nor the camera in game would respond, but the buttons on the keyboard worked just fine. The easiest way i found to fix it was to simply alt+tab the game then bring it back up, and everything worked just fine again. It's annoying, but not game breaking.
There was only one time the game had a loading problem, where it was taking a full 4 minutes to load the level when it was originally only taking 20 or so seconds. Simply quitting out when I could and restarting the game fixed it and I never had the problem since.
Back to the game itself. The game introduces the Nuggets of Truth, a collectible that if you take the time to view it, will tell you a fact about specific places, people, events, or items you come across in the game. There are a significant amount in the game, and while some are easy to find, the rest you will probably need a guide to locate, as they are well hidden off the beaten path. The other modes, Arcade and Duels, are just as they sound. Arcade Mode places you in an area in the game, and tasks you with killing all the people. The more you kill in a bigger combo in a faster time gets you a better score, and if you kill everyone in one huge chain (the placements and pathing of the level always allows you to do this), you are basically guaranteed a 3 star rating, and if you manage to do all 10 levels like this, you get an achievement and serious credit for taking the time and having the patience to accomplish the feat.
Dueling is by far the most difficult mode, unless you are REALLY good with honorably killing the guys without dying horribly. There is an achievement for killing all 15 guys honorably (thankfully there's no stipulation where you cannot die yourself) as well, each fight getting noticabally harder to complete than the last.
In conclusion, if you can get this game on sale, buy it, definitely. If it won't be on sale for a long time, you may just want to pay the 15$ anyways, it's a great game that you're sure to enjoy, if not for the story or the locations or the characters, just for the thrill of slaughtering an entire army of outlaws with a pair of revolvers and some dynamite.

After spending hundreds of hours loged in game (and even more before I started using the steam client version), I have to say this game is my obsession. Everything about it oozes quality from the brilliant music, to the way all the classes work so well together to the storyline that pulls you in. The game as enough pull for casual players and enough grinding and raiding for the hardcore. Best Final Fantasy ever? Probabily not, that still sits as VI for me, but the game's pretty damn close.

So after almost putting 1000 hours into the game, here is the lay down.
- First MMO that I've actually put effort into.
- Easy to get into and the EXP curve is not harsh. (Doing the main quest alone, with some side quest and you can reach the Level limit no problem) (Leveling up other classes though takes time)
- I'm enjoying the story, as do many others, though if you don't want to, it is all skippable.
- You only need to make one character because that one character can be any-class as you can switch on the fly. First you must get to level 15 to one of the classes then you can switch to whatever else you want if you don't feel like it suits your role you want to be. Or you can be like me and level up all the classes. (I main Monk)
- Want to just be a crafter? There is that too and they make money (gil persay) if you join a good FC willing to support the mats (materials you need).
- End-game content is very captivating if you want to raid. There are many raid groups always looking to fill spots if that is what you seek. It is enjoyable and worthwhile. Trust me, it takes a lot of wipes (sometimes one or if your raid team is excellent, only one try), but its feel good.
- Great community
- Square Enix will not disappoint. They always have something awesome planned for this.
- Heavensward Expansion!
Would highly recommend trying it out first. It might not be for everyone, but if you like Final Fantasy (and this game as soo many tibbits to its other titles, ex. Void Ark (FF5) , Crystal Tower (FF3), Gilgamesh, and others), you will enjoy this MMO.
June, 14th, 2016 Update.
So with the Heavensward Expansion out and it being on the current patch of 3.3 at this time, I just want to give an update. Ok, I don't write reviews very often but I felt the need to on this game.
I was skeptical about theHunter at first due to the overwhelming number of negative reviews on Steam. I weighed it out and thought "well, it's free", so I wasn't out anything by giving it a shot...and I'm glad I did.
I like hunting. In real life, I love hunting. Unfortunately, I can only do so certain times in the year...and this game fills that void. This isn't a "game" in a traditional sense, it is practically a hunting simulator and it is done
.
The negative reviews all come from people who hate micro-transactions and expect completely free things. The game itself is free. You can hunt whitetail deer, european rabbits, and pheasant any time, along with two other animals which are selected/rotate on a weekly basis. Right now it's black bear and bison I think. If you like the free stuff, you can
by buying a membership, or different guns, or licenses...whatever floats your boat. I personally bought the Trailrunner membership for $49.99
. I normally spend $50 or so on any other game I play, I have absolutely no problem spending the same for something I truly enjoy. It nets me a year of hunting any animal, plus all sorts of other goodies like weapons, outfits, treestands, etc.
To summarize: This is not a game for just anyone, and it's definitely not fast-paced. It's hunting. But it doesn't deserve negative reviews based solely on how the developers have chosen to take their profit from it. The game is free. The REAL game is going to cost you a bit if you so choose.

For those of you who don't know. ADOM is (originally) an extremely hard, ascii based rouge-like which has been around on multiple formats since the late 90's. Personally I think it's by far the best traditional rogue-like, and I've tried a few over the years.
Even with what would easily be over five hundred hours playing this game over the last 15+ years or so, first on Amiga, then on Windows. I've only ever completed this game once, and even then I was cheating by backing up my save file. Something which is uneccesary in this Steam version, as there is the option to disable perma-death in exchange for a big reduction in points. There are also options to selct optimal birth month, stat rolls, etc. Which saves a LOT of time if you play ADOM as I do with a specific charachter class in mind.
The graphics and sounds actually add quite a bit to the gameplay.  Especially the sound which allows you to hear if you've hit or missed or been hit. And graphics for example; It's much easier to locate the tiny girl in Terinyo when you can see a graphic of a tiny girl instead of a red "t" which under the Windows version could look almost identical to an orange "t" on some monitors.
For those who are unfamiliar with ADOM, even if familiar with other rogue-likes such as Angband, the keyboard configuration will seem a bit alien. But the list of keybindings is readily available in-game by pressing "?" as well as on the title screen, so it shouldn't take too long to get comfortable. For those familiar with ADOM, you'll be pleased to know that it's exactly the same.
Oh, and I don't know if I'm just being distracted by the beautiful hand-pixelled graphics and atmospheric music, but it seems to be just a little bit harder that the text-based ADOM, especially the small mountain cave. Getting a character over level ten can be an achivement.
Is it worth paying fifteen bucks to play a game you can get for free without the graphics/sound? Hell yeah! The only thing I can think of which is wrong with it is the text can be a bit small, but then the display has more lines, so it evens out I guess.
