Alright, so I thought that I would make the actual review right now due to the release of it being availible on Steam Early Access. And to be honest, my opinion still stands.
At this point? Save your money. Trust me. - My inital thought.
When I wrote this down and made it public for you to see, this was during the Second Beta Weekend that they had where people could get a code and activate it on steam, and I obviously took part in this.
When I first played Minimum, I instantly liked the visuals that they had to offer. The simplistic design is something you will either love or hate. I personally love them, but with the lack of detail it would be understanding why you would not like the visuals.
Now when I first started to play Minimum, I did not know what to think. The game just throws you in without no explanation what so ever, which could be a problem for many new players coming into the game. Without you looking up or knowing ahead of time you would have no clue on what the armor does, or may not even know that it exists! A huge downfall.
Balancing is also a major problem. As you get kills with your chosen weapon, they level up becoming more powerful and more unique. The problem with this is that one or two people on the enemy team can kill you in one shot while you try to kill them with a whole clip. A huge problem.
At this point, there is only one game mode, that being Titan. Titan being a Team DeathMatch which has an emphasis on killing an enemy titan to get your titan to move up and destroy There titan factory. (Or whatever its called.) You can also power up your titan by killing creep which spawn when both titans are destroyed, adding a MOBA element to a 3rd person shooter, which is quite unique in itself. But that being the only game mode, it can get quite boring really fast.
At this point, I still say do not buy this game unless you like the concept. However, I would still say that you wait for new game modes, new guns and new blueprints to be added to the game.

So after almost putting 1000 hours into the game, here is the lay down.
- First MMO that I've actually put effort into.
- Easy to get into and the EXP curve is not harsh. (Doing the main quest alone, with some side quest and you can reach the Level limit no problem) (Leveling up other classes though takes time)
- I'm enjoying the story, as do many others, though if you don't want to, it is all skippable.
- You only need to make one character because that one character can be any-class as you can switch on the fly. First you must get to level 15 to one of the classes then you can switch to whatever else you want if you don't feel like it suits your role you want to be. Or you can be like me and level up all the classes. (I main Monk)
- Want to just be a crafter? There is that too and they make money (gil persay) if you join a good FC willing to support the mats (materials you need).
- End-game content is very captivating if you want to raid. There are many raid groups always looking to fill spots if that is what you seek. It is enjoyable and worthwhile. Trust me, it takes a lot of wipes (sometimes one or if your raid team is excellent, only one try), but its feel good.
- Great community
- Square Enix will not disappoint. They always have something awesome planned for this.
- Heavensward Expansion!
Would highly recommend trying it out first. It might not be for everyone, but if you like Final Fantasy (and this game as soo many tibbits to its other titles, ex. Void Ark (FF5) , Crystal Tower (FF3), Gilgamesh, and others), you will enjoy this MMO.

I bought this game because I loved Bastion. Its witty narrator and gorgeous soundtrack were simply amazing. So I was quite surprised that none of the things that made Bastion a great game are present in Transistor.
- The narrtor came off as a bland and diatribe. In fact, the voice acting of all characters was really lifeless. I realize the city is rotten and dying, but having a lifeless narrator destroys the game.
- Your character's singing doesn't match the background music. More importantly, the soundtrack doesn't match gameplay.
- The gameplay itself was boring. I absolutely hated how slow my character walked around. Combat is tedious and not well-balanced.
- There's not much of a story. Whatever barebones tale Transistor attempt to tell didn't make much sense. By the end of the game, I didn't care for a single character. It wasn't like the ending of Bastion, where I was nearly heartbroken when character X dropped everything to save character Y.

If you played and liked Bastion, or if you're a fan of story-rich action RPGs, this game is definitely for you.

The theme around psychological entrapment induced by intellectual pursuits disguised as enlightenment is an interesting one and very applicable to us millenials.  We are the first generation to be "raised" with the intellectual freedoms afforded by the internet and thus the first to also have to deal with the dark side of such freedoms.  Although this theme has been explored by generations of humans as far back as the ancient Greeks (in other words as far back as our record keepings will allow us to see), ours is the first where access to such vast amounts of information and sufficient time to ponder on it is available to so many people.  When in times ancient only the elite had the time to ponder and discuss, now anybody with a part time job has such freedoms.  Although this game, what I can only assume to be a way to illustrate deeper a possible dark side to this freedom, throws apocalytic events into the mix and has the protaganist go to carnally tribal extremes to fend for himself, I believe the dark sides of reality are much more boring.  One of them being - me.  Any you.  And anybody playing this game, writing a review, watching a movie, investing endless hours in exploring the entertaining products that have been produced as a result of such freedom instead of exploring a much scarier product, our own minds.

Note: It's Early Access for now, but I'm pretty sure the basics of the game aren't going to change dramatically between now and release.
Remember a flash game by the name of Pandemic 2? (Some of you will probably recall cursing Madagascar for ruining your runs on it. Yeah. That one.) PIE is similar (in fact, I suspect its "casual" difficulty setting is based on that game), but a more well-researched and broad title. You start with nothing but bacteria as your plague of choice, but victories will unlock gene modifiers (for starting boosts) and new types of medium. That last chunk is where the craziness comes in: sure, viruses basically play like a more mutatable bacteria, but then you begin unlocking the real weird ones, like a fungus (such a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥to spread...), or mind-altering worms (suddenly, the goal can go from "kill the world" to "enslave every living thing"), or nanobots trying to thwart their kill-switch... the list goes on, more are still being added, and each plays distinct from the others while keeping the basics of the game, so what you learn with one can carry over to the others.
If you worry it's just going to be a pushover, play with the varying difficulty settings or some of the mutator genes you get for victories. Figure out what types of symptoms combine to make you more effective, or take on the double-edged sword of being incredibly mutation-happy. All of a sudden, your disease isn't communicable ENOUGH, and your hosts are dying before infecting others...
I really dig this, but you've gotta keep in mind, this is a dark game. It's a frighteningly-realistic simulator of ending the friggin world with disease (or worse). Victory is literally a mass extinction in most scenarios. I would absolutely NOT recommend this for everyone just based on that.

If you do not own the original, then yes, I would recommend you buy this, as Sleeping Dogs is, in my opinion, a very brilliant and under-rated game.  If you do own the original, then, no, I wouldn't recommend it unless you like the look of enough of the DLC available that you don't already have that this will actually end up being cheaper than buying that DLC.  Why do I say this?  Well, the graphics, once you actually get them working right, do show improvement over the original, and the world feels a bit more populated, but the difference is more of a case of a minor nip and tuck, rather than a jaw-dropping overhaul, so it's not really worth even the discounted price for that alone.
More missions, more blood, more enemies to kill or break bones (Death by a Thousand Cuts). Buy it. You won't regret it.

My initial impression of this was it struck me as slightly intimidating, like it was going to be a full on, hardcore puzzler that would probably require lots of knowledge of mathematics and note-taking, or just generally prove to showcase my ignorance as I'd have to hit Google a lot to find information for the answers, but I couldn't have been more wrong. It's much more about observation and curiosity and how savvy the player is at uncovering a secret hidden in plain sight.
The game is divided into five chapters, each literally revolving around some kind of object, be it a safe or table or elaborately decorated box, and it's up to the player to investigate every part of it for hidden compartments and objects to further unlock ever more secrets inside. I loved how unassuming every object looked, only to then find huge sections of it popping open to reveal some intricate mechanism to interact with and figure out. There are some slightly more conventional style puzzles along the way, but like the larger objects that house them, they're really more about poking and prodding at something to find out how it works rather than being a test of knowledge. It really is incredibly accessible, even for those who conventionally wouldn't ever go anywhere near puzzle games.
It's surprisingly atmospheric as well, giving a feeling that the more you strip away of the puzzles and the deeper you get into these contraptions, the more you're digging into something you probably shouldn't be and into a world much bigger than you. That also ties in with the story, told through notes tucked away by a slightly mad scientist as he searches for some mystical form of energy. This is also helped by occasionally switching views to a special eye glass which reveals a world hidden behind the shadows of everything you see around you. It's a really clever element that ties to both the puzzles and the story and gives something extra to what could have easily been a straightforward game about playing with a puzzle box.
I'm trying to think of any downsides worth mentioning before you go into this, but I really can't think of any. There may not be a massive amount of replay value, since discovery is the main objective of the game, but even so I really look forward to going through it all again some day. It helps too that it's only about 2 or 3 hours long as well. Maybe it could have been a little bolder in challenging the player with some of the puzzles, but that's really a minor complaint to what was an otherwise fun and enjoyable experience, and maybe they'll up the ante a little if the second and third games in the series ever make their way to PC. I really hope they do release them here, and if they do then I'll be first in line to play them, but to those who haven't had the pleasure yet, I could easily recommend this to all without a moment's hesitation.

The Room: A Puzzle Solving Game. I'm sat on the fence while I review this game; and here is why...
I picked this game up in the Halloween Sale 2015, for a small fee of £1.99. I didn't know how difficult the game would be so I decided to see how far I could get in one sitting. Less than 3 hours later, I'd completed the game.
For value? The entire 3 hours I played it, I was hooked. The clue solving, forever unfolding treasure chest of mystery is very well designed. The playthrough was smooth, nothing too challenging - however I find to be the downfall of the game. It was a little too easy. I'd highly recommend the game for at least one playthrough, and I hope they release either DLC or another follow up game around the same price (to then snag on the sale for a little cheaper).
I know it's only half price down from £3.99, however if I'd payed the extra to get the game; I'd have been a little more disappointed. Content is good, just not enough.
The atmosphere of the game is captivating and the way new sections of the chest are revealed are gripping!
For me, this game gets 7/10. Needs more content, but the content that's there DOES make you think for the entire sitting.

MMOs are incredibly hard to review.
They require a very different consumption model than the one which follows any other game constuct.
As having almost 4000 hours played would imply, I have a deep invesment into the game if, anything, to prove that I have not wasted over three months of my life playing it.
But it is far more enjoyable than any MMO I have played in the last 10 years.
Being able to play one character who can level anything? Godsdamned priceless.
A crafting system that (before Heaven's Ward) rewarded multiclassing? Superb.
Gathering that is wholly necessary to advance crafting returns? Essential to a proper balance of skills and classes.
A variety of class roles and requirements, wholly integral to endgame content? Fascinating and complicated.
This is the MMO that brought me back after nearly 7 years of exile from WoW.
Enjoy it, love it, find solace in the various game design decisions that benefit the solo player and bring so many options to the multi-player.

Amazing art, sound, script and story telling. A truely beautyful game with the same real time narrative storytelling as its predecessor Bastion. Transistor's game mechanics are different from Bastion's as the prior uses a sort of turn() based / real time hybrid where are the latter was pure real time.  The games however share some elements related to character progression.
My personal recommendation: As you play this game, take the time to listen to the story and take it in. The best part of the game is the narration.

Well, it's no Bastion but it's by no means bad. In fact, it's rather good.
The look and sound is as top knotch as we've come to expect from Supergiant with a surprising eye for the little details.
Controls are tight and responsive although I feel that the ability management could have been better. More than once I found myself grappling with the controls, teleporting when I wanted to shoot or shooting when I wanted to move. Still, the Turn() ability made it easier to manage a chaotic battlefield even though it broke the flow sometimes.
The nature of the gameplay was very innovative, especially mixing a Magicmaker style modular abilities and a vaguely Fallout style turn based ability.
Story is a bit hard to chew through. Oh sure it's solid but I was about a quarter of the way through before I got a grasp on who I was playing as and why was I fighting these strange robot things. I still don't grasp the nature of the setting, something to do with programing.
Overall? Yes, it's a good game and well worth the $20 I paid for it.

Rating: 8.5/10
Overview:  Isometric RPG
The Good
+ Cyberpunk noir setting
+ Customization is fantastic. As you level up you gain skills. You can assign skills to 3 things. You can make it an active skill, assign it to another skill to make your active skills more powerful or you can turn it into a passive skill granting you specific bonuses. By mixing and matching the different skills you acquire you can eventually find a character build that is suitable to your play style. What I love about this system, it's so simple yet produces so many different variation in how you want to play the game. Going online and searching for the best build will result in a lot of different answers.
+ The battle system allows you to use your active skills in real time however if things get too crazy you have the option of pausing and manually inputting a series of commands. Doing this will make you invincible for a brief period of time while you execute all your commands, however this will leave you vulnerable afterwards while you wait for your meter to recharge. The combat is fun, fast and at times requires a bit of strategy to win the battle.
+ In addition to the main story you can also compete in a series of different challenges. Some of these challenges include speed- completing a battle in a certain time, stability - surviving for a certain amount of time, performance - fight wave after wave of enemies, and planning- defeat all enemies in a single turn. These are all optional.
+ Similar to Bastion is the use of limiters. These allow you to customize how difficult you want combat to be but doing so also gives you a bonus to your experience gain.
+ Great soundtrack
Average
The game is roughly 4 to 6 hours depending on skill level.
The game is very linear which is disappointing given the setting
The story although good wasn't executed as well as it should have been. I was playing the game more for the customization and combat.
Conclusion
Another great game from SuperGiant games.  I would love to see the mechanics in this game expanded and put into a more fleshed out game and world.  Regardless, this is a great game and should be played by all. SuperGiant are proving they know how to make smart design decisions in their games.

The world needs more games like this. Beautifully crafted world, fantastic music and lyrical approach to the lore and story-telling is what makes this game a piece of art. The story is not, as opposed to many games, just an information dump with no meaning to it, but rather a fluid path through concepts and ideas. It let's you use your artistic imagination to "fill in the gaps", relate to your own life and let's you use your emotions to experience it.
The mechanics are also fantastic, I would compare them to blizzard's Diablo 3 - you combine skills, thus getting different results and ways to fight. The combination of real time and turn based combat is very interesting and enjoyable.

One of those artsy indie games that does it right.

Not to mention she wields a sword which doubles as a compliment pez-dispenser.
But besides that it has virtually no big cons. Gameplay is original and cool, not what I expected at all. Fights are actually pretty challenging at times, which surprised me as there's no difficulty setting. The combat system simply works.
The music is what you would expect from the makers of Bastion, so are the environments, effects, monsters etc.
The story is decent but nothing amazing; Transistor's gameplay, music and aesthetics are what it's about.
$20 might be a bit steep - I feel it's the absolute maximum they could charge for a game like this.
Yet I have to say it's very much worth it.

This game takes us on a roller coaster of not knowing what is going on until you start piecing things together. That's when the magic of Transistor comes together in a beautiful story, unlike any other I've experienced.
The gameplay mechanics are really solid, providing you with many combinations and ways that you can defeat your opponents. With this, it gains replay ability as well as its achievements and different difficulty "perks".
Transistor joins videogames, visual art and sound together in a massive heartfelt composition that will stun you for a long time.
I don't think this is an experience that can be put on words, only by playing will you understand it.
I definitely recommend it.

I physically can't stop playing this game.  It is just as polished and thorough and evocative as the trailer promises, because Lucas Pope knows how to set up and deliver story elements in clever, sometimes very subtle ways.
That said, it's very dark humor and it's very much a dystopia, so watch out for those.  In particular, if you have any kind of gender dysphoria, DO NOT PLAY THIS.  You're expected to identify male and female entrants based on whether their graphic looks masculine or feminine, and if a very feminine man shows up with an M on his passport then you literally have to scan his body and confirm that he has secondary sex characteristics consistent with someone AMAB.  If he doesn't, you can't allow him in without consequences, and if you fail to scan people with the wrong graphic you get penalized.  So be aware.
Also be aware the game defaults to nudity for body scans (NOT the underwear as depicted in the trailer), but you can change this in the options before you ever start playing.
As for the story, it doesn't really work if you don't empathize at all with the people who've been standing in line for eight hours with passports and friends and family they haven't seen for years on the other side, who suddenly find a typo or an expiration date standing between them and their lives.  If your reaction to "No, please wait, I'm desperate!" is to roll your eyes and complain that we all got problems, then you're going to miss out on some emotional impact.  Because if, on the other hand, you find yourself VERY empathetic starting out, and don't think you'll ever get to a point where you get frustrated enough with someone's faulty papers to have them jailed out of pure spite--you'll see.
There's a lot to this game.  Remember your place.

Honestly, I feel the review page for the game now is clogged with people criticising it unjustly without realising just how good parts of the game are, and where the true faults lie.
Reign of Kings is first and foremost a survival game- from nothing you came, and to nothing you will return. Whilst you will absolutely be proud of what you built- whether it be a mighty Stone Keep to a humble seaside cottage- you shouldn't get attached to it to the point of quitting the game if it is destroyed. By all means, fight to the bitter end to defend your home as I and my friends have so many times, as it is in the tension of a battle that could destroy your hard work, as you stand on the precipice of losing all that fond memories are made as you stave off invaders with whatever blade or stick you can lay your hands on- and pulling a pyrrhic victory from the jaws of defeat- with your fortress broken, but still standing, your body bruised- but alive, is some of the most satisfying results I have ever experiences playing a game.
The game devolving into kill or be killed, conducting night time raids on assailable settlements, making desperate, one sided agreements with others more powerful than yourself in the hopes they can stop an enemy are prominent aspects of my play time. Finally arming your own and having prepared enough siege equipment to breach the citadel of people who wronged you, storming the walls and slaughtering them is such a great end to the struggle, and among my greatest gaming moments. Remember what is best in life, to crush your enemies, see them driven before you and hear the lamentations of their women folk.
Thus, if you are not a fan of PVP, and have a great deal of trust in society, it is probably not the game for you.
However, there are some fundamental problems in the game that must be addressed. Number 1 is the desync in the game. With combat being such a huge part of the game, the lag and desync involved with really harms the experience of the game itself. This, I believe, is the main problem with the game, and if the developers spent some time working on a fix (although I have little faith they will) the game would be one of the best I have ever played.
Tied into the previous problem, Codehatch are notorious for abandoning games, claiming they're released whilst leaving them in a state below completion. This is true, and the previous problem is not the only aspect. The game does generally feel unpolished. Most of it, I can certainly look past, however when it greatly impacts the core aspects of the game as the desynch in combat does, it is simply not acceptable to be unfixed.
I also believe it is necessary I mention the hacking problem so many people complain about. Apparently, hacking is quite prolific in the game. Whilst I personally have never experienced it (although I only play on community servers) as so many people have complained about it it is impossible to deny it isn't a problem.
If you're a fan of player driven roleplaying games (like Altis Life on ARMA), an afficionado for PVP, or a survival/medieval game enthusiast I can guarentee you that Reign Of Kings would provide you with great experiences if you can find the right communities.
If you expect to be left to your own devices to play at your own pace, can't stand occasionally losing, loathe PVP, or simply dislike survival games and want a purely RP driven experience (to which I believe there are better platforms for that)- then Reign Of Kings isn't for you. However, it is rather stupid to buy a PVP orientated game, end up getting raided and/ or killed in game and then giving the game a negative review for its community. Most of the people who play are out for themselves. That's not to say they won't help you, it will generally happen if they believe it is in their best interests. many times my friends and I have answered the call to arms of somebody we struck a deal with, to go to war and die for their feuds.
If you're among the people the game is aimed at, I am sure you will find it to be an excellent game, if you give it a chance. Whilst it has its flaws, and the desynch in combat MUST be fixed, I can't help but feel that the game is so much better than the swathes of reviews it recieves paints it out to be. Reign Of Kings is fundamentally a good idea, and for the most part a good game. It only needs some more attention from its devellopers to become a masterpiece.

Obligatory header to the review: I focus on four primary areas whenever I review a game: gameplay, story, graphics, and sound/audio/general things that go into your earholes. Gameplay and Story get a rating scale from 1 to 10, and the AV stuff gets a rating from 1 to 5. My philosophy on this is that there are some instances in which a game may not necessarily have that much in the way of gameplay (take Amnesia for example), but the story/atmosphere/whatever it may be is reason enough to pick it up. Also, take the cumulative score with a grain of salt; it's just a numerical feeling about the game as a whole. That's part of why I do these subscores. Also, keep in mind that I'm not going off of school grade based rankings. A 5/10 denotes what I feel to be an average game. Likewise, 7/10 is a game that I think is pretty cool, and something that gets a 2/10 is near-abomination level. Pinning scores to an even further obfuscated rating scale is kinda senseless, but for the sake of my backloggery, I'll repeat again that 1.0-2.7 is a one-star game, 3.0-4.7 is a two-star game, 5.0-6.7, 7.0-8.7, and 9.0-10 are three, four, and five stars, respectively.
Gameplay: Man, Atlus sure does publish a lot of weird games. This game is no exception to that. Rock of Ages is a game where you roll a boulder down a hill at a tower gate and try to break in; most commonly requiring three boulders; although requiring four if any one boulder gets particularly roughed up. This roughing up comes from the placement of towers in the pre-rolling phase that both you and your opponent go through. Yes, this is a tower defense game technically, but don't think you can win on strategy alone. It certainly helps; especially in a resistance-based setup involving the world's supply of Ballistae and stone towers, but there's more often than not a crafty way of bypassing these cheap setups with some crafty platforming.
One of the things that you'll learn while playing this game is that keyboard control is only half the story. Your main method of steering the ball is with the mouse, which feels quite natural and works well. The boulder, as one can imagine, has quite a bit of inertia to it, so you have to plan accordingly for harsh turns. You can see a mirror reflection of the stage on your side, but you cannot see the enemy's side apart from when you are rolling. While I would've liked an outline map of the other side, it's not too big of a deal. The stages themselves can either be as simple as a straight line or a simple one turn spiral down or as complex as a multi-leveled complex of paths. There are some shortcuts that you can take throughout the stages; some are easy to defend against, while some are more difficult, if not impossible. Nevertheless, you have access to the same shortcuts, so it remains fair.
This is one of the easier Atlus games that I've played, and the average player will find a reasonable difficulty curve to it. I have noticed a weird AI bug that came up a couple of times where the opponent got stuck in a reset loop, thus throwing the match. I'm not too sure on what causes that, as I have tried to replicate the bug, but to no avail. When the AI doesn't throw a match, however, you'll find that they are pretty decent at setting up their defenses and breaking through yours. There are boss fights in this game, but they're definitely not highlights. I've talked in the past about games that don't really need boss fights but still have them, and this is one of those games. They're not bad by any measure; they just feel out of place.
Overall, I can recommend this game well enough on the gameplay alone for providing an interesting take on the tower defense genre as well as being a pretty fun strategy game. It'd definitely be even more fun with a friend. 8/10.
P.S. cool kids use the Block of Ages
Story: This game has roughly the storyline of a Terry Gilliam sketch, which is basically a sentient rock and his buddy travel through the years to become the best rock. Each stage has their own intro, which can be a groan-worthy reference to a meme, a very loose reference to an historical event, or just a general bout of silliness. Nevertheless, the ones that weren't solely based on predictable memes did get a laugh out of me. The cutscenes are worth a watch; that's for sure. 7/10.
Graphics: The comedic nature of this game certainly does not stop with the writing. Remember the Terry Gilliam comparison? Pretty much all of the cutscenes in the game are done in Gilliam's style. The stages themselves have a very "painted" feel to them, and the skyboxes can be absolutely gorgeous with the lighting working with the paintings in the skybox perfectly. All of the characters are basically ripped from classical paintings, but it all feels consistent in the very weird (and very good) visual design of the game. Regarding the technical aspects of the game, it does run with minimal impact on my system at 1080p max settings at 60FPS. Shadows do that weird thing where it looks like blinds have been cast, which can be a bit distracting at times, but other than that, the game runs well enough. I'd imagine that a low end graphics card or maybe even one of the newer integrated graphics chips could run this game perfectly. 4/5.
Sound: I'm not an expert on classical music (nor do I claim to be), but I do recognize a couple of songs in this game, and that leads me to believe that the soundtrack is almost entirely non-original. That's not a bad thing, though; it fits very well and is often comically overdone for the scenario. The stage music does feel like something from the period that you're in, so that's something. There's no voiceacting, apart from some random mumbling and comically cliched screams. Again, the audio helps propel the very silly nature of this game. Rating: 8.5/10
Overview:  Isometric RPG
The Good
+ Cyberpunk noir setting
+ Customization is fantastic. As you level up you gain skills. You can assign skills to 3 things. You can make it an active skill, assign it to another skill to make your active skills more powerful or you can turn it into a passive skill granting you specific bonuses. By mixing and matching the different skills you acquire you can eventually find a character build that is suitable to your play style. What I love about this system, it's so simple yet produces so many different variation in how you want to play the game. Going online and searching for the best build will result in a lot of different answers.
+ The battle system allows you to use your active skills in real time however if things get too crazy you have the option of pausing and manually inputting a series of commands. Doing this will make you invincible for a brief period of time while you execute all your commands, however this will leave you vulnerable afterwards while you wait for your meter to recharge. The combat is fun, fast and at times requires a bit of strategy to win the battle.
+ In addition to the main story you can also compete in a series of different challenges. Some of these challenges include speed- completing a battle in a certain time, stability - surviving for a certain amount of time, performance - fight wave after wave of enemies, and planning- defeat all enemies in a single turn. These are all optional.
+ Similar to Bastion is the use of limiters. These allow you to customize how difficult you want combat to be but doing so also gives you a bonus to your experience gain.
+ Great soundtrack
Average
The game is roughly 4 to 6 hours depending on skill level.
The game is very linear which is disappointing given the setting
The story although good wasn't executed as well as it should have been. I was playing the game more for the customization and combat.
Conclusion
Another great game from SuperGiant games.  I would love to see the mechanics in this game expanded and put into a more fleshed out game and world.  Regardless, this is a great game and should be played by all. SuperGiant are proving they know how to make smart design decisions in their games.

The world needs more games like this. Beautifully crafted world, fantastic music and lyrical approach to the lore and story-telling is what makes this game a piece of art. The story is not, as opposed to many games, just an information dump with no meaning to it, but rather a fluid path through concepts and ideas. It let's you use your artistic imagination to "fill in the gaps", relate to your own life and let's you use your emotions to experience it.
The mechanics are also fantastic, I would compare them to blizzard's Diablo 3 - you combine skills, thus getting different results and ways to fight. The combination of real time and turn based combat is very interesting and enjoyable.

$20 might be a bit steep - I feel it's the absolute maximum they could charge for a game like this.

Not much I can really say about Borderlands that hasn't been said already: it's your standard run-gun-loot FPS with a fun art style, the replay value is high, most of the dialogue aged like milk in the sun, and the game got additional content released over a span of a whopping eight months after its initial release. I can probably make a few (a lot of) jabs at the plot if I want to nitpick, and Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode definitely isn't nice to casual/leisure players, but in all it's a solidly-built game that does its job well and remains fun while doing it. If you don't like replaying things (you can only reach max level by replaying the main story 2-3+ times, depending on which DLC you have), then you'll get about 35 hours total out of the base game (and a solid 20-25 hours atop that with all the DLC).
I'm writing this review in 2017, five years after its release, and I can confirm that the multiplayer scene is still alive as well. As a matter of fact, in the 400+ hours I've spent playing this game, a good half of it comes from joining the games of complete strangers, helping others, sharing loot, and -- to get cheesy for a second -- making friends. Once you feel confident with a character (or even just right off the bat!) I can't recommend trying out the multiplayer enough. By no means is it mandatory (not until UVHM at least, if you're like me and bad at games), but it really changes the way the game plays.

Overall, it's a wonderful and unique experience that I will continue to come back to.

So this is a slight thumbs up. In Vitras has a good story, likeable characters and an interesting setting. It took me 5.5 hours to beat the game and do all the subquests, so don't expect a Dragon Quest or Persona length RPG. I never had a full party wipeout in the entire game and in fact, much of the game was really easy past the halfway point. My main character was taking 0 damage from hits aside from magic and this was with out me grinding.
The game's difficulty is all over the place. Never truly hard, but there are times when you will go from taking 0 damage to about 10% of your life in a hit. This is really only noticable in the early stages of the game where you have little gold and so it's a lot of returning to an inn to rest and unintentionally grinding because of all the backtracking. Once you hit the halfway point though, you're not taking any damage and you have loads of gold to spare. Perhaps one of the problem is you have a character who has a special attack which wipes out 40% of an enemy's life - INCLUDING BOSSES. I killed the end game boss in three turns since I had enough MP to do this attack three times and then his henchmen were wiped out in another two turns. Five turns for the last boss. That's a bit anti-climatic. But In Vitras had balance issues across the board and because of things being all over the place, I was able to just routinely choose attack for everyone and go into auto-mode. My mage was doing more damage with her rod than with her spells towards the end as an example. So had the game been a little more refined in combat (and random battles weren't hitting me every five steps like a PSX era JRPG), I could give this a higher thumbs up. Instead, while I had fun with the game, the balance and length don't really meet the price point for this game.
FInally there is the ending. Yes, it's the dreaded "TO BE CONTINUED." Note only is this lame, but the game didn't need it. Had it just ended without this trailing off, it would have been a perfect end. It's bizarre and surreal, but it would have been a fantastic way to end things and just let the game imagine what happens next. Bumblebee sold themselves short by promising more to come...even though they still haven't delivered on Days of Dawn.
In short, this is fine for what it is, but don't expect a challenge and wait for a sale so you don't feel a bit let down by the length and bare bones nature of the game. What's here is fun but it is certainly flawed.

Edit: This game was made with Smile Game Builder, NOT RPGMaker.
Edit (4/8/17): I finished the game and added a final verdict below.
In Vitra is the developer's first foray into the RPG world and, while it may not knock any socks off, it's still a solid title. You play as Noa, a young man who lives in the port town, Porta Nova, and are quickly joined by a trio of other young'uns within the first few hours.
Fun fact: Noa and his friend, Luke, are based off of the developer's son and his son's friend respectively. The developer's son also helped program a couple of the game's puzzles, which are simple push-the-box-out-of-the-way puzzles.
You can play with keyboard and mouse or with controller, which is a nice surprise. Both work well, so it's really up to your preference. I personally like playing with a controller, which consists of using the left stick to move, right stick to adjust the camera, holding X while moving to run, B for the menu, and A to navigate menus and dialogue. Nothing unusual there. Y, however, can be used to change your point of view from third person to first person (but only in specific locations)--which is a pretty cool feature and immerses you in the gameplay a bit more; at least while exploring as this does nothing to change combat.
Right off the bat, the game's lack of a journal or any way to keep track of quests is made evident as you are given a series of fetch quests to get you acclimated to the game mechanics. While you could argue that this is an old school decision, the inability to check your progress for quests or even what quests you've picked up unless you go back to the quest giver swiftly becomes tedious--especially if you stop playing the game for a period of time. This is my biggest gripe with the game and hopefully one that can and will be amended.
The majority of the game is presented in 3D models and you are able to enter buildings, interact with specific objects, and talk to NPCs.  Another minor issue I had was the appearance of the NPCs themselves: while the art style is nice, 3/4th of the male NPCs look *exactly* the same without even a re-colouring as I've seen some games resort to. As a result, the game world felt a bit hollow and the immersion was lessened. Battle is presented as 1D images that are much more detailed and colourful than the on-screen sprites.
Battles are turn-based affairs during which the fastest person attacks first and will happen at random while you explore outside of towns. If you've ever played an RPG, you'll be right at home here. You can use skills, items, defend, or run away during your turn. The enemies are much more varied than the NPCs and fit well with the fantasy theme.  The attack animations are nice to look at; the characters change expressions much like characters in a visual novel and the slashes and spells are projected onto the enemy. Your foes don't have HP bars, which means you'll have no idea how close to death one is unless you've faced the creature before and have a general idea of how tough it is. This feature (or lack thereof) means you'll need to be cautious when engaging in combat with stronger foes.
Battles in In Vitra are pretty challenging as a whole and being properly outfitted will make all the difference between life and death. A challenge is fine, but the game doesn't do a very good job of scaling enemy level and that adds a measure of unnecessary difficulty because you can easily walk into the next area that you're supposed to visit in your linear journey only to be flattened by monsters that you should have been able to handle. I found that I had to go back to the previous area and grind up a level and/or gather up some cash to buy new gear in order to progress on more than one occasion. Quests have the same issue: you pick them up from random NPCs along the way and, since you'll likely lose track of it if you leave the area, you'll try to do them as soon as possible... only to find that the monster you're asked to kill can one-shot you.
Your characters gain experience, money (DUC), and items after you've defeated enemies and as they level up, they'll automatically learn new abilities. You have no control over what stat points go where, but you do have the ability to outfit your characters with equipment. Each hero and heroine fits into the standard RPG job classes--attacker, support, mage, tank-- that will limit what they can and can't utilize.
There's a brief loading message between areas which aren't marked so you get a seemingly random "now loading" message. Otherwise, the game runs as it should; no crashes or freezing.
It took me roughly 8 hours to finish the game. It was very linear, with only a handful of side quests, and it ended on a "to be continued." I still recommend it, but now with a grain of salt. A sale would sweeten the deal, but if you're looking for an RPG that you can play during your down time, this is a relatively cheap investment at full price,  The ending was heavily hinted at and didn't really come as a surprise to me, but I *am* curious as to how a sequel will (or won't) answer some of the questions I still have.
.Pros.
.Cons.
.Bottom Line.
These issues aside, In Vitra offers you a pretty standard RPG experience.
The 7.99 USD price tag is fair--about a dollar spent per hour; though I'm sure if you rush, you can finish it in around 6 hours-- and, as long as you don't mind the lack of a quest counter and the subsequent wandering around it causes and you're not easily deterred by a game over that probably would not have happened had the game been more balanced, you'll enjoy the game for what it is: a solid JRPG.
There's a demo available and it'll give you a good idea of what to expect, so give it a shot if you're still on the fence after reading this.

*Just scroll down to the lower half of my review if you want proper Pros and Cons instead of a story*
This game caught me off guard. I was bored one day, hopping from store page to store page of F2P games. All of them seeming like the same cash-grab garbage. So I stumble upon this game with it's Mostly Negative rating and assumed it was another cash-grab that needed to be purged.
I downloaded it because I had been angered by the sheer amount of F2P cash grabs and decided I should throw a negative review at one of them.
So I played this game for a bit. I enjoyed the game-play quite a bit actually, perhaps the only good hunting sim out there at the moment. Played without paying any money for a little over a week and was ready to post a nice little negative review. However, I noticed people that posted positive reviews did not seem like blind fan-boys trying to avoid regretting the money they put into the game.
Noticed the monthly subscription fee was among the smallest I had ever seen ($3.33 per month) and there are 3 Starter packs of different prices that offer some items along with a few months of membership. So I decided "F*** it" and bought the Wayfarer Starter Pack.
I eventually came to the conclusion that this game is pretty damn good with a low price. If you want to play this game without spending a dime then run fast and run far.
The nice little "Free-to-Play" label next to Play Game isn't quite true. It should say "$14.99 | Add to Cart" and have "Download Demo" off to the side.
So for the game:
PROS:
+ Slowpaced relaxing game-play.
+ Many species of animal that require different methods to hunt. (Many share different styles while some are unique)
+ Rather low-entry fee compared to other "Free-To-Play" games.
+ Decent community. Only encountered one troll in multiplayer who was quickly banned by the admin.
+ There is an in-game currency earned by completing missions which can be used to buy consumables and temporary licenses for non-members.
+ Still supported and updated by the developers. The developers have also relaxed some of the restrictions for non-members, such as adding a free animal rotation and making all the reserves free.
+ An actual hunting simulator with tracking, flushing, etc. Instead of those low-budget shooting galleries that are on store shelves.
+ A huge variety of equipment to allow constant play-ability and variation.
+ Low cost membership grants access to all animals to hunt. You start with a 12 Gauge shotgun which can be used to hunt every animal except for Bison.
+ There is a wonderful satisfaction in going for a group hunt then taking a group selfies in front of the kill.
+ Nice sound design.
+ Looks decent without causing FPS drops on my potato rig.
+ Servers are stable most of the time.
CONS:
- All equipment cost real money.
- The "Earn EMS" system to gain money via methods other than directly paying does not work at all. I've taken enough surveys to earn over $100 in in-game currency and haven't received a dime.
- Some animals are clearly added just to sell specific equipment. Bison require high-powered rifles, Black Bears are so skittish you almost always need a bait barrel and you cannot hunt ducks without buying a plethora of equipment to the point it feels like you purchased the "Duck Hunting" DLC. I personally haven't delved into most of the equipment yet so I cannot say if they're worth it or not yet.
- Slow-paced gameplay is not for everyone.
So far I have spent $60 on this game. 15 of which went into the Wayfarer starter pack.
Overall I recommend this game IF you are willing to put some money in it. If you're open to putting money in it I recommend getting it for free and seeing if it is for you. If you are adamant about not spending a dime then stay away.

Ok we'll try keep this short and simple. Yes this game CAN cost a lot of money (I've put in around $500 USD just because I enjoy it and my financial status allows me to) to play but there are lots of things you can do for 100% free. First off do the missions they give you gm$ which can in turn be used to buy ammo, camping supplies, licenses, and a lot of other stuff.
After you get enough gm$ buy a license for a different animal which you can then activate the missions which require you to kill said animal (if you don't have the weapon needed for the mission just ask players that do have that gun many will be glad to help you.) Oh and some missions can be done by just tracking or spotting an animal so theres some gm$ you can get and not have to buy a license. I would buy the Trailrunner membership it gives you tons of things like weapons, camoflauge, scopes, calls, stands, tents, camping supplies, etc. Along with a memebrship to hunt all animals ingame for one year. The cost for the trailrunner is $49.99 USD which equates to 7 cents a day (rounded) It costs more to live per day than it does to play an awesome game!
Oh and after your year is up if you decide to keep on playing, the basic one year memebrship costs $34.99 USD and you still get to hunt all the animals and you get 3 of the deployable hunting stands. Another thing is that 90% of the negative reviews never put at least 50 hours in the game they play for 10 minutes then cry because the game isn't free to play. This game is also very realistic there are more animals than in real life but the developers needed to make this game a bit more fun, which they did perfectly. This is why I recommend this game, if you need help with anything ingame add me on theHunter at Charlielolyoloswag I've been playing for a bit over a year.  Also the devs recently did a lot for their Free to play memebers they gave them 5 new species to hunt 2 of which switch every week, and they gave us all the Single Shot shotgun with free ammo for it. One of the most (if not the most) important features in every audiovisual experience from a movie to a game.
In this case, Fingerbones displays mainly a dark ambient tune that progresses with the gameplay. And the sound effects are just the icing on the cake, they're the main tension holder, appearing in the right moment.

I personally liked it a lot, despite having some hard events behind, and some other things that are not explained (but don't really need to be, they're just the background of the ideas that are trying to be exposed), some philosophical aspects are treated within the plot, they're in fact the plot itself I would say.
If you are up to dedicating a few minutes of your time to this game, you'll probably find yourself thinking about the subjects the game talks about time after finishing it, or even relating to some ideas/thoughts.
It also deals with a serious issue, that's all I can say without spoiling it.
It made me want to give a try to "The Music Machine", wich I knew of its existence not long ago, but I was not completely sure if trying it or not.
So, overall,
By the way, thanks to Danek Le Sanek for writing that passionate review that convinced me definitely to try Fingerbones.

This is a very creative genocidal game where you play as a plague, your mission: Destroy the world
you start by creating your pathogen while choosing from different types: Bacteria, Virus, Fungus, Parasite, etc. each giving you special "abilities", like the virus being able to mutate fast or the Bacteria being very hardy and survivable in harsh environments. then you pick from several gene sequences that give you extra bonuses to certain attributes, like transmission by air or extra DNA (currency) to start with
you then pick a country to first infect one person there, from that person the infection starts spreading into other people in the country and into other countries. each country has certain attributes you need to look at. such as Canada being rich and cold, or China being urban or India being Hot,Humid and rural. these affect how your virus spreads and how you want to mutate it.
you receive DNA when infecting people, that is your currency in the game, which you spend on gene modifications, those are split into Transmission which is how your plague transfers from one person to another, like by air, water, birds, rodents, insects, blood, and each corresponds to a certain country attribute, like insects thriving in hot countries and paying DNA into that makes it progress faster.
Symptoms is the second plague feature, which can start with the cheap coughs, nausea, anemia and progress into Comas and Seizures and Heart Failure and Tumors which are completely lethal and what you eventually want to get to. be careful though, the more lethal the plague the more the world wants to cure it, but we will get to that later
the last feature you can progress in is the abilities, like resistance to cold and heat which allows your plague to spread faster in such areas, or resistance to medicine in rich countries or hardening DNA so the cure becomes harder to make. in addition to this is the special abilities to the pathogen you have selected such as Bacteria hardening or Virus mutation speed
The failure state in this game is when the world discovers a cure and manages to wipe out your plague, this can be combated by being either very stealthy by not advancing symptoms while you infect the world as they cannot notice that they actually have the virus and then attack them in one swoop by spending all the DNA you accumulated over the years to get to the most lethal symptoms and wipe out humanity before it gets the chance. or by going super aggressive and killing people as they get infected, there are different possibilities and they all depends on what pathogen you pick really.
another failure state which is very annoying is that some of the island nations (Greenland, Madagascar, Caribbean) can actually escape infection by noticing the plague and closing off borders, In my english video linked at the end of this review i have a situation where i wiped out the whole world and Greenland remained clean.
to sum it up, this is a very fun game and is highly recommended. check my videos below for a video review in both arabic and english and don't forget to like and subscribe and share. also follow on twitter @bigbarazishow

Transistor is a tragic drama set in a digital town, built and changed by the whims and votes of the people inhabiting it. The game opens with the hero, Red, standing over a figure impaled by a glowing, robotic blade: the Transistor. Releasing the blade, Red finds it talking to her, imploring her to run from the city with it. She does just the opposite, seeking revenge on those who attacked...
Transistor is a blend of real-time action and turn-based strategy. The action is quick and the strategy deep: as you unlock modules for the Transistor, you can use precious points to choose to use them as attacks, or to modify other other attacks. It quickly becomes a game to find the best combination that matches total destruction with your preferred playstyle. The combat is quite enjoyable, although there's a point in between you finding the best combination of modules and the enemies ramping up their death-dealing that can be frustrating at times.
The story is quite engaging, and ended rather surprisingly. The music is wonderful, and the world quite beautiful. Transistor was a pleasure to play.
There are a few problems here and there--in one of the challenge modes you occasionally find the game frozen on your opponent's turn, and sometimes the at-death prompt to either keep limiters removed or put them back in place does the opposite of  what you click, but these are minor issues. Play the story!
Sumptuously. Truly a beautiful game.

Bastion was a major case of "came for gameplay, stayed for aesthetics". Transistor is more like "came for aesthetics, stayed for aesthetics". Gameplay is ok, but does not become tedius only because the game itself is rather short. Planning the turn and combining the effects are interesting mechanics, but have little actual depth and are fun only for the 6-7 hours it takes to beat the game once. Which is kind of perfect.
Now, the aesthetics are brilliant. A futuristic sci-fi city where programming code is a part of everyday reality, is painted in the most unlikely style of Art Nouveau, and this unexpected combination provides a unique experience. Like in Bastion, sound is very tightly knit to the visual, to an almost synaesthetic effect.
The story has two very different layers. The big picture is vague: to the very end we can only guess what the city actually is, can one leave it or not, what is the nature of the forse destroying it, and so on. This, however, is not sloppy worldbuilding, but rather a deliberate refusal to focus on the minutae of the narrative background and keep it blurred to focus on the story of Red, which is told with all the immediacy. A human story of hard work, love, betrayal, retribution and redemption gets through, from the first cue of the man in sword, to the last pictures in the credits.

The game mechanics start out simple, with you only needing to examine one or two pieces of information, but by the end, you will need to be on the tips of your toes, scanning many documents for discrepencies in a matter of seconds. The game has 20 different endings, but only 3 or so of them are actually different. You have the option of doing your job without question, supporting the insurgent group trying to bring down the government, or fleeing the country. All of these different endings have fun twists to them, and are all worth trying to get. If you are looking for a fantastic game, this is it.

ADOM save file folder location:
My Documents\ADOM\adom_steam\savedg
Then you can create a .bat file for the save file backups.
Create a folder called "backup"
Then create a backup.bat file
backup.bat
echo off
copy yourcharactername.svg backup
then a restore.bat file
restore.bat
echo off
delete yourcharactername..svg
copy backup\yourcharactername..svg
Then you can enjoy ADOM with a character save backup.
However, if you do beat the game, the system will still know how many times you have died and came back.

So there are roguelikes, and then there are roguelikes. ADOM is a pretty venerable one, not quite as old or well-known as games like nethack but it's an important one. Why? Well, one thing people attribute to roguelikes pretty often is that they are hard and obtuse. To a certain degree this is true, but not always. Playing a valkerie and knowing how to write Elbereth makes nethack pretty easy, or you can play something like Dredmor or a Mystery Dungeon game to have an easier time.
But ADOM takes being weird and hard to higher levels. Cats are a constant menace. Funny lizards make you think that wasn't a good idea. Why does this level have so many corpses in it and why does my mouth have tentacles in it? ADOM probably won't give you the answers to these questions without making you work for it.
And yet we find ADOM here on Steam, with shiny new features that make playing an old fashioned roguelike a little more palatable for people who weren't doing it in the 90s. The updated tileset is excellent, letting characters have personality and making the screen much more clear than the old ASCII symbols while retaining the ability to switch back when you want to see the whole level at once. Perhaps the biggest change is the ability to save and reload (at the cost of reducing your final score, of course). This makes the many, many fatal mistakes that one can encounter in the Draklor Chain a little less punishing. It might not help you from starving right off, but it could keep you from losing right at the start in the Puppy Cave. Then there are the weekly challenges, to add spice to players who are constantly looking for new ways to play.
All things considered, ADOM is a classic roguelike and the Steam release has a lot to recommend it. If you are a fan of newer roguelikes like Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup or Dungeons of Dredmor and want to dip into older titles, this is the place to be. Plus you can use it as an excuse to send postcards to strangers.

Through ADOM I've found a window to the world of roguelikes many years ago and learn to cherish the simple graphics, I'm still rooting for those classics and I'm glad ADOM landed on steam and is still worked upon. Looking forward for more :)

Transistor is a game not comparable to any game I know. It's an excellent combination of RPG and fast-paced puzzle, in an action hack-and-slash style (Yeah, the genre is kind of hard to describe). The soundtrack is original and it adds compelling ambience to the stunning hand-drawn visuals that add feeling to all the rooms, streets, and courtyards you find yourself in. The actual gameplay seems to get more and more complex as you play, showing you new ways to defeat enemies and avoid death, some limiting your abilities or making you work harder for a better reward. The second you jump into the game, it gives you a hundred choices as to how you choose to play. The storyline - As far as I can tell - is very engaging and well-written, first shrouded in mystery but slowly being revealed as you progress in the game.
The only thing I have a slight problem with - And I'm sure many others agree - Is that the controls are definitely meant for a controller. Though they still function on keyboard and mouse, it feels a bit complex.
I'd give this a 5/5, though I think the background of the storyline and characters could use a bit of work.
Final rating: 4.5/5

Really cannot reccomend this game enough, if video games can be considered pieces of art Transistor would be a masterpiece.
Story: Story elements are weaved throughout the experience though it is largely left up to the player to decide for themselves about the events that happened in Cloudbank prior to game's start. Types of diary entries can be unlocked for completing certain accomplishments within the game which adds a deeper layer to the game's plot.
The game has certain breaks where cutscenes made from gorgeous art detail events and Red is accompanied and guided throughout by the voice a man- the Transistor.
Gameplay: The combat is, I would argue, slightly puzzle based where the player has the ability to pause time (pausing time changes the soundtrack from instrumental to Red humming, which is beautiful) and consider their combat options by running around the battle feild using attacks which fill up an 'action bar'. Once the action bar is full or the player confirms the attack process, the game play out the sequence and you will have to wait a few moments until the bar refills to do another sequence. While this may sound simplistic, I assure you that you have to be very alert to how you move and attack while in this mode to amplify the efficiency of your assult, and there is a section in the game (no spoilers) where you can put your combat efficiency to the test.
Overall: Again, I really adore this game and reccomend it highly. If you are interested in a wonderful gaming experience complete with amazing soundtrack, visuals and gameplay you should deffinately pick transistor up.

Definitive Edition has a busier environment, but some of the graphical eye candy has been toned down. (No lens flare etc...)  It's a good game to experience something set outside the west.  Hong Kong (that's China for all you Americans) is a fascinating place to be the stage for this GTA like game.  Worth playing.  Runs smoothly on high end systems and looks PS4 quality.

Having never played the original despite owning it, I found that getting the Definitive Edition with its enhancements and all the DLC to be a rather good investment. it certainly worked out cheaper than buying all the DLC on their own.
My first impression video goes through the graphics performance, improvements, and gameplay.
Given that I have been thoroughly enjoying the game, and the graphical improvement are extremely good. Especially the new density improvements making mini Hong Kong come alive and bustle with crowds.
Performance is good, although sadly so far AMD Crossfire doesn't seem to be working for me. Even so even with a single card, the game can easily be maxed out at 3440x1440 with AA set to Normal aka FXAA. I have not seen any improvement using the high AA settings at my resolution.
Word of warning though, if you use an Ultrawide monitor or multimonitor setup, all cinematics are rendered in 16:9. Resulting in pillar boxing.
None of which detracts from the game, and it is very good. The story is compelling, and there is a variety of sub missions, and favours which can be done. There is a small RPG element, allowing you to visually customise your character via unlocking or buying new clothing. Along with upgrading skills. Which are in three main categories. Police, Triad, and Martial arts.
They all complement each other, and levels are gain in each by doing their respective faction's missions.
If you already own the original and enjoyed it, but you're missing the DLC and want those. The Upgrade cost to the new version is easily worthwhile, and you gain the new improvements with it.
For new players I would happily recommend this as a sandbox action game, with a very good story, and great gameplay.

Sisyphus, an immortal Greek Titan, has a job to do. For the rest of eternity he must push a giant boulder up a hill in Hades until a magical enchantment causes it to roll back down to the bottom again. Understandably enough, Sisyphus eventually decides this un-life isn’t for him and swiftly breaks out of Hades, taking his giant boulder and some Titan buddies with him.
Rock of Ages is a hilariously chaotic mixture of Insane Obstacle Course and Tower Defence, alternating between guiding your boulder into the enemy gates to break them down, and building medieval weaponry to stop your rival boulder from breaking your own gates. It’s a genuine pleasure to watch your hastily erected dynamite finish just in time to blast your opponent completely off-course with white-knuckle timing.
As you progress through the campaign by massively interrupting famous European historical events, you unlock more Tower Defence items to stymie your opponents efforts and more rock types to destroy the enemy gates which does an excellent job of keeping the gameplay of Rock of Ages fresh and delightfully experimental; will only using War Mammoths stop your opponent wrecking your gates more than wall after wall of dynamite?
Rock of Ages also shines in the cutscenes between levels with both a unique art style and hugely funny direction. Famous characters and events are played out on screen in a 2D mumble-speech cinematic, with the famous opponents (normally accurate, although Plato and Aristotle probably never came back from the dead) highlighted in a massively dramatic way. It brilliantly furthers the light-hearted and joyfully silly theme.
It quickly becomes apparent when playing Rock of Ages that it is a game wholeheartedly about the joy of play. Each level is short enough that progress is never too far away and you will never guess what the game is going to throw at you next. With a depth of silliness that will bring a smile to any face Rock of Ages is a pure joy to play and happily provides many hours of shameless fun.

I have been playing MMOs since starting on Everquest and moving on to Guild Wars and World of Warcraft and unfortunately for several years there haven't been any games which have really been able to grab my attention in the way the earlier MMOs did.  Modern MMOs seem to have devolved into a quick single player race to maximum level where there is no incentive to even read a quest log, before jumping onto the gear grinding treadmill and ultimately running out of things to do shortly afterwards.
FINAL FANTASY XIV: A Realm Reborn has finally changed that, this is the first MMO I have played in recent years which has an interesting, well written story line and actually forces you to complete multi player content in order to progress from time to time.  The crafting system in this game is also incredibly well thought out and rewarding, it is not simply a case of gathering a few materials and pressing a button instead you have to think carefully about strategies to craft each item.  The other thing that also grabbed me about this game was just how beautiful the world is, from the scenery to the chaaracters the game looks stunning and the soundtrack is also top notch.
The game isn't without its faults, one of the main issues at low level is the combat system has a very long GCD and until your character gets some extra skills which are off the GCD this can make combat seem very slow at first.  I think the developers should have introduced a few more 'off GCD' skills earler in the levelling process for some of the classes as this was my main gripe at low level.  That said it doesn't take too long before things start to improve and later on in the game once you have all your skills you can often find yourself wishing the GCD was a bit longer!
One last point worth mentioning is that the community seems to be great, obviously I can't generalise for everyone playing the game but I have found most people are very friendly and helpful.  This goes as much for people outside of your Free Company (guild) as those in it.  I have bumped into more random strangers who have offered to lend a helping hand and explain things in this game than any other I can remember.
To sum it up this is a great game that you can really immerse yourself in.  It has plenty of depth and everthing before maximum level seems tangible and enjoyable rather than something to grind through.  This means you can enjoy the journey rather than worrying about the destination.

Been playing this game since patch 2.3, have played through a full expansion, and were just getting started with a second. This game is amazing, and if your a fan of Final Fantasy in general, as well as looking for a good MMO to play, I can GREATLY reccomend it.

At this point, writing a review is a bit like asking Gordon Ramsay if he likes to cook. I have nearly 300 hours in this game as of writing, and I've enjoyed every single one of them. Also I manage perfectly well to balance my study with this game. If anything it actually IMPROVED my performance, it drives me to work harder during the day so I have more free time during the evenings to play.
The good:
+ Summarized: This game takes everything from other MMOs that works, strips out what doesn't work, and innovates on features in its own way.
+ The dev team is very much aware that the original FFXIV had a horrible start, and their mantra is "earn and deserve the players' trust". They deliberately chose to keep the game subscription-based because it offers them and the players more stability.
+ The cross-server Duty Finder lets you queue up for every form of cooperative content from wherever you are in the world.
+ Big bonuses for people who repeat old content in the Duty Finder (sadly only once per day), to encourage keeping storyline content populated so you won't get stuck just because you can't find anyone to play with.
+ Classes are varied and the handful I've tried are fun to play. At level 30, every class evolves into one or two Jobs that are even more specialized.
+ You can train every class on a single character. In fact most Jobs have a secondary class requirement that also needs to be trained.
+ There are two levels of subscription, Entry and Standard. Entry is cheaper than Standard, but doesn't allow recurring payments and restricts you to 1 character per server, 8 in total. But since you can just train every class on a single character anyway, this won't actually lock you out of anything.
+ The world is beautiful and feels alive.
+ The lore and story are of true Final Fantasy levels, and better than I've seen in any other MMO.
+ The game tries to do that "chosen one in a world of chosen ones" that story-heavy MMOs are all guilty of, but actually executes it very well. In-storyline, your character becomes something of a living legend after a while, and everyone acknowledges that you faced off with terrible monsters and lived to tell the tale. When someone does question your skills in the storyline, it's usually because they actually are a fool.
+ Boss battles are extremely memorable, and all have interesting mechanics.
+ The music. Oh God, the music. The regular zone music is already plenty good and immersive, but the composer went completely wild with the dungeon and boss themes. Expect epic choires, punk rock and heavy metal. One boss in particular has 5 different phases, and every phase has its own song.'
The middle:
~ Truly understanding the mechanics of your class/job and the role you fulfill in party dynamic takes quite some time and willingness to learn. If someone gives you good advice, listen to it. I learned the most by making mistakes, and getting tips on what I should have done differently from people who were there with me. This process still continues today, and I only get better by it.
The bad:
- Levelling alternate classes gets quite grindy. You get massive XP boosts when you level classes that are below the level of your highest class, but even with that you'll need to invest a lot of time past level 30. Your primary class should be fine doing only Main Story Quests most of the time, at least until you reach Heavensward.
- You start with a lot of inventory space and even an armoury chest to store your equipment in, but you will inevitably run into the limits of this with how many crafting materials there are in the game, and how many different sets of equipment you need if you play multiple classes. Rather than a bank the game features retainer NPCs which can do something to alleviate the burden, but I think the game would really benefit of a Guild Wars (2) type of crafting material specific storage.
- There is a shortage of Tanks and Healers in the Duty Finder queues. But this isn't really the game's fault, and multi-classing makes it easy to just ask a friend to jump in for a role if you really can't find anyone.
- Not all parts of the story are equally good, and some characters are very annoying.

Released in Japan with the title:Sora o Aogite Kumo Takaku is an excellent action RPG released on Steam by DebonosuWorks Inc. the developers of Kagura Douchuuki,these are the elements that make A Dragon Girl Looks Up At The Endles Sky an excellent gaming experience.
-Excellent visuals,at max setting the game will look great,very good art,character designs,detailed enviroments and A LOT of CGs for the many events the characters a will go through during the course of the game.
-A deep character progression system with a a vast range of option that will allow you to choose skills and moves that will shape the heroine's fighting style according to your preferences.
-The game will run perfectly on a broken toaster.
-The game is fully voiced in japanese and the soundtrack is very nice too.
-While the gameplay itself is focused on dungeon crawling,randome encounters and action packed real time battles between the heroine and her foes,the story itself is well written and it's experienced through the very lenghty visual novel segments that would easily make up a game of their own dungeon,it bears mentioning again that entire game is voiced in japanese and that the visual novel segment that make up the story can be skipped,in case you just want to focus on the dungeon crawling and the fights against the monsters.
-The combat system is very satisfying,especially as you unlock more moves and abilities.
-The game has a lot of longevity,the game world is pretty big,there are countless quests to embark upon,enemies to fight and events to unlock.
-Several levels of difficulty will allow you to have a great time regardless of your skill level with lower difficulties that will allow you to easily go through the entire game without too much effort and harder ones that will put to the test the even the most talented hardcore gamers.
If you like dungeon crawling,sidescroller beat'em up or visual novel you'll love this game and if you like both,you owe to yourself to play this game.

I know, it's the third Demon Hunter game that I review, and I've always written extremely short reviews about these awesome games.
And for some reasons (related to epic discounts XD) I played them without an order: 2, 3 and 1 (this one).
I think there's literally little to say.
Point and click adventures at their best.
Great story, awesome artworks.
Full of puzzles of any kind.
Hints, if you're stuck.
Plots full of mystic themes, magic, riddles..
The Demon Hunter series to me has everything an adventure puzzle game should have, from the hidden objects to the logic thinking, from the great art and soundtracks to the intriguing plot in constant need of player's input. Fully single-player, of course, for the sociopath that I am.
I stress "adventure", since I adore even more minimalistic puzzles, logic puzzles, physic puzzles and so on, but they're games with tons of levels and with no plot. This is another genre!
What's the only downside?
The price.
10€, or 10$, are definitely too much. But really TOO much. This isn't the new Final Fantasy and not even your favourite FPS. It's great, but it's still a point and click puzzle adventure.
But this series is so so awesome that I'd suggest to anyone to play it from the beginning, when the games are on heavy sales, like 0 or 90% down.
It will be worthy, trust me!
Oh, the other downside is the translation but I don't even mention this point in my review 'cos I somehow started to play everything in American English in the early '90s and went on. 9 games out of 10, they can come from every developer you want, have horrible translations and this whole series (as I said also in the other reviews) is no expection. So, English. :)

The original Sleeping Dogs was a hidden gem of a game, this version adds more polish and turns it into jewel.
Atmospheric effects, moving elements which were originally static, improved character models for NPCs and a lot, lot more people walking around.
If you never played Sleeping Dogs, get it!
If you already have it, it is difficult to say if you think there is value to this edition, but I think there is, and I'm certainly not regretting my purchase.

So is the definitive edition of Sleeping Dogs worth it if you have already played Sleeping Dogs on pc. Well from the get go you will notice the little details like Facial features.car textures,colors & the streets of hong kong are more populated with people I have never seen before & I have seen a lot in the original Sleeping Dogs in my 59 hours of playing it .
The lighting has also been imporved as well to give it that more realistic feel. There is also a legendary clothing shop which makes all the dlc clothing available for purchase & not just in your wardrobe which makes the process of going out collecting the red envlopes & opening lockboxes more enjoyable when you actually have to spend the time to work towards buying all your outfits instead of having a large sum of money towards the end game.
There are also some new cop missions as well from taking out gangs members to stopping a street race by taking out All the street racers before the race finishes.
Add that in with the bonus of getting all the dlc & you have yourself one of the best looking games on pc for a reasonable price.
For those that haven't played Sleeping Dogs yet what are you waiting for go & experience Wei Shen's Amazing story now.
